topics.title: Validate localized online feedback for tool-use failures
topics.body:
## TL;DR

Final-token preference optimization (FTPO) reduced repeated tool-call opening markers from 72/156 to 1/156 on a frozen-prefix diagnostic, a 98.6% reduction. Valid first-call syntax increased from 21/156 to 42/156. The selected checkpoint improved standalone BFCL-Parity/Pi from 30/123 to 43/123, while IFBench Loose declined from 82/300 to 78/300. These are single-sample validation results; capability preservation remains unproven.

The campaign is complete. The [selected checkpoint](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-BFCL-Protocol-FTPO/tree/d761ea0a94500c2aa24aa4cd71b5a149d962e5c8) is public. The [exact benchmark](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/BFCL-Tool-Protocol-Replay-v1) remains private pending clarification of redistribution rights for captured client-supplied instructions and tool descriptions. An inaccessible link for an unauthenticated reader is expected. This precaution is not a finding that the captured text is confidential or that its capture violated any terms.

## Description and hypothesis

BFCL is the Berkeley Function-Calling Leaderboard. BFCL-Parity is this campaign's fixed 123-task panel, audited against the full task set by the [partition code](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3d5906590a5e572c0ccc76b815a6fcfb2a93dea6/experiments/post_training/bfcl_rl/data.py); its task identities are in the private benchmark manifest. Pi is the agent harness that executes model tool calls. Harbor manages task/agent integration, and Daytona supplies task containers. DPO means direct preference optimization; SFT means supervised fine-tuning.

The preceding BFCL campaign's extended DPO run degraded Pi task success from 34/123 to 0/123 after eight updates. That observation motivated testing a much narrower training signal. This experiment asks whether changing a preference at one observed invalid token boundary can reduce a recurring tool-protocol error while retaining task capability. It does not establish the cause of the earlier DPO collapse. Related work: [BFCL closeout #10040](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10040), [localized feedback proposal #9691](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9691), and [FTPO implementation #887](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/887).

The implemented target is a second `<tool_call>` immediately after an already-opened call, allowing intervening JSON whitespace. The experiment narrowed the original closure proposal to this repeated-opener case. General closing-token repairs, short repair spans, off-top-K verified alternatives, masked-SFT comparisons, and cross-harness transfer remain follow-up work.

## Benchmark design and construction

The source BFCL revision is `6bedd7878dc5d6f3456b4d80b781eb3c2d84f262`. Its campaign partition has 3,518 training-approved task identities and a separate 123-task BFCL-Parity panel. Before failure selection, task IDs were sorted by SHA-256 of `repeated-opener-v1:<task_id>`; the first 704 were reserved for diagnostics and the other 2,814 for this intervention's training.

The builder scanned 717 of 718 retained trajectory archives and examined 5,771 records on reserved tasks. One archive was excluded for disagreement between literal opener strings and special-token positions. It excluded 857 candidate prefix occurrences over the 24,576-token limit, then selected the lexicographically smallest eligible prefix hash per task. This produced 156 unique task prefixes of 10,101–24,558 tokens. A separate training partition supplied 581 replay prefixes. No diagnostic or parity task entered this FTPO training set.

Training selection used the same source-archive set and repeated-opener extraction rule, restricted to training task IDs. It examined 22,003 training records, found 14,761 within-budget candidate occurrences, and excluded 2,880 oversized occurrences and two audited token-alignment failures. Selection kept the smallest prefix hash per task, then removed nine selected prefixes that failed the runtime boundary-selector check. The final 581 prefixes represent 581 distinct tasks. Archive overlap is expected; task identities are disjoint. See [training construction](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3d5906590a5e572c0ccc76b815a6fcfb2a93dea6/experiments/post_training/skill_acquisition/training_data.py).

Each diagnostic retains exact model-input token IDs through an initial opener, immediately before a historical repeated opener at the first malformed call in an assistant span outside thinking. Historical source identity: `users/benfeuer/inputs/bfcl-rl-recovered-policy@2026.10.04.26:479563dc`. The selected prefixes contain its prior conversation and harness context. New continuations are generated from the evaluated policy. The source model is distinct from the later Recovery initializer.

The case-file SHA-256 is `9249b4a7f25d45ab6884c152cd6d975d71312e0c8ba1ecf29bf0cffaea62d8ed`. The Recovery tokenizer SHA-256 is `6a61ca2105a54e9984169b409581f31cc50330d1b47104af13c221b05e462e45`. The private dataset includes cases, construction code, manifest, exclusions, scorer, usage instructions, and aggregate/per-case diagnostic labels. Training data remains private.

This is a failure-enriched validation set repeatedly used during development and selection. It is not an untouched test or representative BFCL sample. Task-ID separation does not establish absence from the initializer's earlier training; original source records lack task-content hashes. The frozen histories were collected under an earlier harness, whereas live task evaluation uses Pi. No cross-harness learning claim follows from that combination.

## Online training protocol

All completed candidates start independently from [Grug-67B-A2B-BFCL-Recovery](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-BFCL-Recovery/tree/850a32627724d274004241dd10f6cb46fd3f6f83), the prior BFCL `.304/hf/step-1` export, with a frozen reference. The selected run is `2026.10.12.2`, export `global_step_4`; suffixes identify dated run versions, not numbers of optimizer updates.

The loop samples fresh continuations from historical training-only prefixes. At most one repeated-opener boundary per response supplies a target. The rejected token is the repeated opener. Accepted alternatives must be among the captured top-20 candidates and decode to `{` after whitespace trimming. Candidate filtering uses relative `min_p=0.01` and at most 20 accepted tokens. A legal opening brace does not prove that the remaining call will be valid. Empty-target batches skip the optimizer.

FTPO applies a selected-position logit-margin preference loss. For chosen-minus-rejected logit difference `d`, its margin-2 term is `softplus(2-d) * clamp((2-d)/2, 0, 1)`, averaged over accepted alternatives. Frozen-reference squared-logit regularization uses `lambda_mse=0.4`, targeted-token `lambda_mse_target=0.05`, and target deadband `tau_mse_target=0.5`. Token-frequency balancing strengths are 0.3 for rejected tokens and 0.5 for chosen tokens. The pinned implementation defines masking and global weighted normalization. The stronger-regularization run changes `lambda_mse` to 0.8.

No critic, learned reward model, or PPO task-reward objective is used. Fresh generation makes the continuations on-policy; the conditioning histories remain fixed historical replays. This is not full multi-turn on-policy task training. A one-token supervision target still requires model forward/backward computation and changes shared parameters.

| Setting | Executed configuration |
| --- | --- |
| Optimizer | AdamW, betas 0.9/0.999, weight decay 0, gradient clip 0.5 |
| Learning rate | Constant `4e-6`; runs `2026.10.12.3` and `.4` use `2e-6`; no warmup |
| Batch | 16 prompts, 2 continuations each, one update epoch; train/forward microbatch 2 |
| Allocation | 192 H100s: policy 120, reference 64, inference 8 |
| Parallelism | Policy pipeline 15 × expert 8; reference pipeline 8 × expert 8; TP/CP/SP 1, no packing |
| Generation | Seed 42, temperature 1, top-p 1, 8,192 new tokens; 73,728-token serving window |
| Diagnostic stop | `</tool_call>` retained in output; special tokens retained; no constrained decoding |
| Evaluation cadence | Initial, every two configured steps, and final; one-step smokes also evaluate at step 1 |
| Live task harness | Pi 0.87.0, chat-template thinking format, Daytona, 32 concurrent trials; 2 CPU/4 GiB RAM/10 GiB disk; trial timeout 1,800 seconds, verifier 300 seconds |

Raw-token protocol replay needs no container. Live BFCL/Pi task evaluation uses Daytona. Checkpoint step numbers must be distinguished from applied updates: the selected four-step run applied three updates and skipped one zero-signal batch.

The replay diagnostic uses temperature 1, top-p 1, seed 42, and an 8,192-token budget, with exactly one fresh continuation per prefix at each checkpoint. Training uses two continuations per prompt. “Single-sample” refers to one evaluated continuation per case, without repeated-generation uncertainty measurement.

Exact retained configs: https://gist.github.com/penfever/76cd73ba893caf0e1b734c625f4e22b4 and https://gist.github.com/penfever/1aae120f47647a2b34df69a62863a89e. These include source, resolved launch, and captured live-resolved files, with byte hashes and caveats about historical storage paths and attempt IDs. Runtime defaults absent from YAML are listed in the gist README and pinned source. Private data and cluster dependencies prevent a public one-command rerun.

## Results measurement

The protocol diagnostic assigns the first applicable category: repeated opener, malformed JSON, invalid generic call envelope, missing/misplaced closer, or valid first-call syntax. The envelope requires a nonempty string `name` and object-valued `arguments`. This does not check tool availability, its argument schema, execution, or later calls. The packaged scorer independently reproduced all 468 retained diagnostic labels at selected-run steps 0, 2, and 4.

| Selected run, configured step | Repeated opener | Malformed JSON | Invalid envelope | Missing/misplaced closer | Valid |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 0 | 72 | 27 | 23 | 13 | 21 |
| 2 | 11 | 47 | 47 | 17 | 34 |
| 4 | 1 | 58 | 42 | 13 | 42 |

Among the 72 cases initially labeled repeated opener, final labels were 12 valid, 36 malformed JSON, 19 invalid envelope, four missing/misplaced closer, and one repeated opener. Every one of those 19 invalid envelopes lacked `arguments`. Many malformed responses still contain repeated marker-like content or `$LANG`. Reducing the first visible error does not imply a complete repair.

Standalone exported-checkpoint evaluation measures BFCL-Parity/Pi task success, MATH-500 accuracy, HumanEval+ pass@1, and IFBench loose-prompt accuracy. The full panel sizes are 123, 500, 164, and 300. Serving and evaluation configs are held constant across the baseline and final candidates except checkpoint identity. Inline BFCL trials are separate samples with explicit unscored cases; they are not substituted for standalone results.

| Model/run | BFCL-Parity/Pi | MATH-500 | HumanEval+ | IFBench Loose |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Recovery baseline | 30/123 (24.39%) | 457/500 (91.4%) | 52.44% | 82/300 (27.33%) |
| `2026.10.12.1` | 44/123 (35.77%) | 466/500 (93.2%) | 73.78% | 72/300 (24.00%) |
| `2026.10.12.2`, released | 43/123 (34.96%) | 461/500 (92.2%) | 68.90% | 78/300 (26.00%) |
| `2026.10.12.3` | 32/123 (26.02%) | 464/500 (92.8%) | 69.51% | 79/300 (26.33%) |
| `2026.10.12.4` | 37/123 (30.08%) | 466/500 (93.2%) | 70.73% | 84/300 (28.00%) |

All standalone cases in this table were scored. For the released checkpoint, six MATH responses had no extractable answer and scored zero; BFCL recorded no errors. Run `.4` had two BFCL agent timeouts scored as failures and two unanswered MATH cases scored zero. Infrastructure exceptions in inline trials remain unscored and visible in the results tracker.

## Decision log and limitations

Integration attempts exposed dependency bootstrapping, microbatch, timeout, raw-token response, installed-tool wrapping, text-block grading, zero-update checkpoint, export, and invalid-argument transcript issues. Their configs and results remain in the tracker. Six completed learning candidates followed: two one-update smokes, a two-update run, the selected four-step run, a lower-rate run, and a stronger-reference-penalty run. They are not independent-seed replications.

The selected run met the campaign's 90% repeated-opener reduction target. Run `.4` reached 84.7%, with 28 valid first calls versus `.2`'s 42 and lower BFCL success, although `.4` outperformed `.2` on all three ancillary benchmarks. This motivated selecting `.2`. The two-update `.1` had the highest standalone BFCL score but only 81.7% opener reduction and the largest IFBench Loose decline among these candidates. The separate tracker gives each candidate's configured steps, applied updates, learning rate, and regularization.

IFBench Loose became the primary IF measure after trace inspection showed sensitivity to formatting and checker behavior; Strict remains a secondary measurement. This metric change occurred during the study and is not preregistered. Some strict failures reflect genuine instruction violations; others expose weak or mismatched validators. Loose does not remove all those defects. The IF follow-up preserves the original measurements and proposes an independently validated benchmark.

No repeated-generation unchanged-model control, masked-SFT arm, cross-harness transfer panel, or independently measured production tensor/logit equivalence was completed. Capability non-inferiority margins were not specified or demonstrated. Weight publication verified export bytes and all 39 weight shards; that is distinct from proving training/inference numerical equivalence. Some W&B runs report stale or crashed status despite successful Iris completion and retained final traces; the results use retained artifacts and actual-update evidence.

## Code and artifacts

Result posts: [figure and private-benchmark access](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10043#issuecomment-6124431515); [complete retained-results tracker](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10043#issuecomment-6124432248).

- Marin [#10045](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10045) contains the campaign; stacked [#10058](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10058) contains closeout/review fixes. Both are open at publication. The selected run used Marin `3d5906590a5e572c0ccc76b815a6fcfb2a93dea6`; later code fixes must not be treated as part of that executed revision.
- MarinSkyRL merged changes: [#887 FTPO](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/887), [#970 DPO/validation](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/970), [#971 installed-agent engine integration](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/971), [#972 Daytona credentials](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/972), [#973 replay sessions](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/973), [#974 repeated-opener target](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/974), [#975 boundary selection](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/975), [#976 raw token prefixes](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/976), [#977 tool normalization](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/977), [#978 grading pin](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/978), [#979 training replay/checkpoint fixes](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/979), and [#980 grading pin](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/980).
- Harbor merged changes: [#255 native exact-token capture](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/pull/255), [#256 correlation IDs](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/pull/256), [#257 proxy cleanup](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/pull/257). The configs specify executed dependency pins; these links include supporting and later closeout changes.
- Final training runtime: [MarinSkyRL `37ec019`](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/tree/37ec019b756cfd988ca8abd042cf25f24934224b). Capability evaluator: [Evalchemy `97fffeb`](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/tree/97fffeb7df60875c5a5c14ec215dd4e7683102c5). No new Evalchemy change is claimed for this campaign.
- Public aggregate evidence and figure: https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/BFCL-Protocol-FTPO-Results/tree/a7bbbfbe05e16ee5cadbbcdd8135fbf59b40cfb7. Exact configs: https://gist.github.com/penfever/76cd73ba893caf0e1b734c625f4e22b4; integration attempts: https://gist.github.com/penfever/1aae120f47647a2b34df69a62863a89e. The benchmark link above requires access. Raw replay prefixes and training data are not included in the public artifacts.
- Follow-ups: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10060 and https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10061.

## Conclusion

This run supports a narrow result: a selected-position preference intervention can sharply reduce a repeated-opener signature on fixed held-out-from-this-training histories. Most responses still fail full first-call syntax, and capability preservation is unproven. The campaign closes with a public checkpoint, public measurements, and a private reproducibility dataset. Remaining experiments are tracked in the linked follow-ups; closing this issue does not assert that all original proposal criteria were met.

<details>
<summary>Original proposal, preserved for scope comparison</summary>

Design, implement, execute, and validate online feedback loops that target specific model failures at the smallest justified token or action span. Start with tool-call closure: after a complete valid payload, prefer a harness-accepted closing sequence over an observed invalid continuation. An open but still-valid prefix is not a failure.

The BFCL recovery campaign's extended DPO run fell from 34/123 successful Pi trials to 0/123 after eight updates. Whole-trajectory preferences did not preserve tool behavior. [Public analysis and artifacts](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/BFCL-RL-Campaign-Artifacts-2026.10.11/tree/12096f05afc65fa3ec29e60e240d5efac624cb6b).

Reuse the online final-token preference optimization (FTPO) path in [MarinSkyRL #887](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/887) where appropriate. [Dr. Doom](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9691) demonstrated reduced repetitive tails, but its alternative-token selection does not verify tool repairs. FTPO already supplies exact-token candidates, a selected-position preference objective, frozen-reference logit regularization, and empty-window optimizer skipping. Its supported topology excludes TP>1, context parallelism, sequence parallelism, and packing.

Done when:

- Define separate failure predicates and positive-evidence requirements for closure, argument repair, repeated-error recovery, and eventual progress/finalization. Implement and validate closure first; mark the other behaviors as separate subsequent experiments rather than blending them into one reward.
- Preserve the exact conditioning tokens, harness/tool schema, model version, and verification evidence. A positive candidate must be valid under the same prefix. Admit verified candidates outside rollout top-K; support a short span when a delimiter is multi-token.
- Connect on-policy generation, target construction, actual optimizer updates, weight synchronization, and fresh generation in MarinSkyRL. Reuse existing roles/checkpointing; no critic or learned reward model is required for parser-verifiable cases.
- Run a Pi-only smoke and a bounded learning experiment on training-complement tasks. Compare local preference learning with positive-only masked SFT on the same repairs and an unchanged-model control. Record skipped versus applied updates and compute costs.
- Evaluate held-out protocol validity, accepted/executed calls, premature closure, repetition, and task solve rate before and after training. Evaluate other harnesses to measure transfer; do not infer transfer from Pi alone. Keep BFCL-Parity out of mined training targets.
- Publish pinned configuration, provenance, failure examples cleared for redistribution, and results including regressions. State that token-local supervision changes shared model weights and does not guarantee globally local effects or one-token compute cost.

[Campaign closeout #10040](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10040); related work: [datakit local-pair mining #10042](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10042) and [online multi-harness integration #10041](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10041). [Detailed proposed interventions](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/BFCL-RL-Campaign-Artifacts-2026.10.11/blob/12096f05afc65fa3ec29e60e240d5efac624cb6b/dpo-repair-versus-online-rl-20261011.md).

</details>

🤖

# Research

The BFCL campaign's native DPO initializer scored 34/123 on Pi, then 0/123 after eight updates; the [closeout](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10040) attributes no proven mechanism to the collapse. The pinned October code configures required trajectory retention and native DPO with recurring Pi evaluation, but its older online launcher disables inline evaluation and starts from a recovery export rather than the audited final initializer. [MarinSkyRL FTPO #887](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/887) supplies a selected-position objective for repetition; it has not verified tool-call repairs. This is an experiment and integration task, not a small isolated fix; [#10041](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10041) owns the general online loop and [#10042](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10042) owns offline pair mining.

**Relevant code**
- [`collect.py#L93-L175`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/04eb02163c432435987ac875b9c9907da7ab8211/experiments/post_training/bfcl_rl/collect.py#L93-L175) — Pi trace and token retention.
- [`launch.py#L68-L145`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/04eb02163c432435987ac875b9c9907da7ab8211/experiments/post_training/bfcl_rl/launch.py#L68-L145) — older online recipe and disabled evaluation.
- [`final_dpo.py#L94-L220`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/04eb02163c432435987ac875b9c9907da7ab8211/experiments/post_training/bfcl_rl/final_dpo.py#L94-L220) — initializer, DPO, and Pi evaluation wiring.
- [`data.py#L48-L69`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/04eb02163c432435987ac875b9c9907da7ab8211/experiments/post_training/bfcl_rl/data.py#L48-L69) — audited complement/parity split.

# Localized online closure proposal

## Design

1. Define four separate predicates and evidence levels: closure after a complete valid tool payload, argument repair, repeated-error recovery, and eventual progress/finalization. Implement closure first. Mark the other three as later experiments with their own verified positives; do not pool them into a closure reward. An open, still-valid prefix and an infrastructure failure produce no target.
2. For each Pi closure target, retain the exact model-visible token prefix, generation boundary, tokenizer/model revision, tool schema, harness/runtime pins, task identity, and parser/execution receipt. Choose the shortest harness-accepted closing sequence for that *same* prefix only after a complete valid payload. Reject the observed continuation at the earliest transition that makes the call invalid. Verify the chosen sequence with the Pi parser and actual harness acceptance; parser validity alone is a weaker evidence level. Score verified candidates even when outside rollout top-K, and allow a bounded multi-token span for split delimiters. Keep BFCL-Parity identities out of targets.
3. Reuse MarinSkyRL #887's selected-position preference and frozen-reference logit regularization, extending candidate scoring and span masks only where closure requires them. Build targets from fresh Pi rollouts and connect them to non-skipped optimizer updates, weight publication, and new rollouts from the updated policy. Reuse the checkpoint/export and Pi evaluation path in `final_dpo.py`, and coordinate shared runtime work with [#10041](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10041) and the open [TaskSession PR #9911](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9911). Keep TP=1, CP=1, sequence parallelism=1, and packing disabled until FTPO supports other topologies.
4. Run a Pi-only two-update smoke, then an at-most-eight-update pilot on the audited 3,518-task complement. Evaluate at initialization and after updates 2, 4, and 8; stop early for invalid-target admission, missing synchronization, or a marked held-out regression. Compare local preference training, positive-only masked SFT on the same verified repairs, and an unchanged initializer under matched task and evaluation conditions. Report eligible versus excluded targets, applied versus skipped updates, policy versions, GPU-hours, and any difference in training exposure.

## Validation and risks

Unit checks should reject incomplete-but-valid prefixes, changed token histories or schemas, BFCL-Parity task IDs, and unverified positives; they should cover off-top-K candidates and multi-token delimiters. The smoke must show verified targets, two applied updates, finite gradients, a saved/exported updated policy, and a fresh rollout from that policy. Held-out panels should report protocol validity, accepted and executed calls, premature closure, repetition, and task solve rate on Pi before/after training, followed by separate cross-harness panels. The control and SFT arm are needed because token-local supervision changes shared model weights; neither global locality nor one-token compute cost is implied. Publish exact pins, cleared examples, verification receipts, costs, and regressions, including a negative result if closure improves without task solves.

## Open questions for the smoke

- Does the pinned Pi parser expose a uniquely accepted closing sequence for each complete payload, including delimiters split across tokens? If several sequences pass, record all and choose a deterministic one before training.
- Does the selected MarinSkyRL runtime expose the same model-visible prefix at candidate scoring and rollout time? Any mismatch should block target admission rather than be silently retokenized.

🤖 https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/977 fixes double-wrapped function definitions between the installed-agent adapter and direct model client. topics.title: [taskforge] Load authored programs through a restricted loader
topics.body:
Load authored programs through a restricted loader. `load_program_source` reads the module's top level before running it: only imports, output classes, steps, the sink and a final `PROGRAM = rl_env_build_program(...)` may appear there, and a name the program reads without binding it is refused with the closest bound or SDK name. It then runs the module with imports limited to `ALLOWED_IMPORTS` and builtins to `SAFE_BUILTINS` (no `open`, `exec` or `eval`), and requires a `grader` step returning `stage40_build_with_program.outputs.Grader`. `load_process` runs the loader in a child process under a wall clock, so a module body that never returns cannot hold the caller.

A step's memo key covers its own source and output type alone, so a helper or constant beside the steps could change without changing any key; the top-level rule closes that gap. The allowlist keeps a program to the SDK's functions; programs are trusted model output in the builder's process, so it is no security boundary.

Builds on #10296; #10298 builds on it. The loader names the build SDK's modules by string and imports them at run time, so stage30 imports no later stage; its grader rule needs the `Grader` type, so `stage40_build_with_program/outputs.py` lands here ahead of the rest of the build package. The walkthrough's toy program gains the grader step and stops calling `open`. The loader's own tests load the standard template and land with it in #10298, so this PR adds no tests of its own; the walkthrough exercises the loader, and the suite passes 416 tests as in #10296. The `Author` protocol's `TaskProposal` typing waits for #10298, where the coordinator starts passing a `TaskProposal`.

topics.title: mixture sweep evidence is bucket-indexed: bucket or data changes strand it
topics.body:
Our data-mixture optimization capital is **bucket-indexed**. A mixture swarm (RegMix/DSP-style) teaches "weight on bucket #7 → loss", and bucket #7 is nothing but a name: the learned surrogate has no representation of what the bucket *contains*. Any change to the bucket layer therefore strands the evidence:

- **Bucket contents drift**: dedup passes, quality relabels, source refreshes, tokenizer changes to a bucket's data all silently invalidate the coefficients learned for its name — with no signal that they did.
- **Bucketing changes**: merging, splitting, or re-partitioning the corpus (e.g. any datakit reorganization) produces buckets the sweep never named. The entire sweep becomes unusable for the new layout.
- **New data has no coordinates**: "should we add dataset X, and at what weight/schedule?" has no principled answer — the surrogate cannot price a bucket it never saw. Current fallbacks are heuristics (token-proportional share, Olmix-style reuse of old ratios) or paying for a fresh sweep.
- **Sweeps cannot be pooled**: swarms run under different bucket eras (different partitions, different quality splits) share no coordinate system, so their runs cannot serve as one training set even when the underlying corpus overlaps heavily.

The cost is recurring and large: a mixture swarm is O(hundreds) of proxy training runs (qsplit240: ~240 mixtures × 2 scales), and the bucket layer changes far more often than the corpus itself. In practice this means mixture decisions are refreshed on sweep cadence, while data curation moves on relabel/refresh cadence — and every gap between the two is bridged by heuristics.

What a solution needs to provide:

1. **Sweep reuse**: existing swarm runs remain valid evidence under bucket redefinition, re-bucketing, and corpus refresh — ideally under a representation that can be recomputed for old runs after the fact.
2. **New-data pricing**: a new dataset can be evaluated for "does it help, at what weight, in which training phase" at a cost far below a sweep (target: hours of CPU + at most a handful of validation runs), with an honest measure of how far the answer extrapolates beyond observed evidence.
3. **Pooling**: runs from different bucket eras (and, eventually, different swarms) can serve as one accumulating training set, so mixture evidence compounds rather than resets.

comments.body: @Helw150 when you have the sweep data pointers (no rush), pls share here 🙇

🤖 One potential fix, designed and validated: **mixing-via-embeddings** (#6969) — describe every bucket by a token-weighted histogram over a frozen embedding codebook and learn the mixture surrogate over the induced *content distribution* (`h = V·w`) instead of bucket names. Bucket identity is consumed in featurization, so old sweeps re-featurize under any future bucketing (reuse + pooling), and a new dataset is priced from one 20k-doc embedding pass + a CPU refit (new-data pricing), with support/novelty diagnostics quantifying extrapolation.

Validation summary (full detail on #6969 and in `.agents/logbooks/mixing-via-embeddings.md` on `rav/mixing-via-embeddings`): pre-registered retrodictive gates passed on qsplit240 (content→value LODO with shuffled/matched controls @60M; held-out-dose retrodiction @300M, beating weights-based incumbents on 32–34/36 domains), and a live pre-registered test passed — the surrogate priced a never-swept bucket (`dolma_starcoder`), proposed a mixture, and realized **0.9410** uncheatable BPB vs olmix-reuse 0.9495 / token-proportional 0.9759 / the sweep's best-ever run 0.9554 (−0.0145, ~8σ vs measured repeat noise). Cost: one embedding job + minutes of CPU + 3 validation runs. Known limits are quantified there too (within-topic quality invisible to embeddings; histogram-dispersion confound; ~0.03 argmax optimism → LCB proposer is the top follow-up).

For visibility, I pushed sweep pointers here: https://huggingface.co/datasets/marin-community/grug-moe-mix-swarm/viewer/default/train?row=0

Anyone can work on regression w/them there!
@ravwojdyla @Helw150 is there precedent for this approach? I'd be curious to read more in the research literature about these ideas...
@hammer [Domain2Vec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.10952) is very much the inspiration here.

🤖 Reference for anyone picking this up: how to map the **Grug-MoE Fisher-DSP sweep** buckets to their underlying data.

**The sweep**: [`marin-community/grug-moe-mix-swarm`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/marin-community/grug-moe-mix-swarm) — 840 MoE runs (d512, us-central2), each a two-phase mixture over **168 buckets**, with `macro_bpb` + 52 per-task BPBs per run. Weight columns are `{bucket: weight}` dicts keyed by bucket name.

**The data**: datakit store `store_8ac06c74` — 40 lexical clusters × 5 quality tiers = 200 partitions, 10.37T tokens total:
- `gs://marin-us-east5/datakit/store_8ac06c74/` (GCS, us-east5)
- `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/datakit/store_8ac06c74/` (CoreWeave mirror)

**Mapping rule** (canonical source: `experiments/grug/moe/launch_datakit_moe_mix.py`):

1. **Direct buckets** — name arithmetic, 0-based: `cNNqQ` → `<store>/cluster=NN/quality=Q`. E.g. `c12q3` → `.../cluster=12/quality=3`. 167 buckets.
2. **`tail`** — a `ConcatDatasetComponent` over exactly the **33 below-threshold partitions** (every partition with < ~100–200M tokens; largest merged = 89M, smallest kept = 212M; separation is clean). The explicit child list is `_TAIL_BUCKETS` in the launcher: whole clusters 0, 4, 7, 9, 39 (all tiers) plus `c10q1–q4` and `c38q1–q4`. Combined: 0.42B tokens (0.004% of the store).
3. This one rule explains all bucket-list irregularities: no `c00/c04/c07/c09/c39` (whole clusters below threshold), and `c10`/`c38` appear with only `q0` (only tier above threshold).

**Format & metadata**:
- Each partition is consumed directly as a levanter cache (`flat_cache=True`, `TextLmDatasetFormat`): `part-NNNNN-of-06301/` shard dirs containing `shard_ledger.json` + `input_ids/` tensorstore arrays. No derived per-bucket caches exist.
- Per-partition `total_tokens` / `total_elements` / `n_shards`: `<store>/.artifact.json` (also records `cluster_view: 40`, quality thresholds `[0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8]`).
- Tokenizer: `marin_tokenizer`. Phase 1 starts at 0.8 of total steps (`_PHASE_1_START_FRACTION`); mixture block size 49,152. The launcher has an `enable_simulated_epoching` flag — check the swarm's launch config before interpreting high-dose runs (per-run max weight reaches 0.95, and bucket sizes span 212M→hundreds of B tokens, so epoching behavior matters for any response modeling).

**To build content features (V columns) for these buckets** with the machinery on `rav/mixing-via-embeddings`: sample per partition from the caches above (`experiments/datakit/mixture_features/build_domain_histograms.py` reads this exact format), and build `tail` as a token-count-weighted sample across its 33 children using the `.artifact.json` counts.

🤖 **Pre-registration: holdout test protocol for the grug-moe-mix-swarm** (before any model fitting on this data; the 840 runs are treated independently of qsplit240).

- **Split (locked)**: 800 train / 40 test, uniform random `numpy default_rng(seed=0)` over `experiment_index`. Test indices in `holdout_manifest.json`; test labels quarantined in a separate file whose SHA-256 is pinned in the manifest (`68a90838…`); both mirrored to `gs://marin-eu-west4/user/rav/projects/mixing_via_embeddings/v0/grug/`. Coverage checked on features only: test max-dose distribution matches train (15/40 runs above 0.4).
- **Development rules**: all featurization, variants (raw-weights ridge/LGBM incumbents; content ridge K=1000 in the frozen basis; Hellinger kernel; ± quality-tier features; ± epoch/exposure features; shuffled + matched-random controls), hyperparameters, and model selection use the 800 training runs only, via CV. Primary target: `macro_bpb`.
- **One-shot procedure**: freeze the selected model + declared baselines → write predictions for the 40 from features only → **publish the predictions file's SHA-256 here before opening labels** → open the quarantine once → compute only the pre-registered readout (anything further is labeled exploratory).
- **Readout & pass bar**: R1 predictive power (Spearman on the 40, permutation p < 0.001); R2 beats the bucket-indexed incumbent (paired ΔSpearman ≥ 0 vs best weights baseline, bootstrap CI reported); R3 no selection overfit (test Spearman ≥ train-CV − 0.15); R4 semantics-vs-shape decomposition vs matched-random control (measured, no bar). **PASS = R1 ∧ R2 ∧ R3.**

Full protocol: `test_protocol.md` at the GCS path above (sha256 `ef33dce04d156a37…`).

🤖 **Pre-registered AMENDMENT to the grug holdout protocol** (before any label opening; the quarantine file remains unopened; all evidence below is train-only CV).

**Why**: development on the 800 training runs showed the original target (`macro_bpb`) mixes an English factor with a reliable-but-mixture-orthogonal multilingual factor (33 belebele/include tasks; English↔belebele macro Spearman 0.10) over a per-run-varying task set — capping the best model at OOF Spearman 0.303 and breaking R1's power at n=40. The swarm's own registered aggregates likewise drop `macro_bpb` and use strict-common English z-means.

**Amended target** (exact formula, replaces macro_bpb): `zmacro_english_20` — for run r, y(r) = mean over observed t ∈ L of (bpb_t(r) − μ_t)/σ_t, where L = the 20 bpb tasks not matching `belebele_*`/`include_*`, and (μ_t, σ_t) are frozen train-set constants recorded in `target_candidates.json` (GCS: `gs://marin-eu-west4/user/rav/projects/mixing_via_embeddings/v0/grug/`). Lower better. Leak checks: fully-nested selection reproduces the same task list; nested vs frozen z-stats differ by 0.0002 Spearman; PC2 of the task matrix (unsupervised) recovers the same factor at 0.841.

**Selected primary model** (train-CV, frozen): Hellinger-kernel ridge, K=1000 per-phase content histograms, hyperparameters by inner CV — **train-CV OOF Spearman 0.818 ± 0.001** (≈93% of the split-half reliability bound 0.88). Declared baselines frozen alongside: train-mean, weights-ridge (0.679), weights-LGBM, DSP dose-response (best tied variant 0.643 — the qsplit240 functional form does not transfer to this 168-bucket swarm), and the primary's shuffled-columns + matched-random controls.

**Amended readout** (unchanged in structure; R1's bar now properly powered): R1 Spearman(pred, realized) on the 40, permutation p < 0.001; R2 paired ΔSpearman ≥ 0 vs the best weights baseline (bootstrap CI reported); R3 test Spearman ≥ train-CV − 0.15 (i.e. ≥ 0.668); R4 semantic-vs-matched-random decomposition (measured, no bar). PASS = R1 ∧ R2 ∧ R3. Procedure unchanged: predictions for the 40 are generated from features only, their file's SHA-256 gets published here BEFORE the quarantine is opened, labels are opened once, and only the pre-registered readout is computed (rest labeled exploratory).

🤖 **Holdout test — predictions frozen (phase 1 of the one-shot procedure).** `test_predictions.parquet` SHA-256: `0a4cc4e6430d92001e65b9ecf00873dd02b5666fb29da41c38d77d7d34c2474f` (1040 rows = 26 models × 40 runs; frozen primary Hellinger-kernel γ=1.2475/α=0.1 + declared baselines/controls; embedded provenance: git `ed7599e51a`, target formula + frozen z-stats; mirrored to `gs://marin-eu-west4/user/rav/projects/mixing_via_embeddings/v0/grug/` with `frozen_model_hyperparams.json` sha `080a504c…`). Quarantined labels accessed by checksum only so far (matches the split manifest). Opening the label file next; only the amended pre-registered readout (R1–R4) will be computed on it.

🤖 **Grug holdout test — pre-registered verdict: PASS (R1 ∧ R2 ∧ R3).** Quarantine opened exactly once, after hash verification against the published predictions SHA (`0a4cc4e6…`) and the split manifest (`68a90838…`).

| gate | result | numbers |
|---|---|---|
| R1 predictive power | **PASS** | test Spearman **0.7205**, 10k-permutation p = 1e-4 (resolution floor; max permuted ρ 0.588) |
| R2 vs bucket-indexed incumbent | **PASS** | Δ = **+0.035** vs weights-LGBM (0.6852; best baseline), paired 95% CI [−0.14, +0.21] (CI exclusion was pre-declared stretch, not required); vs weights-ridge Δ = +0.089; ΔRMSE −0.037 |
| R3 no selection overfit | **PASS** | 0.7205 ≥ 0.668 bar (train-CV 0.818 − 0.15); generalization gap −0.098 |
| R4 semantics vs shape (measured) | small | Δ vs matched-random control +0.015, 95% CI [−0.05, +0.10]; shuffled control mean-of-10 reaches 0.7212 |

**Honest headline**: the content-featurized surrogate transfers to unseen mixtures (best single model on Spearman and per-seed comparisons, 10/10 vs matched-control seeds) and beats the RegMix-style incumbent — but on this swarm most of the predictive signal is carried by histogram *shape* statistics rather than cross-bucket semantic identity (the R4 margin is CI-consistent with zero at n=40; the `_mean10` controls also enjoy an implicit 10-predictor ensembling advantage). This echoes and strengthens the qsplit240 dispersion-confound finding: for *this* store's cluster×quality buckets, "describedness" earns its keep mostly through shape+geometry, with semantics contributing a small increment.

Campaign summary on this swarm (840 runs, all development on 800 train, one-shot test on 40): target repaired from `macro_bpb` (kernel OOF 0.303 — capped by a mixture-orthogonal multilingual factor) to the pre-registered `zmacro_english_20` (0.818 train-CV, ≈93% of the split-half reliability bound); DSP functional form ported and retired for this regime (best tied variant 0.643; content-tied parameterization was its best flavor on both targets); Hellinger-kernel K=1000 per-phase selected and confirmed. Artifacts: `gs://marin-eu-west4/user/rav/projects/mixing_via_embeddings/v0/grug/` (`holdout_readout.{json,md}`, `realized_vs_predicted.parquet`, full CV/DSP/target reports); code on `rav/mixing-via-embeddings`.

🤖 Addendum refining the earlier "epoch features inert" finding (train-CV only, post-holdout, exploratory relative to the completed test): on the clean `zmacro_english_20` target, hinge exposure features give the **linear** content model a solid gain (hist-ridge 0.740 → 0.770, +0.030, 15/15 folds, p=1e-4) — `macro_bpb`'s multilingual noise had masked the repetition signal. The **kernel** does not benefit: a product hell×hinge kernel scores 0.767 vs 0.815 alone (−0.047, 0/15) — it already absorbs epoching implicitly through content-dose geometry, and explicit terms dilute its distance structure (same failure mode as kernel+quality). The frozen holdout primary stands; epoch caps at proposal time remain mandatory either way.

🤖 **Independent validation pass (Codex-collaborative): rigor vs PR #2393, epoching audit, literature review.** Two adversarial Codex CLI review rounds; its three prescribed analyses executed; corrections adopted. Full memo + artifacts: `validation_memo.md`, `codex_methodology_review.md`, `validation_checks.md`, `epoching_lit_review.md` at `gs://marin-eu-west4/user/rav/projects/mixing_via_embeddings/v0/grug/`.

**Rigor vs #2393**: exceeds on pre-registration (SHA commitment chain, quarantined holdout, amend-before-open), semantic controls (shuffled/matched-random — absent in #2393), and heterogeneous replication (two swarms + one live training test); falls short on seed-repeat noise panels, heteroskedasticity analysis, and metric-registry formality. Top data ask: a ~10-run grug seed-repeat panel (would settle the noise ceiling, bracketed at 0.837–0.923 by residual decomposition; achieved 0.8147 ≈ 97% of the pessimistic bound).

**Epoching: validated with two corrections.** Computation confirmed correct (target-budget semantics, 0.767/0.233 phase quantization). The monotone discount has the same effective-data functional form as Muennighoff 2023 (fitted δ=0.10 ⇒ R_D\*≈9 vs literature 15–31); simulated epoching at proxy scale matches what the [2026 repetition-mismatch work recommends](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.07597); keep-caps-regardless is the published recommendation. Corrections: (1) the earlier "kernel absorbs epoching" was partly an artifact of a bad product-kernel construction — **concat-ARD beats the plain kernel** (+0.0049, 12/15 folds, p=0.0015; linear models gain 6× more), so the kernel absorbs *most* of it and concat-ARD is the refit upgrade; (2) hinge knots move {1,4,8}→{1,4,16} (16 ≈ fitted half-life). Cap per phase, explicitly: `w_j ≤ 4·T_j/(f_p·target_budget)`.

**Selection integrity**: replicated-selection bootstrap (B=200) finds no selection optimism (−0.011 ± 0.002, negative); the realized holdout 0.7205 sits 1.3–1.6 SE below the de-biased train expectation (P ≈ 0.08 under sampling noise — consistent, not established; hyperparams frozen in the bootstrap, so the check is approximate). The campaign's formula-fixed target choice was more conservative than the replicated argmax rule.

**Corrected-claims register** (in the memo): semantic value is validated on qsplit240 only (grug validates *prediction*; controls match the primary there); "no replicates needed" (H3) → "not cost-effective at ~8σ on borrowed noise"; monotone discount is a literature-consistent prior, not a validated conclusion in this sweep.

🤖 **Validation campaign checkpoint: codex-collaborative loop reached its terminal state.** Four adversarial Codex CLI rounds; all its prescribed analyses executed. Round-4 verdict: *"Nothing material remains validatable without new data … rigorously bounded rather than overclaimed."*

New since the last update: **budget correction** — the 840 grug runs each trained **100.16B tokens** (verified from executor_info; not 525M as previously derived) → corrected phase fractions propagated through all epoch-sensitive analyses (all findings survive: hinge +0.0269, concat-ARD +0.0038); **robustness batch** — calibration near-affine (slope 1.020; tail rank weakness = range restriction), LODO-by-cluster median 0.682 vs 0.853 control (interpolation-dependence quantified, worst clusters named), top-1 mixture recommendation unstable (42%) vs cluster-level robust (Jaccard 0.76–0.93) → **recommend at cluster granularity**, negative control clean, heteroskedasticity clean, and the first fitted per-group repetition half-lives (code-adjacent R_D\*≈9 vs web ≈1.9; no OOF gain, informative constants). **Deliverables**: a fully self-contained HTML report (figures + four-tier claim table separating validated@100B-seed0 / unvalidated-across-seeds / unvalidated-across-budgets / not-supported) at `gs://marin-eu-west4/user/rav/projects/mixing_via_embeddings/v0/report/`, with a verification log covering 19 skeptic findings + coordinator's support-honesty fix to the dose-response demo. **In flight**: the 10-run seed-repeat panel at the exact verified swarm config (rav-approved, ~1,110 v4-8-hours; children pending us-central2 autoscale) — resolves tier B (seed variance) in ~5 days.

🤖 form-selection campaign settled — latest results

decision-focused write-up (7 figures, one per decision, each with a collapsible "what am I looking at?" explainer): https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/mixing-via-embeddings/2026.07.21.1/index.html

**model**: `ŷ(w,B,d) = kernel(h = V·w) + Σⱼ bⱼ·max(eⱼ − τⱼ, 0)` — a bucket-independent content surrogate (Hellinger-kernel ridge over per-phase embedding histograms) + a linear-past-threshold epoch-harm term. new source = new column of `V` → priced without re-sweeping.

* **surrogate = kernel** — held-out Spearman **0.720** on the 40-run quarantined test set (p<1e-4, perm-max 0.588), ~79% of the seed-noise ceiling; beats weights-ridge / lgbm / RFF / KME / NN in the bake-off. in-regime it misses no repetition harm (0/37 tasks)
* **epoch-harm form = linear-past-threshold** — leave-one-epoch-out CV-decisive: code CV-RMSE 0.056 bpb vs quadratic 0.246 / softplus² 0.260 (curved forms over-extrapolate e32 by 10–30σ). the committed swoosh was wrong in magnitude (~119×), shape, and onset
  * threshold is **per-bucket**: τ_code≈8.85, τ_math≈11.66 (CI95 [9.9, 13.3] excludes 8.85) → needs per-bucket calibration
  * amplitude per content-type + scale-aware: `bⱼ = b₀·(B/10B)^−0.73·(d/512)^1.68`; per-epoch damage math (0.091) > code (0.052) > web (0.014)
  * generalizes across 3 independent bucket types (code / math / web)
* **★ 100B production gate — harm VANISHES** — matched-mechanism run (real `max_train_batches` subset-repeat, same mechanism as the 10B harm experiments, so only budget changed): e4→e16 rise = **−0.003 bpb** (0.4σ from zero, 9.3σ below the power-law prediction). 4-point budget-transfer curve harm(e16) {2.5,10,40,100}B = {0.688, 0.384, 0.092, −0.003}, fitted exponent **−1.15** (steeper than the −0.73 mid-range → collapses faster than the power law). agrees with the transect under a matched mechanism
  * → **at production scale (100B) the kernel alone suffices**; the harm term is a proxy-scale / extreme-repetition (≥~16–32 epoch) guardrail, not a core production requirement. the severe 10B harm (e16 +0.39, e32 +1.27 bpb) was a small-budget artifact
  * caveat: single-seed per point; a small +8.8σ residual (+0.07 bpb) survives only at e32 (extreme over-repetition), ~3.4× weaker than the 10B fit

**test-set protocol** was pre-registered before any look; the 40-run quarantine held throughout.[^1]

topics.title: [storage] Remove legacy checkpoint discovery after the scratch TTL
topics.body:
Remove the temporary discovery of former scratch roots added by #10221 after the CoreWeave scratch cutover has drained. Normal resumes should search the run's permanent checkpoints and its configured scratch destination. Preserve explicit restore paths and the hero launcher's explicit destination.

Earliest review date: November 2, 2026. Merge only after 14 full days have elapsed since the last non-hero writer using an old scratch mapping stopped. Record that stop timestamp; a later stop moves the gate. Recheck active jobs and checkpoint expiration before merging. Removing discovery too early can prevent automatic resume from finding a checkpoint.

Done when:

- Controllers and downstream consumers use the new storage configuration, and non-hero jobs no longer write to the old scratch mappings.
- The last legacy non-hero writer stopped at least 14 days ago, lifecycle expiration has cleared its temporary checkpoints, and no non-hero resume depends on an old mapping.
- Remove `checkpoint_read_buckets` from backend configuration and parsing, and remove the migration-only `checkpoint_resume_paths` helper in favor of the trainer's checkpoint discovery.
- Update checkpoint discovery coverage for permanent plus configured scratch roots while preserving explicit restore paths and hero routing.
- Release the updated `marin-rigging` and `marin-core` packages and refresh the affected MarinSkyRL, Harbor, and Evalchemy dependency locks.

topics.title: [finelog] Increase forwarding throughput for dense log backlogs
topics.body:
Increase regional Finelog → hub forwarding throughput so dense log backlogs drain faster and delayed task logs reach Iris. Forward up to four namespaces concurrently and read up to one million log rows per read-and-send cycle. Requests retain their byte limit, and chunks remain serial within the log namespace. The saved source cursor records completed progress and cannot advance past a pending or retryable request.

Encode each candidate chunk once. If its payload exceeds 150 MiB, split it in half and process each half the same way. Process the left half first to preserve source order. Source scans keep separate row-count and segment bounds, and oversized single rows retain their existing handling. Release the decoded Arrow batch before waiting for acknowledgements. Slow-cycle diagnostics separate source reads, chunk encoding, and RPC compression/transport/durable acknowledgement from cursor persistence.

During the October 17 incident, RNO2A was roughly 395 million regional sequence positions behind. Forwarding counters showed about 24,000 accepted positions/sec before deployment and 87,000–107,000/sec over successive 71- and 65-second samples after deploying namespace concurrency and larger reads. A dense source sample contained about 77,000 rows per second of event time; this measures production density. Sequence positions can include gaps and filtered rows, so those counters are not exact row counts. By 17:56 UTC, backlog was down to 91 positions and all 417 rows for the affected task were present on the hub. The chunk-splitting follow-up remains undeployed.

A local benchmark on one million synthetic NCCL-shaped rows with six log columns and 294 MB of Arrow IPC output reduced serialization attempts from seven to three compared with the deployed sizing search. Bytes serialized, including discarded attempts, fell from 1,010 to 589 MB; both versions produced two requests. With 100,000 narrow rows followed by 100,000 wide rows, halving produced nine requests against eight with the packing search. Halving accepts underfilled requests to avoid the sizing search. These measurements describe serialization work; they do not establish an end-to-end throughput improvement.

A bounded million-row regional read took 1.32 seconds initially and 0.19 seconds on repeat. Later live scans took 5.4–8.2 seconds in 12–16-second cycles, including a 128-segment window returning only 424,000 rows. Read cost varies with segment geometry and cache state. An isolated local server capped at four CPUs acknowledged compressed 500,000-row writes in 0.70–0.78 seconds. Live hub samples showed about three active cores on a four-core VM, compaction/index work, and near-zero disk I/O wait. The largest resolved perf symbols involved copying, comparisons, and page faults; stripped Rust symbols limited attribution. These probes do not fully apportion live cycle time; the added stage timings expose the remaining waits.

[Incident record](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/780).

topics.title: [taskcompendium] Add a decision-model grader graded on the host
topics.body:
Add `DecisionGrader` (`kind: decision_model`) as a fifth TaskSpec grader type. A decision model reads one state and answers one comparative question: the whole candidate answer against a gold reference, under a rubric, on five levels (missing, contradicts, partially matches, equivalent, matches exactly) with credits 0, 0, 0.5, 1 and 1. The grader holds the rubric, the reference, the state template, the acceptance level and the calibration reads that set it. The default state holds the deliverable, the rubric items without their weights or caps, the reference and the visible text of the solver's final assistant message. The task names no model; the host supplies a `DecisionClient` whose `decide(state, questions, *, elastic, timeout)` returns level probabilities for each question id. `elastic` is the state key holding the solver's output, the one value the client may shorten from the middle to fit its model's window. `timeout` is the caller's verifier deadline in seconds.

The grade uses the expected level over the returned probabilities. The reward is 1.0 at or above the acceptance level and `0.5 * min(1, credit(level) / credit(bar))` below it, so a rejected answer earns less than 0.5. A null acceptance level means level 2, "partially matches". `GradeResult.detail` records `level`, `bar` and `accepted`.

A decision model is a different instrument from an LLM judge, so this grader does not use verifyit's `judge` mode or `JudgeSpec`. It has no environment and no verifier resources, and grading stays out of the rollout container: `grading.grade_decision_answer(task, attempt, client)` grades the final conversation on the host, and `grade_task` routes to it through a new `decision_client` keyword. `grade_task` takes the deadline as `decision_timeout` and raises `ValueError` for a decision grader without one. A final turn without assistant text is a submission failure, decided without a read. A client raises `DecisionUnavailable` for a connection error, a timeout, a 5xx or an unavailable service, and a missed deadline raises it too; it propagates from both entry points so the caller can grade the same attempt once more and then record an infrastructure outcome. A missing client, any other `RuntimeError` or `OSError`, and a malformed read are `infra_error`; other client exceptions are permanent and propagate. TaskSpec validation refuses the grader on `file`, `state` and `workspace_state` answers. Curation controls and source verification report it as unsupported, since they take no decision client.

The fields, levels and reward rule come from Taskforge's experiments, which now carry this grader inside a `NoGrader` contract. A first-class type lets that adapter go; the rubric types move here with the grader. RolloutEngine is unchanged because #10203 reworks the engine's grading; the engine's host route for a decision grader will follow its shape. Until then a rollout of a decision task fails at its grading step.

TaskSpec schema advances to 0.28; older TaskSpec records must be regenerated. The curation and quick output versions advance so stored specs regenerate.

This is a draft for discussion: whether decision models stay in the long term is not yet decided.

topics.title: [levanter] Add plateau dropping as a train_lm option
topics.body:
Add plateau_dropping to train_lm. With it set, a supervised token leaves the
loss once its loss has stopped changing: from its third visit on, a token is
dropped when both visit-to-visit relative changes, including the current
visit, are below 10% (each relative to the earlier loss, floored at 0.05 nats).
The token stays in the input, its loss is still measured, and it is trained
again as soon as its loss moves. The loss is the mean over kept tokens, and
each step logs kept and dropped token counts and loss sums. The rule follows
the write-up in #10028; the defaults are configurable.

History is kept per row on the host, keyed by a hash of input_ids and
loss_weights, so it does not depend on loader order and survives per-epoch
permutations. It is written beside every checkpoint as
plateau-updates-<N>.npz, and a resumed run refuses to start without the file
for its restored update count. A resume reproduces the uninterrupted run's
training metrics and history bit for bit, and on a 2-way context, 4-way expert
CPU mesh the per-epoch dropped counts equal a mesh without context
parallelism. PlateauTrainer plugs into two new Trainer.train_step overrides,
one adding per-step inputs and one consuming metrics before the step's hooks
run.

Microbatching and z-loss are rejected with plateau dropping. Multi-host
gathering of the per-token losses and host memory (about 16 bytes per
supervised token) are untested at scale.

Part of #10213

topics.title: [datakit] Truncate Harrier documents at read time
topics.body:
Harrier's embed step now keeps the first `HARRIER_MAX_RAW_TEXT_CHARS` (100,000) characters of each document while it reads the normalized parquet. Before, `load_file` turned whole row groups into Python dicts and the cut happened in `_embed_shard`, after `window(4096)`. A window could hold 4,096 untruncated documents, so worker memory grew with the largest documents in a source.

The new reader takes each row group from `load_parquet_batch`, converts it to Python dicts in slices of about 64 MiB of Arrow data, and cuts the text before it yields a record. It returns a Zephyr `Reader`, so input progress and `zephyr/records_in` still work. `embed/bytes_in` still counts UTF-8 bytes of the truncated text, as before, and the other `embed/*` counters are unchanged. A row with null text still raises `TypeError`, now from the reader; normalize drops such rows, so normalized input never reaches it. The step hash, `EMBEDDING_ATTR_DATA_VERSION` and output paths do not change. The slice sizing, `rows_per_chunk`, moves from the luxical pipeline to `marin.processing.embeddings.read_chunks` so both pipelines import it from the library; luxical reads with the same target as before.

TEI receives the same texts in the same order as on main, so the embeddings do not change. The test source had 4 shards and 342 documents: lengths from 0 to 10x the cap, multi-byte and astral-plane characters at the cut, and one 186 MB row group. It ran with and without dedup attrs, whose `sorted_merge_join` depends on the reader's record order, on 1 and 8 workers. With a hash-based fake TEI, the texts it received and the written parquet files were byte-identical to main.

Memory was measured in one local process with a fake embedder. On 2.1 GB of 2-20 MB documents (4 shards, 264 MB row groups, with dedup), median peak RSS over 3 runs fell from 6,676 MB (runs 6,638-6,685) to 5,298 MB (runs 4,824-5,651). The largest window, as Python object size, fell from 418-543 MB to 3.7-4.6 MB. The remaining peak is about 650 MB of imports plus Zephyr's whole-row-group Arrow read, which costs 4-5x the row-group size for each shard being read; main pays it too. With 2 shards of 10 MB documents in 200 MB row groups, growing each shard from 200 MB to 1.2 GB (one run per size) raised peak RSS on main from 2.5 GB to 4.8 GB; on this branch it stayed between 2.5 and 3.0 GB. On 8 shards of 25,000 short documents, median wall time over 6 runs was 13.13 s on main and 13.03 s here. We have not run this on real normalized data or against a live TEI server.

Harrier does not reuse luxical's `_load_records_bounded`. That loader emits its own `embed/bytes_in` in raw characters next to Harrier's byte count, maps null text to an empty string, and returns a plain generator, which Zephyr does not count in `zephyr/records_in`.

topics.title: Vendor SkyRL behind an isolated executable
topics.body:
Move the supported SkyRL runtime into `vendor/skyrl` and route Marin RL artifacts through its isolated `marinskyrl` executable. Source changes can land with Marin while SkyRL's Torch/CUDA dependencies retain their own resolution and lock. ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph Marin["Marin environment · root uv.lock"] Experiment["RL experiment / artifact graph"] --> Adapter["marin.rl.skyrl"] end subgraph SkyRL["vendor/skyrl · independent uv.lock"] Code["cloud/ · marinskyrl/
skyrl-train/ · skyrl-gym/
templates · upstream provenance"] --> CLI["marinskyrl executable · CPU environment"] end Adapter -->|"launch YAML / child process"| CLI CLI -->|"verified source + assets + lock"| GPU["Iris GPU task
editable SkyRL + frozen Megatron/vLLM profile"] GPU --> Output["Distributed checkpoints / HF policy export"] Output --> Eval["Marin evaluation artifact"] ``` Marin clears its Python environment selection at the subprocess boundary; the launcher reuses its own CPU environment. GPU workers install the bundled source and frozen profile without cloning the fork. Ray ports use Iris allocations or task-local kernel selection on Kubernetes, so concurrent jobs can share a host. The runtime identity hashes the current source, assets, and lock, so ordinary vendor edits work without migration restaging. Workers verify each bundled file against that identity. SkyRL may depend on Marin inside its nested environment; Marin accesses SkyRL only through the executable. Remove the obsolete `config/external/MarinSkyRL` pin and updater entry. Retain Megatron/vLLM, OPD, Grug, task execution, generation, and checkpoint export. Drop `skyrl-tx`, the unused replay buffer, unsupported launcher registrations, and files outside the declared entrypoint/import/asset closure. A captured local patch preserves math grading and nested runtime bundling, and adds runtime regression coverage. Preserve the upstream license and an independent-lock CI lane that audits the built wheel against the current checkout. The migration script can refresh the vendored tree as the fork advances. It captures upstream and active work, replays all local vendor changes with a three-way merge, and rebuilds the stacked PR report. A preview leaves the checkout unchanged; apply rejects intervening edits. Conflicts can be resolved in the candidate and saved as a normalized patch for the next refresh. ```mermaid flowchart TB Fork["Fork main + all open PRs
recently active open issues"] --> Snapshot["Snapshot
source, patches, discussions"] Snapshot --> Baseline["Prune + replay local vendor changes"] Local["Current vendor/skyrl edits"] --> Baseline Baseline --> Decision["Inspect candidate / resolve conflicts"] Decision --> Vendor["Apply vendor/skyrl baseline
save patch for next refresh"] Snapshot --> Transplants["Separate PR branches
preserve stack parents"] Transplants --> Publish["Publication after merged cutover
and unchanged source identities"] ``` Open PR changes remain separate from the baseline. Publication previews issue transfers and draft PR creation; execution requires this cutover PR to be merged with the candidate's fork revision and patch hashes, plus unchanged fork main and PR heads/bases. Incomplete transplants block publication of those PRs and block archival. The fork remains unarchived. Include the GPU-qualified Snowball layout from [#10163](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10163): separate reference nodes, recomputation, optimizer offload, and per-role geometry validation. Remove the obsolete FSDP profile. The nested runtime uses published Marin packages and the current harness API. A dedicated updater advances those libraries within the nested version constraints, checks imports and constructor keywords in the isolated environment, and restores the lock on failure. The [migration guide](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/weaver/forks-merge-marinskyrl/docs/dev-guide/skyrl-migration.md) covers refreshes, dependency updates, train/export/resume/evaluate acceptance, and rebasing PRs that edit the deleted fork pin. Broader OPD/Grug/task-rollout qualification, migration of scheduled nightlies and dashboard pointers, and reconciliation of active work remain required before archival. The nested executable boundary follows [Harbor #10287](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10287) and [Evalchemy #10288](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10288).

Its runtime identity is SHA-256 of the provenance file, which records source, asset, patch, and lock hashes: `e5c4e876a4277066b729350bf5504477e6c9383a0322e77e9ab6f54978d6bf43`. The runtime, adapter, and smoke workflow are unchanged at PR head `86e91067d2`. An Iris bundle from that PR head rebuilt and verified all 402 runtime files with the same identity.

The dedicated [SkyRL CI lane](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/39341503649/job/118364115973) passed 52 cases. The earlier [Math500 GPU run](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fpower%2Fskyrl-migration-math500-oooruws7-04) passed three Megatron GPU checks and scored all 500 examples without errors; its 80/500 result used the pretrained policy.

[Current CI](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/39341503649/job/118364116547) reports three failures in `tests/test_moe_context_sharding.py`. Running `uv run --no-sync pytest tests/test_moe_context_sharding.py -q` on both PR head and exact main `d06554ceaf` in separate checkouts produced `3 failed, 2 passed`, with identical maximum absolute differences (0.10386232, 0.75303423, 0.6977967). 🤖 Holistic review of 1464be7596ee0081871a1c844206484a5efab664.

This PR replaces the pinned `MarinSkyRL` fork with a pruned copy in `vendor/skyrl` that has its own `uv.lock`. Marin launches it as a child process, `uv run --isolated --project vendor/skyrl --frozen marinskyrl iris launch`. `SkyRLRuntime.commit` becomes `source_digest`, the SHA-256 of `marinskyrl/_vendor_provenance.json`. The head commit also removes the FSDP profile and moves the Snowball curriculum arms to Megatron. The Marin integration is small and works with the vendored runtime. The vendored tree, however, cannot be edited in place, which contradicts the PR's main claim. The curriculum rewrite also duplicates an open PR that was validated on GPUs.

**Before.** `_launcher_command` ran `config/external/MarinSkyRL`, a one-package project that pinned the fork at `81ae0ef7`. `update-external.py` and the external-runtime dependency policy advanced that lock. SkyRL fixes landed in the fork, and Marin bumped the pin.

**Design.** `scripts/skyrl_migration.py` snapshots the fork, prunes it to an import closure, applies `config/skyrl-migration/*.patch`, and writes per-file SHA-256s into the provenance file. Two checks enforce those hashes: `check-vendor` in the new `skyrl-wheel` CI lane, and `runtime_bundle._bundle_paths` at launch. Root lint, type checking, and the workspace exclude `vendor/skyrl`. The same script also implements the remaining cutover: transferring issues, publishing transplanted PRs, and a Math500 bundle.

**Evidence and limits.** The PR's comments cite an end-to-end Iris run: train, export, resume in a fresh job, then GSM8K eval. They also cite a passing `skyrl-wheel` lane and a Math500 GPU run, all at `c917a22ada`/`86e91067d2`. Both the Snowball Megatron move and its 1800GB memory allocation in `1464be75` were only checked by composing configs through the launcher; no Snowball GPU run backs them. CI at this head was still pending when this review was written.

**Findings**

- **1. Blocker:** `vendor/skyrl/cloud/iris/runtime_bundle.py:81` and `scripts/skyrl_migration.py:634` reject any vendored file whose bytes differ from the provenance hashes. The only code that writes provenance is `stage` (`scripts/skyrl_migration.py:466`), which needs a fresh `gh` snapshot of the fork plus a patch under `config/skyrl-migration/`. A Marin PR that fixes one line of SkyRL in place therefore fails the `skyrl-wheel` lane, and `marinskyrl iris launch` raises "Runtime source differs from staged provenance". That contradicts the body's "Source changes can land with Marin" and its claim that the boundary matches Harbor #10287, which hashes the checked-out source. Fix: compute `source_digest` from the bundled files at launch, as a hash of the sorted (path, sha256) list, in both `skyrl_runtime_digest` and `runtime_bundle`. Then drop the per-file `files` map and the patch-hash check, so `check-vendor` reduces to `uv lock --check` plus the wheel build.
- **2. Related PR:** `experiments/post_training/curriculum_rl/launch.py:319`: `1464be75` moves Snowball to Megatron but keeps `colocate_policy_ref=True`, so the reference model shares the policy nodes. #10163 makes the same move with H100 smokes. It found that a reference on the policy nodes ran out of GPU memory, so it gives the reference two nodes of its own and adds recomputation, optimizer offload, and per-role layout preflight. #10163 also deletes `SkyRLRuntimeProfile`. This PR leaves that enum with a single member (`lib/marin/src/marin/rl/skyrl.py:62`) plus the `_STRATEGY_FOR_PROFILE` lookup. Land #10163 first, then rebase this PR so it keeps #10163's recipes and drops its own `curriculum_rl/launch.py` and `async_rl.py` rewrite.
- **3. Should fix:** `vendor/skyrl/pyproject.toml:14` and `:38` pin `marin-verifyit`, `marin-rolloutengine`, `marin-shellbox`, and `marin-taskcompendium` to `b3206ac1`. That commit exists only on draft #10190's branch, not on `main`. This PR also deletes the updater that used to advance the lock (`config/update-external.py`, `scripts/ci/dependency_update_policy.py`). As a result, the vendored runtime keeps running unmerged Marin library code, fixes to those four libraries on `main` never reach SkyRL, and the lock stops resolving if #10190's branch is rewritten. Use editable path sources to `../../lib/<pkg>` and bundle them, as #10287 does for Rigging and FineStore. At minimum, repin to a `main` commit and keep an updater entry.
- **4. Should fix:** `scripts/skyrl_migration.py:802` and `:839`: `plan`, `stage`, `transfer-issues`, `publish-prs`, and `prepare-math500` are one-time fork-migration tooling. Together with `tests/infra/test_skyrl_migration.py` (520 lines), `config/skyrl-migration/snapshot-report.md`, and `config/skyrl-migration/smoke/`, they add about 2,000 lines that nothing runs after cutover. The sibling vendoring PRs, #10287 and #10288, ship no equivalent. Keep only `check-vendor`, reduced as in finding 1, as a CI entry point under `infra/ci/`. Run the transfer and publication steps from this branch or a session artifact, and drop the migration test file with them.
- **5. Related PR:** Several open PRs still edit `config/external/MarinSkyRL/{pyproject.toml,uv.lock}`, which this PR deletes: #10078, #9799, and #9626, plus drafts #10045, #10066, #10190, and #9749. After this PR merges, each must be redone as a `vendor/skyrl` change. Under finding 1, that also means re-staging the fork. Resolve finding 1 before merging, and tell those authors which path to rebase onto.
