topics.title: Marin eval policy roadmap
topics.body:
OVERVIEW

Our first task for you concerns the next iteration of our eval policy! As you are no doubt aware, we are very excited to have you help create and source new high quality evals for Marin, and help direct our eval policy. We have many directions we are excited to explore that the current iteration either does not cover, or covers with insufficient granularity.

Therefore, your first assignment at Marin is to create a *roadmap* for Marin’s eval policy. Look into the details of the current policy and consider -- what, in your estimation, are the most crucial areas for us to improve upon? Here are some candidates we could consider; please treat these as suggestions or starting points, not as mandates. You are free to pick your own priorities. Also, please treat this as an unordered set rather than an ordered priority list!

OPEN QUESTIONS

1. Marin currently does not explicitly evaluate the multilingual capabilities of its models under the policy. This stands in contrast to projects like OpenEuroLLM, which are explicitly emphasizing multilingual ability. There are many evals of this type we could consider including, such as [JudgeArena](https://github.com/OpenEuroLLM/JudgeArena). We could also start evaluating our models’ capabilities in the realm of culturally idiomatic language.
2. simpleQA (or a miniaturized version of it) is a benchmark we are excited to evaluate under our policy, because we believe it has the potential to correlate well with our out-of-distribution AAII target. That said, our current implementation of simpleQA is producing extremely depressed estimates of model capability. We believe this warrants some investigation; a repaired simpleQA would be a useful addition to our cohort.
3. We should consider adding a more realistic long context eval to our policy to complement MRCR and give a more holistic picture of our models’ retrieval capability.
4. We currently do not evaluate deep research or search capability directly.
5. We lack a comprehensive overview of the long tail of agentic benchmarks which now appear in many frontier labs’ model cards. Should we consider adding some of these to our policy?
6. IFBench scores are depressed and do not seem likely to be a realistic reflection of model instruction following capabilities; a well-designed benchmark derived from the [Snowball conversation lab](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/snowball-conversation-lab) might be a good replacement for this.
7. We have several biology / medical benchmarks we could consider incorporating into future eval policies; biomedical knowledge: MedXpertQA or PubMedQA, Clinical reasoning: HealthBench Professional/ Bedside Bench /ASCENT, Biological discovery: Longevity — genetics regression; LAB-Bench cloning / DNA methylation age comparison, Medical coding: MedConceptsQA — ATC Hard/ MedConceptsQA ICD-10 procedures, hard

DONE WHEN

We have a document that proposes a priority list of what we should focus on in our next eval policy (limitations) and sketches out potential solutions. Ideally, the document will also include an estimated timeline for the next eval policy release.

REFERENCES:

Marin Eval Policy 10-16-26: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10197

Snowball V0 vs Baselines -> issue 10199

comments.body:
🤖

# Research

[Policy #10197](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10197) has 26 in-distribution benchmarks, including eight agent tasks and BixBench, plus three reserved out-of-distribution benchmarks. It has no explicit multilingual or search measure; MRCR is its only dedicated long-context benchmark. The [#10199 selection record](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10199) and policy name different Snowball release checkpoints, and the policy documents an Evalchemy timeout/scoring mismatch. Those validity issues should be resolved before expanding the canonical panel.

**Relevant code**
- [Campaign configuration](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/5d5f405e097b0062c7b008d3b45c40d2dd73cff7/experiments/evaluation/campaigns/eval-campaign-09-25-unlabeled/campaign.yaml) — current benchmark selection.
- [Campaign validator](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/5d5f405e097b0062c7b008d3b45c40d2dd73cff7/experiments/evaluation/campaigns/eval-campaign-09-25-unlabeled/validate-campaign.sh) — pinned run checks.
- [Campaign implementation #9569](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9569) — existing launcher and records.

# Proposed Fix

Target a policy decision by **November 30, 2026** (six weeks); publish the next version only after a full baseline campaign. The ranked work is:

1. **P0, October 19–23: repair policy evidence.** Reconcile the selected checkpoint and source hashes between [#10197](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10197) and [#10199](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10199). Resolve the Evalchemy timeout rule against the pinned implementation and version any scoring change. Define one admission sheet for every candidate: capability measured, task provenance and contamination check, scoring audit, baseline discrimination, runtime, failure rate, and ID/OOD assignment. Do not use reserved AAII scores to tune an in-distribution candidate; the current policy forbids inspecting them before model freeze.
2. **P1, October 19–November 6: pilot factuality and multilingual coverage.** Diagnose depressed SimpleQA results by replaying a fixed model sample through Marin and the [reference scorer](https://github.com/openai/simple-evals/blob/main/simpleqa_eval.py), then adjudicate parser, abstention, and judge disagreements before considering a pinned mini-subset. Pilot a balanced language-by-task panel with per-language scores and native-speaker review of idiomatic prompts; [JudgeArena](https://github.com/OpenEuroLLM/JudgeArena) is a candidate runner, with judge and language bias checked against human labels. Admit either benchmark only if its protocol is reproducible and separates relevant baselines beyond measurement uncertainty.
3. **P2, November 2–13: add realistic long-context evidence.** Pilot a predeclared, common-item, length-stratified subset of [LongBench v2](https://github.com/THUDM/LongBench) alongside MRCR. Report accuracy by context bin, tokenizer fit, truncation, and cost; use the same item set for models being compared. This tests multi-document and other realistic tasks that MRCR does not cover.
4. **P3, November 9–20: gate larger tracks.** Use [#10189](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10189)'s fixed-corpus BrowseComp-Plus baseline to decide whether search/deep research is ready for a later policy; keep retrieval and answer accuracy separate. Audit IFBench failure traces and a held-out Snowball conversation alternative before replacing its score. Review the existing eight agent tasks for missing capabilities, and coordinate any new biomedical task with [#9258](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9258), where grading ambiguity and coverage are still open.
5. **November 23–30: freeze and release.** Select only pilots that pass the admission sheet, pin data/prompts/judges/serving configs, run the complete baseline cohort, preserve traces, and meet the policy's ≥90% scored-trial coverage rule. Publish per-benchmark scores with uncertainty, costs, failed/graded coverage, ID/OOD status, and the reasons for deferring each candidate. If a full cohort or audit misses the gate, move the release date rather than publish a partial canonical panel.

🤖

The [2026 hallucination benchmark review](https://gist.github.com/penfever/432308318dc38eaf8c32e69a8a491288) recommends a battery because closed-book factuality, grounded faithfulness, abstention, long-form verification, and detector localization measure different failures.

For the next in-distribution policy, pilot these additions:

1. [HalluLens](https://aclanthology.org/2025.acl-long.1176/) NonExistentRefusal and PreciseWikiQA for false-premise acceptance, refusal, and dynamic short-form factuality.
2. [RAGTruth](https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.585/) plus [FaithBench](https://aclanthology.org/2025.naacl-short.38/) for grounded response-level and span-level hallucination detection. FaithBench is a disagreement-selected hard set, so report it as a stress test rather than a prevalence estimate.
3. [FactBench](https://aclanthology.org/2025.acl-long.1587/) or a pinned [LongFact/SAFE](https://github.com/google-deepmind/long-form-factuality) slice for claim-level support in long-form, open-world answers. Preserve retrieved evidence and judge inputs because search and judge changes can move the score.

For the SimpleQA work already proposed here, use [SimpleQA Verified](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.07968) rather than SimpleQA-mini and report correct, incorrect, and abstained rates separately.

Exclude AA-Omniscience and all other Artificial Analysis tasks. They are out of distribution under the current policy. The candidates above are not components of the current AAII 4.3 panel. Keep TruthfulQA as a narrow misconception benchmark instead of treating it as comprehensive hallucination coverage.

topics.title: [rolloutengine] History resets silently discard earlier TITO training actions
topics.body:
RolloutEngine can silently discard earlier generated actions from training when an agent changes its next request. Exact-token checks still pass because the reset clears their reference state. A whole-task training sample can therefore contain only the final segment while carrying the reward for the entire attempt.

Confirmed at Marin `f45f04b293128bd8a5b1567e03bef59c7f59e1d0`, with MarinSkyRL `97415bb1432688bc3d316b94e0f649a8d04d2ad7` and Harbor `a85964704593b7d89428ef480238ffce8be3a63c`. These are the pins of [Smartie run 2026.10.19.57](https://wandb.ai/dogml/snowball-smartie-rl/runs/v1vksnkr), using Mini SWE Agent 2.1.0, exact-token tracing, requested behavior logprobs, and whole-task training (`step_wise_training: false`). This report does not establish whether subsequent main revisions still have the defect.

Minimal reproduction procedure derived from the pinned code (not yet executed as a standalone test):

1. Run a two-turn `AgentTaskSession` with exact-token tracing. Return a first assistant message and its served prompt IDs, completion IDs, and behavior logprobs.
2. Have the agent send the same history back with an additional null-valued assistant-message field, such as `annotations: null`. Keep content, tools, and generation options unchanged.
3. `AgentTaskSession.advance()` compares raw message dictionaries and returns `reset_conversation`.
4. The engine calls `trace.reset()` and `steps.clear()`. Complete the second turn and grade the task.
5. Inspect the resulting `RolloutData` and training projection: the first action's loss tokens and step record are absent. The second turn passes exact-token checks as a fresh segment.

Changing only `max_tokens` also triggers the reset because the adapter compares the entire options dictionary.

Relevant code:

- [Adapter prefix/options comparison](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f45f04b293128bd8a5b1567e03bef59c7f59e1d0/lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/agent_session.py#L98).
- [Engine reset clears trace, steps, and completed-record fields](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f45f04b293128bd8a5b1567e03bef59c7f59e1d0/lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/engine.py#L368).
- [Exact-token trace reset and prefix validation](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f45f04b293128bd8a5b1567e03bef59c7f59e1d0/lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/trace.py#L45).
- [MarinSkyRL whole-task and step projections](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/97415bb1432688bc3d316b94e0f649a8d04d2ad7/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollouts/task_projections.py#L237) consume the surviving trace; neither can recover cleared actions.

In a sample of 19 training attempts, all 254 completed-turn-to-next-request boundaries satisfied the reset condition: 170 differed only by null fields or empty provider metadata, 82 omitted an assistant response after Mini SWE Agent reported “No tool calls found,” and two changed only `max_tokens`. In 136 of the metadata-only cases, the next served prompt exactly extended the previous prompt plus completion. Those resets were unnecessary even under the strict token-prefix contract. The other 34 had changed token prefixes; the cause of those token differences has not been isolated. The sample consists of 16 seeded random installed-agent directories plus three attempts linked to retained training records; it is not a population-wide frequency estimate. These boundary counts classify captured requests against the pinned reset condition.

Separately, 687 retained Stage 1 training records each contain only one trainable step boundary, although 662 contain multiple assistant messages. One 19-assistant-message attempt retains only a 522-token final segment as trainable. Retention favors failures and loops; this does not establish frequencies in consumed optimizer batches. Raw task traces remain private.

Expected:

- Under token-in/token-out (TITO), changing inference context must never silently delete earlier training evidence. Preserve each generated action's exact served prompt, completion tokens, behavior logprobs, and loss mask.
- A component that rewrites history must satisfy the training contract before the engine accepts the rewrite. In strict append-only mode, reject incompatible compaction, history edits, or tool-definition changes before applying them. This rejection is the minimum acceptable behavior when full preservation is unsupported. Do not turn an invalid whole-task trajectory into a valid-looking final-segment sample.
- Support for non-prefix histories must be explicit. If segmented training is supported, preserve all segments within the same rollout and define reward attribution across them. Do not reconstruct earlier actions under the rewritten prompt.
- Transport metadata and generation-budget changes must not cause false history resets. Genuine prompt changes still require validation.
- Enforce episode completeness separately from token integrity: aligned tokens and logprobs in the surviving segment do not prove that all required actions survived.

Regression tests should exercise a real Mini SWE Agent/LiteLLM serialization round trip, a missing-tool-call response, a budget-only change, and genuine compaction/tool-definition changes. Assert that every action remains represented in training, or that an unsupported rewrite is explicitly rejected. Changing only the projection to step-wise training is insufficient because the engine already clears the step list.

Historical scope: the older successful Terminus-2 path checked captured token streams and marked all continuous completion spans for loss; see [the pinned assembler](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/a03b2773/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/trajectory_runners/trajectory_processing.py#L1761) and [reported training results](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9225#issuecomment-5777718831). That path also had limitations for genuine history rewrites. The newer adapter/integration is described in #10054 and [MarinSkyRL #1010](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/1010). The trace-loss defect is confirmed; its contribution to Smartie's later reward decline has not been isolated experimentally.

🤖
# Research

The pinned Smartie run used the pre-[#10203](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10203) reset path, which discarded completed turns. Current Marin `5ec80e7124` retains each conversation and its token evidence, but `AgentHarness` still starts a new conversation when raw message dictionaries or any option differ. The rollout API permits a trainer to use only the last conversation; the issue's pinned MarinSkyRL projection cannot recover earlier actions, and its current pin and projection need verification during the port.

**Relevant code**
- [`recorder.py#L404-L417`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/5ec80e71242485b353b1f4556d3d68eb0a4dddf5/lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/recorder.py#L404-L417) — retains previous conversation on start
- [`external.py#L89-L105`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/5ec80e71242485b353b1f4556d3d68eb0a4dddf5/lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/harness/external.py#L89-L105) — raw history and options comparison
- [`models.py#L127-L150`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/5ec80e71242485b353b1f4556d3d68eb0a4dddf5/lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/models.py#L127-L150) — per-conversation evidence and trainer choice
- [`test_rollout.py#L697-L720`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/5ec80e71242485b353b1f4556d3d68eb0a4dddf5/lib/rolloutengine/tests/test_rollout.py#L697-L720) — retained masks across a restart
- [`task_projections.py#L237`](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/97415bb1432688bc3d316b94e0f649a8d04d2ad7/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollouts/task_projections.py#L237) — pinned training projection

# TITO training across conversation starts

A training attempt must account for every sampled action before carrying its task reward. The engine's retained conversations make that possible, but they do not make a last-conversation projection complete.

## Challenges

The agent's chat round trip can add null or empty provider fields without changing the rendered prompt. `max_tokens` changes generation, not prior context. A missing assistant message, compaction, or changed tool definition can change the served prefix. These cases need distinct treatment before a request becomes training data.

## Costs / Risks

The initial completeness guard will reject some otherwise useful attempts until continuation classification improves. Existing records from the old reset path cannot be repaired from their final segment. Updating MarinSkyRL's rollout engine pin and training projection must land together.

## Design

1. Port MarinSkyRL to the post-#10203 `Rollout.conversations` API. In exact-token TITO training, reject a rollout with multiple conversations before projecting or assigning its task reward. Record a structured rejection reason and retain the full rollout for diagnosis. Do not emit a final-segment sample. This is the minimum safety gate; keep old-pinned agent TITO training disabled until it lands.
2. At the agent/transport boundary, compare the fields that the real Mini SWE Agent/LiteLLM serializer puts into the model prompt. Normalize only proven transport-only null and empty metadata. Separate generation-only options such as `max_tokens` from context-defining options, and pass the current generation budget through `reply()` without starting a new conversation. Keep exact served-prefix and logprob checks.
3. In strict TITO mode, reject a missing assistant response, compaction, changed tool definitions, or any unclassified prompt rewrite before forwarding the next model request. Surface an explicit contract failure and suppress training projection for that attempt. If segmented training is later supported, project *every* retained conversation with its own served prompt, sampled tokens, loss mask, and logprobs, and specify how the task reward is attributed across segments. Never rebuild earlier actions under a rewritten prompt.

## Testing

Use a real Mini SWE Agent/LiteLLM serialization round trip with two model turns. Null assistant fields, empty provider metadata, and a budget-only change should leave both actions in one exact-token sample when the rendered token prefix is continuous; a changed prefix should fail explicitly. A missing-tool-call response, genuine compaction, and a tool-definition change should fail the strict training gate. Assert sampled-action counts, loss masks, logprobs, and reward assignment at the MarinSkyRL projection boundary; engine tests should continue to show that interrupted or restarted rollouts retain earlier evidence.

## Open Questions

- After the strict guard lands, should non-prefix attempts remain ineligible for TITO training, or should MarinSkyRL train every retained segment? Segment training needs an explicit terminal-reward attribution rule.

topics.title: [canary-datakit-smoke] Fuzzy verification workers miss 7100s wait
topics.body:
The October 19 tier-1 Datakit ferry exceeded the workflow's 7,100-second Iris wait while `datakit/verify_fuzzy_clusters` waited for workers. Verification started at 14:44 UTC; its worker job was pending in the uploaded diagnostics near the 15:48 UTC cutoff. Iris reported `Scheduler: Insufficient memory (need 64.0GB, available 16.7G...)`. The root job was still running with zero failures or preemptions. The worker job was running by 15:52 UTC, after the cutoff.

Reproduce:
1. Run `.github/workflows/marin-canary-datakit-tier1.yaml` at commit `55dd5cc892b3d7578401ade71777c63c9488b81c` under the observed cluster capacity.
2. Inspect the `zephyr-fuzzy-cluster-verify` worker job as the 7,100-second wait expires.

Expected: verification workers start soon enough for the ferry to finish within the CI wait budget, or the scheduling constraint is reported before the deadline.

## Canary run context

- Lane: `datakit-smoke`; date: 2026-10-19 UTC
- Iris job: `/runner/iris-run-job-20261019-134945`
- [Actions run](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/39263384983) and [uploaded diagnostics](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/39263384983/artifacts/12198429340)

topics.title: [levanter] Distill Qwen 32B into a 0.6B student
topics.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

The Qwen3 32B-to-0.6B study is complete. A two-seed, 100 million-token screen compared five research treatments and four controls. Factorized initialization was the only research treatment promoted to a fresh 1.8 billion-token extension, but its early advantage reversed: it ended at mean NLL 2.6644, 0.39% worse than scratch forward KL at 2.6541. Official Qwen3 0.6B Base initialization plus forward KL was strongest at 2.5579 NLL and 0.3934 mean zero-shot accuracy.

Use official Base plus forward KL when checkpoint provenance is acceptable, and plain forward KL from scratch otherwise. Factorized initialization is useful only for short budgets; projected all-layer matching, TAID, weight-saliency initialization, and the 4B capacity-gap control did not justify extension.

### Helpful links
- [Results and methods report](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/7671/files#diff-827dbbb1efb2f80ce249ec12cbef9dafc025f6b43869b04482cfc816fdc793b8)
- [Implementation and report PR #7671](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/7671)
- [W&B run group](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin/groups/QD-qwen32b-to-0p6b)
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Scope

The requested dense Qwen3.5 32B and 0.6B pair is unavailable. The experiment uses pinned Qwen3 32B, Qwen3 0.6B Base, and Qwen3 4B checkpoints, preserving the requested compression ratio but not claiming Qwen3.5 results.

## Protocol

The screen stops after 100,007,936 tokens. The extension stops after 1,800,011,776 tokens. Both use two paired seeds, sequence length 2,048, global batch size 8, a common regional Datakit sample, terminal held-out NLL as the primary endpoint, and zero-shot ARC-Easy, HellaSwag, PIQA, and WinoGrande as a regression check.

The five research treatments are projected per-layer activation distillation, rank-512 factorized initialization, TAID, teacher weight-saliency initialization, and a 4B capacity-gap control. Scratch and official-Base hard-label and forward-KL runs provide four controls.

## Result

Factorized initialization improved mean NLL over scratch KL by 1.47% at 450 million tokens, but finished 0.39% worse at 1.8 billion tokens with both paired seeds worse. Official Base plus KL finished 3.63% better than scratch KL and had the highest mean accuracy on every zero-shot task. Exact online 32B KL ran at about 28,000 tokens/s versus 95,000–97,000 tokens/s for hard-label training.

All ten terminal extension checkpoints restored and evaluated successfully. This includes the four hard-label retries that crossed the former step-10,000 Hugging Face export failure boundary. Late W&B and controller cleanup failures did not affect terminal artifacts; missing metrics were recovered from durable finelog records.

## Conclusion

Use official Base plus forward KL when possible. If training must start from scratch, use ordinary forward KL. Do not carry factorized initialization into a long run based only on a short screen; its benefit was transient in this study.

comments.body:
🤖 **Scope:** research/experiment scaffold, not a bug — no PR. Analysis for a human to review before implementation begins.

# Research

Distillation infrastructure does not exist in Levanter yet. `models/loss.py` has only next-token CE (+ logsumexp/z-loss); there is no KL/soft-target/temperature loss and no teacher forward pass in the training step. The trainer takes a single `ComputeLossFunction` closure, so a distillation loss is pluggable, but a second (teacher) model must be threaded into the step, kept detached, mp-cast, and sharded. Weight loading from HF (both 32B teacher and 0.6B student) is well supported; **model surgery is not** — only vocab resize exists, so methods 3 (factorized init) and 4 (depth/width structured init) need new tree-surgery utilities over the `haliax` `Stacked`/`BlockSeq` layer stacks.

Two open issues cover a *different* regime — on-policy distillation for RL post-training (#5853; RFC #7236: teacher serving, top-K sparse logprobs in an RL loop). This issue is offline logit distillation + teacher-init for pretraining a 0.6B student. Related but not overlapping; align the KL/top-K loss with #7236 so the loss code is shared, not forked.

One factual flag: the TL;DR correctly notes `Qwen3.5-32B` does not exist. Confirm exact HF repo IDs before launch — `Qwen3Config` defaults to `Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B` and Qwen3 dense tops out at 32B, but the `-Base` suffixes in the plan should be pinned to real repos.

**Relevant code**
- [`train_lm.py#L202-L209`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/main/train_lm.py#L202-L209) — loss closure + single-model `Trainer(...)`; distillation loss plugs in here
- [`loss.py#L35-L142`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/models/loss.py#L35-L142) — CE/z-loss only; no KL/soft-target
- [`qwen.py#L299-L396`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/models/qwen.py#L299-L396) — `Qwen3Config`/`Qwen3LMHeadModel`, HF converter ready
- [`model_init.py#L24-L93`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/main/model_init.py#L24-L93) — load pretrained HF model, sharded/dtype-cast (teacher + student)
- [`trainer.py#L260-L309`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/trainer.py#L260-L309) — `ComputeLossFunction` injection point

# Proposed approach

Build the scaffold in three landable pieces, not one PR. Screen all five arms + the scratch control at a fixed token budget; extend finalists only after the matrix completes.

1. **Distillation loss + dual-model step.** New `models/distill_loss.py`: temperature-scaled forward-KL over teacher logits, `alpha`-blended with student CE. Thread a frozen, sharded teacher into the train step (co-located forward; detached, mp-cast). This covers arm 1 (logit distillation) and the scratch control. Keep the KL top-K compatible with #7236 so the loss is shared.

2. **Model-surgery utilities.** `eqx.tree_at`-based helpers over the `Stacked` layer stack: layer selection/slicing (depth) and width projection/factorization of embeddings and attention/MLP blocks. Covers arms 3 (factorized init) and 4 (structured depth/width init). Unit-test each transform on a tiny config against exact shape and parameter-count invariants — real, testable transforms, not wrappers.

3. **Intermediate-layer + assistant arms.** Arm 2 (projected intermediate distillation) needs a learned student→teacher hidden projection and activation capture; materializing teacher activations may dominate step time (the hypothesis already flags this — measure it). Arm 5 (teacher-assistant curriculum) is orchestration over arms 1/3 with a 4B intermediate, best expressed as an `experiments/distill/` config matrix following the `experiments/grug/base/train.py` nested-dataclass + Iris-dispatch pattern.

Open questions before code:
- Exact HF repo IDs for the 32B teacher / 4B assistant / 0.6B student (`-Base` variants).
- Shared token budget and the fixed val-loss and teacher-divergence thresholds (stopping criteria) — needed to define "done" for the screening matrix.
- Memory plan: co-locate teacher forward vs. precompute top-K soft labels offline. Does the 32B teacher fit alongside 0.6B training on `cw-us-east-08a`, or do we cache teacher logits to storage first? This gates piece 1.
- The logbook `.agents/logbooks/qwen32b-to-0p6b-distillation.md` referenced in the issue does not exist in the repo yet.

🤖 Scaffold snapshot: d3c5b9de06

The pinned revision adds exact online forward KL, selected-layer projected hidden loss, TAID, factorized initialization, weight-saliency structured initialization, and the 4B capacity-gap control. The teacher is excluded from optimizer and checkpoint state and reloaded on resume.

Local gates: 12 focused behavior tests pass; Pyrefly and the required changed-file pre-commit suite pass; the Marin smoke graph resolves to a Qwen-tokenized regional Datakit cache and one GB200x4 worker.

Reviewed design: https://loom.rjp.io/s/xd26vay4/artifacts/design

Next gate: materialize the cache on cw-us-east-08a, then complete the 12-step 32B→0.6B smoke before launching the fixed-budget screen.
@dlwh Added a managed experiment TL;DR block, kept the original experiment details below it, linked the research/scaffold updates, and added the `tldr` label.

🤖 The 100M-token screen is complete: all 18 training cells and all 18 zero-shot evaluations succeeded. Factorized initialization (`QD-002`) is the only research treatment that passed the promotion rule. Its mean held-out NLL was 2.2979 versus 2.3315 for scratch forward KL, and it beat the paired control in both seeds without exceeding any zero-shot regression tolerance. Projected hidden-state matching reached 2.3064 on average but lost the paired comparison in seed 1; TAID, structured initialization, and the 4B teacher did not clear the mean-loss gate.

The strongest screen result overall was the official 0.6B Base checkpoint plus forward KL (`QD-C3`) at 1.9236 mean NLL. Ten fresh 1.8B-token runs—four controls plus `QD-002`, two seeds each—are now running at batch priority on `cw-us-east-08a` under `/power/qwen-distill-extended-1db30a` from commit `1db30ae713`.

🤖 The four hard-label extension cells reached step 10,000 and exposed an intermediate Hugging Face export bug: the export hook treated the regional `s3://` tokenizer directory as a Hub repository ID. Native checkpoints were intact, and the six online-KD cells were unaffected.

Commit `dc9a89de63` makes LM HF export explicitly disableable and turns it off for these runs. `/power/qwen-distill-extended-ce-retry-dc9a89` resumed the four cells from temporary checkpoints around steps 8,955–9,325; all have now passed step 13,733 and completed their first held-out evaluation. The fixed 1.8B-token comparison remains valid.

🤖 All four hard-label extension retries reached terminal step 109,863 and committed native checkpoints. Mean terminal NLL was 2.9796 for scratch CE and 2.8739 for official 0.6B Base plus CE.

Iris marked the QD-C2 seed-1 child failed after completion because its pod disappeared during controller reconciliation. The child logs show the terminal regional checkpoint committed, final evaluation completed, and W&B shut down cleanly. The frozen checkpoint evaluation will provide the restore check; this does not block the six online cells, which remain healthy.

🤖 Final report and implementation: #7671

All ten 1.8B-token checkpoints restored and completed evaluation. Mean terminal NLL was 2.9796 for scratch CE, 2.6541 for scratch KL, 2.8739 for Base CE, 2.5579 for Base KL, and 2.6644 for factorized initialization. Base KL also led the four-task zero-shot mean at 0.3934.

Factorized initialization improved early loss but ended 0.39% worse than scratch KL. The report recommends Base KL when checkpoint provenance is acceptable and scratch KL otherwise.

topics.title: [post-training] Compare SFT, rejection-sampled SFT and OPD transfer on Snowball with CruxEval
topics.body: Design doc: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1LVfMDHRBKBk_Bn9PY1J9Lb_MYwdUTFP5PkX2br25TNg/edit?tab=t.izhzsywzorld. Final results and the full ledger: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9920#issuecomment-6076348127 (ledger also at https://gist.github.com/karansag/0ce1a07580bd430bc8c5b890069385b0). ## TL;DR (final, 2026-10-09). ** Given **one expert E** ([open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Expert-E-Step272 @ fb4f8051](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Expert-E-Step272/tree/fb4f8051a344fec59f902bdd2ca876ac1b2f3296) (S3 source `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task133-cruxeval/checkpoints/karan/cruxeval-step92-lr1e-05/2026.10.07.5/hf/step-272`)) built from the Snowball student B ([open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92 @ fdc3c3c5](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92/tree/fdc3c3c5fff489d3fb04dcbc2387c179b1bf3fab)) by SFT on [GLM 5.3](https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-5.3) CruxEval traces, three methods were used to transfer E's gain back into B: * plain SFT on E's traces * SFT on rejection-sampled E traces (RS-SFT) * on-policy distillation from E (OPD). All three recover most or all of E's CruxEval gain on the 1,600 training-is-test prompts (4x sample traces from the test set size). Two-pass CruxEval input / output accuracy on the selected checkpoints: plain SFT 73.9 / 72.0, RS-SFT 80.8 / 77.9, OPD 79.6 / 75.2, against E 79.4 / 71.4 and B 55.4 / 57.8. RS-SFT and OPD are both 3–7 pp above plain SFT; the RS-SFT vs OPD ordering (1.2 / 2.7 pp) is unresolved with one run per arm and two evaluator passes. No arm dropped below B on GSM8K or MATH500. Training cost: plain SFT 61.6 H100-h, RS-SFT 57.4, OPD 376.4 for the full run (286.9 to the selected checkpoint, plus 14–15 per HF export). RS-SFT used ground-truth execution results to select demos; the other arms did not. These numbers measure transfer on seen prompts, not generalization. ## Results (selected checkpoints; CruxEval two-pass means, pass@1 %, 800 problems per direction; "gap closed" = gain over B divided by E's gain over B).** | Model | CruxEval input | CruxEval output | Gap closed (in / out) | GSM8K | MATH500 | Training H100-h | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | B ([baseline Snowball student, HF @ fdc3c3c5](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92/tree/fdc3c3c5fff489d3fb04dcbc2387c179b1bf3fab)) | 55.4 | 57.8 | 0 | 90.4 | 89.8 | — | | [GLM 5.3](https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-5.3) (teacher of E; served as `glm-5.3` through the internal glm53 relay, reasoning effort high) | 94.0 | 90.5 | — | — | — | — | | E (expert; B + SFT on GLM traces, step 272; [open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Expert-E-Step272 @ fb4f8051](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Expert-E-Step272/tree/fb4f8051a344fec59f902bdd2ca876ac1b2f3296) (S3 source `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task133-cruxeval/checkpoints/karan/cruxeval-step92-lr1e-05/2026.10.07.5/hf/step-272`)) | 79.4 | 71.4 | 100% | 92.1 | 92.2 | 35.9 | | Plain SFT on E demos, 400 updates (final; [open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Plain-SFT-Step399 @ 3e34be3f](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Plain-SFT-Step399/tree/3e34be3f884ff737f85354b060ea831ce0c90636) (S3 source `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task145-cruxeval/checkpoints/karan/cruxeval-plain-e-from-b-lr1e-06/2026.10.08.1/hf/step-399`)) | 73.9 | 72.0 | 77% / 104% | 94.0 | 92.6 | 61.6 | | RS-SFT on execution-correct E demos, 283 of 376 updates ([open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-RS-SFT-Step282 @ 073d128c](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-RS-SFT-Step282/tree/073d128cb1e53652126cce37a7cc2c96625d3c80) (S3 source `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task145-cruxeval/checkpoints/karan/cruxeval-rs-e-from-b-lr1e-06/2026.10.08.1/hf/step-282`)) | 80.8 | 77.9 | 106% / 148% | 93.5 | 93.6 | 57.4 (full run) | | OPD from E, 75 of 100 updates ([open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-OPD-Step75 @ 9d189320](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-OPD-Step75/tree/9d1893207226cf72f701187e1d5260d9fc3c931d) (S3 source `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/karan/skyrl/snowball-opd-cruxeval-e-2/exports/global_step_75/policy`)) | 79.6 | 75.2 | 101% / 128% | 92.5 | 90.4 | 286.9 to the checkpoint; 376.4 full run; +14–15 per HF export | ## Models Student B = [`open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92` @ `fdc3c3c5`](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92/tree/fdc3c3c5fff489d3fb04dcbc2387c179b1bf3fab) (Hugging Face commit; the repo received a later commit on 2026-10-13, so the pin matters). E = B after full SFT on 1,454 execution-correct [GLM 5.3](https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-5.3) CruxEval traces (trace collection: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/scratch/karan/glm-bench-traces/`) (LR 1e-5, 3 epochs, 272 updates, 32 H100, fresh optimizer state, frozen router biases), export [open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Expert-E-Step272 @ fb4f8051](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Expert-E-Step272/tree/fb4f8051a344fec59f902bdd2ca876ac1b2f3296) (S3 source `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task133-cruxeval/checkpoints/karan/cruxeval-step92-lr1e-05/2026.10.07.5/hf/step-272`). E keeps B's tokenizer and chat template. E+ (E + 2 epochs at LR 1e-6; 80.2 / 75.1) was built as a separate reference and is not an arm. Every arm starts from B. ## Benchmark CruxEval (800 Python functions; input prediction and output prediction scored separately by executing the assertion). MATH500 was dropped as the target because B already scores 89.8% there; GSM8K and MATH500 are the collapse checks. Teacher gate: B 55.4 / 57.8; GLM 5.3 on the identical 1,600 prompts 94.0 / 90.5; E 79.4 / 71.4 (two-pass mean), passing the gate of B + 10 points on both tasks with no GSM8K drop. ## Frozen evaluator Marin `experiments.evaluation.cli launch` with Evalchemy [`ae362881cf53f869a6ad52c8a59fa17343c0b5f8`](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/commit/ae362881cf53f869a6ad52c8a59fa17343c0b5f8), vLLM on H100x8 (DP8 + EP8), `max_model_len` 32768, `max_gen_toks` 30720, `enable_thinking: true`, reasoning parser `grug`. Configs and pitfalls: https://gist.github.com/karansag/49de943771b98a7a23d9348b58933f71. Evalchemy's chat client sends no temperature, top_p or seed, and B's `generation_config.json` sets none, so every run samples at vLLM's default (temperature 1.0, unseeded). One pass on 800 problems has a binomial 95% half-width of about 3.5 pp; selected checkpoints get two passes. **Arms as run (all from B; AdamW LR 1e-6 constant, betas 0.9/0.999, weight decay 0, grad clip 1.0, router bias frozen; 4 epochs over the 1,600 prompts; one checkpoint per epoch).** - E demos: 8 samples per prompt from E at temperature 1.0, both directions, execution-graded in an isolated container (12,800 samples, 14.6 H100-h, shared by both SFT arms). - Plain SFT: E's first sample per prompt, correct or not (1,600 rows; 1.45M supervised tokens per epoch; batch 16; Levanter, 32 H100). - RS-SFT: first execution-correct sample per prompt (1,503 rows; 97 prompts with no correct sample stay in the eval denominator; 1.06M supervised tokens per epoch; Levanter, 32 H100). - OPD: [MarinSkyRL](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL), 4 on-policy rollouts per prompt at temperature 1.0, E as the teacher (sampled reverse KL on chosen tokens, no verifier), 64 prompts per update, 25 updates per epoch; 4 learner + 1 rollout + 1 teacher H100x8 nodes (Megatron). - Selection: the final checkpoint when it is similar or better than the previous one on both CruxEval directions, otherwise a second pass on both and the two-pass means decide. Plain SFT selected its final checkpoint (400 updates); RS-SFT (283 of 376) and OPD (75 of 100) selected their epoch-3 checkpoints after their finals dropped on one direction. ## Artifacts Trace browser (GLM, E, E+ traces, side-by-side compare): https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/072c90b0-281e-4692-a4bf-845874c021b1/. OPD W&B: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/skyrl/runs/p3ie2bg7. Selected exports: plain [open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Plain-SFT-Step399 @ 3e34be3f](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Plain-SFT-Step399/tree/3e34be3f884ff737f85354b060ea831ce0c90636) (S3 source `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task145-cruxeval/checkpoints/karan/cruxeval-plain-e-from-b-lr1e-06/2026.10.08.1/hf/step-399`), RS-SFT [open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-RS-SFT-Step282 @ 073d128c](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-RS-SFT-Step282/tree/073d128cb1e53652126cce37a7cc2c96625d3c80) (S3 source `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task145-cruxeval/checkpoints/karan/cruxeval-rs-e-from-b-lr1e-06/2026.10.08.1/hf/step-282`), OPD [open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-OPD-Step75 @ 9d189320](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-OPD-Step75/tree/9d1893207226cf72f701187e1d5260d9fc3c931d) (S3 source `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/karan/skyrl/snowball-opd-cruxeval-e-2/exports/global_step_75/policy`). Eval records: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals//record.json` (every record id is in the final comment's ledger). GPU-hour method: https://gist.github.com/karansag/500604143668730f8e79277b43f39298. ## Not in scope Weight merging (needs RL-trained experts that share B's init; none exist) and transfer from the older Snowball experts (none beats B under the matched eval). ## Decision log - 2026-10-06: matched eval of B and the existing experts (E6, E17a, E18, SWE, Stage-3) on MATH500/GSM8K; none beats B, so no promotion to teacher. - 2026-10-07: MATH500 near ceiling for B → CruxEval chosen; MMLU-Pro (B 44.1) and GPQA-D (B 41.9) measured as fallbacks and not used. - 2026-10-07: full SFT over LoRA for building E; LoRA kept as the fallback if full SFT collapses out-of-domain. - 2026-10-07: rejection-sampled SFT added as a third arm. - 2026-10-08: E frozen at step 272 for every arm; E+ built as a separate reference only. Arms changed from the plan: one sample per prompt for both SFT arms (not up to 4), no LR sweep, 4 rollouts per prompt for OPD. The arms ran in parallel on Iris. - 2026-10-09: RS-SFT and OPD final checkpoints not selected (drops on one direction with paired CI excluding 0); epoch-3 checkpoints selected on two-pass means. Final results posted in one comment; the running-log comments were removed and are archived with the ledger.

🤖
# Research

Teacher training and three transfer arms make this a gated experiment. As of 23:29 UTC, the owner has submitted the W&B-corrected teacher retry; startup, optimizer progress, and export remain unconfirmed ([latest status](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9920#issuecomment-6048938002)). No open PR targets #9920, while the owner is already preparing the recipe on `task/133`; the earlier coding-teacher spike [#9528](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9528) ended without a usable MOPD transfer result.

**Relevant code**
- [`experiments/sft/launcher.py#L494`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/experiments/sft/launcher.py#L494) — shared SFT specification and training setup
- [`lib/marin/src/marin/rl/skyrl.py#L150`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/skyrl.py#L150) — versioned SkyRL experiment and export contract
- [`experiments/evaluation/cli.py#L147`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/experiments/evaluation/cli.py#L147) — shared evaluation launch path

# Proposed Fix

1. Follow the submitted teacher retry through a completed update, full training, and verified HF exports. Evaluate the planned exports with the frozen CruxEval/GSM8K configuration. Stop the transfer arms unless E clears the stated +10-point gate on both CruxEval directions without a GSM8K drop beyond noise.
2. Pin E, B, prompt IDs, tokenizer/template, grader, evaluator, and one eight-sample-per-prompt teacher generation artifact. Build unfiltered SFT from samples 1–4 and rejection-sampled SFT from up to four execution-correct samples. Record missing-correct-sample prompts, actual supervised tokens, and teacher-generation GPU-hours; a matched prompt set alone does not equalize training tokens.
3. Start OPD from the same B and prompts. Check teacher/student token-score alignment and one update plus export before the full run. Match the planned sweep and student update budget across arms, and record teacher-scoring GPU-hours separately.
4. Evaluate every selected arm twice with the same pinned evaluator on CruxEval input, CruxEval output, and GSM8K. Report each arm's accuracy, `(arm − B) / (E − B)` per direction, run-to-run spread, prompts and tokens consumed, and total GPU-hours. Label gains as transfer on the trained test prompts; this protocol cannot establish held-out generalization.

🤖 Final results: SFT vs rejection-sampled SFT vs on-policy distillation for transferring the CruxEval expert back into B

TL;DR. All three arms recover most or all of the expert's CruxEval gain. Every arm trains on prompts drawn from the same 1,600 the evaluator scores (800 input-prediction and 800 output-prediction problems; plain SFT and OPD use all 1,600, RS-SFT the 1,503 with an execution-correct E sample), so this is transfer on seen prompts. Two-pass means on the selected checkpoints: plain SFT 73.9 / 72.0 (400 updates), RS-SFT 80.8 / 77.9 (283 updates), OPD 79.6 / 75.2 (75 updates); the expert E scores 79.4 / 71.4 and B scores 55.4 / 57.8 (CruxEval input / output, pass@1 on 800 problems each). RS-SFT's two-pass means are 1.2 / 2.7 pp above OPD's; two passes on one run per arm do not resolve that ordering. Both are above plain SFT by 5.7–6.9 pp on input and 3.2–5.9 pp on output. Training cost: OPD 287 H100-h from allocation to the selected checkpoint (376 for the full 4-epoch run); plain SFT 62 and RS-SFT 57 for their full 4-epoch runs (the RS candidate is update 283 of 376 and was not timed separately). RS-SFT also used ground-truth execution results to pick its demos, which the other arms did not have. No arm dropped below B on GSM8K (B 90.4) or MATH500 (B 89.8); OPD 75 scores 90.4 on MATH500, 1.8 below E, inside MATH500's binomial 95% half-width of about 2.6 pp at n=500. These numbers do not measure generalization to unseen prompts.

Setup (the design doc is linked from the issue body).

- Student B: [`open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92` @ `fdc3c3c5`](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92/tree/fdc3c3c5fff489d3fb04dcbc2387c179b1bf3fab).
- Expert E: B after full SFT on 1,454 [GLM 5.3](https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-5.3) CruxEval traces, LR 1e-5, 3 epochs, step 272 (35.9 H100-h); export [open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Expert-E-Step272 @ fb4f8051](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-CruxEval-Expert-E-Step272/tree/fb4f8051a344fec59f902bdd2ca876ac1b2f3296) (S3 source `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/task133-cruxeval/checkpoints/karan/cruxeval-step92-lr1e-05/2026.10.07.5/hf/step-272`). E+ (E + 2 epochs at 1e-6, 80.2 / 75.1) is a reference only.
- Evaluator: Evalchemy [ae362881](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/commit/ae362881cf53f869a6ad52c8a59fa17343c0b5f8) (corrected 2026-10-13: the revision that actually ran is `ae362881cf53f869a6ad52c8a59fa17343c0b5f8`, recorded in every record's `eval_runtime` field; `c131e5ab` was the code constant in `eval_policy.py`, which the launcher did not use. The scorer and sampling settings are the ones at ae362881 throughout, so no number changes.), vLLM H100x8, 32,768 context, 30,720 generation cap, thinking enabled, unseeded sampling at vLLM's default temperature 1.0 (the lm-eval chat client sends no sampling parameters). One pass has a binomial 95% half-width of about 3.5 pp at n=800 (p≈0.55) and 3.0 pp at p≈0.75. Paired deltas use a problem-resampling bootstrap conditional on the sampled completions. Gist of all evaluator configs: https://gist.github.com/karansag/49de943771b98a7a23d9348b58933f71.
- Matched AdamW hyperparameters across arms, in different implementations (Levanter for the SFT arms, Megatron for OPD): LR 1e-6 constant, betas 0.9/0.999, weight decay 0, grad clip 1.0, router bias frozen (E froze it too; all exports verified to carry B's 26 router-bias tensors).
- Plain SFT: B + 4 epochs on E's first sample per prompt (1,600 rows, unfiltered), batch 16, 32 H100. 1,452,363 supervised tokens per epoch.
- RS-SFT: all 12,800 E samples (k=8) execution-graded in an isolated container; first correct sample per prompt kept. 1,503 of 1,600 prompts covered (774 input / 729 output); the 97 uncovered prompts stay in the eval denominator. 4 epochs, 376 updates. 1,056,479 supervised tokens per epoch.
- OPD: MarinSkyRL, B samples 4 rollouts per prompt at temperature 1.0, E scores them (sampled reverse KL on the chosen tokens, coefficient 1.0, reward replaced by the distillation signal, no verifier). 64 prompts per update, 25 updates per epoch, 4 epochs. 4 learner nodes (PP2 × EP8) + 1 rollout node + 1 teacher node, all H100x8.
- Selection procedure used (the rule 'prefer the final checkpoint when similar or better on both directions' was agreed before the final checkpoints were scored; the operational reading of similar as 'paired 95% CI includes 0' was fixed while applying it): if the final checkpoint is similar or better than the previous one on both CruxEval directions on the first pass, select it; otherwise run a second pass on both checkpoints and choose on the two-pass means. GSM8K and MATH500 run on the selected checkpoint and on any terminal checkpoint that lost the selection.

Results. CruxEval pass@1 (%), input / output. "Gap closed" is the gain over B divided by E's two-pass gain over B (24.06 pp input, 13.63 pp output). GSM8K (flexible-extract, 0-shot) and MATH500 are single pass for every model.

| Model | Input | Output | Gap closed | GSM8K | MATH500 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| B | 55.4 | 57.8 | 0 | 90.4 | 89.8 |
| E (CruxEval 2-pass mean) | 79.4 | 71.4 | 100% | 92.1 | 92.2 |
| GLM 5.3 (teacher of E) | 94.0 | 90.5 | — | — | — |
| Plain SFT, 400 updates (2-pass mean) | 73.9 | 72.0 | 77% / 104% | 94.0 | 92.6 |
| RS-SFT, 283 updates (epoch 3) (2-pass mean) | 80.8 | 77.9 | 106% / 148% | 93.5 | 93.6 |
| OPD, 75 updates (epoch 3) (2-pass mean) | 79.6 | 75.2 | 101% / 128% | 92.5 | 90.4 |

Learning curves (single pass per checkpoint; the training trajectory, not the selection basis):

| Arm | Epoch 1 | Epoch 2 | Epoch 3 | Epoch 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Plain SFT (101/201/301/400 updates) | 69.6 / 67.5 | 73.5 / 69.9 | 69.4 / 71.8 | 74.8 / 71.3 |
| RS-SFT (95/189/283/376 updates) | 75.5 / 72.0 | 82.0 / 75.8 | 81.4 / 77.1 | 77.0 / 76.5 |
| OPD (25/50/75/100 updates) | 74.9 / 68.9 | 81.8 / 75.8 | 79.0 / 76.8 | 80.9 / 72.3 |

Selection. Plain SFT's final checkpoint was similar or better than its epoch-3 checkpoint on both directions (+5.4 / −0.5 pp), so it was selected and repeated (second pass 73.1 / 72.8). RS-SFT's final checkpoint was 4.4 pp below epoch 3 on input, and OPD's final checkpoint was 4.5 pp below epoch 3 on output, each with a paired CI excluding 0. Both arms got a second pass on their last two checkpoints. RS-SFT: 376 updates 76.1 / 76.2 against 283 updates 80.8 / 77.9 (two-pass means); the final is lower on both directions, so 283 was selected. OPD: 100 updates 79.875 / 72.0 against 75 updates 79.625 / 75.19; input differs by 0.25 pp and the final is 3.19 pp lower on output, so 75 was selected. The terminal checkpoints are reported in the curve table, not as the method result. The second passes reuse the same runs, so the four pass pairings per arm are one comparison, not four. Same-checkpoint pass pairs moved by up to 3.1 pp (OPD 75 output: 76.75 on pass 1, 73.6 on pass 2, paired CI [−6.0, −0.25]), so the conditional problem-bootstrap intervals do not capture all generation variability; two repeats are too few to estimate it. The final-checkpoint drops are therefore suggestive, not established.

Paired comparisons at the selected checkpoints (pass 1 vs pass 1; 95% bootstrap CI): RS-SFT 283 vs OPD 75: +2.4 [−1.0, +5.8] input / +0.4 [−2.5, +3.3] output on pass 1, and 0.0 [−3.4, +3.3] / +5.0 [+2.0, +8.0] on pass 2. RS-SFT 283 vs plain 400: +6.6 [+3.1, +10.1] / +5.9 [+2.8, +9.3] (pass 2: +7.1 / +5.9). OPD 75 vs plain 400: +4.3 [+0.9, +7.9] / +5.5 [+2.3, +8.8] (pass 2: +7.1 / +0.9 [−2.3, +4.0]). Against E (pass 1): RS-SFT 283 +2.0 [−1.5, +5.5] / +6.9 [+3.8, +10.1]; OPD 75 −0.4 [−3.8, +3.0] / +6.5 [+3.5, +9.5]; plain 400 −4.6 [−8.4, −1.0] / +1.0 [−2.4, +4.5]. Pass-1 and pass-2 pairings share the training runs; they are two draws of the evaluator, not two experiments.

Response shape: B leaves no final answer after the thinking block in 1,110 of 1,600 CruxEval responses; E in about 90. The same count was not made for the three arms, so part of each arm's gain may be this shape change. The 97 prompts with no execution-correct E sample among 8 (26 input, 71 output) score low for every model. Correct/n on pass 1 and pass 2: B 1/26, 1/71; E 2/26, 1/71 and 1/26, 4/71; plain 400 0/26, 3/71 and 0/26, 4/71; RS-SFT 283 4/26, 8/71 and 4/26, 9/71; OPD 75 3/26, 6/71 and 2/26, 2/71. The slice was selected by E failing all 8 samples on these prompts, so E's low score is selection-induced. RS-SFT saw no demos for these prompts. Comparing different methods on 97 selected prompts does not identify the effect of omitting them, so these are counts only.

Cost (H100-hours, Iris task-runtime accounting). Training figures are full-run costs for 4 epochs and include in-gang startup, native saves and exports; they exclude CPU preprocessing, demo generation and evals. The selected RS-SFT checkpoint is update 283 of 376 and the selected OPD checkpoint is update 75 of 100; costs are not pro-rated to the candidate. OPD's allocation-to-checkpoint figure comes from the run's log timestamps and ends at the checkpoint request, so it excludes the native save; plain SFT's 61.6 runs through its final HF export and job teardown. The two selected-cost endpoints are therefore not identical.

| Arm | Training (full 4-epoch run) | Demo generation | Exports | Allocation to selected checkpoint |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| E (expert) | 35.9 for 3 epochs (+15.3 in aborted attempts) | GLM traces via relay, no GPU-h on our side | in-gang | — |
| Plain SFT | 61.6 | shares the one k=8 E collection (14.6 measured once for all 12,800 demos, plus a 0.7 pilot; plain used 1 of the 8 samples, and no standalone 1-sample generation run was timed) | in-gang | 61.6 (final checkpoint selected) |
| RS-SFT | 57.4 | the same k=8 E collection (14.6, counted once for both SFT arms) + CPU execution grading | in-gang | full run 57.4; update 283 was not timed separately |
| OPD | 376.4 (6 nodes × 7h50m) | none (on-policy) | 58.8 (4 export-only jobs, 14–15 each) | 286.9 from allocation start to the update-75 checkpoint request (before the native save completes), plus its 14.2 export job |

OPD also spent 73.5 H100-h on smoke tests, debugging and the export path and 4.6 on a startup failure (missing W&B key) before the full run. These training-only figures are not the experiment total; the ledger adds evaluation (about 3.3 per CruxEval pass), failed-eval overhead, E and E+ training, and the reference runs. OPD per-update wall time was 4–5 min (256 sampled responses, 30,720-token cap) against about 17 s per SFT update; one prompt epoch is 4 rollouts per prompt for OPD and 1 demo for SFT, so epochs are matched on prompts, not on tokens or compute. One CruxEval pass costs about 3.3 H100-h; the ledger lists every eval run. Failed eval groups (serve preemption with a stale endpoint in the eval runner, and one preflight disconnect; see below) cost about 11 H100-h.

Confidence. The gains over B are large relative to noise (the lower 95% bound of every arm's paired gain over B is at least 9.8 pp). Between arms, the measured two-pass means put RS-SFT 1.2 / 2.7 pp above OPD and both 3–7 pp above plain SFT; each arm is one training run with no LR sweep, same-checkpoint pass pairs moved 0.5–3.1 pp on the six repeated checkpoints, and two repeats do not estimate run-to-run variance, so the RS-SFT vs OPD ordering is unresolved and the gap to plain SFT is the better-supported difference. The last-checkpoint drops in RS-SFT (input) and OPD (output) are each supported by two passes but one training run; see the selection paragraph for the statistical limits.

Deviations from the plan in the issue body.

- Plain SFT used one sample per prompt (E's sample 0, 1,600 rows), and RS-SFT used the first execution-correct sample per prompt (1,503 rows), instead of up to 4 samples per prompt. Uncovered prompts stayed in the eval denominator.
- No LR or epoch sweep was run for any arm; every arm used LR 1e-6 and 4 epochs, with per-epoch checkpoints as the only sweep.
- OPD used 4 rollouts per prompt, so its prompt epochs are not token- or compute-matched to the SFT arms.
- GSM8K and MATH500 are both reported as collapse checks (the plan named GSM8K only).

Material failures and fixes.

- Levanter could not HF-export from an S3 reference checkpoint; fixed by plumbing `hf_save_reference_code=False`.
- MarinSkyRL accepted teachers only as HF repo ids; added staging of the teacher from S3. The export-only job's config inherited the run's distillation objective, which requires a teacher the export job does not start, so the export failed at config validation; the fix drops the distillation block from the export config. Learner nodes ran out of host memory at checkpoint save with 512 GB; the full run reserved 1024 GB.
- MarinSkyRL does not convert checkpoints to HF format during training; it writes a small export request per checkpoint, and the conversion is a separate 4-node export-only job (about 14–15 H100-h each).
- The Marin eval runner keeps the serve address it first resolved. When the serve job is preempted and re-registers on another host, the eval loops on connection errors until its timeout. Two RS eval groups were lost this way and relaunched as fresh groups; no partial outputs were reused. Not fixed yet.
- Evalchemy sends no temperature or seed, so every run samples at vLLM's default. One GSM8K run failed Evalchemy's preflight request 9 s after the serve registered (server disconnected); relaunched alone, it passed.
- GPQA-D (41.9%, needs an HF token and a 28,672-token generation cap) and MMLU-Pro (44.1%) were measured on B while choosing the benchmark, as fallbacks in case CruxEval failed the teacher gate; they were not used further.

## Weight deltas against the student

A reader asked what the weight changes behind these transfers look like. Table and method below; numbers are percentages.

| Model (vs student B) | ‖Δ‖/‖B‖ all, % | attention % | expert MLPs % | shared expert % | router % | LM head % | weights changed, % | cos(Δ, Δ_expert) all | attention | expert MLPs | LM head |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Expert E (CruxEval SFT, LR 1e-5, 3 ep) | 0.036 | 0.65 | 0.047 | 0.069 | 0.17 | 0.13 | 13.7 | — | — | — | — |
| Plain SFT step 399 | 0.123 | 0.30 | 0.27 | 0.31 | 0.022 | 0.41 | 41.2 | 0.05 | 0.08 | 0.05 | 0.68 |
| RS-SFT step 282 | 0.094 | 0.24 | 0.21 | 0.25 | 0.015 | 0.34 | 34.5 | 0.06 | 0.09 | 0.07 | 0.71 |
| OPD update 75 | 0.035 | 0.12 | 0.077 | 0.12 | 0.006 | 0.060 | 20.3 | 0.08 | 0.12 | 0.12 | −0.32 |

Reading:
- Everything is a small perturbation: no checkpoint moves more than 0.13% of B's weight norm overall, and the largest component change is the expert's attention at 0.65%.
- The expert (LR 1e-5, 3 epochs, 1,454 rows) concentrates its change in attention, the router and the LM head and leaves the MoE expert MLPs almost untouched (0.047%, 13% of weights changed). The two SFT transfer arms (LR 1e-6, 4 epochs, 1,500–1,600 rows of the expert's text) do the opposite: they move the expert MLPs 4–6× more than the expert did and touch 35–41% of all weights. OPD moves least of the three arms (0.035% overall, comparable to the expert) and touches 20%.
- Direction: none of the arms re-creates the expert's weight change. The cosines between an arm's delta and E's delta are 0.05–0.12 in attention and the expert MLPs (random directions in this dimension give ≈0). The one shared direction is the LM head, where plain SFT and RS-SFT align with E (cosine 0.68 and 0.71) while OPD moves the LM head the opposite way (−0.32). Recovering the expert's CruxEval score therefore does not require copying its weights; three different weight changes produce it.
- RS-SFT changes the weights less than plain SFT (0.094% vs 0.123% overall) while scoring higher; it trains on fewer, verifier-correct rows.

Method: every tensor of each checkpoint was compared with the student B (open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-10T-Mixed-RLVR-Sync-Step92 @ fdc3c3c5) in float32 after widening the bf16 exports; ‖Δ‖/‖B‖ is the relative Frobenius norm over all 67.1 B weights or over one component (attention q/k/v/o and attention gates; the 26 layers' fused MoE expert MLPs, 65.4 B weights; shared experts; router weights and biases; embeddings; LM head), 'weights changed' is the share of scalars whose bf16 value differs from B's, and cos(Δ, Δ_expert) is the cosine between the checkpoint's delta and the expert's delta over the same weights. Embeddings and norms are omitted from the table (relative change ≤ 0.01% everywhere). Caveat: the exports are bf16, so training-time changes below half a bf16 ulp of a weight are invisible; magnitudes and 'weights changed' are lower bounds, and the cosines are computed only on what survived rounding. Script `experiments/tutorials/weight_delta_stats.py` (eval worktree); per-tensor results at `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/scratch/karan/mopd2/review/wdelta-<model>.json`, all summaries in `wdelta-all-summaries.json`.

From a task interference standpoint, this seems like it would favor OPD; smaller magnitude changes, much closer frobenius norm to the original expert update, and fewer weights changed overall -- despite that it gets roughly comparable skill transfer.

@karansag

> much closer frobenius norm to the original expert update

Yes, but the direction seems almost orthogonal (0.08 here, 0.05 in  #9984 )? So it doesn't seem like it's making a "similar" update in that sense. 

The simple retained tasks we used here (GSM8K, Math500, and GPQA in #9984 ) didn't show much regression, though. Small drop in IFEval-Instruct on #9984.  SFT w/rejection sampling showed what seems like a significant improvement in GPQA-D, actually. 

If there are known typical examples of interference, we could test on that, but maybe it's fine so long as we watch retained task performance?

topics.title: [evaluation] Resume brokered evals and expose serving status
topics.body:
Await inference responses asynchronously so waiting requests do not consume AnyIO’s 40 worker threads. Expose an HTML status page at `/status` with queue counts, dispatch delay, worker registration, response errors, and proxy timeouts and rejections. Report prompt, output, and total tokens from completed responses, rolling 60-second and lifetime token rates, and the fraction of completed generation responses containing token usage.

Run multiple serving instances behind one broker with `--instances` and bound simultaneous evaluator jobs with `--max-concurrent`. Evaluation serving workers allow 64 concurrent HTTP requests each; proxy capacity is `max(256, 64 * instances)`, including requests already running. GPU evals use a 4,096-token scheduling budget and TPU evals retain 512, with model-level overrides.

Make `launch --run-id` reuse evaluation identities and output archives when only evaluator code, dependencies, endpoints, or concurrency change. Model and scoring-setting changes produce distinct steps. Evalchemy validates model identity and configuration, task, prompt, generation, judge, and saved request inputs; implementation and dependency versions remain provenance.

Read aggregate scores from Evalchemy’s result table, retain evaluator-owned benchmark metadata, and derive rollouts from normalized samples. Retain valid partial aggregates and report dropped requests, requiring at least 90% of attempted documents to have scores when infrastructure errors occur. Missing results, empty aggregates, and inconsistent scored counts still fail validation. Set broker worker, lease, and proxy deadlines 60, 120, and 180 seconds beyond the configured request timeout (30 minutes by default), with a transport retry budget three times that timeout and 40 minutes for serving startup.

Leave Marin’s Evalchemy pin unchanged for the nightly `ops-external-dependencies` updater. Cross-runtime request replay and partial-score production are supplied by [Evalchemy PR #216](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/pull/216); the updater can adopt them after that PR merges. The first pass below used Evalchemy [cf5c040](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/commit/cf5c040b5e7896923713e1b2f4e670f78f6cf8db), and recovery used [cc3ddcf](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/commit/cc3ddcfa85c622ca626b58128ef39af1d00752c8).

Observed Qwen3-8B timings on cw-rno2a with eight one-H100 vLLM workers, eight simultaneous evals, and 64 concurrent requests per evaluator:

| Run | Wall time | Work and outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [First brokered pass](https://iris.oa.dev/job/%2Fpower%2Feval-qwen3-8b-20261016-full-2722ecef) | 2h 42m 24s | Nine evals reused; 20 executed. Ended with 25/29 complete and four partial archives; 160,612 responses matched to pending requests, with no proxy timeouts, rejections, or dropped responses. |
| [Recovery with the same run ID](https://iris.oa.dev/job/%2Fpower%2Feval-qwen3-8b-20261016-full-2f6845c9) | 12m 13s | 25 evals reused; four resumed. All 29 records saved as succeeded. Only 14 generation requests were retried: 13 succeeded, producing 174,063 output tokens; one DROP context-limit request remained unscored (9,535/9,536 scored). |

The first pass’s longest tasks were MMLU-Pro (2h 4m 43s), MMLU (1h 47m 26s), and HellaSwag (1h 14m 52s), running alongside other evals. For a fresh run of all 29 evals with the same model, settings, and eight H100s, allow roughly 3–3.5 hours (24–28 H100-hours) for planning, after capacity is available. This is a planning estimate from the 20-eval pass and the extra work of the nine cached evals; a fresh, complete 29-eval run has not been measured. Cluster queue time and cold package/model downloads can add time. Recovery reused saved requests and retried 14 generations; its 12-minute duration does not measure full-suite throughput.

Incident and recovery details: [brokered Evalchemy timeout incident](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/779).

🤖 Holistic review of b37c75fd8f64008e3c3beea691e33b3c7bf6e26c.

This PR lets one evaluation launch run N candidate serving instances behind a shared request broker, moves Marin onto Evalchemy's FineStore result table (pin now `cf5c040`), and adds a resumable `--run-id` launch plus a `/status` page on the broker proxy. Earlier findings 1 and 2 are resolved. One identity inconsistency remains open, along with three related-PR notes.

**Serving.** Before this PR, the evaluation path always passed one instance, and a brokered launch would have used iris's default `BrokerConfig()` deadlines (180 s worker, 300 s proxy). Now, when `instances > 1` and no broker is given, `inference_config_for_model` (`serving_config.py:251`) derives every deadline from `EVALCHEMY_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 1800`, which `evalchemy/client.py` exports. The worker deadline is that budget plus 60 s, the lease plus 120 s, and the proxy plus 180 s. Each worker allows 64 in-flight requests, and the proxy allows `max(256, 64 * instances)` pending requests. `InferenceProxy.forward_raw_request` is now `async`. It still submits through `anyio.to_thread`, but it waits on the response with `asyncio.wait_for(asyncio.shield(asyncio.wrap_future(future)))` (`proxy.py:249`). A request waiting on inference therefore no longer holds one of AnyIO's 40 worker threads. The new proxy test drives 64 concurrent requests through the ASGI app to cover this. `InferenceBroker.status()` returns a `BrokerStatus` with queue counts, lease counts, response counts, and queue-wait figures. Through the actor handle that `_start_brokered_inference` casts to `InferenceResponseProvider`, `/status` renders that snapshot as escaped HTML.

**Results.** `read_evalchemy_results` (`lm_eval_samples.py:791`) now fails in two cases: a configured task prefix has no `evalchemy_results` row, or a row has `scored=False`. Callers pass the expected prefixes from `eval_task_directory`. `BenchmarkMetadataRef` switches to `extra="allow"`, so evaluator-owned metadata such as source, reducers, and prompt length survives into the record.

**Resume.** Before this PR, a CLI launch drew a fresh `uuid4` run ID for each eval, so a relaunch could not reuse anything. Now `group_id = spec.run_id or _group_id(...)`. Each eval's run ID is `uuid5` over a JSON identity that includes the run ID. On the CLI path, that identity excludes `serve.{max_num_batched_tokens,max_num_seqs,gpu_memory_utilization}`, `source_digest`, and `evalchemy.num_concurrent`. Relaunching with the same `--run-id` and records prefix therefore lets `StepRunner` skip completed evals and reuse the partial FineStore archives. Evalchemy `cf5c040` accepts the changed endpoint and concurrency during partial recovery. `test_launch.py` covers both outcomes through the real CLI: a relaunch with changed concurrency keeps each eval's identity, and a change of model or limit gets new ones.

**Evidence.** At this head, I ran `test_launch.py`, `test_inference_proxy.py`, `test_evaluation.py`, and `test_eval_archive.py` locally: 154 passed. Nothing exercises brokered serving or Evalchemy partial recovery on a cluster. The concurrency arithmetic, the 4,096-token GPU scheduling budget, and the claim that `cf5c040` preserves its model and dependency checks rest on the PR body.

**Findings**

- **3. Related PR (open, unchanged):** #10033 still imports `scored_results` from `marin.evaluation.evalchemy.client` in `tests/evals/test_evalchemy_config.py:25`, and this PR deletes that function. Land this PR first. #10033 should then drop that import and its `test_scored_results_rejects_empty_results_dict`, and assert endpoint-follow behavior against `read_evalchemy_results`'s `scored`/missing-prefix checks.
- **4. Should fix:** `experiments/evaluation/launch.py:338-355` applies the serve and concurrency exclusions only when `spec.cache_key is None`. The `eval_step` pipeline path (`pipeline.py:106` sets `cache_key`) still hashes `evalchemy.num_concurrent` and the serve-tuning fields. Two consequences follow. First, this PR's own default change (`DEFAULT_NUM_CONCURRENT` 16→64, `runner.py:44`) gives every default-concurrency Evalchemy eval under an immutable pipeline version new inner run IDs. A pipeline step that is re-run after this PR merges then repeats inner evals that already completed, and it abandons their partial archives. Second, the stated rule "concurrency changes preserve identity" holds for `launch --run-id` but not for `eval_step`. Fix: define the exclusion sets once as module constants and apply them unconditionally. Then drop the two `if spec.cache_key is None` branches and the `source_digest` asymmetry with them. Add a `cache_key` case to `test_relaunch_changed_request_concurrency_preserves_identity`.
- **5. Related PR:** draft #9718 (`lib/marin/src/marin/inference/proxy.py`) addresses the same 40-thread cap in a different way: it keeps `forward_raw_request` synchronous and runs it under an `anyio.CapacityLimiter(max_pending_requests + 16)`. With this PR's async wait, that limiter has nothing to protect, and its call site no longer exists. Land this PR first. #9718 should then drop its `_FORWARD_LIMITER_HEADROOM`/`_forward_limiter` hunk and keep only its worker `httpx.Limits` change.
- **6. Related PR:** #10169 adds in-step Evalchemy retry after inference preemption around `FineStoreEvalchemyResult` in `evalchemy/runner.py`. This PR restructures the same function into `run_evalchemy` → `read_evalchemy_outcome` (`runner.py:300`). #10169 also rejects resumed archives that contain saved transport failures and tells the operator to delete the archive, while this PR's tutorial (`run-lm-evals.md`, relaunch paragraph) says a `--run-id` relaunch restores those same archives. Land this PR first. #10169 should rebase its retry loop onto `read_evalchemy_outcome` and add its delete-and-retry instruction to the `--run-id` paragraph in the tutorial.

Earlier findings: 1 resolved (`read_evalchemy_results` rejects unscored rows and missing task prefixes; parametrized regression added); 2 resolved (broker deadlines derive from the exported client timeout and exceed it).

topics.title: [post_training] Add a recovery arm to the SFT shootout row builder
topics.body:
Add a recovery arm to the shootout row builder. It inserts masked failed attempts into plain's rows before selected teacher turns, so the student sees a failure and the harness reply before the turn it trains on.

A seed selects 20% of each family's plain rows. Each selected row has one or two injection points, never at the first or last teacher turn, with one to three failed attempts per point. Attempt counts follow Marianna's published mix (`marianna13/grug-sft-mix-v4-40M-think`); failure styles follow v0's format errors.

For TMax (Terminus-2), the failed attempt re-renders the teacher turn as v0 fails: prose first, then broken or missing JSON. The reply uses the error and warning from Terminus-2's parser, vendored from Harbor 016dd78b. For SWE-smith (mini-swe-agent 2.1.0), mini-swe-agent drops replies it cannot parse. By default, an injection therefore consists of one to three consecutive user turns with its fixed "No tool calls found" message. `--recovery-swe-mode with_failed_reply` also inserts the failed reply.

Injected turns and error messages provide context. The builder checks that every injected row trains exactly the tokens in its plain counterpart, so B and the replay cut equal plain's; only context grows. To meet the 32k cap, an oversized injection loses one attempt at a time, then one point at a time. A row that cannot fit one attempt retains its plain rendering and is counted.

`--recovery-handoff`, off by default, also adds conversations 1+ of passing summarized TMax trials while holding B constant by dropping clean TMax rows. Pool v5 has only 74 such rows across all 21 TMax shards, so the option stays off. The manifest's `recovery` block records, per family, rows selected, injected, reduced to fit, and skipped; points, attempts, styles, and harness errors; and context added.

The production recovery arm used the same 43 pool v5 trace files as plain at 0673b18b7d, with handoff off. B is plain's 28,933,580, and the replay rows match plain's. SWE-smith injected 280 of 1,398 rows (20.0%) and added 0.35% context. TMax injected 279 of 1,482 rows (18.8%) and added 2.52% context. Seven TMax rows took a smaller injection, seven could not fit even one attempt, and ten had no eligible turn. `verify_arms` (#10254) passed on this arm: it uses the same trials as plain, every row trains exactly plain's target tokens, and every row not marked injected is byte-identical to plain's.

Stacked on #10253, which adds the row builder. Part of #10213

---
