topics.title: [iris] Capability proxy returns 502 while a preempted serve task is being replaced
topics.body:
When a served model's Iris task is preempted and replaced, the native capability proxy answers requests that arrive during the replacement with HTTP 502 `upstream transport error: client error (Connect)`. Clients see a hard failure for a gap Iris is already recovering from.

Impact: on 2026-10-18 an Evalchemy GSM8K screen on H100 lost 112 of 1,319 rows. Kueue preempted the serve task at 00:14:07 UTC; Iris rescheduled it and the replacement was initializing from 00:14:55. At 00:19 the proxy returned 502 to the queued requests, the client exhausted its retries, and the rows were recorded as `EVALCHEMY_INFRASTRUCTURE_ERROR` (`model_transport`). Recovery needed a manual selective rerun of the 112 doc ids and a cached regrade before the record could be merged (1,215/1,319 after recovery).

A second instance on 2026-10-19 lost 960 of 1,319 GSM8K rows. Kueue preempted the serve task at 03:42:04 UTC. Requests in flight at that moment got 502 `client error (SendRequest)` (15 responses at 03:42). Requests sent afterwards got 502 `client error (Connect)` (985 responses from 03:42 to 03:47) until the client gave up, and the rows were recorded as `EVALCHEMY_INFRASTRUCTURE_ERROR`. The same serve task was preempted six more times over the next 11 hours (attempts 1 to 6) at interactive priority. That record needed a full GSM8K rerun.

The 502 comes from the native proxy's upstream error path ([`lib/iris/rust/src/lib.rs` L1243-L1246](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8e99858a17df0463daac6b104f5eddb0ffa79ffd/lib/iris/rust/src/lib.rs#L1243-L1246)), which maps any connect failure to `BAD_GATEWAY`. [`lib/iris/docs/federation.md`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8e99858a17df0463daac6b104f5eddb0ffa79ffd/lib/iris/docs/federation.md) documents this message as "cannot connect to its upstream".

Reproduce:
1. Serve a model through a capability URL (for example the eval launcher with Harbor or a capability-routed Evalchemy run).
2. Send a steady stream of requests through the capability URL.
3. Preempt or cancel the serving task and let Iris start a replacement under the same endpoint name.
4. Requests sent before the replacement registers return 502 with the message above.

Expected: while the endpoint's job is still live and a replacement task is pending or initializing, the proxy holds the request until the endpoint registers again (bounded by the request timeout), or returns 503 with `Retry-After`. Clients retry connect errors and 503s with backoff for at least the documented serve replacement time. A replacement can take much longer than a request timeout: in the second instance the serve stayed unavailable for the rest of the GSM8K client's retry budget. Holding requests therefore covers short gaps only. Long gaps need the 503 signal so that the client can pause instead of recording failures.

Done when: a serve-replacement test through the capability proxy completes requests sent during the gap, or receives 503 with `Retry-After`, and no 502 is returned while the job is live.

Related: #10237 covers the direct-route client (`remote_inference`) keeping a stale address after rescheduling.

Evidence (Iris task events and the Evalchemy client log, URLs omitted):

```
2026-10-18T00:14:07.473Z attempt 0  k8s/kueue        WorkloadEvictedDueToPreempted  Preempted to accommodate a workload (UID: 3fc9af02-…)
2026-10-18T00:14:50.525Z attempt 0  iris/controller  TaskRetryScheduled             Backend reported PREEMPTED; controller returned the task to PENDING.
2026-10-18T00:14:55.578Z attempt 1  k8s/container    PodInitializing
[00:19:08] eval-gsm8k-0shot-2a8d8acc/0 | API request failed! Status code: 502, Response text: {"error":"upstream transport error: client error (Connect)"}. Retrying...
[00:19:09] eval-gsm8k-0shot-2a8d8acc/0 | API request failed! Status code: 502, Response text: {"error":"upstream transport error: client error (Connect)"}. Retrying...
```

Second instance: serve task `/karan/eval-20261019-025403-task238-arm-recovery-lr1e-06-step791-04d5/inference-177d09d0c73a4f048310e082db087746/0` (Kueue `WorkloadEvictedDueToPreempted` at 03:42:04, 05:19:02, 07:12:39, 10:56:25, 11:04:59, 14:19:01 and 14:24:54 UTC), evaluator task `/karan/eval-20261019-025403-task238-arm-recovery-lr1e-06-step791-04d5/eval-gsm8k-0shot-4ac3cd86/0`, record `20261019-025403-task238-arm-recovery-lr1e-06-step791-gsm8k-0shot-6554` (`infra_failed`, 359/1,319 scored).

First instance: serve task `/karan/eval-20261018-000555-task204-lr1e-06-step1095-1b9b/inference-a54b7942d3b34ffba92e5f0d4192aa69/0`. Evaluator task: `/karan/eval-20261018-000555-task204-lr1e-06-step1095-1b9b/eval-gsm8k-0shot-2a8d8acc/0`. Record: `20261018-000555-task204-lr1e-06-step1095-gsm8k-0shot-77c1`.

comments.body:
🤖
# Research

Iris keeps a serving endpoint's last address until its lease expires (at most 10 minutes). The native proxy can therefore route a request to a preempted task; its upstream transport error path returns 502. Once the lease expires, the registry omits the endpoint and the same live job can instead return 404. The registry has no replacement state, so changing 502 to 503 alone would leave that later gap unresolved. [PR #10033](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10033) handles Evalchemy's direct-route relay and does not change this capability path.

**Relevant code**
- [`endpoint_service.py#L40-L49`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/endpoint_service.py#L40-L49) — ten-minute registration lease.
- [`endpoint_service.py#L165-L177`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/endpoint_service.py#L165-L177) — live mappings enter the proxy snapshot.
- [`lib.rs#L230-L264`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/iris/rust/src/lib.rs#L230-L264) — expired mappings are skipped.
- [`lib.rs#L1190-L1240`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/iris/rust/src/lib.rs#L1190-L1240) — transport failures become 502.
- [`client.py#L79-L93`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evalchemy/client.py#L79-L93) — Evalchemy allows eight request retries.

# Proposed Fix

The failure chain is task preemption → old endpoint address remains routable → connect/send fails → proxy returns 502; after lease expiry, lookup returns 404. This needs a controller/proxy availability contract and a capability-client retry budget, so it is larger than a local status-code patch.

1. Preserve an authenticated endpoint name while its owning task is being retried. Publish `ready` versus `replacing` in the controller's proxy snapshot/deltas; preemption and lease expiry make the old address unavailable, replacement registration restores `ready`, and terminal job/task state removes the route. Reconstruct the same state after controller restart.
2. Return 503 with `Retry-After` for `replacing` and for connect/send failures to task-owned endpoints, including a race before the registry update. Keep ordinary 404 for unknown names and 502 for unrelated upstream/protocol failures. Do not replay an in-flight POST inside the proxy.
3. Verify the pinned Evalchemy and Harbor capability clients retry 503 according to `Retry-After` with a time budget tied to the evaluation deadline and stop on terminal serve state. Extend their policy where needed; leave the direct-route relay in #10033 alone.
4. Add a real HTTP capability-proxy test that sends requests before preemption, during replacement, after the old lease expires, and after a new address registers. Assert no 502/404 during the recoverable gap, 503 plus `Retry-After` until recovery, successful forwarding afterwards, and terminal/unknown routes ending promptly. Cover an in-flight send failure and the federated capability relay as separate cases.

Open decision: the repository documents a 10-minute endpoint lease but no upper bound on serve replacement. Use the evaluation's overall deadline as the retry cap unless a shorter serve-replacement contract is established; eight immediate request retries are insufficient for the observed multi-minute gaps.

topics.title: [hero] Sample vibe-check completions at temperature 0.7 from step 270k
topics.body:
Raise the hero checkpoint completion sampling temperature from 0.2 to 0.7 and
bump the sampler release to hero-native-v6-temperature-0.7, so the report labels
and sorts the new samples separately from earlier results.

0.2 was giving overly repetitive responses. A one-off sample at 1.0 on step 270k
(release hero-native-v5-temperature-1) was tried first; 0.7 sits between the two.

A spec change re-identifies every sample request, so discovery now skips
checkpoints before FIRST_SAMPLED_STEP (270k) instead of backfilling the full
lineage. Earlier releases keep their results in the report.

topics.title: Automated eval system
topics.body:
# Requirements  
1. For a given checkpoint, run our complete list of evals (or a specified subset) on it
2. Publish the results on the eval leaderboard (from a single-source-of-truth database) (tracked here: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6043) 
3. This should work for our own models and others (see https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/4827) 
4. There should be a defined path (and agent skill) for adding more evals + the set of evals should be visible on the leaderboard

This should work for our own models and others that we support inference on (e.g. on vLLM). 

# Definition of done
New checkpoint trigger (TBD below how) → configured eval subset runs via the OpenAI-HTTP contract (#4827) → results land in the DB → appear on the leaderboard (#6043), with zero manual steps.

# Decisions to make
- **TPU vs GPU, or both** Should we start with TPUs, or focus on having this run on GPUs? (Do we need to make this decision?) Our default path is both (#6041 and #6042).
- **Trigger definition**: Do we want this to run on all model checkpoints as they land (where?) How do we want the system to determine which specific checkpoints to automatically run on?


# Related issues

- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6041

### What #7405 delivered vs. what remains in #6503

#7405 (merged, closed #7345) built the **eval execution + reporting engine**. Mapping it against this issue's requirements:

| # | Requirement | Status | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|

| 3 | Works for our models **and** others via vLLM/OpenAI-HTTP (#4827) | ✅ Done | Demonstrated on snowball + 5 HF models; serves over the OpenAI-compatible contract; TPU (v5e→v6e→v5p sizing) and GPU (CoreWeave). |
| 4 | Defined path + **agent skill** for adding evals; evals visible on leaderboard | 🟡 Partial | README "Adding a model or eval" documents the path (`EvalSuiteConfig`→`EVALS`, `EvalModelConfig`→`MODELS`); evals are visible as dashboard columns. **No agent skill exists** (only `evaluate-zephyr-perf`, unrelated). |

### Remaining work

**1. Automated checkpoint trigger — the core gap (blocks the Definition of Done).**
The DoD is *"New checkpoint trigger → eval subset runs → results in DB → leaderboard, with zero manual steps."* #7405 provides only **manual** entry points: the `launch` CLI and a `pipeline.py` `eval_step` `ArtifactStep`. There is no code that watches for new checkpoints and auto-launches evals — no watcher/webhook/poller in `experiments/evaluation/`. This is the "Automated" in "Automated eval system" and is still entirely open. It also subsumes the open **"Trigger definition"** decision in the issue: *which* checkpoints auto-run, and *where* the trigger lives (checkpoint-export step hook, GCS-landing poll, WandB/registry event, cron sweep, etc.). The `eval_step` ArtifactStep is the natural building block — remaining work is wiring it to fire automatically.

**2. Leaderboard reconciliation (#6043).**
Evaldash exists and reads the SSOT records, but the issue asks for results on *the leaderboard* (#6043). Need to confirm whether evaldash **is** that leaderboard or whether records/DB still need to feed the #6043 surface. Likely a scope/ownership question rather than net-new plumbing.

**3. Agent skill for adding evals (requirement #4).**
Requirement #4 explicitly asks for a defined path **and an agent skill**. The README path exists; the skill does not. A `.agents/skills/add-eval/` playbook (mirroring `add-dataset`) would close this.

**4. Decision now resolved by #7405: TPU vs GPU.**
The issue flagged "TPU vs GPU, or both" as undecided — #7405 does **both** (TPU sizing heuristic + CoreWeave GPU shapes), so this decision can be marked resolved.

### Summary
#7405 nails requirements **1** and **3** and most of **2/4** (execution, multi-backend serving, durable SSOT records, a dashboard, a documented add-eval path). What remains for "Automated eval system" to be done:
- **the automatic checkpoint trigger** (biggest item; also resolves the open "Trigger definition" decision),
- **reconcile evaldash with the #6043 leaderboard**, and
- **add the `add-eval` agent skill**.

This matches @rjpower's "partly fixed in #7405" — the manual pipeline is there; the automation and leaderboard-integration layers are not yet.

topics.title: [tpu-inference] Qwen3.5 hybrid GDN prefill ~10x slower than pure attention on v6e
topics.body:
Serving Qwen3.5-9B (hybrid GDN attention, `Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration`) on v6e-8 at fork main (`e8809d49`), prefill runs at ~6-7k prompt tokens/s through the `chunked_jax_pd` kernel — roughly 10x slower than Qwen3-8B's pure-attention prefill on the same slice. The engine sits at ~2 running requests with KV cache 0.1% used, so the batch is kernel-compute-bound, not budget- or memory-bound; raising `max_num_batched_tokens` 512 -> 2048 changed neither throughput nor concurrency.

Observed impact: a full 5-shot MMLU (56k echo+prompt-logprobs requests) takes ~3.2h for Qwen3.5-9B vs ~3-10 minutes for Qwen3-8B on identical hardware and pins. Decode throughput looks unremarkable; the gap is prefill.

Repro: serve `Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B` on v6e-8 (defaults, tensor_parallel per the sizing heuristic), then drive prompt-heavy traffic, e.g. lm-eval `local-completions` MMLU with `echo=True` + prompt logprobs at concurrency 16. Watch prefill tokens/s in the engine stats.

Marin-side context: marin-community/marin#7345 (eval system) — the Qwen3.5-9B column of the eval grid pays this cost on every MMLU-class run.

comments.body:
🤖 ## Research

Actionable — clear repro, named kernel, expected vs actual, and good reporter diagnosis (compute-bound: ~2 running reqs, KV 0.1%, insensitive to `max_num_batched_tokens`).

But the slow code is **not in this repo**. The `chunked_jax_pd` TPU Pallas GDN-prefill kernel and `Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration` live in the `marin-community/tpu-inference` fork; Marin only pins its SHA. No Marin-side config change fixes a 10x kernel-compute gap, so this is a fork-side kernel investigation rather than a Marin PR.

**Relevant code (Marin side — knobs, none of which are the fix)**
- [`pyproject.toml#L182-L183`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/pyproject.toml#L182-L183) — pins fork `rev 734d2842` (reporter served fork main `e8809d4` — tip skew).
- [`serving_backend.py#L150-L152`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/inference/serving_backend.py#L150-L152) — `max_num_batched_tokens=512`; reporter's 512→2048 no-op is consistent with compute-bound.
- [`vllm_server.py#L119-L123`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/inference/vllm_server.py#L119-L123) / [`serve_and_eval.py#L116-L119`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/evals/evalchemy/serve_and_eval.py#L116-L119) — `--gdn-prefill-backend triton` is **GPU-only** (FlashInfer-vs-triton); the TPU path goes through `chunked_jax_pd` and this flag does not touch it.
- [`quick_serve.py#L114-L154`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/inference/quick_serve.py#L114-L154) — TP-size heuristic; not the bottleneck (batch is compute-bound, not sharded-comm-bound).

## Proposed approach (fork-side, human review before implementation)

Root cause is in the fork's TPU GDN chunked prefill kernel. The signature — 10x vs pure attention, compute-bound, flat under batch-size changes — points at the gated delta-rule chunk recurrence in `chunked_jax_pd` being poorly tiled on v6e: likely a small chunk length serializing the intra/inter-chunk scan, or the GDN state-update matmuls not saturating the MXU (vs. Qwen3-8B attention which does).

Next steps:
1. TPU-profile `chunked_jax_pd` on a Qwen3.5-9B prefill in `marin-community/tpu-inference` (fork main); capture chunk length, MXU utilization, and scan structure.
2. Fix (chunk-tiling / MXU packing / chunk-parallel form) lands in the **fork**, then a Marin pin bump via `.agents/skills/refresh-tpu-vllm-forks/`.

Not opening a Marin PR — the fix is out-of-repo and kernel-scoped. Suggest routing to the tpu-inference kernel owner and tracking against #7345.

topics.title: [iris] Follow re-registered serve endpoints from Evalchemy evals
topics.body:
## tl;dr

While doing evals for another experiment ( https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9984), agent found that serve endpoints that got pre-empted permanently lost their connection. This should fix that.


## Full Explanation (agent)
Evalchemy children now reach their serve through a loopback relay that looks
the endpoint name up in the Iris registry, instead of a host:port resolved once
at launch. When Kueue preempts the serve and its retry registers on another
host, the old address refuses connections, hangs, or answers 404. The eval used
to retry that address until the group timed out: nine groups on cw-rno2a were
lost this way on 2026-10-09/10, some after 16-20 h.

The relay (iris.cluster.client.endpoint_relay) looks the name up every 30 s and
after each connection failure or 404. It aborts requests still waiting on a
replaced address and replays requests that have no response yet once the
endpoint is registered again (for up to 1 h, then 503). A response that has
started is never replayed; the relay drops the client connection so lm-eval's
own retries apply. Each relay thread keeps a pooled direct connection, so evals
keep the direct routing that #9480 chose over the hub proxy.

The fix sits in an Iris client module so any in-cluster client can use it. A
stable cluster-level address (a per-endpoint Kubernetes Service, or
controller-side forwarding) would cover every client without a helper process,
but it needs a controller deploy and work in each backend. The hub proxy
already follows re-registrations, and it is the path #9480 moved away from. The
relay ships in the job bundle and takes effect on the next eval launch.

While the Evalchemy job runs, the parent now reads the serve job states every
60 s. When one is terminal, it cancels the Evalchemy job and the record becomes
infra_failed with the serve job ID and state. A failed status read does not end
the eval. Before, the parent waited with no bound.

Tests drive the relay with real HTTP servers and a fake registry whose endpoint
moves mid-run. On a local in-process Iris cluster, the relay CLI in a client
task followed a serve job that was cancelled and replaced under the same
endpoint name; the request in flight during the gap waited about 4 s and was
answered by the replacement. A [CoreWeave smoke test](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10033#issuecomment-6136856836)
also passed task-token registry lookup and failover to a replacement port through
the `$IRIS_VENV` relay subprocess. Both serve tasks ran on the same node, and
the helper ran in a plain Iris task. Cross-host relocation and the actual
Evalchemy child's isolated uvx environment remain untested by that smoke.

Fixes #10030
topics.head: a70c24c5cfc497c7e840ef5f6ad068c64ca6c300

comments.body:
🤖 CoreWeave smoke at 38bcc8b65a (cw-us-east-08a, CPU only, job `/karan/smoke-relay-10033-d`): passed.

A coordinator task started a fake serve job that registered `/serve/smoke-relay-<id>`, then opened the relay through the Evalchemy child's `endpoint_relay()` helper, which launches `$IRIS_VENV/bin/python -m iris.cluster.client.endpoint_relay`. The relay's registry lookup used the task token. It then cancelled the serve, waited until the old address stopped answering, started a replacement under the same name, and sent a request through the relay.

```
02:23:33 relay up; request 1 answered by first (http://10.186.213.131:10241)
02:24:03 relay: Endpoint moved: http://10.186.213.131:10241 -> None   (periodic refresh)
02:24:07 old address is down; request 2 sent
02:24:20 relay: Endpoint moved: None -> http://10.186.213.131:10243
02:24:20 request 2 answered by second after 13s
```

Limits: both serve tasks landed on the same node, so the move changed only the port, not the host. The relay ran in a plain Iris task, not under the uvx environment of a real Evalchemy child; the helper and `$IRIS_VENV` are the same. Earlier runs showed a cancelled serve pod keeps answering for about 30 s while Kubernetes stops it; the relay correctly kept using it while it answered.

🤖 Addressed the review follow-ups in 10755536e0 and a70c24c5cf: shared monotonic timing, bounded recovery waits, explicit request-body naming/order, and Python-first relay documentation. The Evalchemy entry point now selects the Iris interpreter and passes it explicitly to the helper.

Kept `_in_flight` cancellation: the relay and lm-eval both allow 1800-second responses, so relying only on timeout retries can leave a request blocked for 30 minutes after its endpoint has moved. The regressions for a stalled pre-header request and a stalled response body still pass; started responses are closed, never replayed. Kept the resolver/server structure and the focused 404 policy rather than expanding this fix into a proxy redesign or replaying arbitrary HTTP errors.

The six findings from the required lint-catalog review were addressed: log socket-shutdown errors during cleanup; move interpreter selection to the entry point; replace implementation narration with a boundary comment; remove three assertions tied to human-readable messages. Serve-failure tests now also check structured stage/job fields.

`./infra/pre-commit.py --changed-files --fix` passes, including pyrefly. The affected safe-test runner passes all 168 tests. The PR body now records the successful CoreWeave smoke and retains its actual limits: same-node replacement and no real Evalchemy uvx-child execution. No additional cluster run was performed.

topics.title: [grug] Add GB200 launch and H100 validation support
topics.body:
Stack the GB200 launcher, checkpoint/data support and H100 validation runner on the pipeline foundation in #9279 for the model recipe from main `89ac0d770506f7e27ca217760ec5ca3246694e7e`. The launcher uses FP32 parameters, BF16 compute, compute-scaled MuonH, SM100 ragged transport and Flash Attention. Executable `0da04acccf7b0842319a8668d71ccc697a7b10ec` completed the corrected eight-GB200 synthetic gate with two full-width layers, PP2/EP4 and sequence length 4096. The two losses were 11.806337356567383 and 0.4912489652633667. All eight native GPU processes, both Iris GPU tasks and the coordinator exited zero. All 48 startup task ABI records had zero input memory-kind mismatches. Both coordinator failure and preemption retry caps were zero; the SDK launch example sets both explicitly because the CLI retry option controls failure retries only. [GB200 setup and standalone commands](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/hero-gb200-pipeline/experiments/grug/moe_hero_pipeline/GB200.md) record prerequisites and acceptance criteria.

The combined H100 runner was validated at `a1e3ab278eeb05bb645db641dd3e7dabedf90dbb` on 16 H100s with two full-width layers, PP2/EP8 and sequence length 4096. Ten synthetic updates had finite losses from 11.804966926574707 to 0.4793720245361328. Twenty fresh Harrier updates consumed 2,621,440 tokens with finite losses from 11.8075590133667 to 7.612007141113281. All 200 raw components remained nonempty with their original mixture weights and order. Both GPU tasks and supervisors exited zero; fresh-data logs retain 15 individual rank exits, while the supervisor's child-reaping contract certifies all 16. Save/restore support is included, but hardware checkpoint validation is limited to the historical reduced-model comparison: a 90,018,826-byte scratch checkpoint and a resumed-versus-uninterrupted loss difference of 9.5367431640625e-7, within unchanged 1e-5 tolerances. These runs used the explicit SM90 pooled-wave/FA4 adapter with SYRK disabled and establish no H100 ragged-transport parity. [H100 reference](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/hero-gb200-pipeline/docs/references/hero-pipeline-h100.md) separates these runs from the historical reduced-model checkpoint comparison.

The runtime pins upstream JAXPP `328f75a80cecf22c7cc030a82d8941d3c1e220b6` plus a tracked host-memory/startup overlay. JAX 0.11.1 overrides JAXPP's declared compatibility cap and remains experimental; CUDA dependencies with lower bounds are recorded per launch. Installer recovery avoids duplicate global reinstall flags, including on deployed older worker wrappers. The [Iris installer incident record](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/600) distinguishes the initiating GitHub fetch failure from the broken recovery command. Shared pipeline configuration, process ownership, array predicates, data scheduling and loader cleanup consolidate the overlapping work from #9279 and #9460.

The combined executable, runtime and test source is identical to the previously published `5c2d91a6e48a43573b7f0b09be7e5f16bfc3eddc` snapshot. topics.title: [grug] Balance attention work across batch shards in hero train step
topics.body:
The hero train step now permutes the rows of each global batch so that each batch shard gets a similar amount of attention work. Document packing gives rows very different attention costs. When rows stay in loader order, the busiest of the 64 shards does 2.10x the mean global-attention work on real 16K hero batches. All other shards wait for that shard at the next collective.

`balance_attention_rows` uses the FA4 segment bounds of each row to count its attended query-key pairs. Padding tokens do not add to this count. The function sorts the rows by this cost. Before the forward pass, it deals the rows to the batch shards in snake order. Even rounds go from the first shard to the last shard, and odd rounds go back. Each shard then keeps its rows in loader order.

Expert capacity drops the later tokens of a shard first. If each shard kept its rows in cost order, the tokens of short-document rows would be dropped first. The permutation adds one all-gather and one reshard of each per-row batch array. Every token still enters the loss and the router statistics. However, the row placement can change which assignments exceed expert capacity, so the loss can also change.

On real batches at 16K, the ratio of busiest-shard work to mean work decreases from 2.10 to 1.17 for global layers and from 1.46 to 1.05 for local layers. At 4K, the ratio decreases from 1.29 to 1.01.

We measured both arms on the same GB200 NVL72 rack, with 106 scored steps per arm. Each arm restored from hero step 240000. At 16K context, the step time decreases from 13.131 to 13.055 s/step (+0.58% tokens/s). At 4K, it decreases from 12.764 to 12.732 s/step (+0.25%). The loss stays within same-code noise of the control. The drop fraction changes by less than 3%.

The companion PR changes the FA4 mask. With both changes on a second rack, the 16K step time decreases from 13.046 to 12.833 s/step (+1.66%). In that stack, balancing alone gives +0.29%, because faster masked attention also makes the imbalance smaller.

All numbers above come from the code before two later fixes. The cost now excludes padding, and each shard now keeps its rows in loader order. We did not measure again after these fixes.

All measurements used one rack. The all-gather sends the whole global batch to each GPU, so its cost increases with the number of racks. We did not measure this cost at the 11-rack hero size.

topics.title: [smallquery] Stand up long-running Ballista Scheduler with baseline warm pool
topics.body:
#### **Context & Goal**
Currently, `smallquery` stands up a transient Ballista scheduler and executor pool on-demand per step, introducing a ~1-minute Kubernetes pod scheduling delay and requiring ad-hoc cluster lifecycle management inside python pipeline steps. 

To provide instant query submission for interactive queries, we want to stand up a persistent, long-running Ballista cluster on Iris with a non-preemptible scheduler and a baseline warm pool of preemptible, low-priority executors.

---

#### **Proposed Architecture**

1. **Non-Preemptible Scheduler (24/7)**:
   * Run a lightweight, non-preemptible Ballista Scheduler task (`cpu=0.5, memory="1Gi"`) on Iris with a stable service endpoint.
   * Running 24/7 incurs negligible cost (~$10/month) while guaranteeing that query DAGs and state are never lost due to node eviction.

2. **Preemptible & Low-Priority Executor Pool with Baseline Warmth**:
   * Maintain a baseline warm pool of **2–5 preemptible (Spot) executor workers** running continuously for instant query execution on small queries.
   * **Low Iris Priority**: Configure baseline warm workers with low Iris job priority so Iris can automatically preempt them to yield cluster capacity whenever higher-priority jobs (e.g., training, ferries) require resources.
   * Support dynamic bursting to **80–100 preemptible workers** when large batch pipeline stages are submitted.
   * Schedulers handle worker evictions mid-query by automatically re-assigning lost task partitions to remaining workers.

3. **Idle Scale-Down**:
   * Burst workers scale back down to the baseline warm pool (2–5 workers) after an idle timeout (e.g., 10–15 minutes of query inactivity).

---

#### **Key Requirements & Implementation Tasks**

* [ ] **Deployment Config**: Add launcher manifest / script to register the long-running Ballista Scheduler on Iris with non-preemptible resource constraints.
* [ ] **Preemptible & Low-Priority Provisioning**: Configure baseline warm executor task specs with preemptible constraints (`max_retries_preemption=10`) and low Iris job priority so Iris can preempt them for higher-priority work.
* [ ] **Baseline & Burst Management**: Update `smallquery.deploy` / client launcher to target the stable scheduler endpoint and scale the executor pool dynamically between baseline warmth and peak stage requirements.
* [ ] **Idle TTL Scaling**: Implement an idle timeout worker reaper that returns the executor pool to baseline size when no queries are active.

topics.title: [grug] Run the production hero with a PGLE latency profile
topics.body:
The hero's step is about 1.5-1.9% shorter with a PGLE (profile-guided latency estimation) profile, and production does not use one yet. The hero schedules with one collective in flight, and XLA's default latency estimator gives every collective the same small latency, so the scheduler treats a multi-millisecond ragged transport as hidden under a single GEMM. A profile built from the program's own trace replaces those estimates with measured costs.

All four runs below are on the same 64-GPU rack (restore step-180000, seed 0, 100 steps); the same code ran 0.8% faster on another rack, so only same-rack comparisons count.

| Program | No profile | Own profile |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stack #9830-#9836 with #9835, plus #9829 | 12.695 s | 12.506 s (+1.51%) |
| The same without #9835 | 12.763 s | 12.522 s (+1.92%) |

With a profile, #9835's hand-placed transport ordering was worth 0.13% (12.506 against 12.522 s), so #9835 was closed and its scheduling left to PGLE. Without a profile it was worth 0.54%, which production gives up until it runs with one.

`experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/pgle_profile.py` (#9831) builds a profile from one XProf trace, and the hero README describes the trace, build and rerun loop. Automatic PGLE (`JAX_ENABLE_PGLE`) cannot profile with one process per GPU. A profile matches instructions by name, so it applies only to the program it was traced from: production needs a profile traced on its own 11-rack mesh, rebuilt after any change to the model, mesh or XLA flags. A stale profile loses the gain without an error.

Done when: the production hero runs with a profile built from its own program, the launcher warns or fails when the profile does not match the compiled program, and the production step-time change is recorded here.

Part of #9636.

comments.body:
🤖 Two ways a profile can break a hero run, both found on one rack while testing the stack (#9830-#9834). A production rollout needs a guard for each.

**1. XLA compile abort (fixed in a candidate plugin, not yet promoted).** With `--xla_gpu_enable_host_memory_offloading` (#9831), rematerialization may offload values to host when its estimate of the step exceeds its budget. One profiled schedule overshot the budget (124.77 GiB against 114.09 GiB inside the layer loop), and remat picked an f32[] operand of an all-reduce whose start was scheduled before the loop and whose done came after it. `GetCostOfHostOffload` counts users reached through the all-reduce's alias; `OffloadInstruction` places the reload before direct users only, found none unplaced, and failed `CHECK(!place_before_list.empty())` at hlo_rematerialization.cc:2118 on every rank. The bug is unchanged on openxla/xla main and has no upstream report.
- Fix: skip candidates whose buffer `has_indirect_uses` in `GetCostOfHostOffload`, as recomputation already does. Branch `marin/remat-offload-indirect-uses` (0f6dc61dee) on marin-community/xla. A plugin built from it on Iris (`0.11.1+marin.0f6dc61dee6d`, 15 minutes) compiles the case that aborted.
- A second branch, `marin/remat-no-offload-strategy` (ff858b5447), also keeps the flag's host accounting but turns the offload strategy off. Its cost model prices host copies at HBM bandwidth. It is built but untested on the rack.

**2. Out of memory at runtime.** With the fix, the same program compiled and then failed to allocate its 143.75 GiB pool on the first step. Remat estimated the profiled schedule about 26 GiB above the unprofiled one. A near-identical program (the shared expert as two custom VJPs instead of one) trained with its own profile at 119.5 GiB peak, so this depends on the schedule. I have not traced which buffers grow.

What this adds to the done criteria: before a long run, a preflight that compiles the profiled program and runs a few steps, with a fallback to no profile when either fails. Both failures appear within minutes of start.

topics.title: [Evaluation] Safety audit: Snowball Smartie vs. Qwen 3.6
topics.body:
## TL;DR

A manual audit of 100 completed head-to-head conversations found no direct unsafe actions by either model. The main risk was unreliable truthfulness: Snowball Smartie showed false-success behavior in 16 cases versus 7 for Qwen, while hallucinations appeared in 13 and 12 cases, respectively. Qwen won 59 reviews, Snowball Smartie won 19, and 22 tied.

## Description

The deterministic sample compares `open-athena/Snowball-Smartie-RL-2026.10.15.32-step14` with `Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B` across 67 chat and 33 ShellSim agentic conversations. The report covers legal, clinical, food-safety, engineering, privacy, data-integrity, and operational failures.

The sample includes only completed conversations, so it has survivorship bias. Its mostly benign prompts and sandboxed agentic tasks provide limited evidence about adversarial safety.

## Status

Complete. The public artifact contains the sample manifest, raw case records, readable transcripts, run configuration, aggregate statistics, and case-level manual annotations. The public release redacts personal and internal identifiers plus one credential-shaped example string; these changes are documented in the dataset card and manifest.

## Links

- [Safety and Alignment Report](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-smartie-vs-qwen36-v3-final4-safety-audit/blob/main/SAFETY_AND_ALIGNMENT_REPORT.md)
- [Public artifact repository](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-smartie-vs-qwen36-v3-final4-safety-audit)
- [Source conversation run](https://applets.marina.oa.dev/a/25f504c6-c6fb-4e14-8401-07dd8e6fbfba?run=smartie-rl-step14-vs-qwen36-20261019-v3-final4)

## Conclusion

Qwen was more reliable overall in this sample. Both models produced plausible factual errors, while Snowball Smartie more often claimed execution or completion without supporting tool evidence. Neither model showed overtly antisocial behavior or attempted credential theft, exfiltration, destructive host commands, targeted harassment, or real-world self-harm assistance.

comments.body:
🤖 ## How the cases were generated and flagged

The safety sample was random. GLM's prior judgments did not affect which cases entered it.

1. **Seed and task synthesis.** For each case, the worker chose a random entry from `allenai/WildChat-1M` at revision `7d6490e462285cf85d91eabea0f9a954fbddcd1f`. GLM-5.3 used at most 6,000 characters as loose inspiration and was told to transform the source without copying personal details. The scheduler cycled through 11 capability categories and alternated chat and agentic modes. An operator-supplied idea from the app queue could override the focus or mode. GLM then produced the opening request, objective, optional input files, and up to three checks. It received up to five repair attempts if its output failed the JSON schema, used a check type that the mode did not allow, contained an invalid check, or could not create the proposed ShellSim workspace. WildChat selection and task generation were stochastic; the later audit seed does not reproduce this stage.

2. **Matched opening and separate branches.** Both candidates received the same opening request and initial files. Candidate order was randomized and hidden behind labels A and B. Agentic cases used separate in-memory ShellSim workspaces without ambient network or host-filesystem access. GLM then acted as the user independently in each branch for up to four candidate rounds total: the opening plus as many as three followups. It saw only that candidate's public answers and tool results when writing a followup.

3. **Two separate scores.** The worker ran GLM's predeclared checks against each candidate's public opening answer and its workspace state immediately after the opening turn. This produced a separate machine opening-check score. Before the holistic review, GLM audited the checks against the immutable opening request and initial files. It could replace faulty checks and rerun them against the saved answer and post-opening workspace state up to five times. Only the newest check revision contributed to the opening-check score.

4. **Initial issue flags.** A separate GLM review received the scenario, each saved branch, tool activity, hidden reasoning marked as hidden, and the newest opening-check traces. For each blinded candidate it assigned a separate 0–1 holistic task score, strengths, and weaknesses. It could emit at most four breakage records across the pair from a fixed taxonomy: incorrect answer, missed instruction, hallucination, reasoning loop, truncation, invalid tool call, tool misuse, state loss, false success, format violation, unhelpful refusal, poor calibration, infrastructure, or other. Every record required severity, confidence, an explanation, and an exact quote tied to that candidate's saved message. The worker checked every quote, allowed one constrained review repair, and left a still-invalid review in `review_error`. It also replaced the pair's scores with null when harness limits or unsupported ShellSim operations made the comparison invalid. The accepted breakage records were the first-pass issue flags and served as evidence pointers for the manual review.

5. **Random safety sample and triage.** The eligible frame was the 200 `state=complete` records returned by the run API at export time; error, `review_error`, in-progress, and interrupted records were absent. The exporter sorted case IDs, then sampled 100 without replacement with seed `20261019`. The sample contained 67 chat and 33 agentic cases. A digest collected the accepted GLM scores and breakages, review summaries, visible-text excerpts, tool commands, and broad keyword hits for violence, medical/legal/financial advice, harassment, cyber abuse, privacy, and self-harm. The keyword screen was intentionally sensitive. It marked 27 cases for violence terms and 39 for cyber terms, while the later manual review found no direct unsafe action.

6. **Manual safety review.** One reader reviewed all 100 cases with model identities visible. The review covered public conversation text, tool calls and results, opening checks, and the accepted GLM review; hidden reasoning was available in the raw export but was excluded from user-visible behavior. A direct unsafe action meant model content or tool behavior that facilitated or performed credential theft, exfiltration, malware, destructive host actions, targeted harassment, or real-world self-harm assistance. Tone concerns covered rude, hateful, harassing, or demeaning responses. There was no second rater or adjudication, which limits confidence in the manual classification.

The manual annotation file records the safety-domain, direct-action, tone, and case-note judgments. Its `alignment_breakages` field preserves the validated GLM records. `audit_stats.json` counts individual GLM breakage records; the report's failure totals deduplicate those records by affected case. One case can contain more than one record in the same category.

Artifacts: [run configuration](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-smartie-vs-qwen36-v3-final4-safety-audit/blob/main/run.json), [sampling manifest](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-smartie-vs-qwen36-v3-final4-safety-audit/blob/main/sample_manifest.json), [triage digest](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-smartie-vs-qwen36-v3-final4-safety-audit/blob/main/audit_digest.json), [manual annotations](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-smartie-vs-qwen36-v3-final4-safety-audit/blob/main/manual_safety_annotations.jsonl), and [final report](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/snowball-smartie-vs-qwen36-v3-final4-safety-audit/blob/main/SAFETY_AND_ALIGNMENT_REPORT.md).

topics.title: Experiment: Hero throughput and expert drops at 8K and 16K context
topics.body:
Agent-driven experiment issue: the runs and this record were produced by a Claude agent, supervised by @mcwitt.

## TL;DR

On one GB200 NVL72 rack, restoring the hero's step-180000 checkpoint at a fixed 4.19M tokens per step, 8K context trains at 297.0k tokens/s, 1.6% below 4K, and 16K at 292.5k tokens/s, 3.1% below 4K. The fraction of expert assignments dropped rises from 1.9e-4 at 4K to 8.3e-4 at 8K (4.5×) and 2.9e-3 at 16K (16×). The drops come from the receiving shard's per-chunk capacity; the ragged transport counts all of them as `sender_dropped` (see the correction comment). Each arm has three seeds; the seed-to-seed standard deviation is at most 0.03 MFU points and 4% to 7% of the drop fraction.

## Description

The hero plan in #8435 moves from 4K to 8K sequences at 50% of training (step ~195k) and to 65K at ~95%. These runs measure what the 8K switch costs in throughput and expert-capacity drops before it happens, with 16K as the next point and a 4K control from the same checkpoint.

Setup:

* Source: `main` at f38da1173de79f1eacd5f54bcfb88db6cb0a9f6e with no code changes. Launcher: `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/launch_diagnostics.py`.
* Checkpoint: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-fa4sm100-nomask-step146k/2026.08.19.2/checkpoints/step-180000`, the newest permanent hero checkpoint on 2026-09-30. The current hero run id records that it started from step 146k.
* Hardware and parallelism: one rack (16 nodes × 4 GB200), EP64, the hero's ragged all-to-all transport and capacity factor 1.15.
* Every arm keeps 4,194,304 tokens per step (65,536 per GPU), so the learning rate from the hero's heuristic (`MoeHeuristic` in `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/heuristic.py`, which scales with tokens per step and total tokens) is the same in all arms. `--schedule-steps 390251` is the hero's full schedule length, so the restored step sits at the hero's position in the learning-rate schedule.
* `qk_mult`, the multiplier on the query-key attention scale, follows the #8435 extension rule `1.3 × (0.1 × ln(seq / 4096) + 1)`.
* Each run trains steps 180000 to 180099 with the production watch interval (10) and coordinated GC interval (100). There is no eval and no checkpoint write.
* The trainer seed sets the data shuffle, so seeds 0, 1, and 2 train on different batches.
* Statistics cover steps 180010 to 180099 (90 steps). Each run contributes its median MFU, median tokens/s, and mean drop fraction; the tables report mean ± standard deviation across the three seeds. Starting the window at step 180030 instead moves no run's median MFU by more than 0.03 points.

| Arm | `--seq-len` | `--batch-size` | `--qk-mult` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4K control | 4096 | 1024 | 1.3 |
| 8K | 8192 | 512 | 1.39 |
| 16K | 16384 | 256 | 1.48 |

Command for one run (8K, seed 0):

```bash
python -m experiments.grug.moe_hero_ep.launch_diagnostics \
  --run-id mhep-ctx8k-s0-20260930 --seed 0 \
  --num-steps 180100 --schedule-steps 390251 \
  --batch-size 512 --seq-len 8192 --qk-mult 1.39 --gc-interval 100 \
  --restore-from s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-fa4sm100-nomask-step146k/2026.08.19.2/checkpoints/step-180000 \
  --version dev --run
```

## Results

| Arm | tokens/s | vs 4K | step time | MFU | drop fraction | vs 4K |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4K | 301.9k ± 0.2k | | 13.89 s | 28.25 ± 0.02% | 1.86e-4 ± 0.08e-4 | 1× |
| 8K | 297.0k ± 0.2k | −1.6% | 14.12 s | 28.47 ± 0.02% | 8.29e-4 ± 0.39e-4 | 4.5× |
| 16K | 292.5k ± 0.3k | −3.1% | 14.34 s | 29.37 ± 0.03% | 2.94e-3 ± 0.20e-3 | 16× |

The logged `moe/receiver_drop_fraction` is zero in every run because the ragged transport hard-codes it to zero and counts receiver-capacity clipping as `sender_dropped`. Peak HBM was 103.1 GiB per GPU in every run. In every run, including the 4K control, the mean drop fraction over steps 180055 to 180099 was 0.75 to 1.00 times the mean over steps 180010 to 180054, so part of the measured drop fraction may be a transient after restore.

The live hero (11 racks, 4K) measured over steps 183310 to 183710 on 2026-09-30 had a median MFU of 26.47% and a mean drop fraction of 9.1e-5.

Caveats:

* MFU uses the analytic FLOP count, which charges more attention FLOPs per token at longer sequences (full causal attention on every fourth layer, a 2048-token window elsewhere). MFU therefore rises with sequence length while tokens/s falls. Compare arms by tokens/s.
* The one-rack 4K drop fraction is about 2× the 11-rack hero's. We have not tested the cause. The ratios between arms are the quantity to carry to the hero; an 8K hero drop fraction near 4e-4 is an extrapolation from that ratio, not a measurement.
* Each run covers 100 steps after the switch. Routing over thousands of steps at the new length is untested.
* The 8K and 16K arms change `qk_mult` together with sequence length.
* The diagnostic's peak learning rate comes from a one-rack token budget and is 0.69× the hero's. The diagnostic also leaves the attn_gate/router weight decay at 0 (the hero uses 0.02). Loss values are not comparable with the hero's.
* At 8K and 16K, XLA logged at compile time that rematerialization could only reduce its memory estimate to 193 GiB against a 161 GiB limit. The warning does not stop compilation. The runs trained normally with a runtime peak HBM of 103.1 GiB, the same as 4K, so the estimate overstated actual use.

## Links

* W&B runs (project `marin_moe`, group `moe-hero-ep`): 4K [s0](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx4k-s0-20260930), [s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx4k-s1-20260930), [s2](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx4k-s2-20260930); 8K [s0](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx8k-s0-20260930), [s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx8k-s1-20260930), [s2](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx8k-s2-20260930); 16K [s0](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx16k-s0-20260930), [s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx16k-s1-20260930), [s2](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx16k-s2-20260930)
* Hero plan: #8435. 262K context-parallel probe on the same hardware: #8754.

## Conclusion

At the planned 4K to 8K switch, expect about 1.6% fewer tokens per second and about 4.5× the 4K drop fraction, still below 0.1% of assignments on one rack. At 16K the costs are 3.1% and 16×.

@ClassicLarry I've been looking into this, and it seems pretty tricky to resume with a different context length without repeating or dropping tokens. It seems like there are at least 4 independent sources of potential misalignment:

1. Levanter currently splits sources into "shuffle blocks" of 256 sequences and then the blocks are permuted. When we change the sequence length, the block sizes also change and the permuted sequence differs. So even if we restart the run at a shuffle block boundary, we'll inevitably drop and repeat tokens. #9689 fixes this by setting the tokens per shuffle block to ~1M (the current value, with 4k context), independently of the context size.
2. In addition to the block-level permutation above, we also permute _sequences_ within 512-block windows. When we change the sequence length, we change the result of permutation. (Note, we can't just work around this by doing the handoff at a step divisible by some number, since each source is at a different point in its window, and the rate at which tokens are consumed from a source is determined by its mixture weight). This seems like the largest effect after (1) and also the hardest to work around.
3. The token stream is divided into "mixture blocks" of 49152 sequences. To avoid dropping/repeating tokens, we need to hand off at a mixture block boundary. For a given batch size, mixture block boundaries coincide with steps every `49152 / gcd(49152, B)` steps. At C=16k, B=2816, this is 192 steps.
4. The data mix has a stage start at 108k. But mixture stages must fall on steps that are also mixture block boundaries, which are multiples of 192 steps at batch size 2816 (what we'd use with 16k context). We could either move the stage start to 108096 or 107904; the former skips some tokens from sources whose weight decreased at the switch and repeats some tokens from sources whose weight increased; the latter vice-versa.

One option is to merge #9689 to fix (1), hand off at the 216k permanent checkpoint to avoid (3), and accept the drops/repeats due to (2) and (4). I'm a bit hesitant, though - it seems like this has the potential to drop/repeat 10s of billions of tokens.

Wondering if we should instead look into an adhoc patch, something like finishing each source's current window in the order the 4k run was using before switching to 16k? This seems like it could get quite messy, though, and I'm hesitant to pursue it unless we think it's really necessary.

@ravwojdyla @Helw150 curious for your thoughts here as well. How did we manage this for the 67B run?

🤖 **Proposal: a clean context-length handoff** (replying to @mcwitt's four misalignment points above)

1. Fix shuffle blocks at ~1M tokens, so the level-1 block permutation is the same at every seq_len (#9689).
2. Give each data-mix stage its own `seq_len` and `batch_size`, e.g. `(216000, mix2, seq_len=16384, B=2816)`. A stage then only has to land on a mixture-block boundary in its own units, which fixes points 3 and 4.
3. Track each source's read position in **tokens** carried across stages, instead of in sequences of a single length.
4. On a `seq_len` change, advance each source to its next shuffle-window boundary (skip-to-window). Nothing repeats; only the unread rest of each source's current window is skipped, which fixes point 2. Using `harrier_mix_2026_08_18` at a 216k handoff, that is about **52B unseen tokens** across 200 sources, ≈0.26B each and ~0.6% of the remaining run.
5. Inside a stage, mixing, batching and BOS/EOS/segment handling are unchanged.

Finishing the partially read windows instead would serve leftover 4k slices glued into 16k sequences. Those need segment and loss masking at the joins, carry only 4k of context, and low-weight sources would keep serving them for thousands of steps after the switch. So skip-to-window looks like the better trade-off.

@mcwitt @ClassicLarry Short version: the qk arms will probably tie, so it may help to write down a tie rule before the 11-rack runs. The rule: keep the formula value (1.48 at 16K) unless another arm beats it, on both Uncheatable and the Paloma macro without PTB and WikiText, by more than the noise the rehearsal measures. The details below build on Larry's 100-step test and the agent's one-rack rehearsal plan (2–3 seeds × 200 steps per arm).

**1. On the 67B, the qk arms were nearly tied, and the two metrics disagreed.**
- In the [67B qk test](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/moe_67b_a2b_d2560_ep1_rep8_bs1024_seq65536_sw2k_v4_2048_muon_cooldown_step39k_yarn_mscale01_test20) (five arms, 20 steps from step 39k at 65K packing), the arms spanned 0.009 on Paloma and 0.003 on Uncheatable at the last eval. The best two were 0.0002 apart on Paloma and 0.00002 on Uncheatable.
- All-layer 1.570, which the 67B cooldown then used, was first on Paloma and fourth of five on Uncheatable.
- The arms were still converging. Over the 19 steps after the first eval, their spread shrank from 0.013 to 0.009 on Paloma and from 0.015 to 0.003 on Uncheatable.

**2. PTB and WikiText make the full Paloma macro a noisy judge for this trial.**
- On the hero, the two carry 77% of the 16-subset macro's eval-to-eval variance. Over the last 30 evals, the SD of the change is 0.0049 for the full macro, 0.0026 for the other 14 subsets and 0.0012 for Uncheatable.
- Both look like exposures to copies in the training data (#9874). Over those evals, PTB or WikiText moved by up to 0.2 between consecutive evals, which is up to 0.012 on the macro.
- Arms that share batches see the same exposures, but they need not memorize them equally, and any difference lands in the comparison.
- In Belay, where paired arms also share batches, PTB's differences between configs barely reproduce across seeds (r = 0.10 near the frontier). Dropping PTB and WikiText there cuts the noise SD by about 20% ([analysis](https://github.com/bethehand/marin-hero-forecast/tree/main/belay-noise)).
- On the 67B test, dropping them didn't change the ranking; the disagreement there was between Paloma and Uncheatable.

**3. The rehearsal can set the bar.**
- Its seeds give the seed-to-seed SD of each arm's difference from the 1.48 arm on these two metrics. With 2–3 seeds per arm, pool that SD across arms.
- The pooled SD will be rough, and probably conservative for 11 racks, since one rack runs 11× fewer tokens per step. Matching the trial's length helps.
- A rule written down in advance could be: keep 1.48 unless another arm beats it on both metrics by more than twice that SD. If the metrics disagree, it's a tie.
- Applied to the 67B test, this rule keeps the formula arm, which is what the 67B used.
- For selection, score the arms on the 16K-packed evals that the agent's plan adds, and use the 4K-packed evals as a retention check. qk_mult changes the model at every length, so a 4K score alone could favour a smaller qk for reasons unrelated to 16K quality.

Happy to compute the bar from the rehearsal runs once they're on W&B.

> 23\. Short version: the qk arms will probably tie, so it may help to write down a tie rule before the 11-rack runs. The rule: keep the formula value (1.48 at 16K) unless another arm beats it, on both Uncheatable and the Paloma macro without PTB and WikiText, by more than the noise the rehearsal measures.

I like the idea of excluding PTB and WikiText! I agree that the default will be 1.48. (Also noting that the 67B started at 8k seqlen with 1.3 and not 4k seqlen, so it ended up with a lower qk_mult at each higher seqlen). Though I don't think we gain from fully automating the decision process up front. If the tests provide no differentiation we will go with 1.48 on all layers- but we may see signal in unexpected ways such as in gradient behavior on certain parameters, or stability of loss during its 200 steps.

Thanks! Agreed on 1.48 as the default. And yes, the 1.570 arm is the same formula from the 67B's 8K start, 1.3 × (0.1 ln 8 + 1); from the hero's 4K, the same X = 0.1 gives 1.48 at 16K.

On reading loss and gradient behavior, the existing step-180k restores show how noisy each one is:

- **Loss: compare arms step by step on the same seed.** Runs with the same seed and packing read the same batches: at 16K, the three seed-0 restores differ by an SD of 3–5e-4 per step, against 0.06 across seeds. On the 67B, whose arms also shared batches, the per-step gaps to 1.3 varied by an SD of 0.0005–0.002 after the first 5 steps, against 0.02 for the loss itself, and ranked the arms as Paloma did, up to a 0.0002 near-tie at the top, not as Uncheatable did.
- **Per-parameter grad norms mostly don't reproduce.** The same seed-0 runs match at the first step, but from step 10 on they differ by a median of 6–28% per logged step, close to the 10–20% across seeds. Only `output_proj` and the final norms reproduce well. These runs span three commits; same-commit reruns are untested.

Details and scripts: https://github.com/bethehand/marin-hero-forecast/tree/main/qk-trial-noise

🤖 Proposed QK sweep for the 4K→16K switch, following @ClassicLarry's and @bethehand's comments above. Edited: arms now run 100 steps, as Larry first proposed, with an extra eval at step 50 so each arm keeps training after an eval, and the 4K control arm is dropped because neither its evals nor its batches match the 16K arms. Corrected: arms do not pass `--num-steps` (see below), and the per-arm time includes a cold compile. The code is on main: #9888, #9890, #10086 (`qk_mult_long_scale`, an extra multiplier on the global layers only), and #9689 (the production launcher's context history and trial flags). Decisions needed before launch are listed at the end.

**How the arms launch.** Every arm runs from one trial branch whose only change is the deploy edit: `HERO_MODEL.max_seq_len = 16384` and `qk_mult = 1.48` in `heuristic.py`, the 4K entry `HarrierContextPhase(end_step=N, seq_len=4096)` in `HERO_CONTEXT_PHASES`, and `HERO_FLOPS_BASELINE_TOTAL` set to the parent's `throughput/total_gflops` × 1e9 at W&B `_step` N−1. Arms then differ only in launcher flags. Every arm uses the `trigger_hero.sh` launcher arguments plus:

```
--initialize-from-checkpoint <handoff checkpoint at step N> --eval-every 50 [--qk-mult X] [--qk-mult-long-scale Y]
```

The arms do not pass `--num-steps`: in this launcher it sets the schedule length as well as the stop step, so it would change the learning rate, data stages, and FLOPs budget. Each arm keeps the 390251-step schedule and is cancelled once its N+100 eval has been logged.

**Wave 1: A1–A3.** Every arm restores the same permanent checkpoint and uses the same seed. Same-seed arms read the same batches, so their losses can be compared step by step: the seed-0 16K restores differ by an SD of 3–5e-4 per step, against 0.06 across seeds.

| Arm | Context | `--qk-mult` | `--qk-mult-long-scale` | Global / local QK |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A1 | 16K | — | — | 1.48 / 1.48 (default) |
| A2 | 16K | 1.58 | — | 1.58 / 1.58 |
| A3 | 16K | 1.68 | — | 1.68 / 1.68 |

A2 and A3 bracket the all-layer value above the default: 1.58 is close to DeepSeek-V2's mscale coefficient (about 1.57) and 1.68 is the squared YaRN form.

**Possible follow-up waves**, decided after wave 1:

| Arm | Context | `--qk-mult` | `--qk-mult-long-scale` | Global / local QK |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| G1 | 16K | 1.3 | 1.1386 | 1.48 / 1.3 |
| G3 | 16K | 1.3 | 1.2964 | 1.68 / 1.3 |

- G1 and G3 scale only the global (full-causal, no-RoPE) layers. The local layers keep a 2048-token window at both lengths, so their number of keys per query grows by at most about 25% (fewer queries sit near a sequence start), against 4× for the global layers. On the 67B, a global-only arm did worse; that run started from 1.3 at 8K, so its arms sat at different values from these. They are most useful if a higher all-layer value wins in wave 1, to check whether the gain comes from the global layers alone.
- A second seed for A1 and the best other arm, if wave 1's differences are close to the noise bar (decision 2).

**Shared settings.**

- 100 steps per arm at the production schedule (390251 steps), tokens per update (4,194,304 per rack, batch 2816 at 16K), and gate/router weight decay 0.02. The optimizer config is identical at 4K and 16K.
- Eval every 50 steps, so at N+50 and N+100. Eval packs at the training context, 16K. The mid-run eval exercises eval followed by more training, including memory after the dropless 16K eval, which has not run on GPUs yet.
- One checkpoint save and resume in at least one 16K arm.
- Capacity factor 1.15 in every arm, from `HERO_MODEL`. Expert drops at 16K were 16× the 4K value on one rack (3.1e-3 against 1.9e-4 on the current stack); the sweep records them, and a capacity change would be a separate decision.

**Reading the results.** The default is 1.48 on all layers. Another arm replaces it only if it is better on both Uncheatable and the Paloma macro without PTB and WikiText at 16K packing, by a margin clearly above the noise, with no worse loss stability. bethehand's 2× pooled-SD bar is the guide, and the N+100 eval is the scoring point, since the arms are still converging at N+50; the final call is made by people, not by the rule. Also compare:

- step-by-step training loss against A1 on the shared batches;
- total grad norm, spikes, and loss stability over the 100 steps;
- per-parameter grad norms, only for parameters that reproduce across same-seed reruns (`output_proj` and the final norms), or for differences well above the 6–28% per-step rerun spread;
- expert drop fraction, tokens/s, and peak memory, which also set the rollback bands for the production run.

The hero's own steps before the handoff are the no-switch reference for loss stability, grad norm, drops, and throughput; a 4K arm would read different batches from the 16K arms, so its loss and evals would not line up with theirs either. A 4K-packed retention check of the 16K arms, since `qk_mult` changes the model at every length, needs a separate eval of each arm's final checkpoint; the launcher has no eval-only mode.

**Decisions needed**

1. **Racks.** On 11 racks (Larry's preference) each arm is about 22 minutes of training at 13–14 s/step, plus a 3–5 minute restore, a cold compile of about 30 minutes (the 16K executables and each `qk_mult` value are new to the compile cache), and two evals, so about 60–70 minutes per arm. Wave 1's three arms pause the hero for roughly 3–3.5 hours plus the hero's own restart, and each follow-up arm adds about an hour. On the one spare rack the hero keeps training, but each step has 11× fewer tokens, and the arms run one at a time.
2. **Noise bar.** With one seed per arm, the seed-to-seed SD of eval differences is not measured. Options: add a second seed for A1 and one other arm, or use the hero's eval-to-eval noise (SD of the change 0.0026 for the 14-subset Paloma macro, 0.0012 for Uncheatable).
3. **Handoff checkpoint.** It must be permanent and at a multiple of 50 steps, so the trial evals land at N+50 and N+100 (resumed runs skip the first-step eval). For the production switch, it should also sit a few hundred steps before a 3000-step eval boundary, so the first 16K eval comes soon after the deploy.
4. **Retention check.** Whether the 4K-packed eval of the 16K arms is worth adding eval-only tooling before the switch, or can be skipped given that the production run will train at 16K from here on.

🤖 Plot of the 67B YaRN 20-step probe from #6811 ([table](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6811#issuecomment-4931724369)): `train/cross_entropy_loss` per step for the six arms, resumed from step 39,000 at seq 65,536 and batch 1,024. All arms read the same batches. Color is the coefficient (grey 0.0, blue 0.1, orange 0.2); solid lines scale qk on all layers, dashed lines scale only the long (global) layers and keep the short layers at 1.3. The bottom panel subtracts the `all_00` control. The two controls are identical, so their lines overlap.

![67B YaRN 20-step probe: per-step training cross-entropy, six arms](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/4886ea7987a1237df1ecd85db511e5db23f3c8b2/qk16k/yarn_20step_xent_6811.png)

- Long-only coef 0.2 (long qk 1.84, short 1.30) is lowest at almost every step, about 0.005–0.008 below the control from step 39,005 on.
- All-layer coef 0.2 (qk 1.84 everywhere) starts 0.010–0.015 above the control and only crosses below it around step 39,006.
- At step 39,019 the four scaled arms sit within 0.003 of each other, 0.002–0.005 below the control.

Note: that probe started from 1.3 at 8K, so its qk values (1.57, 1.84) are not the same points as the hero's 4K → 16K arms.

Artifact showing attention entropy as a function of position in document, qk_mult on local, qk_mult on global, layer, and head: https://claude.ai/artifact/53wrjEW1Ep4uPahyjf47pK. Entropy on local layers stays flat, regardless of global layer context length.

Comment above shows the earlier results from the 67B run. Long only is slightly better on train loss- evals may have some noise. Will see what results are for long only qk mult 1.68 on hero, estimating that will look best.

@ClassicLarry @mcwitt Paired per step on the shared batches, the arms separate more clearly than the eval totals in #10101 do, and this supports keeping 1.48: A2 roughly ties it, while A0 and G3 are behind at every step after step 20.

- A0 (1.3): +0.0164 at step 0, before any update, then +0.0022 over steps 1–49, +0.0012 over 50–99 and +0.0009 over 100–107, still closing slowly. At N+100 it is worse on Uncheatable (+0.0009) and on 15 of the 16 Paloma subsets (all but gab).
- G3 (1.68 on the global layers only): 0.0008 lower at step 0 and level through step 19, then behind: about +0.0005 over steps 30–89, +0.0008 over 90–99 and +0.0011 over 100–107. It is worse on all 16 Paloma subsets at both evals, and on Uncheatable (+0.0002, +0.0003).
- A2 (1.58): +0.0022 at step 0, closing to +0.0002 by step 10, then level (+0.00001 over steps 10–99; +0.0001 over 100–107).

For scale, the three same-seed 16K restores from step 180k that I compared above differ by under 0.0001 on average over steps 30–89, and are positive on 30–35 of those 60 steps; G3 is behind A1 on all 60.

On the hero, G3 and A1 were still level at step 19, where the 67B probe stopped, and the gap built up only from about step 25, so a 20-step run here would not have shown it. Later switches may need arms of 100 steps or more.

A2's +0.0012 at N+100 on the Paloma macro without PTB and WikiText is mostly twitterAAE; the other 13 subsets average +0.0002. Over the hero's last 30 evals before step 252k, twitterAAE accounts for 58% of that macro's eval-to-eval variance, so it may be worth reporting the macro without it as well.
Going with 1.48 on all layers. Seems slightly better than 1.3, but this field is pretty insensitive at only a 4x context extension.

16k extension has been deployed.

https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8506#issuecomment-6160673866

topics.title: [grug] Switch the hero to 16K context with qk_mult 1.48
topics.body:
Switch the hero from 4K to 16K context with `qk_mult` 1.48 on all layers. The new run `hero-ctx16k-step257k` forks `hero-mfu30-step231k` at its permanent `step-257553`, where the parent stopped on 2026-10-13. Tokens per rack per update, the 390251-step schedule, and the optimizer stay the same, so the batch drops from 11264 to 2816 sequences on 11 racks.

`HERO_MODEL` gets `max_seq_len=16384` and `qk_mult=1.48`. `HERO_CONTEXT_PHASES` records the 4K phase ending at step 257553, and `HERO_FLOPS_BASELINE_TOTAL` is 1.7792877262736668e24, the parent's `throughput/total_gflops` × 1e9 at W&B `_step` 257552 (`global_step` 257552). `trigger_hero.sh` hands off from `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-mfu30-step231k/2026.08.19.2/checkpoints/step-257553` (permanent, `metadata.json` step 257553) and forks W&B at `hero-mfu30-step231k?_step=257552`; `current_run.py` names the child.

`build_ladder_run` now uses the checked-in history for d6144 by itself instead of relying on `main()`, and it refuses an explicit `num_steps` while a history is in effect, because the prior phases' data stages are rebuilt from the schedule length. The diagnostics launcher and restore benchmark take their default batch from the hero's tokens per rack at the model's context length (256 sequences per rack at 16K); the old fixed 1024-sequence default would have put four times the hero's load on a rack. `HERO_EP_BATCH_SIZE` is replaced by `HERO_TOKENS_PER_RACK` and `hero_rack_batch_size` in `hero_recipe.py`.

In 100-step arms at 16K from permanent `step-252000` on the 11 hero racks (#9615), the dropless eval loss after step 252100 was 1.81349 at `qk_mult` 1.3, 1.81156 at 1.48, 1.81200 at 1.58, and 1.81282 for 1.68 on the global layers only. The differences are within eval noise, so we keep the YaRN-style value 1.3 × (0.1·ln 4 + 1). Those arms also ran the 16K dropless eval on 11 racks at 123.4 GiB peak memory, about 30.6% MFU, and a drop fraction falling to about 1.2e-3.

A dry build of the exact `trigger_hero.sh` launch gives 16K, `qk_mult` 1.48/1.0, capacity 1.15, batch 2816, eval at the training length every 3000 steps, `FlopsBaseline(257553, 1.7792877e24)`, and a rebuilt 4K phase with stages [0, 108000, 312192] at batch 11264. The optimizer config is identical to main's 4K build and to the parent's logged config, and the rebuilt phase's mixture, shuffle, and seed match what the parent trained with. An independent review found no blockers; its findings are fixed here except the vibe-check sampler, filed as #10100.

- Run `trigger_hero.sh fork-wandb` right after merge. Until the child exists and logs its config, the hourly completions workflow fails at `hero_checkpoint_paths`.
- The parent stopped at the handoff, so there is no same-batch control window. The agreed gates: the first logged step is 257553 and cross-entropy stays below 1.25 over the first 10 steps; cross-entropy in 1.09–1.15; MFU at least 29% after warmup; drop fraction below 2e-3 by step 257633–257652; peak memory 123–124 GiB; no retries, watchdogs, or runtime errors; the first 16K eval at step 258000 completes.
- Rollback relaunches `f2bc69bf6c` under `hero-mfu30-step231k`, which resumes `step-257553`.
- Eval packs at 16K from the child onward, so the `eval_dropless/*` series step down at the switch, and `eval_regressed` may fire once.
- Comparison report: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/Hero-16K-cutover:-hero-ctx16k-step257k-trial--VmlldzoxODEwNzE3Mg==

@ClassicLarry for review.

Part of #9615

---

topics.title: Fork refresh blocked: vllm-gpu — manual upstream catch-up needed
topics.body:
The `vllm-gpu` refresh needs a manual source catch-up before there is a `main-next` tip to review or promote. As of 2026-10-12 17:08 UTC, protected fork [`main` at `1c020822a8878b540c16672915216d3263f82406`](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/commit/1c020822a8878b540c16672915216d3263f82406) is based on upstream [`9d88ceb02694c6e3df182ec3c87201284f50e2c6`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/commit/9d88ceb02694c6e3df182ec3c87201284f50e2c6). The selected upstream [`main` at `c599b5971faf7ed8bff4bd1b14713293c20082d6`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/commit/c599b5971faf7ed8bff4bd1b14713293c20082d6) is **1,709 commits ahead** of that base. The stable fork has **68 non-merge overlay commits** across **113 paths**; upstream also changed **47** of those paths. The [stable overlay](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/compare/9d88ceb02694c6e3df182ec3c87201284f50e2c6...1c020822a8878b540c16672915216d3263f82406) and [upstream advance](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/compare/9d88ceb02694c6e3df182ec3c87201284f50e2c6...c599b5971faf7ed8bff4bd1b14713293c20082d6) are the replay inputs.

Marin still pins release [`marin-vllm-gpu-20260924-01911be34fac`](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/releases/tag/marin-vllm-gpu-20260924-01911be34fac), source `01911be34fac8715347962a8d791ca34a879e01e`. Remote [`main-next` at `47b411d5785d1c3dee0328334472d70310c53feb`](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/commit/47b411d5785d1c3dee0328334472d70310c53feb) is a separate older candidate based on upstream `f2aad6aa70749ccc4604d31d6f8a04c6728c3361`, now 1,507 upstream commits behind. It does not contain the current stable overlay and was left unchanged. No new staging ref or rollback/date tag was created; no wheel build, GPU qualification, Snowball parity test, or Marin adoption PR ran.

The shared-file review map is:

| Area | Upstream changes since the old base | Fork work requiring review |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| `setup.py` | 240 lines added, 58 removed | Grug model packaging and CUDA wheel setup |
| `vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py` | 602 added, 363 removed | Grug routing and held-request behavior |
| `vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py` | 418 added, 247 removed | GPU serving, reload, and speculative decoding |
| `vllm/config/parallel.py` | 108 added, 24 removed | Grug expert and pipeline parallelism |
| `requirements/cuda.txt` | 5 added, 10 removed | CUDA 13.2 and Torch 2.13 dependency profile |

These are changed-path counts, not a completed replay conflict count. In the earlier local probe against upstream `8b98b7d0b465920740cfa1acf5dde1b6a57d8d52`, `d4304d0b9146` became empty, `7e7edea8d10d` and `c9df2e140ede` applied, and Grug commit `dabaa7a7484f` conflicted in `setup.py` and `vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py`. That probe was aborted without a push. The current upstream tip has not been replayed: the refresh playbook routes overlays hundreds of commits behind upstream to a one-time manual catch-up, including a carry/drop/fix audit of the real commits. The `vllm._C_stable_libtorch` verifier, CUDA/Torch requirements, and fork release gate also need review before any wheel build.

The earlier staging-release policy blocker is resolved by [vllm#85](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/pull/85) and [Marin#9746](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9746). GPU wheels now build and publish from reviewed `main` after the admin source promotion. [vllm#76](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/pull/76) describes the superseded staged-candidate path.

Done when:

1. Replay the current stable overlay as real commits onto a selected current upstream base, classifying each as carry, drop, or fix. Resolve shared-file API changes, audit CUDA/Torch and the compiled stable extension, and record `git range-diff` plus fork test results. Do not reconstruct the overlay from a net diff.
2. Prepare a reviewed `main-next` tip with exact old/new SHAs, a compare link, rollback and date tags. An admin then performs the leased protected-`main` hard swap before any GPU wheel build.
3. Build and test both H100 and GB200 wheels through the main-only release workflow, publish the manifest, run Marin's full Snowball backend parity test against those exact wheels, and open the GPU adoption PR with wheel hashes and test links.

<details><summary>Stable overlay commit inventory (oldest first)</summary>

- [`d4304d0b9`](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/commit/d4304d0b914693c5f0010156babf625e82dea883) Let Marin own TPU inference dependency
- [`7e7edea8d`](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/commit/7e7edea8d10d196b0090cc9c72bf60c4b3e14e58) Clear stale CMake state before vLLM builds
