topics.title: [taskforge] Add machine factories, task images and the image builder
topics.body:
Add the `sandbox` package to select shellbox machine factories by host: ShellSim and Docker on laptops, ShellSim and gVisor on Iris, and the local backend for lock-only graders where bubblewrap works. `sandbox.factories` rejects a lowered task up front with the factory's own message, warms the local backend's CPython once, and gives ShellSim the package catalog its CPython comes from.

Grader images use the base image, `DockerBuild` context and limits, and `ImageBuilder` protocol in `sandbox.images`. Build and validation both classify the host-failure messages in `sandbox.host_failures`. `scripts/build_image_job.py` builds a directory's `DockerBuild` on Iris and prints the digest-pinned reference.

`IrisImageBuilder` builds with kaniko in one Iris CPU job and pushes with `crane` in a second job, so the registry credential never shares a container with the model-authored Dockerfile. It takes the credential at construction and reads no secret store, so it runs on a host without `gcloud` or Google credentials, such as a coordinator in an Iris task. Only the laptop helper `registry_credential_json` calls `gcloud`.

Builds on #10292; #10294 builds on it. Two manual machine tests that build their requirements with `spec.draft` land there. The taskforge suite passes 212 tests here (25 more than #10292).

topics.title: [taskcompendium] Start grading in the grader workspace
topics.body:
The grading machine now starts in the grader's workspace unless its environment specifies a `working_directory`. This restores the behavior before #10021 when the environment names no directory and preserves an explicit directory when it does.

Since #10021, every script-graded task has failed while creating its grading machine on Iris. `_grade_staged` previously passed `workdir=grading.workspace`; the move to `prepare_machine_spec` dropped that argument. When the grader environment names no directory, `prepare_machine_spec` retains the spec's workdir, which is empty for an image machine because `rolloutengine._machine_spec` leaves it empty. Docker interprets an empty workdir as the image's `WORKDIR`, so laptop grading continued to work. Iris instead runs `mkdir -p ""` and fails:

```
RuntimeError: Failed to create Iris workdir : mkdir: cannot create directory ''
```

The Taskforge ladder dry run on cw-rno2a hit this failure in every grader sandbox. Solver and control machines were unaffected because `draft.requirements` names `/workspace`.

A test checks the spec passed to the factory with and without an explicit `working_directory`; the grader-workspace case fails on main. The ShellSim-backed taskcompendium suite passed locally. The bubblewrap-backed tests require Linux, and CI runs the full suite.

---

topics.title: [grug] Add an AMD Grug attention layer benchmark for one or more GPUs
topics.body:
Add `lib/levanter/scripts/bench/bench_grug_attention_amd.py`, which times one Grug attention layer on one or more AMD GPUs. It exits unless the backend is ROCm: it targets the AMD Pallas-Triton kernel, and the NVIDIA FA4/CuTe kernels need packed segment IDs that its inputs do not have. For each mask (2048-token sliding window, global causal) and each implementation passed to `--impl`, it reports forward and forward-plus-backward time and the max absolute output difference against the first implementation. With `--sweep --sweep-part fwd|dq|dkv` it times a grid of tile sizes, warps and stages for one of the three Pallas-Triton flash kernels (forward, dQ, dK/dV) and keeps the defaults for the other two. `--block-q`, `--block-k`, `--num-warps` and `--num-stages` replace that kernel's default values for one axis of the grid. TFLOP/s counts only the FLOPs the mask needs over the allowed (query, key) pairs. Each time is the median of ten 0.2 s windows after a 1 s warmup. Results are printed as `RESULT {json}` lines.

`--num-devices N` runs on the first N GPUs with the batch sharded over an explicit `data` mesh axis, as in Grug training. `--batch` is per GPU, so the global batch is N times it; TFLOP/s are reported in total and per device.

Defaults are the June per-GPU shape at global batch 64 on 8 GPUs: 8 x 4096 tokens, 20 query heads, 5 KV heads, head_dim 128, bf16.

```bash
python lib/levanter/scripts/bench/bench_grug_attention_amd.py --impl reference xla_flash gpu_pallas_triton_flash
python lib/levanter/scripts/bench/bench_grug_attention_amd.py --sweep --sweep-part dkv --block-q 64 128 --num-stages 1
python lib/levanter/scripts/bench/bench_grug_attention_amd.py --num-devices 8
```

Forward plus backward time on one MI350X with jax 0.11.1 and the ROCm 10.1 plugin (job 460980):

| Mask | reference | xla_flash | gpu_pallas_triton_flash |
|---|---|---|---|
| window 2048 | 18.84 ms (96 TF/s) | 22.66 ms (80 TF/s) | 6.74 ms (268 TF/s) |
| causal | 20.89 ms (115 TF/s) | 22.89 ms (105 TF/s) | 10.02 ms (240 TF/s) |

In the same job, the dK/dV sweep with the window mask ran all 36 configs. The default tile, 128 queries x 64 keys with 4 warps and 1 stage, was the fastest at 6.80 ms.

On one Vultr MI355X node with jax 0.11.0 in the TheRock 7.14 container (job 11645), 8 GPUs at global batch 64 run within 1% of one GPU at batch 8, so per-device throughput holds under batch sharding. Forward plus backward, TF/s per GPU:

| Mask | GPUs | reference | xla_flash | gpu_pallas_triton_flash |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| window 2048 | 1 | 15.60 ms (116 TF/s) | 21.47 ms (84 TF/s) | 5.87 ms (307 TF/s) |
| window 2048 | 8 | 15.78 ms (114 TF/s) | 21.77 ms (83 TF/s) | 5.91 ms (305 TF/s) |
| causal | 1 | 15.08 ms (160 TF/s) | 21.57 ms (112 TF/s) | 9.19 ms (262 TF/s) |
| causal | 8 | 15.24 ms (158 TF/s) | 21.81 ms (110 TF/s) | 9.23 ms (261 TF/s) |

On 8 GPUs, the default dK/dV tile was again the fastest of the six block sizes swept (block_q 64 or 128, block_k 32, 64 or 128, 4 warps, 1 stage), at 5.91 ms.

The script imports `TritonFlashBlockSizes` and `pallas_triton_flash_attention` from `levanter.grug.attention._amd_pallas_triton_flash`, which #10014 added.

topics.title: Floppy Phoenix-ing a few different timelines
topics.body:
# Floppy Phoenix schedules for December (and maybe January)

Building on @ClassicLarry et al. candidate work in [the GB200 TPS tracker (#7201)](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7201), I've been Rick Rubin-ing on [Floppy Phoenix](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/floppy-phoenix/2026.07.24.3/index.html) to see how post-training changes model choice under a few different timelines that @ihodes was curious about at our last hero run meeting.

Under the very heavily asterisked assumptions below, d6144 4-of-128 seems about right so not actually a huge prior update here. One thing I'd raise is that (if we want a more pretrained model that we think can support longer RL runs) d7168 (or another larger model via sparsity or depth scaling) is worth benchmarking to see how much it tanks our MFU v.s helps our model size.

## TL;DR

My current recommendation is to plan around d6144 4-of-128. If December 24 is fixed, the unresolved choice is whether to hand off on November 15 or December 1. I would consider d7168 only for a January 15 release, and only if its measured pretraining and RL pace are close to the estimates here.

We are trying to ship a broadly useful model, roughly at the capability level tracked by the [Artificial Analysis index](https://artificialanalysis.ai/). Everything below assumes that pretraining starts August 15. The MFU estimates use Larry et al.'s measurements and the extrapolation formulas in #7201. RL is modeled as fully on-policy, so rollout generation and policy updates happen in sequence. I assume 15% downtime from operational issues, plus seven pretraining days for long-context extension and early cooldowns.

No row is measured end-to-end. The d6144 pretraining pace is projected from one rack, d7168 pace is forecast, and every RL figure is an unmeasured ceiling.

| post-training start | release | provisional model | pretraining tokens | illustrative RL response-token upper bound<sup>1</sup> | decision status |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| December 1 | December 24 | d6144 4-of-128 ([scenario inputs](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/floppy-phoenix/2026.07.24.3/index.html?fam=marin&C=3.18e24&steps=13889&tps=4000000&c_total_mult=17.75)) | ≈20.8T | ≈0.5T | stretch; the upper bound reserves no time outside RL |
| November 15 | December 24 | d6144 4-of-128 ([scenario inputs](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/floppy-phoenix/2026.07.24.3/index.html?fam=marin&C=3.18e24&steps=25000&tps=4000000&c_total_mult=17.75)) | ≈17.4T | ≈0.9T | open trade: 3.3T pretraining tokens for 13.6 post-training days |
| December 1 | January 15 | d7168 4-of-128 ([unmeasured scenario](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/floppy-phoenix/2026.07.24.3/index.html?fam=marin&C=3.74e24&steps=22222&tps=4000000&c_total_mult=17.757)) | ≈14.5T | ≈0.8T | only if measured pace supports it; d6144 is the fallback |

<sup>1</sup> This spends the full effective post-training window on one synchronous RL loop. It reserves no time for SFT, evaluation, verifier work, recovery, safety work, or release packaging. We also have not decided whether "response tokens" means generated, accepted, or learner tokens.

All d6144 calculations use 20.0B active parameters. That convention is still unresolved in #7201.

## Why doesn't the fastest model win?

For a December 1 handoff, the fastest d5120 row gets 27.4T pretraining tokens versus 20.8T for d6144. The loss fit assigns a penalty to the smaller active model, even though it gets more pretraining tokens and can run more RL cycles.

[ScaleRL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.13786) motivates a sigmoid in log RL compute. [Floppy Phoenix](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/floppy-phoenix/2026.07.24.3/index.html?fam=marin&C=3.18e24&steps=13889&tps=4000000&c_total_mult=17.75) then assumes that the RL ceiling grows with model size. The [Nicholas Roberts et al. overtraining paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01411) is another reason to include inference-time compute when sizing the pretrained model. None of these results calibrates final Marin capability.

Under those assumptions, d8192 has the lowest predicted reducible loss in all three schedules. I do not trust that result enough to train d8192: there are no d7168–d8192 throughput points, the loss fit has no prediction interval, and we do not have a Marin RL scaling curve. This is useful as sensitivity analysis, not as a model ranking. I would measure d7168 and d8192 to see where MFU falls off.

## The three schedules

### What if post-training starts December 1 and we release December 24?

This is tight: 19.6 effective post-training days. The [d6144 4-of-128 plan](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/floppy-phoenix/2026.07.24.3/index.html?fam=marin&C=3.18e24&steps=13889&tps=4000000&c_total_mult=17.75) gets about 20.8T pretraining tokens and an illustrative 0.5T RL response-token ceiling.

The [d5120 4-of-64 plan](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/floppy-phoenix/2026.07.24.3/index.html?fam=marin&C=3.18e24&steps=22222&tps=4000000&c_total_mult=8.8356) gets 27.4T pretraining tokens and a 0.8T RL ceiling. The current loss fit ranks it below d6144; we do not have a measured released-model quality comparison.

If its MFU holds up, [d6144 4-of-256](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/floppy-phoenix/2026.07.24.3/index.html?fam=marin&C=3.18e24&steps=11111&tps=4000000&c_total_mult=35.35) gets about 16.7T pretraining tokens and a 0.4T RL ceiling. Its quality advantage over 4-of-128 is unmeasured, and the current fit assigns it none.

### What if pretraining ends November 15?

For [d6144](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/floppy-phoenix/2026.07.24.3/index.html?fam=marin&C=3.18e24&steps=25000&tps=4000000&c_total_mult=17.75), the earlier handoff gives up about 3.3T pretraining tokens and adds 13.6 effective post-training days. We could use that time for more shots at goal on the recipe, or raise the illustrative ceiling from 0.5T to 0.9T response tokens.

The 0.9T figure is closer to the scale in the [MAI technical report](https://microsoft.ai/pdf/mai-thinking-1.pdf), but the comparison is pretty fuzzy. Their token accounting and post-training stages might not match ours.

We do not have much signal on shorter pretraining versus shorter post-training. The ongoing A2B run might give us some: if much lower pretraining loss does not make RL easier, maybe we should take the earlier handoff.

### What do we buy by waiting until January 15?

Releasing January 15 instead of December 24 adds 18.7 effective post-training days, 2.8e24 post-training hardware FLOPs, and 18% more total hardware compute.

[d7168](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/floppy-phoenix/2026.07.24.3/index.html?fam=marin&C=3.74e24&steps=22222&tps=4000000&c_total_mult=17.757) gets about 14.5T pretraining tokens and has a 0.8T illustrative RL ceiling. I would only use it if measured training and RL pace make those two estimates credible. [d6144 is the fallback](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/floppy-phoenix/2026.07.24.3/index.html?fam=marin&C=3.74e24&steps=27778&tps=4000000&c_total_mult=17.75): 20.8T pretraining tokens and a 1.0T RL ceiling.

## What would be helpful to measure

- Define the RL token accounting, then run one complete synchronous RL cycle for each viable width. Report prompt, generated, accepted, and learner tokens; group size; response lengths; policy updates; and generation, update, synchronization, and total wall time.

- Measure d7168 and d8192 MFU with the same accounting as #7201. If d7168 is already falling off the throughput curve, use d6144 for every schedule.

- Cut another A2B cooldown so that Ben can run his existing post-training recipe on top of it. Knowing whether lower pretraining loss makes post-training easier in our setup would help us choose which phase to compress.

<details>
<summary>Full candidate table</summary>

| candidate | params, B (active / total) | TPS basis | 11-rack TPS | 11-rack 6NT utilization<sup>2</sup> | assumed RL cycle, seconds | pretraining tokens, T<sup>3</sup> | RL response-token ceiling, T<sup>4</sup> | modeled reducible-loss gap vs d8192<sup>5</sup> |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| d5120 4-of-64 | 14.6 / 129 | projected from 8 racks | 3.740M | 18.6% | 8.5 | 27.4 / 23.0 | 0.8 / 1.3 / 1.6 | 10.1% / 9.4% |
| d5120 4-of-128 | 14.5 / 250 | projected from 2 racks | 3.346M | 16.5% | 11.2 | 24.5 / 20.6 | 0.6 / 1.0 / 1.2 | 10.5% / 9.9% |
| d5120 8-of-256 EP | 14.5 / 249 | projected from 2 racks | 3.254M | 16.1% | 11.4 | 23.8 / 20.0 | 0.6 / 1.0 / 1.2 | 10.6% / 10.0% |
| d6144 4-of-128 <sup>C</sup> | 20.0 / 355 | projected from 1 rack | 2.833M | 19.3% | 13.2 | 20.8 / 17.4 | 0.5 / 0.9 / 1.0 | 5.5% / 5.0% |

| d8192 4-of-128 <sup>E</sup> | 35.6 / 631 | MFU forecast | ≈1.434M | ≈17.4% | not estimated | 10.5 / 8.8 | not estimated | reference |

<sup>2</sup> `6NT utilization = 6 × active parameters × tokens per second / peak hardware FLOP/s`.

<sup>3</sup> December 1 / November 15 post-training starts.

<sup>4</sup> December 1→December 24 / November 15→December 24 / December 1→January 15. These are unmeasured ceilings from the assumed cycle times, not forecasts.

<sup>5</sup> Relative gap in the reducible part of the base-loss fit for December 1 / November 15. This is uncalibrated to released-model quality and has no prediction interval.

`C` marks the unresolved active-parameter convention. `E` marks a pace forecast with no measured throughput point.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Schedule math and assumptions</summary>

`hardware FLOPs = effective days × 86,400 × 704 × 2.5e15`

| pretraining start | post-training start | release | calendar days (pre / post) | effective days (pre / post) | peak hardware FLOPs (pre / post / total) |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| August 15 | December 1 | December 24 | 108 / 23 | 84.8 / 19.6 | 1.29e25 / 2.97e24 / 1.59e25 |
| August 15 | November 15 | December 24 | 92 / 39 | 71.2 / 33.2 | 1.08e25 / 5.04e24 / 1.59e25 |
| August 15 | December 1 | January 15 | 108 / 45 | 84.8 / 38.3 | 1.29e25 / 5.82e24 / 1.87e25 |

- Assume an average of 11 active NVL72 racks, 10–12 in practice, or 704 working GB200s for 1.76e18 peak BF16 FLOP/s.
- Effective pretraining days are `0.85 × calendar days − 7`; effective post-training days are `0.85 × calendar days`. The 7 pretraining days are 4 days for long context and 3 days for cooldown checkpoints.
- TPS projections come from #7201 and scale from 12 racks to our 11-rack average. d7168–d8192 use an MFU forecast.
- Useful pretraining FLOPs are `6 × active parameters × tokens`.
- The Floppy Phoenix links use compute normalized to its 20% reference MFU: 3.18e24 for the December 24 budget and 3.74e24 for the January 15 budget. This is not directly comparable to the peak hardware FLOPs above.
- The post-training calculation uses a 4M-response-token batch. Generation, policy update, and synchronization happen in sequence.
- The loss fit does not model a quality benefit from total expert count.

</details>

comments.body: cc @yonromai @penfever to tell me where I'm being dumb on RL flops/tokens/inference speed

🤖 A more concrete comparison to the related work:

| model | parameters (active / total) | base-model training tokens | approximate base-training FLOPs | RL tokens / FLOPs |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| [MAI-Thinking-1 / MAI-Base-1](https://microsoft.ai/pdf/mai-thinking-1.pdf) | 35B / ~1T | 30T pretraining + 3.55T mid-training | 6.30e24 pretraining; 7.05e24 including mid-training | about 1.8T packed learner tokens and 3.8e23 policy-update FLOPs for the plotted STEM climb under the reconstruction below; full RL total is higher and not recoverable |
| [OLMo 3 Think 32B](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.13961) | 32B / 32B | 5.5T pretraining + 2×100B mid-training branches + 100B context extension | 1.06e24 pretraining; 1.11e24 including both mid-training branches and context extension | not reported; the published hyperparameters imply at most 25.2B response tokens and about 6.4e21 nominal model FLOPs for generation + one learner pass |
| [Arcee Trinity-Large-Thinking](https://www.arcee.ai/blog/trinity-large-thinking) | 13B / 398B | 17T | 1.33e24 | not reported; the final model followed two months of SFT/RL pipeline work across 1,152 H100s. Continuous use for 60 days would be about 5.9e24 peak hardware FLOPs, but this is a mixed program envelope, not reported RL spend |
| [Kimi K2 (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.20534) | 32B / 1.04T | 15.5T | 2.98e24 | not reported |
| [DeepSeek V4 Pro](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19348) | 49B / 1.6T | 33T | 9.70e24 | not reported; the report describes specialist RL followed by on-policy distillation, but gives no total |

The base-training FLOPs above are my `6 × active parameters × training tokens` calculations. They are useful-model FLOPs, not measured hardware FLOPs, and they do not include ablations or failed runs. In particular, they are not directly comparable to the peak hardware-budget FLOPs in the issue without an MFU/goodput conversion.

<details>
<summary>MAI RL derivation and caveats</summary>

MAI does expose enough to estimate the learner side of its main STEM climb. The report gives a packed global batch of 7,040 sequences, a rollout-length curriculum of 8K → 16K → 32K → 64K → 128K, and a STEM curve that reaches about 5,000 steps. Reading that curve as roughly 1,000 steps at each length gives:

`7,040 × 1,000 × (8,192 + 16,384 + 32,768 + 65,536 + 131,072) = 1.788T packed learner tokens`

At 35B active parameters, that is about `3.75e23` policy-update FLOPs using `6NT`. One rollout-generation pass over the same tokens adds about `1.25e23` using `2NT`, for about `5.01e23` nominal model FLOPs across the accepted generation + learner path.

This is still not the full MAI RL bill. The paper does not tabulate the exact step boundary for each length, so the approximately 1K steps per stage is an inference from the approximately 5K-step plot. Generation also includes early-exit samples and rejected rollout groups. In addition, MAI trained separate STEM, agentic, and helpfulness/safety specialists, then ran consolidation SFT and a final RL stage. The report plots about 1.3K agentic steps, but does not expose enough trajectory-length accounting to convert those cleanly; it does not give corresponding totals for the helpfulness/safety or final consolidation climbs. The report’s largest RL job used 4,864 GB300s—4,096 for inference and 768 for the learner—but gives no duration.

One correction to the earlier discussion still stands: MAI’s 3.55T-token number is mid-training, not RL. The separate reconstruction above is why “roughly 2T RL learner tokens” is nevertheless a reasonable description of the main STEM climb.

</details>

<details>
<summary>OLMo 3 RL derivation and caveats</summary>

For OLMo 3, `750 steps × 128 prompts × 8 responses × 32,768 max response tokens = 25.2B` maximum response tokens. Applying `2NT` for rollout generation and `6NT` for one policy update gives about `6.4e21` FLOPs. That is not a reported total: real responses are usually shorter, while prompt prefill, verifiers, reference/teacher work, failed samples, and systems overhead add compute.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Arcee checkpoint distinction and hardware ceiling</summary>

The February [Trinity Large technical report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.17004) covers Trinity-Large-Preview, not the final Trinity-Large-Thinking post-training run. Preview was instruction-tuned on [20B tokens](https://huggingface.co/arcee-ai/Trinity-Large-Preview) and received a “short RL stage”; Arcee does not give its RL tokens or FLOPs.

Trinity-Large-Thinking is a separate checkpoint built from Trinity-Large-Base. Arcee’s April release report says it followed two months of work improving and scaling the SFT/RL pipeline, with post-training across 1,152 H100s. As a loose ceiling, `1,152 × 989e12 BF16 FLOP/s × 60 days = 5.91e24` peak hardware FLOPs. That period includes SFT, recipe development, experiments, and the final model run, and Arcee does not report full-cluster uptime or MFU. I therefore would not call 5.9e24 the model’s RL FLOPs or infer an RL-token count from it.

</details>

topics.title: Marin 67B-A2B (65k and 262k checkpoints) vs Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-Base and Gemma 4 26B-A4B: Paloma and UncheatableEval BPB with lm-eval-exact scoring
topics.body:
🤖 Comparison of the Marin 67B-A2B checkpoints from #6044 and #8813 against Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-Base, scored the same way lm-eval scored the open-weight baselines in #8824.

## TL;DR

- On the Paloma test split, the 65k-context checkpoint (step 156k) gets **0.7812** macro BPB and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-Base gets **0.8397** (−7.0%). Our model is lower on 15 of 16 subsets; M2D2 S2ORC is the exception (+2.4%).
- On the 7 legacy UncheatableEval subsets, it gets **0.5178** vs **0.5245** (−1.3%). We are lower on Wikipedia, BBC News and AO3. Qwen is lower on C++ (by 5.7%), arXiv Physics and arXiv CS; Python is a tie.
- Against Gemma 4 26B-A4B, the pre-trained base (`google/gemma-4-26B-A4B`; the instruction-tuned model is the separate `-it` repo), the 65k checkpoint gets **0.7812** vs **0.8494** on Paloma (−8.0%). Our model is lower on 14 of 16 subsets; Gemma is marginally lower on M2D2 S2ORC (by 0.2%) and RedPajama (0.5354 vs 0.5356). On the 7 UncheatableEval subsets Gemma is lower: **0.5138** vs our **0.5178** (ours is 0.8% higher). We are lower on GitHub Python, arXiv Physics and arXiv CS; Gemma is lower on Wikipedia, GitHub C++, BBC News and AO3. #8824 scored Gemma only on the newer 15-subset UncheatableEval snapshot, so these 7-subset numbers are our own rerun with the same lm-eval setup (see Method).
- The 262k context extension (qk_mult 1.75, 8× long-document skew, step 157k) is slightly lower again: 0.7795 Paloma, 0.5171 UncheatableEval.
- Marin's in-training Paloma numbers are not directly comparable to the #8824 open-model rows: Levanter scores Paloma **val**, lm-eval scores Paloma **test**, and Levanter packs documents. See "Why earlier Marin numbers differ" below.

![BPB per eval: 65k ckpt, 262k ckpt, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-Base, Gemma 4 26B-A4B base](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/7bfc4c75cf0f74e70263690ebce2fddaa907f302/experiments/grug/moe/eval_67b_a2b_vs_open_bases_bpb.png)

## Results

All numbers are bits per byte (lower is better). Document counts match Qwen's lm-eval run exactly for every subset.

| Paloma subset | Docs | 65k ckpt | 262k ckpt | Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-Base | Gemma 4 26B-A4B | 65k vs Qwen | 65k vs Gemma |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 4chan | 404 | 0.8254 | 0.8245 | 0.8828 | 0.8415 | -6.5% | -1.9% |
| C4 100 domains | 14,131 | 0.6513 | 0.6503 | 0.7045 | 0.6576 | -7.6% | -1.0% |
| C4 English | 2,124 | 0.6982 | 0.6972 | 0.7549 | 0.7205 | -7.5% | -3.1% |
| Dolma v1.5 | 4,481 | 0.6183 | 0.6173 | 0.6582 | 0.6411 | -6.1% | -3.6% |
| 100 programming languages | 7,832 | 0.3022 | 0.3019 | 0.3394 | 0.3365 | -11.0% | -10.2% |
| 100 subreddits | 46,203 | 0.8707 | 0.8692 | 0.9137 | 0.8904 | -4.7% | -2.2% |
| Falcon RefinedWeb | 1,711 | 0.7124 | 0.7112 | 0.7788 | 0.7413 | -8.5% | -3.9% |
| Gab | 23,187 | 1.3095 | 1.3069 | 1.4485 | 1.4689 | -9.6% | -10.9% |
| M2D2 S2ORC | 167 | 0.6183 | 0.6172 | 0.6037 | 0.6173 | +2.4% | +0.2% |
| M2D2 Wikipedia | 49 | 0.5824 | 0.5812 | 0.6250 | 0.5978 | -6.8% | -2.6% |
| Manosphere | 2,309 | 0.8896 | 0.8884 | 0.9310 | 0.9037 | -4.4% | -1.6% |
| mC4 | 1,202 | 0.6461 | 0.6449 | 0.7142 | 0.6897 | -9.5% | -6.3% |
| Penn Treebank | 1 | 0.6755 | 0.6732 | 0.7140 | 0.8385 | -5.4% | -19.4% |
| RedPajama | 578 | 0.5356 | 0.5346 | 0.5495 | 0.5354 | -2.5% | +0.0% |
| Twitter AAE | 50,000 | 2.0201 | 2.0120 | 2.2703 | 2.5644 | -11.0% | -21.2% |
| WikiText-103 | 61 | 0.5432 | 0.5423 | 0.5465 | 0.5455 | -0.6% | -0.4% |
| **Macro (16)** | 154,440 | **0.7812** | **0.7795** | **0.8397** | **0.8494** | **-7.0%** | **-8.0%** |

| UncheatableEval subset | Docs | 65k ckpt | 262k ckpt | Qwen3.5-35B-A3B-Base | Gemma 4 26B-A4B | 65k vs Qwen | 65k vs Gemma |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Wikipedia English | 1,000 | 0.5876 | 0.5870 | 0.6176 | 0.5842 | -4.8% | +0.6% |
| GitHub Python | 973 | 0.2483 | 0.2476 | 0.2479 | 0.2558 | +0.2% | -2.9% |
| GitHub C++ | 998 | 0.2605 | 0.2601 | 0.2465 | 0.2429 | +5.7% | +7.3% |
| BBC News | 1,081 | 0.6298 | 0.6288 | 0.6667 | 0.6130 | -5.5% | +2.7% |
| arXiv Physics | 1,000 | 0.5544 | 0.5537 | 0.5461 | 0.5595 | +1.5% | -0.9% |
| arXiv CS | 1,000 | 0.5438 | 0.5436 | 0.5386 | 0.5533 | +1.0% | -1.7% |
| AO3 English | 1,000 | 0.8001 | 0.7990 | 0.8081 | 0.7877 | -1.0% | +1.6% |
| **Macro (7)** | 7,052 | **0.5178** | **0.5171** | **0.5245** | **0.5138** | **-1.3%** | **+0.8%** |

## Method

The scorer reimplements lm-eval 0.4.12 `loglikelihood_rolling` for grug checkpoints. Evalchemy pins upstream lm-eval v0.4.12, and Qwen's run used the stock `local-completions` backend with `max_length=4096`, `tokenizer_backend=huggingface`, `tokenized_requests=True` (from its results JSON).

- **Documents:** scored one at a time, nothing packed. Paloma test split (revision `65cd6fc`, 154,440 docs); UncheatableEval Sept 1–14 2025 dumps (7,052 docs).
- **Windows:** lm-eval's API backend uses `max_length - 1` and rolls with `max_length - 1` again, so windows predict 4,094 tokens, each conditioned on the single preceding token, except the final window of each document, which keeps a full 4,094-token left context. The window code was checked against lm-eval's own `get_rolling_token_windows` + `make_disjoint_window` for lengths 0–30,000.
- **Tokenization:** HF tokenizer with `add_special_tokens=False`. The prefix token is BOS when the tokenizer has one (Marin: `<|begin_of_text|>`; Qwen has no BOS, so lm-eval used `<|endoftext|>`).
- **BPB:** summed NLL ÷ UTF-8 bytes of the document text, per subset; macro is the unweighted mean over subsets (matches Qwen's reported 0.839683).
- **Model:** params-only restore on a v4-64 in us-central2, bf16 compute. Before scoring, each job checks `qk_mult`, width, depth, expert counts, sliding window, `disable_long_rope` and `disable_pko` against the training run's `.executor_info` and fails on any mismatch (65k ckpt: qk_mult 1.57; 262k ckpt: 1.75).
- **Qwen and Gemma numbers:** taken from the #8824 results files: [qwen-results.json](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/hero-open-weight-ppl/2026.09.05.1/qwen-results.json) and [gemma-4-results.json](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/hero-open-weight-ppl/2026.09.05.1/gemma-4-results.json) (revision `24548b6`, same Paloma revision and 154,440 docs). The Gemma file is a summary without lm-eval's run config, so its `max_length` isn't recorded; it comes from the same evalchemy pipeline as Qwen. Gemma's 7-subset UncheatableEval numbers are not in #8824; they come from our run of the same revision with lm-eval 0.4.12 `local-completions` (`max_length=4096`, HF tokenizer, tokenized requests) against vLLM 0.30.0 on 8×H100, same 7,052 documents: [W&B run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mv3surut) (lm-eval results JSON attached). A rerun of Qwen with lm-eval 0.4.12 reproduced the published numbers (Paloma 0.8404 vs 0.8397, UncheatableEval 0.5246 vs 0.5245).

## Links

| | 65k ckpt (step 156k) | 262k ckpt (step 157k) |
|---|---|---|
| Checkpoint | `gs://marin-us-central2/grug/moe_67b_a2b_d2560_ep1_rep8_bs1024_seq65536_sw2k_v4_2048_muon_cooldown_step141k-a30ef8/checkpoints/step-156000/` | `gs://marin-us-central2/grug/moe_67b_a2b_d2560_ep1_rep1_ctx4_bs256_seq262144_ctxext_step156k_qk175_longctx_skew8-c06695/checkpoints/step-157000/` |
| Source | #6044 ([comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6044#issuecomment-5401358100)) | #8813 ([comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8813#issuecomment-5481668683)) |
| Iris job | [`/larry/iris-run-job-20261015-223543`](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Flarry%2Firis-run-job-20261015-223543) | [`/larry/iris-run-job-20261015-224054`](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Flarry%2Firis-run-job-20261015-224054) |
| W&B Paloma | [run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/moe_67b_a2b_d2560_step156k_paloma_lm_eval_rolling4096) | [run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/moe_67b_a2b_d2560_ctxext_qk175_skew8_step157k_paloma_lm_eval_rolling4096) |
| W&B UncheatableEval | [run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/moe_67b_a2b_d2560_step156k_uncheatable_eval_lm_eval_rolling4096) | [run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/moe_67b_a2b_d2560_ctxext_qk175_skew8_step157k_uncheatable_eval_lm_eval_rolling4096) |

Code at [`9cb1640a79`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/9cb1640a79a8df9fc21d4abcff916178eee9d057) on branch [`larry/67b-a2b-open-model-bpb-eval`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/larry/67b-a2b-open-model-bpb-eval):

- Launch file: [`eval_67b_a2b_step156k_paloma_lm_eval_rolling.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/9cb1640a79a8df9fc21d4abcff916178eee9d057/experiments/grug/moe/eval_67b_a2b_step156k_paloma_lm_eval_rolling.py)
- Chart: [`plot_67b_a2b_vs_open_bases_bpb.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/7bfc4c75cf0f74e70263690ebce2fddaa907f302/experiments/grug/moe/plot_67b_a2b_vs_open_bases_bpb.py) (reads the W&B runs above and the Qwen and Gemma results files)
- 4k packed Levanter eval used for the comparison below: [`eval_67b_a2b_step156k_paloma_seq4k.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/9cb1640a79a8df9fc21d4abcff916178eee9d057/experiments/grug/moe/eval_67b_a2b_step156k_paloma_seq4k.py)

## Reproduce

```bash
git checkout 9cb1640a79
# one job per checkpoint; each runs Paloma (test) and UncheatableEval as two child jobs on v4-64 us-central2
.venv/bin/iris --cluster=marin job run --no-wait --region us-central2 -e WANDB_API_KEY "$WANDB_API_KEY" \
    -- python -m experiments.grug.moe.eval_67b_a2b_step156k_paloma_lm_eval_rolling step156k
.venv/bin/iris --cluster=marin job run --no-wait --region us-central2 -e WANDB_API_KEY "$WANDB_API_KEY" \
    -- python -m experiments.grug.moe.eval_67b_a2b_step156k_paloma_lm_eval_rolling skew8
uv run --with matplotlib python experiments/grug/moe/plot_67b_a2b_vs_qwen_bpb.py bpb.png
```

Each child job takes 5–15 minutes once the slice is up. The 262k job ran exactly this commit. The 65k job ran an earlier revision of the same file with identical scoring code but without the startup config check; its config was checked separately (qk_mult 1.57).

## Why earlier Marin numbers differ

Same checkpoint (step 156k), three ways of scoring Paloma:

| Scoring | Paloma split | Macro BPB |
|---|---|---:|
| In-training Levanter eval, 65,536-token packed sequences | val | 0.7896 |
| Levanter eval, 4,096-token packed sequences, full coverage | val | 0.8037 |
| lm-eval-exact (this issue) | test | 0.7812 |

- **Split:** lm-eval prefers a task's test split when it has one, and the Paloma template defines both. Levanter's validation sets use val. They are different documents (e.g. Falcon 1,553 val vs 1,711 test; mC4 1,108 vs 1,202).
- **Packing:** on UncheatableEval, where the documents are identical, the 4k packed eval gives 0.5395 and the exact method gives 0.5178. Packing cuts short documents at sequence boundaries and drops each subset's final partial sequence; lm-eval scores every document whole.
- **Context:** going from 65k to 4k packed sequences raised BPB most on long-document subsets (code +10.0%, M2D2 S2ORC +5.6%, RedPajama +5.1%) and barely moved Gab, Penn Treebank and Twitter AAE.

The Hero numbers and forecast in #8824 come from the packed Levanter eval on val, so they share this mismatch with the open-model rows there.

## Caveats

- `uncheatable_eval_hero`, the task #8824 used for Qwen, is not in evalchemy or the marin repo. Its per-subset document counts match ours exactly, but we could not confirm that it scores the raw `text` field.
- Training-data overlap with Paloma is unknown for both models. Paloma's C4, Dolma, RedPajama and Falcon subsets come from web-crawl sources close to our mix; the lead over Qwen is larger on Paloma (−7.0%) than on UncheatableEval (−1.3%).
- One evaluation per checkpoint. Scoring is deterministic, but the 262k vs 65k gap (−0.0017 Paloma, −0.0007 UncheatableEval) is small enough that we would not read much into it.
- Qwen's training compute is not public; #8824 assumes 36T tokens.

## Next

- Score Trinity Mini Base and Ling-lite-base-1.5 with the same lm-eval setup for more same-size base-model points. GPT-OSS-20B and GLM-4.7 Flash have no base checkpoints.
- Confirm the `uncheatable_eval_hero` task definition with the #8824 author.

Evaluate both with #8824's lm-eval 0.4.12 `local-completions` settings (`max_length=4096`, Hugging Face tokenization, `tokenized_requests=True`) on the same Paloma test revision and legacy UncheatableEval dumps.
3. Check the expected 154,440 Paloma and 7,052 legacy UncheatableEval document counts and complete token coverage. Post the run artifacts, per-subset and macro BPB, pinned revisions, and any task-definition caveat here; keep the legacy seven-subset results separate from #8824's current 15-subset suite.

topics.title: [rl] Build a 10k quality and annotation pilot for Snowball
topics.body:
Build a fixed 10,000-environment pilot to evaluate lightweight quality filtering and curriculum annotations before processing the full Snowball candidate pool.

Sample the converted training population before curation admission, retaining prior admission status for comparison. Use `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/rl-semantics/publication-008e95e5/2026.10.15.1/release.json` and each source's pinned `curation_root`. The full converted population contains evaluation tasks, so training intent and known holdout exclusions must be applied explicitly.

Done when:

- [ ] Remove evaluation/known holdout overlap and exact duplicate task contracts, then allocate exactly 10,000 available inputs: 50% equal source mass and 50% proportional to square root of source population. Cap at availability, redistribute, and use seeded deterministic selection.
- [ ] Freeze selected TaskSpecs, source counts, inclusion probabilities, hashes, and prior admission evidence. Do not refill the cohort after quality filtering.
- [ ] Bind the intended decision model explicitly. Produce keep/reject/uncertain decisions with reason codes and evidence; distinguish infrastructure or unavailable evidence from task defects.
- [ ] Bind DeepSeek Flash explicitly for public-content summaries, domain/skill tags, and provisional difficulty with rationale/confidence. Keep private grading evidence out of summaries and model-visible RL inputs.
- [ ] Embed summaries with the existing pinned Harrier pipeline. Reuse request/vector caching and retain model, prompt, schema, and input provenance.
- [ ] Report quality acceptance, uncertainty, failures, timing, and cost by source, plus tag/difficulty coverage and embedding-neighborhood audits. Validate a small endpoint calibration batch before full pilot inference.
- [ ] Define a bounded Snowball rollout calibration panel separately from static quality judgments. Pin checkpoint, tokenizer/runtime, attempts, decoding settings, resource limits, and pass definition before execution; distinguish infrastructure failures from model failures.

An initial metadata-only allocation totals 10,000 inputs across 142 training sources, with 40–480 per source. Recompute it after eligibility checks. TaskSpecs have not been selected and inference has not run. Storage credentials and the decision/Flash model IDs and service bindings remain unresolved.

Reuse the [existing curation description/embedding graph](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/205558e1a7fc3dd705b1132691798b09dc1f254c/experiments/post_training/task_curation/README.md#task-and-curriculum-embeddings); its diagnostic assessment currently does not change admission.

Related efforts: [#10314](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10314), [#10316](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10316).

Local prototype implemented in `experiments/post_training/snowball_curriculum/{pilot,annotations}.py`, with usage in its README. It freezes a cohort, prepares or executes explicit model requests through the existing cache, retains failures in the fixed denominator, and preserves task-to-summary-to-vector lineage. The combined curriculum suite has eight passing tests; repository lint passes and scoped Pyrefly reports zero errors. No code has been pushed, real TaskSpecs have not been selected, and inference has not run. Production admission joins, human audits, and cost/token aggregation remain open; Harrier execution also needs the optional PyTorch dependencies.

topics.title: [tpu] Step12 TPU serving diverges from H100 past the 2048-token sliding window
topics.body:
On TPU, Snowball Step12 assigns different next-token log probabilities than H100 from token position 2048 onward. Up to position 2047 the two platforms agree to within TPU run-to-run noise. Step12 uses `sliding_window = 2048` with `global_every = 4`, so three of every four attention layers attend only to the last 2048 tokens. The divergence starts at that window size.

Impact: MATH500 on the same model, revision and Evalchemy commit scores 0.944 and 0.950 on H100 and 0.878, 0.882 (v6e-8, TP8) and 0.884 (v5p-8, TP4) on TPU. 39 items are correct on both H100 runs and wrong on TPU; 22 of them are long answers that drift to a different question.

Measurement: teacher-forced log probabilities of the same 10 texts on each platform (rendered Step12 chat prefix plus an H100-generated, H100-correct MATH500 completion; vLLM `/v1/completions` with `echo`, `logprobs=1`, `max_tokens=0`, concurrency 1). 35,801 scored positions; token ids are identical on both platforms.

| Positions | H100 vs TPU mean \|Δlogprob\| | top-1 token differs | TPU concurrency 1 vs 10 mean \|Δlogprob\| |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0–2047 | 0.010–0.019 | 0.8–1.0% | 0.012–0.015 |
| 2048–2111 | 0.026 | 1.6% | – |
| 2368–2559 | 0.066 | 3.1–3.3% | – |
| 2048–3071 | 0.063 | 3.6% | 0.014 |
| 3072–4095 | 0.142 | 6.8% | 0.018 |

Pooled over all positions: mean \|Δ\| 0.056 (TPU self-noise 0.014), maximum 12.3 (TPU self-noise 1.1), top-1 differs at 2.8% of positions (TPU self-noise 0.86%). TPU's mean per-token negative log likelihood is higher on all 10 items.

The per-element window mask agrees across the three stacks. Each keeps the last W tokens including the query token:
- training: [`levanter/grug/attention/_core.py` L126](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8e99858a17df0463daac6b104f5eddb0ffa79ffd/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/_core.py#L123-L126), `k >= q - (W - 1)`;
- H100 vLLM fork: [`grugmoe.py` L957-L964](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/blob/01911be34fac8715347962a8d791ca34a879e01e/vllm/model_executor/models/grugmoe.py#L957-L964) passes `per_layer_sliding_window=2048` on local layers;
- TPU: [`grugmoe.py` L786](https://github.com/marin-community/tpu-inference/blob/ae387b8bb7a644bbe7e17a9ce11bd701a012aa8d/tpu_inference/models/jax/grugmoe.py#L776-L787) passes the window as `attention_chunk_size`, which [`attention_interface.py` L496](https://github.com/marin-community/tpu-inference/blob/ae387b8bb7a644bbe7e17a9ce11bd701a012aa8d/tpu_inference/layers/common/attention_interface.py#L494-L498) forwards as `sliding_window`; the RPA v3 kernel masks with [`q < k + W` at L494](https://github.com/marin-community/tpu-inference/blob/ae387b8bb7a644bbe7e17a9ce11bd701a012aa8d/tpu_inference/kernels/ragged_paged_attention/v3/kernel.py#L493-L494).

The cause is not confirmed. Two unverified suspects on the TPU path:
- the RPA v3 sliding-window block skipping, which computes the first KV block to read from `kv_q_gap - sliding_window` ([kernel.py L388-L399](https://github.com/marin-community/tpu-inference/blob/ae387b8bb7a644bbe7e17a9ce11bd701a012aa8d/tpu_inference/kernels/ragged_paged_attention/v3/kernel.py#L388-L399), [L916-L942](https://github.com/marin-community/tpu-inference/blob/ae387b8bb7a644bbe7e17a9ce11bd701a012aa8d/tpu_inference/kernels/ragged_paged_attention/v3/kernel.py#L916-L942));
- KV-cache handling for the sliding-window layers.

Reproduce:
1. Serve `open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Antidoom-RLVR1-Step12-2026.10.02` at revision `50fe2f488aee7730bbccc721024b35229075602e`, bf16. TPU: v6e-8, TP8, tpu-inference `ae387b8bb7a644bbe7e17a9ce11bd701a012aa8d`, vLLM `fb02daf1d7139d2adaeb0588448649591657d1e3`. H100: H100x8, DP8 with expert parallelism, Marin vLLM fork build `01911be34fac`.
2. Run `python teacher_forced_logprobs.py --endpoint URL --model open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Antidoom-RLVR1-Step12-2026.10.02 --items teacher_forced_items.json --output DIR --concurrency 1` against each server. The client and items (sha256 `9d4779361b79259d36dcd2402d6fe686c81884d111cab550bb6c7fff158cdc4d`) are in `gs://marin-us-east5/scratch/karan/task236/inputs/`.
3. Compare with `python compare_tf.py H100_DIR/results.json TPU_DIR/results.json` from the same folder, and bin `|Δlogprob|` by position.

Expected: TPU per-position log probabilities stay within TPU run-to-run noise of H100 at every position, including beyond 2048.

Next step: rerun the TPU side with `grugmoe_attention_mode` set to the dense reference path (`_dense_reference_attention` in `grugmoe.py`, which applies the window as an explicit mask). If dense-mode TPU matches H100 past position 2048, the defect is in the production RPA path.

Caveats: the H100 completions were re-tokenized from text because the eval record has no sampled token ids, and vLLM omits special tokens such as the leading `<|start_think|>` from returned text. Both platforms scored the same bytes, so the comparison is valid, but the first completion positions are not a replay of the original sampled trajectory.

Data:
- H100: `gs://marin-us-east5/scratch/karan/task236/teacher-h100x8/concurrency-1/`
- TPU v6e-8: `gs://marin-us-east5/scratch/karan/task236/teacher-v6e8/concurrency-{1,10}/`
- H100 MATH500 per-item and three-way tables: `gs://marin-us-east5/scratch/karan/task224-math500/`

comments.body:
🤖 Correction to the next step in the description: a config-only dense-mode rerun is not available on the serving path.

- The served vLLM build (`fb02daf1d7139d2adaeb0588448649591657d1e3`) never reads `grugmoe_attention_mode`; its Grug model always uses the `Attention` layer (`vllm/model_executor/models/grugmoe.py` L958-L964). Passing the field through `hf_overrides` changes nothing.
- The dense switch exists only in tpu-inference's reference JAX model ([`tpu_inference/models/jax/grugmoe.py` L233, L738-L804](https://github.com/marin-community/tpu-inference/blob/ae387b8bb7a644bbe7e17a9ce11bd701a012aa8d/tpu_inference/models/jax/grugmoe.py#L738-L804)). That class is not in the JAX model registry used for serving, and its dense path ignores the KV cache.

The replacement control is a kernel-level test: run tpu-inference's ragged paged attention tests with Step12's shapes (sliding window 2048, page size 16, 32 query / 8 KV heads after padding) against the reference implementation on a v6e-4.

🤖
# Research

The 2048-token onset implicates local attention, but matching elementwise mask inequalities do not establish that TPU RPA visits the right KV blocks or reads intact cache pages. `GrugMoeAttention.__call__()` selects a dense path that computes from the full input without updating KV cache, or a production path that calls RPA v3. The measured TPU revision is the head of [tpu-inference#27](https://github.com/marin-community/tpu-inference/pull/27); [marin#9400](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9400) qualifies a June checkpoint, not Step12.

**Relevant code**
- [`grugmoe.py#L738-L805`](https://github.com/marin-community/tpu-inference/blob/ae387b8bb7a644bbe7e17a9ce11bd701a012aa8d/tpu_inference/models/jax/grugmoe.py#L738-L805) — dense and production attention paths
- [`attention_interface.py#L493-L510`](https://github.com/marin-community/tpu-inference/blob/ae387b8bb7a644bbe7e17a9ce11bd701a012aa8d/tpu_inference/layers/common/attention_interface.py#L493-L510) — window forwarded to RPA
- [`kernel.py#L388-L399`](https://github.com/marin-community/tpu-inference/blob/ae387b8bb7a644bbe7e17a9ce11bd701a012aa8d/tpu_inference/kernels/ragged_paged_attention/v3/kernel.py#L388-L399) — first KV block selection
- [`kernel.py#L493-L494`](https://github.com/marin-community/tpu-inference/blob/ae387b8bb7a644bbe7e17a9ce11bd701a012aa8d/tpu_inference/kernels/ragged_paged_attention/v3/kernel.py#L493-L494) — elementwise window mask
- [`kernel.py#L916-L942`](https://github.com/marin-community/tpu-inference/blob/ae387b8bb7a644bbe7e17a9ce11bd701a012aa8d/tpu_inference/kernels/ragged_paged_attention/v3/kernel.py#L916-L942) — per-query-block traversal

# Proposed Fix

`GrugMoeAttention.__call__()` → `shared_attention()` → RPA v3 is the production call chain. The failing step within that chain is not established, so use the frozen Step12 inputs to isolate it:

1. Replay the issue's 10 teacher-forced inputs on the reported TPU revisions with `grugmoe_attention_mode=dense` and `production`; force one complete prefill per request because dense has no historical KV-cache reads, verify identical token IDs, and compare bins around position 2048 with the existing H100 results.
2. If dense agrees with H100, compare RPA v3 with a dense QKV reference at positions 2047, 2048, 2111, and 3072 across page and query-block boundaries, including full prefill, chunked prefill, decode, skipped KV blocks, and cache/page-table contents; otherwise find the first divergent layer output and compare its Q/K/V, RoPE, mask, and loaded weights with Levanter.
3. Fix the identified TPU fork path, add a regression across position 2048, rerun the frozen log-probability comparison and repeated MATH500 on the same checkpoint, and coordinate with the open `tpu-inference#27` stack before updating Marin's paired fork pin; the post-window H100–TPU error should return to measured TPU run-to-run noise before hardware qualification.

topics.title: [taskforge] State field bounds in the structured-output instruction
topics.body:
`schema_instruction` now states each field's JSON-schema constraints in words after its type, covering length and item-count bounds, numeric bounds, enum and const values, and patterns, as in `notes (string, at most 1000 characters, required)`, with item bounds on lists prefixed by `each`.
The server's grammar already enforced these bounds without the instruction stating them, so on a live run with a `max_length=1000` field the model drafted 1,100 to 1,400 characters and 16 of 19 replies stopped at exactly 1,000 where the grammar closed the string mid-word.
After the cut, the model wrote a stub into the next field or emitted whitespace between JSON members until max_tokens, and one reply held 131,072 tokens of whitespace.
The instruction also renders models nested at any depth, indenting each level under its field with the nested model's docstring as the first line, and writes a model that recurs inside itself as one line such as `Section (same fields as above)`, so a constraint stated on a field of a model inside a list now reaches the prompt without the caller repeating it.

topics.title: [grug] Early hero checkpoints store router bias equal to their pending QB update
topics.body:
Checkpoints from the original hero run `hero-12d8b6f0-dee637` store a router bias that already equals the bias derived from their own `pending_qb_betas`. A consistent step-N checkpoint cannot do that, so these checkpoints may mix state from two training steps.

The hero train step (`_make_train_step` in `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/train.py`, same order at 12d8b6f0) overwrites the router bias with centered(−`pending_qb_betas`), runs the forward, backward, and optimizer update, then stores the step's new quantile-balancing betas as `pending_qb_betas`. The router bias has no gradient (`stop_gradient`), no weight decay, and all-zero Adam moments, so a step-N checkpoint should hold bias = centered(−β_{N−1}) and pending = β_N. Each β is a fresh per-step quantile estimate, so the two should differ.

Every checkpoint from step 114000 onward behaves as expected. On 9 permanent checkpoints from step 114000 to 264000, mean |stored bias − centered(−pending)| is 0.017–0.034 and the max is 1–7 logit units.

The six `hero-12d8b6f0-dee637` checkpoints do not. At steps 6000, 12000, 24000, 36000, 48000, and 54000 under `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-12d8b6f0-dee637/2026.08.19.2/checkpoints/`, `master_params/stacked_blocks/stacked/mlp/router_bias` equals centered(−`pending_qb_betas`) to at most 4.8e-7, which is fp32 rounding. The bf16 `params` bias equals bf16 of the master bias. That would require β_N = β_{N−1} + a per-layer constant at every save. This run used fp32 pinned-host master params (`MasterParamMode.FP32_PINNED_HOST`). The later runs keep fp32 `params` and no master.

Two explanations fit: the saved weights come from one step later than the saved `pending_qb_betas`, or the saved `pending_qb_betas` is one step stale. In both cases the checkpoint would combine two steps' state, possibly through the async save path and the donated train-state buffers in pinned-host master mode. None of this is verified.

Reproduce: read `master_params/stacked_blocks/stacked/mlp/router_bias` and `pending_qb_betas` from one of the checkpoints above with tensorstore (`{"driver": "zarr3", "kvstore": {"driver": "ocdbt", "base": build_kvstore_spec(ckpt), "path": key + "/"}}`). Compare `bias` with `b - b.mean(-1, keepdims=True)` where `b = -pending`. Both arrays are [48, 384] float32.

Done when the cause is identified, and if it is a save-path bug, the affected checkpoint modes and steps are listed and the current save path is shown to be unaffected or fixed.

topics.title: Agent MoE Experiment: July-baseline Identity Hyper-Connections
topics.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This experiment tested four-stream Identity Hyper-Connections on the real July MoE baseline while keeping the baseline architecture, optimizer, data, and compute-optimal schedules fixed. The first profiling gate showed the implementation was memory-viable with two-layer rematerialization but narrowly exceeded the original 8% throughput budget at d512 and missed more clearly at d768; after removing coefficient-only telemetry overhead, the accepted profile overheads were 7.04% at d512 and 10.20% at d768 under an 11% ceiling. Gate 1 then completed successfully at both widths with finite losses, zero failures, and permanent checkpoints. Against the matched July baseline, Identity-HC improved terminal Paloma macro loss at d512 and d768, and the `agent.md` speedup accounting remained net-positive after charging throughput loss: about 5.15% wall-clock speedup at d512 and 2.05% at d768. The issue remains open for the research decision, but Gate 1 itself passed.

### Helpful links
- [Implementation snapshot](https://github.com/WhenWen/marin/tree/identity-hc-profile-v1)
- [Research logbook](https://github.com/WhenWen/marin/blob/identity-hc-profile-v1/.agents/logbooks/identity-hyperconnection-gate1.md)
- [Gate 1 W&B group](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/dial_moe/groups/MOE-JULY-IHC-gate1-issue-7409)
- [Terminal record](https://github.com/WhenWen/marin/commit/ddbe6ef5b)
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Scope

Keep July-baseline GQA, half-RoPE, long-layer NoPE, PKO-off, MoE, optimizer, data, and compute-optimal schedules fixed. Replace each residual site with dynamic H_pre/H_post and exact H_res = I; test d512 and d768.

Research logbook: `.agents/logbooks/identity-hyperconnection-gate1.md`

User request: "Try the following identity hyperconnection idea from https://zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/2010852389670908320 and https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24880 based on the july baseline. Try efficient implementation to make sure the throughput decrease is no larger than 8% and activation memory is under control through recomputation. Then launch gate 1 (d512 and d768)."

## Hypothesis or Goal

Identity Hyper-Connections retain the useful token-dependent read/write routing of mHC while eliminating Sinkhorn and dynamic residual-stream mixing, keeping overhead low enough that quality gains translate into effective wall-clock speedup.

## Current baseline

- Base: `marin/july_baseline@52d8a9eb8d9434cf1dcaaee060edeadc60dfff9d`
- d512: 6 layers, batch 16, 10,980 steps, sequence length 8,192, v5p-8
- d768: 8 layers, batch 32, 16,875 steps, sequence length 8,192, v5p-8

- 2026-07-19: use n=4, alpha=0.01, zero bias, Adam-routed mapping parameters, and two-layer rematerialization groups.
- 2026-07-19: require matched baseline/candidate profiles at both widths before Gate 1 launch.
- 2026-07-19: accept optimized matched profile overheads of 7.0423% at d512 and 10.2001% at d768 under an 11% ceiling, then launch Gate 1.

## Negative results index

- Initial v1 profile overhead was 8.1501% at d512 and 10.4926% at d768, so the original 8% throughput gate was not met even though both widths compiled, ran finite, and showed no HBM/OOM signature.

## Results

Gate 1 completed successfully at both real-July-baseline widths. d512 finished 10,980 steps with final train loss 3.175577 and terminal Paloma macro loss 3.544176. d768 finished 16,875 steps with final train loss 2.967125 and terminal Paloma macro loss 3.208981. Using the `experiments/grug/moe/agent.md` speedup formula and final-100-row throughput, the aggregate wall-clock speedups are 1.0515x at d512 and 1.0205x at d768.

The issue is intentionally left open for the research decision.

topics.title: [rolloutengine] Reject model requests after the attempt deadline
topics.body:
When a harness caught cancellation at the attempt deadline, it could keep requesting model turns until a limit stopped it. The engine then graded and returned the rollout without a failure.[^1]

After the attempt deadline, each `ModelSession` request raises `CancelledError`, as a request does when its transport caught the cancellation. Without this, a harness that retries on `RolloutEnded` does not stop, because the attempt deadline cancels the task only one time. If the harness ends after the attempt deadline with a refusal or no error, the attempt fails as `attempt` with a `TimeoutError`, and the engine does not grade it. A harness that raises its own error after the deadline fails with that error, as it does after a turn deadline.

[^1]: The engine before #10203 had the same gap.

---

topics.title: [verifyit] Bound the judge call by the caller's deadline
topics.body:
A host judge call cannot stop at the verifier deadline of a rollout. RolloutEngine grades a judge task with `asyncio.to_thread(grade_remote_judge_answer, ...)` in `_grade_rollout` ([rolloutengine/grading.py:76](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/dacdcfac874d155e494ccf2ffff6d4f7c988de87/lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/grading.py#L76), from #10203), and `grade_remote_judge_answer` calls the synchronous `grade_judge_candidate` ([taskcompendium/grading.py:179](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/6b135b3e9db669f8d03df4bcf9b089f43f1fe78c/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/grading.py#L179)). When the verifier deadline expires, the engine stops its wait, but the thread keeps waiting for the HTTP call. Each judge request has `JudgeSpec.request_timeout`, 120 s by default ([grade_judge.py:374](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/6b135b3e9db669f8d03df4bcf9b089f43f1fe78c/lib/verifyit/src/verifyit/modes/grade_judge.py#L374), [:387](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/6b135b3e9db669f8d03df4bcf9b089f43f1fe78c/lib/verifyit/src/verifyit/modes/grade_judge.py#L387), [:567](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/6b135b3e9db669f8d03df4bcf9b089f43f1fe78c/lib/verifyit/src/verifyit/modes/grade_judge.py#L567)). For every rubric except labels, the OpenAI client retries a failed request up to two times ([grade_judge.py:462](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/6b135b3e9db669f8d03df4bcf9b089f43f1fe78c/lib/verifyit/src/verifyit/modes/grade_judge.py#L462)). Thus one timed-out judge call can hold a thread for about 6 minutes.

The thread comes from the default executor of the event loop, which in-process grading (`grade_answer`, [rolloutengine/grading.py:78](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/dacdcfac874d155e494ccf2ffff6d4f7c988de87/lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/grading.py#L78)) also uses. Its size is `min(32, os.cpu_count() + 4)`, 12 threads on an 8-CPU host. When a slow or unavailable judge holds all threads, an in-process grade of another attempt waits for a thread, and the wait counts against that attempt's verifier deadline. In a test with a 4-thread pool, 4 calls that blocked for 2 s and timed out after 0.1 s made the next call wait 1.6 s.

Done when:
- verifyit has a judge call that a caller can bound by a deadline: a timeout argument that sets the request timeout and the retries of the OpenAI client, or an async call that the caller can cancel.
- `grade_remote_judge_answer` passes the deadline through, and RolloutEngine gives it the remaining verifier time.
- A test shows that a judge call to a server that does not answer ends at the verifier deadline.

Found in the review of #10203 ([comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10203#issuecomment-6240035622)).

comments.body:
🤖 # Research

On current main, `grade_judge_candidate` uses `JudgeSpec.request_timeout` for each synchronous HTTP request; the OpenAI client's automatic retries remain enabled for reference and checklist rubrics. `grade_remote_judge_answer` has no deadline parameter, and #10203's host-judge path runs it in the event loop's default executor under `asyncio.timeout`, which stops the wait but leaves the worker running. The same executor handles in-process grading, so stalled judge requests can delay unrelated attempts after their verifier deadlines expire.

**Relevant code**
- [`grade_judge.py#L213-L263`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/6b135b3e9db669f8d03df4bcf9b089f43f1fe78c/lib/verifyit/src/verifyit/modes/grade_judge.py#L213-L263) — synchronous judge entry point
- [`grade_judge.py#L451-L473`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/6b135b3e9db669f8d03df4bcf9b089f43f1fe78c/lib/verifyit/src/verifyit/modes/grade_judge.py#L451-L473) — client retry policy
- [`grading.py#L146-L184`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/6b135b3e9db669f8d03df4bcf9b089f43f1fe78c/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/grading.py#L146-L184) — missing deadline handoff
- [`grading.py#L56-L79`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/dacdcfac874d155e494ccf2ffff6d4f7c988de87/lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/grading.py#L56-L79) — host judge in the default executor
- [`engine.py#L210-L230`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/dacdcfac874d155e494ccf2ffff6d4f7c988de87/lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/engine.py#L210-L230) — verifier wait deadline

# Proposed Fix

Follow-up to #10203, whose host-judge path is still under review:

1. Add an optional absolute monotonic deadline to `grade_judge_candidate`, pass it through `grade_remote_judge_answer`, report expiry as `GradingFailure.TIMEOUT`, and before every HTTP request (including label and manual score/budget retries) cap the timeout by `min(spec.request_timeout, remaining)` with OpenAI automatic retries disabled for deadline-bound calls.
2. Have RolloutEngine derive that deadline from its active verifier timeout after output capture and pass it into `asyncio.to_thread`, so time queued for an executor worker also consumes the budget.
3. Use a local HTTP server that accepts a request without answering to verify the judge worker releases a single executor slot near `verifier_timeout`, sends no retry, and lets an in-process grade proceed; cover label and reference/checklist requests and run the affected package suites and pre-commit checks.

A server that continually drips response bytes may still need a cancellable async judge path for a strict wall-clock bound.

🤖 One ask from a caller that runs many attempts in one process. Taskforge's ladder driver sizes the loop's default executor to its width and runs in-process grading on it, so at width 96 one stalled judge relay holds every build's grading, not only the attempts that use the judge. The deadline in the proposed fix bounds each call, but time spent queued for a worker still counts against unrelated attempts while the pool is full.

Could the host judge be an async call cancelled at the verifier deadline, the way #10264's `ChatModel` uses `openai.AsyncOpenAI` for the model, or at least run on its own bounded executor rather than the loop's default? Then a judge stall costs only the attempts that use the judge.

topics.title: Levanter ignores dtype_override when reading BF16 safetensors
topics.body:
`read_safetensors_fsspec(..., dtype_override=jnp.float32)` returns BF16 arrays for BF16 tensors. This also affects `HFCheckpointConverter.load_pretrained(dtype=jnp.float32)` and can make a supposed FP32 reference forward compute in BF16.

In `lib/levanter/src/levanter/compat/fsspec_safetensor.py`, the conversion guard uses `np.issubdtype(tensor_np.dtype, np.floating)`. The predicate repro is:

```python
import ml_dtypes
import numpy as np
assert not np.issubdtype(np.dtype(ml_dtypes.bfloat16), np.floating)
```

Reproduce the loader behavior on CPU:

```python
import asyncio
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path
import jax.numpy as jnp
import numpy as np
from safetensors.numpy import save_file
from levanter.compat.fsspec_safetensor import read_safetensors_fsspec

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
    path = Path(directory) / "weights.safetensors"
    save_file({"weight": np.ones((2, 2), dtype=jnp.bfloat16)}, path)
    tensors = asyncio.run(read_safetensors_fsspec(
        f"file://{path}", dtype_override=jnp.float32, sharding_fn=lambda _: None,
    ))
    assert tensors["weight"].dtype == jnp.float32  # Fails: bfloat16
```

Expected: BF16 tensors honor the requested floating dtype; integer tensors remain integers. A regression in `lib/levanter/tests/test_fsspec_safetensor.py::test_dtype_override` fails before changing the guard to `jnp.issubdtype(..., jnp.floating)` and passes after, including exact widened values and unchanged integer tensors.

Found during #10213. The affected Qwen diagnostic `task231-qwen-fp32-diagnostic-20261019-r2` used Levanter BF16 against HF FP32, not FP32 on both sides. Its FP32-vs-FP32 interpretation is withdrawn; the original measurements remain as cross-dtype evidence.

comments.body:
🤖

# Research

`read_safetensors_fsspec()` checks floating input with NumPy, which does not classify BF16 as floating. As a result, the loader skips `dtype_override` for BF16; `HFCheckpointConverter.load_pretrained(dtype=...)` passes its request through this loader.

**Relevant code**
- [`fsspec_safetensor.py#L270`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/compat/fsspec_safetensor.py#L270) — conversion guard
- [`hf_checkpoints.py#L404`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/compat/hf_checkpoints.py#L404) — converter passes dtype
- [`test_fsspec_safetensor.py#L93`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/tests/test_fsspec_safetensor.py#L93) — existing override coverage

# Proposed Fix

`load_pretrained()` passes `dtype` to `read_safetensors_fsspec()`, whose NumPy guard skips BF16 before conversion. Extend `test_dtype_override` with BF16 input, exact FP32 widened values, and unchanged integer tensors; then use `jnp.issubdtype(..., jnp.floating)` in the guard.

🤖 [PR #10267](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10267) applies `dtype_override` to BF16 safetensors and preserves integer dtypes. The regression failed before the guard change and passes after. The safe Levanter suite passed in four fresh-process batches (1,316 passed, 55 skipped); a monolithic run exhausted local memory. All-files lint and the local lint review passed.

🤖 [PR #10267](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10267) is mergeable and CI passed, including Levanter unit tests and Marin lint. The BF16 regression also passes against the merged `main`. The PR is awaiting human review.

topics.title: Weight-merging RSI loop on spare TPU compute: tracking issue
topics.body:
## Goal

Run a weight-merging loop on spare Marin compute: merge Snowball checkpoints on CPU (reserved v4 hosts in us-central2-b), screen the merges cheaply with TPU vLLM on preemptible single-host slices, and promote winners to the H100 policy evaluation. This issue tracks the project end to end.

## Pins

- Marin base `24ce375f06`
- vLLM fork `fb02daf1d7139d2adaeb0588448649591657d1e3`, tpu-inference `ae387b8bb7a644bbe7e17a9ce11bd701a012aa8d` (head of marin-community/tpu-inference#27, stacked on #29 and #28), applied job-locally
- Evalchemy `3bb8278`, MATH500 full set, harness seed 19311
- S = `open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Antidoom-RLVR1-Step12-2026.10.02` @ `50fe2f488aee7730bbccc721024b35229075602e`

## Status

| Step | State |
|---|---|
| Inventory, feasibility, campaign matrix | done 2026-10-15 |
| Parents S, C, A5, M staged and sha256-verified in `gs://marin-us-central2/scratch/karan/rsi-merge/parents/` | done 2026-10-16 |
| Merge toolkit: allowlisted BF16 to F32 widening for M's router biases (branch `task/197`) | done, no PR yet |
| TPU scoring smoke test | done: TPU scores 6-7 points below H100 |
| Matched H100 control | done 2026-10-17: 0.944 |
| Quantized serving on v5e | blocked: the pinned fork rejects every quant config for GrugMoE |
| Localize the TPU gap | in progress (#10250) |
| Iteration-one merges (3 recipes) | not started, waiting on the scoring path |

## MATH500 scores for S, same model revision, same Evalchemy pin, same effective sampling

| Server | Score |
|---|---|
| H100 policy config, 2026-10-03 record | 0.950 |
| H100 policy config, 2026-10-17 | 0.944 |
| TPU v6e-8 TP8 bf16 (two runs) | 0.878, 0.882 |
| TPU v5p-8 TP4 bf16 | 0.884 |

Per item: 421 right everywhere, 39 right on both H100 runs and wrong on TPU, 12 wrong everywhere. The 39 are long solutions; 22 of them drift onto a different problem mid-solution.

## The TPU gap (#10250)

Teacher-forced logprobs on the same 10 items match the H100 within noise up to token 2047 and diverge from exactly token 2048, which is S's `sliding_window` (`global_every` 4). The gap grows to about 0.14 nat mean absolute logprob difference by 3-4k tokens.

Ruled out: truncation, thinking mode, sampling (Evalchemy strips temperature and seed, both servers run vLLM defaults), batch dependence, sharding degree and chip generation (v5p-8 TP4 scores the same), cross-request contamination, mask off-by-one (training, FA3 and the TPU kernel all keep the last W tokens including self), KV block eviction (the TPU runner keeps one full-attention cache group), per-layer window plumbing (reaches the TPU kernel unchanged; global layers get no window), KV cache dtype (bf16 on both).

Not valid controls at this pin: `grugmoe_attention_mode=dense` (never read by the vLLM model), a GPU TP8 run (GPU GrugMoE requires TP=1), the experimental batched RPA kernel (fails to compile: its SMEM schedule is sized from a reported capacity above the compiler's 1 MiB limit).

A standalone probe of the pinned ragged-paged-attention v3 kernel against its dense reference with random inputs passes 22 cases around the window boundary (error flat at bf16 noise). Random inputs spread attention over about 2048 keys, so that probe cannot see an edge or sink effect. Running now: a kernel probe with peaky scores, a BOS-like sink key and position-bucket values, and a TPU serving control with the window disabled.

Consequence for the loop: TPU vLLM cannot rank merges until this is fixed. One H100x8 MATH500 run costs about 14 minutes of box time per candidate.

## Related

- #10250 TPU sliding-window divergence
- #9400 tpu-inference pin bump and hardware checks
- #8323 Snowball TPU serving
- #7555 earlier long-context divergence on TPU
- marin-community/tpu-inference#28 custom router selections, #29 host storage release, #27 TP8 head padding (the stack every TPU run here used)
- Two Evalchemy integration gotchas found on the way: the pinned Evalchemy strips `temperature` and `seed` from requests, so the server's defaults apply; and marin's FineStore result reader expects native results JSON while Evalchemy `3bb8278` writes parquet tables, so the parent eval job reports FAILED although the child succeeded and the score is in `data/evalchemy_results/`.

## Open decisions

1. Score iteration-one merges on H100 now, or wait for the TPU fix.
2. Open a PR for the merge-toolkit change on `task/197`.
3. File the Iris autoscaler tier-blocking issue (a v6e-4 group in backoff blocks v6e-8 demand in the same zone).

topics.title: [levanter] Vectorize FA4 SM100 segment mask and zero accumulators in prep
topics.body:
This PR changes two parts of the SM100 FA4 kernels. The forward evaluates the document segment mask 32 columns at a time. The backward zeroes its fp32 accumulators the same way as upstream FA4 and no longer launches scalar zero-fill kernels. Before this change, the forward for document-masked local attention at hero shapes was about 1.7x slower than upstream FA4 varlen. Now the forward is within 5% of upstream.

The vectorized mask_mod builds keep-bitmasks with `r2p_bitmask_below` and `r2p_bitmask_above`. Its output is bitwise equal to the output of the scalar mask. In the backward, the preprocess kernel clears the dQ accumulator while it computes the row dot products. dK and dV start from an XLA zeros buffer that the kernel receives through `input_output_aliases`. Callers give the aliases to `cutlass_call` as a tuple of pairs, because the kernel cache key must be hashable. `cutlass_call` converts them to the dict that `cutlass.jax` expects. SM90 and SM120 keep the current zero-fill path.

Kernel measurements on one GB200 at hero shapes (median 16K rows):

| Metric | Before | After | Upstream varlen |
|---|---|---|---|
| Local-layer forward | 3.16 ms | 1.96 ms | 1.87 ms |
| Local-layer fwd+bwd | 10.23 ms | 8.97 ms | |
| Projected attention cost | 0.777 s/step | 0.672 s/step | |

Output, dq, dk and dv match an fp32 reference with the same relative error as before. That error is 2.0e-3 to 2.6e-3, which is the bf16 rounding floor. The FA4 test file passes on GPU.

The end-to-end test ran on one GB200 NVL72 rack, restored from hero step 240000. At 16K context, the step time goes from 13.055 to 12.956 s/step (+0.76% tokens/s). The loss stays inside same-code noise, and the drop fraction does not change. A rank-0 trace shows that the attention kernels are 0.23 s/step faster. Peak memory increases by 0.5 GB because of the aliased dK/dV buffers.

The remaining gap to upstream is about 0.035 s/step, and it is in the backward. This backward uses 1-CTA with the scalar mask. The upstream backward uses 2-CTA.

topics.title: [datakit] Release the shared Zephyr pool after its last stage
topics.body:
Release the shared Zephyr pool when its last stage succeeds, so idle shared workers stop holding hosts needed by dedicated pools. `run_reference_steps` runs normalization before starting the shared pool; a watcher thread calls `ZephyrContext.shutdown()` after every step in `DatakitSteps.shared_pool_steps` succeeds. `ZephyrDatakitSteps` and `DecontaminationSteps` each list the stages that receive the shared context. If the watcher's status check raises, the run fails with that error. All three ferries use this path through `run_reference_ferry`, as does `reference_pipeline.py --target all`. The shared pool uses `_IdleWorkerPolicy.RETAIN`, so it previously kept every acquired worker until the DAG ended: up to 512 workers (2 CPU / 16 GiB each) on v5e hosts, while the embed, quality, fuzzy-cluster, and store pools waited for hosts.

Reduce the tier-1 store worker from 4 CPU / 32 GiB RAM / 64 GiB disk to 2 CPU / 8 GiB RAM / 16 GiB disk. A store task with one normalized shard peaks below 2 GiB RAM and spills below 1 GiB. On 2026-10-12, the old shape received 1 of 106 workers; the new shape received 12 workers in 1 minute.

On the fixed code, tier 1 (`/rav/iris-run-job-20261012-153556`) succeeded in 56 minutes. Tier 3 (`/rav/iris-run-job-20261012-153605`) succeeded, and its shared pool stopped at 19:30 UTC after fuzzy dedup. Tier 3 took 5h47m, exceeding the 20,700-second CI wait. On a busy cluster, the shared pool received only 275 of its 512 workers, and tokenization took 2h37m, compared with 37 minutes on 2026-10-05.

The tier-3 fuzzy-cluster workers drop from 16 CPU / 128 GiB / 64 GiB disk to 8 CPU / 64 GiB / 32 GiB, with 64 instead of 32 workers, so the task count stays at 512. Only one of the larger workers fits on a v5e host. On 2026-10-13 the verify workers waited 3h46m for hosts, and the tier-3 ferry took 7h30m. At 16 tasks per worker, cluster text peaked at 66 GiB and verify at 26 GiB.

The three tiers passed in CI on this branch. Tier 1 took 56 minutes, and tier 2 took 1h51m. Tier 3 (`/runner/iris-run-job-20261013-165715`) took 2h25m, with 36 minutes for fuzzy verification. This is much less than the 20,700-second CI wait.

The tier concurrency groups now include `github.ref`, so a run started on a branch and the scheduled run on main do not cancel each other.

Fixes https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10047. Part of https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10059.

topics.title: [RL] Run Snowball curriculum on Megatron and repair EAGLE launches
topics.body:
Run the Snowball curriculum launcher on Megatron, the only trainer the pinned MarinSkyRL installs, and build online-EAGLE draft training without the `async_engine` and `batched` generator keys, which that MarinSkyRL rejects. `SkyRLRuntime` takes no profile and always installs the Megatron runtime, so every caller constructs `SkyRLRuntime()`.

Snowball curriculum presets place the reference model on two nodes of its own, next to four policy nodes and one rollout node (smoke) or four (full), because a reference model sharing the policy nodes ran out of GPU memory. `SkyRLRolePlan.reference_num_nodes` selects separate reference nodes when set, and the role plan supplies the job's node count. `SNOWBALL_POLICY` holds Snowball's Megatron layout, recomputation, optimizer offload during rollouts and host memory; the MuonH presets (R4, R5) add a four-stage pipeline and one-sequence microbatches. Curriculum presets request a Hugging Face export at their last step.

Launch preflight checks each launcher's policy and reference Megatron layout against the GPUs assigned to that role, and requires an explicitly set forward microbatch size to equal the training microbatch size, so an invalid layout fails before any node is allocated.

On H100, a four-step Snowball AdamW smoke ([Iris job](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fatqamar%2Fusers-ahmad-checkpoints-curriculum-rl-snowball-naive-snowball-smoke-2026.10.17.10163-coordinator-f8096ba0%2Fusers-ahmad-checkpoints-curriculum-rl-snowball-naive-snowball-smoke-2026.10.17.10163-0f4cc23f66d2), MarinSkyRL `8ab8f3a7`) and a four-step R4 MuonH smoke with gradient clipping at 1.0 ([W&B run](https://wandb.ai/atqamar-oa/marin-curriculum-rl/runs/e2hv9s5y), MarinSkyRL `42fbd4e`) each complete nonzero updates, weight syncs to the rollout engine and a step-4 checkpoint. MarinSkyRL revisions after those, up to the pinned `32edb00f`, change Harbor agent rollouts, Harbor recipe validation, tests, and the Marin library revisions MarinSkyRL depends on, whose only library change is grading after an agent conversation reset.
