topics.title: [vllm histograms] Store and query cumulative family snapshots
topics.body:
Store cumulative histograms as one record per engine and family. The opt-in Rigging publisher preserves collected integer bins, bounds, and collection metadata using existing `kind=histogram` records and nullable `body_json`. Raw histogram observations and the scalar publisher retain their behavior. No new record kind, table, column, backfill, or database/schema migration is required.

The detailed and compact dashboard readers share publication validation and interval-delta logic for scalar, structured, and mixed histories, including output length and time per output token. Equivalent numeric bounds share schema identity for interval baselines. Duplicate checks retain the original encoded bounds, so differing copies of one identified publication are excluded by both views. Readers suppress scalar twins when a matching structured publication is present. Counts support 0 through 2^63−1; unsupported source families increment telemetry loss counters. Scalar counts at or above 2^53 are unavailable for exact deltas, and a family with multiple bucket schemas in the requested range withholds percentile/distribution estimates. The root lock uses DuckDB 1.5.4, matching Grafana's dependency. The Iris native wheel floor matches the controller's existing per-user-role contract exercised by CI.

The [design and local measurement report](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/773) documents the wire contract, ownership, and September 23–24, 2026 results: 6,208→832 data rows, 8→2 HTTP POSTs, 83.0% fewer compressed request bytes, and 180.17→33.50 seconds ingest in a four-engine, three-hour replay. Detailed client peak RSS was higher (441→474 MB). These historical measurements do not prove current-head performance, training speed, or #9382's seven-day/50-job ten-second target.

The dashboard's ingestion-to-query contract runs against a source-built Finelog server in CI.

The companion producer is marin-community/MarinSkyRL#738. Activation requires the released Rigging API, structured/dual delivery tests against SkyRL's locked dependencies, regional-schema and external-consumer verification, server/reader deployment, and a bounded training canary. Part of #9382.

topics.title: [shellbox] Refuse an empty workdir on the Iris backend
topics.body:
Reject an empty `MachineSpec.workdir` for the Iris backend before submitting a job. The spec check names the image and asks for a directory.

For Docker, an empty `workdir` leaves the image's own `WORKDIR` in effect because the backend passes no `-w`. Iris starts every task container in `/app`, the Docker runtime's default workdir and the Kubernetes pod's `workingDir`, so it cannot honor the image's `WORKDIR`. Previously, the factory ran `mkdir -p ""` after the sandbox started. The resulting error took several launches to read:

```
RuntimeError: Failed to create Iris workdir : mkdir: cannot create directory ''
```

#10102 removes the grading caller that produced an empty workdir. This guard covers future callers and replaces the closed #10103, which attempted to give an empty workdir Docker's behavior on Iris.

With the `iris` extra installed, the Iris test module passed locally (22 tests). The shellbox CI job skips the module when the SDK is absent.

---

~~~markdown
A `MachineSpec` whose `workdir` is empty means the image's own working directory to the Docker backend, which passes no `-w`. RuntimeError: Failed to create Iris workdir : mkdir: cannot create directory ''
```

The spec check now refuses an empty workdir before any job is submitted, naming the image and asking for a directory. #10102 removes the one caller that produced an empty workdir in grading; this guard is for the next one, and replaces the closed #10103, which tried to treat an empty workdir as Docker does and could not.

The Iris test module runs locally with the `iris` extra installed (22 passed); the shellbox CI job skips it when the SDK is absent.
~~~

topics.title: [levanter] Interrupted model-cache mirrors re-download completed shards
topics.body:
An interrupted Hugging Face checkpoint mirror leaves uploaded shards in regional object storage, but retrying downloads and uploads them again. The GLM-5.2 attempt left approximately 295 GB under its pinned cache prefix; the retry overwrote existing shards instead of resuming. At approximately 106 MB/s, repeating the 474 GB snapshot exceeds evaluation's 40-minute startup budget.

Reproduce:
1. Start `cache_hf_model` for a pinned multi-shard checkpoint in an empty prefix.
2. Terminate the worker after several shards upload, before `.cache_metadata.json` is written.
3. Retry against the same prefix and revision. Previously uploaded shard modification times change, and Hugging Face downloads repeat.

Expected: validate existing shards against the pinned source metadata and skip matching objects; download missing or mismatched objects. Use size and a reliable content identity/checksum, not an assumption that every object-store ETag is an MD5. Preserve the distributed lock and write the existing completion marker only after every required file is validated. Cover interruption and resume, mismatched objects, and complete-cache hits in tests.

`lib/levanter/src/levanter/model_cache.py:228` (`_stream_hf_snapshot`) unconditionally downloads and uploads each file. `cache_to_prefix` only recognizes the final completion marker. No implementation is included in this report.

[Incident evidence and affected runs](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/468). Found during #8215 validation.

comments.body:
🤖 Research: _stream_hf_snapshot downloads every repository file whenever the snapshot completion marker is absent; uploaded shards are not checked. Both automatic serving preparation and the standalone CPU job use this path.

Proposed Fix: fetch pinned Hugging Face file metadata, verify existing objects by size and content hash (LFS SHA-256 or Git blob SHA-1), and skip verified files. Retain the distributed lock and final marker. This reads existing regional objects during recovery but avoids re-downloading them over the internet; no object-store ETag assumptions. Add interruption/resume and corrupt-object regression coverage.
@weaverbot  what do you think about this? do you want to create a fix?

On it — https://loom.oa.dev/s/l3qfum0s

- 🟠 `Oct 19 16:01Z` **attention** — PR #10276 open for review: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10276
- 🟠 `Oct 19 17:12Z` **attention** — PR #10276 green; review decision on checksum validation pending: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10276#issuecomment-6272857251

🤖 Research: `_stream_hf_snapshot` uploads every file again when a retry finds no completion marker. The earlier issue analysis identified the same path, and no open PR covers it. [Source](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/levanter/src/levanter/model_cache.py#L230-L253).

Proposed Fix: obtain file size and LFS SHA-256 or Git blob SHA-1 from the pinned Hugging Face tree. Hash existing destination files in chunks before reusing them; verify downloaded files and uploaded copies before the marker is written. Keep the current distributed lock and add interruption, mismatch, and complete-cache tests.

🤖 Fix proposed in [PR #10276](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10276). Incomplete cache retries hash existing shards against the requested Hugging Face size and LFS SHA-256 or Git blob SHA-1, reuse matches, and repair missing or mismatched objects. Downloads and uploaded copies are verified before `.cache_metadata.json` is written under the existing distributed lock.

All 16 model-cache tests pass. The affected safe suite had 506 passes, four skips, and one unrelated Grug compilation timeout under parallel load; that test passed when rerun alone. Regional read throughput for the GLM-5.2 cache has not been measured.

topics.title: [grug] Match inference router bias to training evaluation
topics.body:
Restore the checkpoint's stored router bias for inference and export, matching training-time evaluation. Pending quantile-balancing estimates belong to the next training update; applying them during inference previously selected a different model from the same checkpoint.

Advance the export version so an interrupted export started under the previous bias convention cannot be resumed. Finished exports whose manifest records export_version 1 or 2 carry the pending-estimate bias, as the README now notes. Move apply_qb_betas back into the training module, its only remaining caller. Regression coverage checks stored biases in both current and legacy checkpoint layouts, including checkpoints with authoritative fp32 master weights. Pretraining updates are unchanged.

topics.title: [iris] Capability-URL round trips into cw-us-east-02a take 6–10 s under load (cw-rno2a: 0.15–0.5 s through the same gateway)
topics.body:
**Symptom.** Generation jobs in cw-us-east-02a each serve an OpenAI-compatible proxy as an Iris link endpoint (`/glm-harbor/<run>-<id>`). Agents call it through its capability URL (`https://iris.oa.dev/proxy/t/...`) once per agent step. On 2026-10-20 at about 04:50Z, a `GET /v1/models` on such an endpoint took 6–10 s through the capability URL. The same request sent directly to the endpoint's registered address from inside its container took under 10 ms. At the same time, capability URLs for endpoints in cw-rno2a (vLLM servers) answered the same request in 0.15–0.5 s from the same client. About 900 concurrent agent trials sat behind cw-us-east-02a endpoints then: 28 jobs × 32 trials, 56 registered endpoints. That was roughly double the load before about 03:10Z.

**Measurements**

| | result |
|---|---|
| `GET /v1/models` via capability URL, cw-us-east-02a endpoint (4 endpoints, 3–6 calls each) | 5.9–10.5 s; connect 0.01 s; nearly all of it is time to first byte |
| same endpoint, direct to its registered address from its own container | 0.000–0.009 s |
| `GET /v1/models` via capability URL, cw-rno2a endpoint, same client, same minute | 0.15–0.49 s |
| per agent step, gap from model reply to the next request (job request logs) | p50 0.4–1.3 s before ~03:05Z; 23–28 s after ~03:40Z |
| model backend latency per request, measured at the proxy (same window) | unchanged: p50 0.8 → 1.0 s, 6.7 → 6.9 ms per output token |

**Ruled out**
- The proxy process: it answers directly in under 10 ms, uses 5–7% of a core, and the containers have no CPU limit.
- The model backend: its latency and per-token speed are unchanged.
- The sandboxes (Daytona): command execution takes 20–80 ms per call, CPU speed is normal, host load is 22–37 on 64 cores.
- Client-side connection setup: connect time is 0.01 s, and the delay is all time to first byte.

**Not available.** There are no gateway or endpoint-relay metrics from before the slowdown. Load dependence is inferred from timing: the gap rose from about 03:10Z and leveled off by 03:40Z, as about 450 more trials started behind cw-us-east-02a endpoints. It has not been measured directly.

**Ask**
1. Gateway and endpoint-relay metrics for cw-us-east-02a from 2026-10-20 00:00Z onward: request rate, latency, queue depth and in-flight connections, compared with cw-rno2a.
2. Is there a per-cluster limit on proxied endpoint traffic (connection pool, worker count, a single relay stream to the cluster) that about 900 concurrent clients would saturate? If so, can it be raised, or should high-request-rate clients use another path?

| UTC window | cw-us-east-02a parent / child mean | parent / child completions | child total RPS / mean in-flight |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 00:00–00:15 | 6.35 / 4.57 s | 40,100 / 46,384 | 55.2 / 274 |
| 02:50–03:05 | 3.43 / 3.28 s | 40,025 / 48,026 | 68.5 / 307 |
| 03:40–04:00 | 14.64 / 5.61 s | 32,553 / 33,036 | 54.6 / 339 |
| 04:45–05:00 | 10.48 / 3.51 s | 50,900 / 51,105 | 61.5 / 374 |

At 04:45–05:00, cw-rno2a parent/child means were 5.21/5.23 s (2,458/2,437 completions); cw-us-east-02a's added wait appears in the parent-to-child path. The native proxy has no per-peer semaphore or single relay stream, but its upstream client retains zero idle connections; the metrics do not split decision, connection setup, and Traefik time. Live Traefik middleware inspection was denied by this session's Kubernetes role, so an ingress-side limit remains unverified.

**Relevant code**
- [`lib.rs#L1127-L1135`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/rust/src/lib.rs#L1127-L1135) — parent relay route
- [`dashboard.py#L278-L292`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/dashboard.py#L278-L292) — peer target decision

2. Reproduce the POST and GET request mix on staging at approximately 450 and 900 concurrent clients. Change the measured bottleneck: bounded keep-alive reuse if connection setup dominates, or the identified ingress/decision path if it does not.
3. Verify p95 added relay time below 1 s at 900 clients, with no cw-rno2a regression or higher error rate. Off-cluster clients should continue using capability URLs until another authenticated route is validated; the child ingress is IP restricted.

topics.title: [grug] Fix AMD Pallas flash attention on packed and one-device meshes
topics.body:
`gpu_pallas_triton_flash` failed at trace time on packed batches under an explicit mesh. `_key_lower_bounds` concatenated a replicated `jnp.ones((batch, 1))` with the batch-sharded segment-ID comparison, and explicit sharding rejects operands with different shardings (`ShardingTypeError: All operands should have the same sharding`). Grug's data loader shards segment IDs by batch, so every packed run with this backend failed, on one GPU or many. The first column is now built from the segment IDs, so it shares their sharding.

It also failed on one-device meshes. The wrapper skipped `shard_map` when no axis of size greater than 1 partitioned q, and `pallas_call` rejects operands whose type names a mesh axis (`ValueError: sharded ref ... can only be sliced along unsharded axes`). Grug's meshes keep length-1 axes in every spec, so every single-device Grug or Snowball run with this backend failed. The wrapper now skips `shard_map` only when q's spec names no mesh axis, so Auto meshes keep their current path.

Two regression tests cover the fixes, and each failed on main with the error above: a packed, batch- and head-sharded run on a 4-device CPU mesh, and a packed run on a one-device Grug mesh.

Supersedes #10126, which fixed only the one-device case.

Part of #9812

This PR fixes three things in the AMD Pallas-Triton attention backend: packed batches under explicit sharding, one-device Grug meshes, and masks that carry `fa4_bounds`. topics.title: [finelog] Reduce forwarding serialization and decompression work
topics.body:
Reduce forwarding work by skipping oversized parent IPC encodes, sharing immutable payloads across retry clones, and moving the hub's owned request buffer into Arrow decoding. Decode complete zstd frames with a known content size into a bounded output buffer. Other zstd frame formats retain the existing decoder; gzip and streaming providers retain their existing behavior.

Keep SQL reads, compression level 1, serial log ordering, the wire format, and durable cursor settlement.

On five rotating local replays per variant, median delivery of 1M synthetic rows increased from 284k/sec on main to 409k/sec (1.44×). With only the encoding and copy changes, the same cohort measured 361k/sec. Adding the decoder change reduced median cumulative write/RPC time per replay, across two serial requests, from 1,391 to 1,243 ms. Source and authenticated hub shared four CPUs with release builds, production jemalloc/zstd, warm Parquet source files, and local-disk durability. The decoder comparison's throughput ranges overlap. These runs exclude TLS, cold remote objects, concurrent queries, fleet hub load, and steady small-write coalescing.

[Final measurements and reproduction](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10271#issuecomment-6275161594). [RPC diagnosis and profiling evidence](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10271#issuecomment-6274803649).

comments.body:
🤖 Holistic review of 564482d5e81bf05bfccdddc2c5dab297d5d129a9.

This change replaces the forwarder's SQL source read with a direct Parquet-to-Arrow reader in `store/forwarding.rs`, bounded by sequence span, segment fanout, a 256 MiB retained-Arrow target, and a deadline. The reader logic holds up: the byte budget narrows the examined boundary (`through`) rather than truncating rows, so the `complete_window` flag and its LIMIT reasoning go away and the cursor always settles to a proven boundary.

**Before.** `read_batch` took the visibility guard, snapshotted the namespace, built a DataFusion provider, and ran `SELECT * … WHERE seq > c AND seq <= t AND (cluster IS NULL OR cluster = '') ORDER BY seq LIMIT n`. Uncached object-backed sources were range-read from their remote URL (`ObjectSources::resolve` in `query/provider.rs`), with a background cache fill. Because LIMIT could stop inside the window, the turn advanced past trailing foreign-origin rows only when fewer than `n` rows came back.

**After.** `read_forwarding` keeps the guard and snapshot, localizes every selected source, serially for cold cache misses, then decodes on a blocking thread. It prunes row groups by `seq` statistics, projects each batch to the registered schema, and filters by window and origin. When retained bytes exceed the budget it halves `through` and re-filters what it already holds. Every overlapping file is still examined, so lower sequences in later files are not skipped. A final sort runs only when the batches arrive out of order. `ship_batch`, `bounded_forward_read_through`, and `resume_after_eviction` move unchanged in behavior; the new `scanned_through <= cursor` early return covers the empty-snapshot case that `complete_window` used to absorb.

**Evidence.** The new store tests cover reordered/overlapping segments, foreign-origin filtering, additive schema evolution, and byte-limited resumption without losing lower rows in later files. The server test shows a missing local file leaves the cursor at 0 and delivers once restored. The object-backed sort-order test now also reads through `read_forwarding`, and a cold-cache test shows an uncached object whose remote bytes are missing fails the read, then replays both rows once the bytes return. This review did not run the Rust tests locally (a cold build exceeded ten minutes); `finelog-rust` CI covers them. The throughput numbers are from the PR body; this review did not reproduce them, and OPS.md now states that cold recovery throughput was not measured. No other open PR touches these paths.

No findings.

Earlier findings: 1 resolved; cold localization is now serial per namespace turn, and OPS.md and AGENTS.md count the whole-object download buffer and cache I/O against the read deadline, outside the 256 MiB budget. 2 resolved; the benchmark example and its SQL copy are gone, and the forwarder helpers and reader are private again.

The SQL comparison example is removed, and forwarding helpers and the reader are private to their owning modules or crate. The [measured snapshot and one-time harness](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/0d4ff15fdd46eeb07e0fa44936fc95156b17e14c/lib/finelog/rust/examples/forwarding_bench.rs) remain available for reproduction; the PR body links there. 🤖 Initial RPC diagnosis and follow-up experiments for `a91c68fd9d0e`. The most promising follow-up is a bounded bulk-decompression path in ConnectRPC. On four 1M-row replays per decoder, it reduced hub decompression from 386 to 175 ms and RPC time from 1,362 to 1,125 ms. Paired counter captures showed 16% less RPC-stage CPU time. These are disposable prototypes on `a91c68fd9d0e`; PR #10271 still ships the SQL-based encode/copy change and its earlier 1.39× comparison. ## Where RPC time goes Source and hub ran in one process with affinity CPUs 0–3 on Ryzen 7 3800X, four Tokio workers, production jemalloc, real JWT authentication, and local-disk durable acknowledgements. The large replay delivers exactly 1M rows in two serial requests: 291,596,432 bytes of final IPC, 14,206,613 compressed request-body bytes at zstd level 1, and 4,315,399 bytes of hub Parquet output. | RPC phase, median ms | Current decoder | | --- | ---: | | Client preparation and serialization, measured before compression | 165 | | Client zstd compression | 109 | | Transfer and request-body collection, timing gap | 13 | | Hub zstd decompression | 386 | | Dispatch to Arrow decode, timing gap | 0.3 | | Arrow decode and validation | 215 | | Route, align, stamp origin, and append | 25 | | Durability wait, including the flush | 340 | | Response completion and cleanup, timing gap | 106 | | Complete RPC | 1,362 | Within the durability wait, Parquet encoding was 313 ms, file write/`sync_all`/rename/stat 7 ms, and key-bound/catalog-commit/persisted-watermark work 19 ms. Buffer sealing was under 1 ms. These sub-stages are included in the wait, not added to it. Independent phase medians need not sum exactly to the median RPC. Timing gaps include scheduling and cleanup; the 165 ms interval is not a pure protobuf microbenchmark, and the 106 ms interval has no finer attribution yet. A gated `perf record -e cycles:u -F 199 --call-graph dwarf,32768` captured three 1M-row push passes, excluding reads and packing. It recorded 1,004 samples with no reported loss. The source test thread accounted for 20.7% of sampled cycle weight and runtime workers 79.3%; workers also execute the client's HTTP connection tasks, so that is not a pure client/hub split. Self-sample weights resolved to client zstd 14.4%, worker zstd 18.7%, other Parquet encoding/dictionary work 15.9%, UTF-8 validation 5.1%, other named work 2.6%, unresolved libc addresses 21.4%, and other unresolved addresses 22.0%. Worker zstd combines hub request decompression with Parquet compression. The unresolved samples prevent a complete function-level CPU attribution; the explicit stage timers provide the wall-time breakdown. ## Compression settings These are medians of three unprofiled process runs per setting, with case order rotated between rounds. | Transport setting | Request body MB | Compression ms | RPC ms | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | zstd 1, current | 14.21 | 107 | 1,363 | | zstd −1 | 19.19 | 111 | 1,335 | | zstd −3 | 20.09 | 77 | 1,206 | | zstd 3 | 13.49 | 123 | 1,380 | | Uncompressed | ≥291.60, IPC alone | 0 | 990 | Level −3 saved about 30 ms of directly timed compression but added 41% more compressed bytes. Its larger RPC median difference also includes changes in unrelated Parquet timings, so it cannot all be credited to the level. Level 3 saves about 5% of bytes at higher compression time. Uncompressed loopback transport saves time while sending at least 20.5× as many body bytes. Keep level 1 as the default from this initial evidence. Both transport and Parquet compression already use level 1. ## Decompression and Parquet experiments ConnectRPC 0.6.1's zstd decoder uses bounded streaming `Read::take(limit + 1).read_to_end`, starting with capacity estimated from compressed length × 4. These requests expand about 20.5×, so the output buffer grows; reallocations can copy already decoded bytes. Compressor contexts are already pooled; context construction is not the issue found here. The first prototype sizes that same bounded streaming buffer from the zstd frame's content-size hint. The second uses bulk decompression only when the input is exactly one complete frame with a known output size within the configured limit. Unknown-size, concatenated, or over-limit frame headers retain the current bounded streaming path. Malformed and truncated inputs still error in the contract probe. The bulk API writes into its output buffer without the generic streaming `Read` loop. Tests of the prototype cover single-frame and unknown-size round trips, concatenated frames, exact and exceeded limits, and malformed/truncated input. | Four-round large replay comparison | Current | Sized streaming | Bounded bulk | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | Hub decompression ms | 386 | 248 | 175 | | Complete RPC ms | 1,362 | 1,140 | 1,125 | | Complete replay rows/sec | 386k | 473k | 473k | Bulk decompression cuts this stage by 55% and the RPC median by 17%. All four paired large RPC and full replay timings improved, but source read, packing, and Parquet times also vary. The 22% full replay median-rate increase is exploratory and cannot be attributed entirely to decompression. Bulk RPC ranges were 1,011–1,235 ms versus 1,298–1,429 ms for current; full replay throughput ranges overlap. Four alternating pairs on the smaller 200k-row replay gave 53 → 32 ms of decompression and 237 → 195 ms of RPC time for current versus bulk. Pre-sizing alone had previously reduced small-case decompression by about 9 ms without a clear delivery gain. These smaller trials start a fresh hub: the first flush is immediately eligible. They do not measure a steady stream of small acknowledged writes, where the one-second flush coalescing interval can matter. The large requests cross the force-flush threshold and bypass that interval. Four factorial rounds also disabled Parquet dictionaries only for the log body. Its Parquet encode median improved 349 → 282 ms with the current decoder, but worsened 253 → 322 ms when combined with sized streaming. Source and real JWT-authenticated hub share affinity CPUs 0–3 and four Tokio workers on Ryzen 7 3800X, production jemalloc, optimized release builds, 128 warm local source Parquet files, and local-disk durability. Every replay verifies the delivered row count. The acknowledgement follows Parquet encoding, file write/`sync_all`/rename, catalog commit, and published persisted sequence. Verification/shutdown are outside timing. CPUs are shared, not reserved. No caches were dropped; TLS, cold objects, large catalogs, concurrent queries, fleet hub load, and simultaneous regional senders are unmeasured. A fresh hub's first flush is immediately eligible; the small case does not measure steady small-write coalescing.

Level 1 stays: level −3 saved about 30 ms in direct compression but added 41% body bytes; dictionary removal had inconsistent effects.

The production wrapper accepts the fast path only for one complete frame with known size within the existing decoded-message limit. Unknown size, concatenation, skippable/trailing frames, and oversized declarations retain the stock bounded decoder. Malformed frames preserve stock error codes; compressors, gzip and streaming providers are unchanged.

Local checks: all 659 active Rust workspace tests pass, including compressed authenticated forwarding with every expected value and the persisted hub watermark checked; strict Clippy, Rust formatting, and the required repository checks pass. Use the original private child module from the [encoding/copy evidence](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10271#issuecomment-6273653311) on each revision. Keep its production jemalloc allocator. Build each with `CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_STRIP=none CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/home/power/.cache/cargo-build cargo test --manifest-path lib/finelog/rust/Cargo.toml --release -p finelog --lib --no-run`, then copy the emitted executable to `.cache/finelog-forwarding-profile/baseline`, `candidate`, or `final`. Remove the temporary module afterward; it does not ship.

SHA-256:
- main: `9a288362bc83c6766bf12d75c1a49580217f77210db6b259bc8966628fcaf64c`
- encode/copy: `d9779dc42625412b37471870bed828f0b59f5b3d4a8b6dd66c187387977cc24d`
- final: `62fea361fa8f399126a9b732284339cc05a27a5b3c1a4955a658a1f4e88649c8`

Run the following driver with `uv run --no-project python DRIVER.py CHECKOUT TASK_SCRATCH`. It rotates three variants sequentially across five rounds per workload. Fixture generation, process setup, and context microbenchmark are outside replay timing. The driver captures raw output and fails on incomplete row delivery.

```python
import json
import os
import statistics
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

root, scratch = map(Path, sys.argv[1:])
variants = ["baseline", "candidate", "final"]
observations = []
for workload, rows, body in [("large", 1000000, 232), ("small", 200000, 160)]:
    for turn in range(5):
        for variant in variants[turn % 3:] + variants[:turn % 3]:
            env = {key: value for key, value in os.environ.items() if not key.startswith(("FINELOG_PROFILE_", "FINELOG_PERF_"))}
            env.update(FINELOG_PROFILE_DIR=str(root / ".cache/finelog-forwarding-profile/replay"), FINELOG_PROFILE_REPETITIONS="1", FINELOG_PROFILE_STAGE="all", FINELOG_PROFILE_ROWS=str(rows), FINELOG_PROFILE_BODY_BYTES=str(body))
            command = ["taskset", "-c", "0-3", str(root / ".cache/finelog-forwarding-profile" / variant), "--ignored", "--exact", "server::forwarding::forwarding_profile::profile_forwarding", "--nocapture"]
            proc = subprocess.run(command, env=env, capture_output=True, text=True)
            (scratch / f"final-replay-{workload}-{variant}-{turn}.txt").write_text(proc.stdout + "\n" + proc.stderr)
            if proc.returncode:
                print(proc.stdout[-3000:] + proc.stderr[-3000:], flush=True)
                proc.check_returncode()
            row = json.loads(next(line.removeprefix("PROFILE_RESULT ") for line in proc.stdout.splitlines() if line.startswith("PROFILE_RESULT ")))
            row.update(variant=variant, round=turn, workload=workload)
            observations.append(row)
            (scratch / "final-replay-observations.json").write_text(json.dumps(observations, indent=2))
            print(json.dumps(row), flush=True)
summaries = []
for workload in ["large", "small"]:
    for variant in variants:
        items = [row for row in observations if row["workload"] == workload and row["variant"] == variant]
        numeric = ["read_prepare_ms", "encode_ms", "push_ms", "settle_ms", "elapsed_ms", "rows_per_second"]
        summaries.append(dict(workload=workload, variant=variant, medians={key: statistics.median(row[key] for row in items) for key in numeric}, ranges={key: [min(row[key] for row in items), max(row[key] for row in items)] for key in numeric}, rows=items[0]["rows"], encoded_bytes=items[0]["encoded_bytes"], chunks=items[0]["chunks"]))
(scratch / "final-replay-summary.json").write_text(json.dumps(dict(observations=observations, summaries=summaries), indent=2))
print(json.dumps(summaries), flush=True)

```

</details>

topics.title: [levanter] Honor dtype overrides for BF16 safetensors
topics.body:
Apply `dtype_override` to BF16 tensors when streaming safetensors. NumPy's floating predicate excludes BF16, so requesting FP32 left those weights in BF16, including through `HFCheckpointConverter.load_pretrained(dtype=...)`. Integer tensors retain their source dtype.

The intended FP32 Levanter reference run in #10213 loaded BF16 weights, so it compared Levanter BF16 against HF FP32. Its measurements remain valid for that comparison.

Fixes #10266

topics.title: Vendor Evalchemy with an isolated evaluation runtime
topics.body:
Move Evalchemy into `vendor/evalchemy` with all 42 benchmark dataset generators,
their required data, grading and resume support. Remove database tracking,
benchmark pages, reporting, original benchmark model providers, standalone
rollout drivers and unused model/evaluator configurations. Retain the prompt
processing and scoring code called by the shared runtime.

Evalchemy has its own `uv.lock` and environment, outside the root workspace's
resolution domain. Marin invokes its CLI in a child process. FineStore and
rigging resolve from local sources, so their changes can land atomically with
the evaluator. Runtime provenance includes the vendored source and dependency
lock, and CI checks the independent environment. Remove the external fork pin
and refresh machinery.

Immutable evaluation caches track evaluator source, runtime data, portable
configuration and the dependency lock. Records keep broader local-library and
adapter provenance. Historical policy launches reject Evalchemy selections
before writing configs or starting jobs and require a Marin checkout from
before vendoring with the original evaluator commit. With Iris's existing test
and documentation exclusions, the default bundle is 21.50 MiB, within the
deployed 25 MiB limit.

topics.title: [rolloutengine] Keep the tools of each conversation in ConversationRecord
topics.body:
`ConversationRecord` (`lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/models.py:128`) keeps the messages of a conversation, but not the options of the prompt that started it, for example the tools that the model saw and `tool_choice`. Each request of the conversation sends these options (`lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/recorder.py:80`), and the `ConversationStarted` event gives them to an observer (`models.py:285`). But `_Conversation.record` (`recorder.py:119`) does not put them in the record, so a `GradedRollout` does not tell which tools the policy had.

`analyze_failed_runs` (#10265) shows its agent the tools of each failed rollout. Because the record has no tools, it takes `(TaskSpec, GradedRollout)` pairs and builds the tool list again with `task_prompt`. That list is not complete: it does not have the shell tool or the provider functions that `ShellHarness` adds.

Done when:
- `ConversationRecord` keeps the options of the prompt that started the conversation.
- A test shows that the record of a `ShellHarness` attempt has the shell tool and the provider functions.
- `analyze_failed_runs` takes only `GradedRollout` and reads the tools from the record.

comments.body:
🤖
# Research
`_Conversation` retains the options passed to `ModelSession.start()`, but `record()` omits them from `ConversationRecord`. `ShellHarness` adds the shell and provider functions to those options; the open #10265 analyzer builds each failed-rollout text file's tool header with `task_prompt(task, None, ())`, which omits those runtime-bound functions.

**Relevant code**
- [`recorder.py#L77-L126`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/recorder.py#L77-L126) — options lost when recording
- [`shell.py#L209-L220`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/harness/shell.py#L209-L220) — runtime tools enter prompt

topics.title: [taskforge] Grade decision-model tasks on the host
topics.body:
Grade decision-model tasks on the host. The owner is undecided on this kind of task, so this PR is kept separate from the rest of the stack; its upstream counterpart is #10280.

Verification is now one of five kinds (`answer_in_box`, `decision_model`, `code`, `llm_as_judge`, `composite`), and a composite is a weighted list of at least two other kinds. A `DecisionGrader` is its own grader type, not an LLM judge: the authoring model writes a rubric and a gold reference, and a decision model of fixed strength reads one state, by default the visible output of the solver's final turn, and answers one comparative question on five levels. Grading stays out of the rollout: a trial runs with the grader swapped to `NoGrader`, and the host grades the trial's final conversation afterwards. A read that fails transiently is read once more on the same conversation, and the solver's rollout is never re-run. `ClefDecisionClient` sends the reads to Clef behind the Orion gateway, using the request schema and state budget copied from clefclient into `taskforge.llm.clef`.

TaskSpec has no decision grader type until #10280 lands, so a TaskSpec carries the grader as a `NoGrader` whose contract holds it.

Builds on #10301 and is the last PR of the stack. Its five commits are the restack's own, cherry-picked unchanged. The taskforge suite passes 785 tests here (78 more than #10301).

topics.title: [rl] Build a source-stratified Snowball curriculum v0
topics.body:
Build an immutable 100,000-task candidate curriculum for fast-turnaround Snowball RL. Version `2026.10.19.2` contains 88,366 production-admitted TaskSpecs and 11,634 reviewed historical native closure imports. The [private browser](https://applets.marina.oa.dev/a/e2bd5c9d-0f93-4ce9-b7af-3c78ca55e5d1/v/2/) contains the complete selected pool; sign in with a work Google account.

The approved recipe targets equal shares across five families: 20,000 each. Calendar capacity is 9,115, so its shortfall is distributed over the other four families. Final counts are calendar 9,115; competitive coding 22,722; Reasoning Gym 22,721; STEM 22,721; structural 22,721. This supersedes the initial proposal to reuse [Ben's intended one-sixth/four plus one-third structural weights](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/fed5a9383b92acacbe264c7e601e93d8437218d3/experiments/post_training/smartie/mixture-v2.json).

Sources:

- Calendar: Nemotron calendar and two Task Trove calendar datasets.
- Coding: Nemotron competitive coding, Eurus2, and verified Glaive sandboxes.
- Reasoning Gym: Nemotron puzzles and standalone Reasoning Gym.
- STEM: Nemotron STEM MCQA and OpenScience.
- Structural: all 11,087 selected admitted structured-output tasks plus 11,634 of Ben's synthetic structural-compliance tasks.

The 12 admitted sources have 244,938 eligible contracts after known holdout exclusions. Ben's pinned structural training release adds 57,364 native rows; full-contract deduplication removes 52, leaving 57,312 eligible. Combined candidate population: 302,250. Native additions are sampled as evenly as possible across eight structural families, then their control strata; no row is repeated to fill a quota. Distinct private grading contracts remain distinct and all selected source aliases are retained.

Inputs are pinned in the export:

- Production catalog `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/rl-data/catalog/production`, snapshot `8c5d247ef6c2416fb3d14b2f159f74c4`; admitted `final/part-*.parquet` identities resolve through the verified CoreWeave migration receipt.

- Four evaluation sources and the known 910-task native validation panel. Native holdout checks use effective token prompts and full contracts, not their shared generic instruction text.

Done when:

- [x] Freeze source revisions, admission/import status, holdouts, recipe, and replay code.
- [x] Exclude known exact holdout overlap; deduplicate complete contracts and retain source aliases.
- [x] Select deterministically without replacement, recording quotas, probability denominators and provisional difficulty labels.

- [x] Implement the historical native closure adapter and validate exact prompts and grading through the current CPU engine/trainer.

Retained canonical TaskSpec JSON strings are byte-identical to the same task records in the verified predecessor; native payload strings match the pinned historical release. The immutable pool retains original historical payloads. In its `train.parquet`, `contract_kind` selects either `task_json` or `lowered_task_spec`; the unused payload is null. The remaining 48,085 task payloads, including all native tasks, remain unchanged. The live Linux CPU gate validated the complete pool and returned grades for ten sandbox probes. Model and tokenizer use the exact step-14 revision `6783e9743478bd25a9ce03ab3460e84d6a9814b0` already staged regionally. [Experiment source](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/970d6ce10bb78cda3ac0ed291efa907067dae8da/experiments/post_training/snowball_inventory_smoke.py) pins trainer runtime `8eab996d9a6a46cb6aba9df8f008ce8a783cf1c1` and adapter packages from core `6e2fe1839ea067be147f1ce06aced63a96670f7a`.

The original grader lock expired and its dirty-build bytes could not be verified. This run rebuilds the grader environment using the dependency lock checked into the curation build's recorded base commit and pinned auxiliary data. Equivalence to the expired dirty build is unverified. Its runtime export changes only the lock URI in 51,915 script TaskSpecs and records every old/new contract hash; logical IDs remain unique. The original published pool is unchanged, and all 11,634 native runtime payloads remain byte-identical. Runtime Parquet: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/rl-data/curricula/snowball-v0/runtime/2026.10.20.1/train.parquet`, SHA-256 `61540e2349b89258c3e2be5fb5c7b159f0c2acbb2d109784d22a170fb04040b3`. Published runtime objects match the frozen local export hashes. This establishes byte integrity; live grading behavior and training remain pending.

🤖 The first coordinator failed before creating its CPU child or allocating GPUs: the child pinned its own regional controller as a federation peer. [The placement correction](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/45d293066c0bc79c2d2e13764c7bd8ed5beb89ea) makes the CPU child inherit its coordinator's cluster.

Fresh attempt `2026.10.20.2` is submitted as [/dlwh/users-dlwh-checkpoints-snowball-inventory-smoke-2026.10.20.2-coordinator-d7581925](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fdlwh%2Fusers-dlwh-checkpoints-snowball-inventory-smoke-2026.10.20.2-coordinator-d7581925). It uses the same verified model, full pool, runtime, 10-update recipe, and CPU grading gate. No optimizer update is verified yet.

🤖 Attempt `.2` validated the exact pool hash, all 100,000 TaskRolloutSpecs, and the three installed adapter package revisions, then failed its real bubblewrap capability probe. Both failed attempts are terminal, with no GPU training job submitted.

Attempt `2026.10.20.3` is now accepted as [/dlwh/users-dlwh-checkpoints-snowball-inventory-smoke-2026.10.20.3-coordinator-c0ef8b57](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fdlwh%2Fusers-dlwh-checkpoints-snowball-inventory-smoke-2026.10.20.3-coordinator-c0ef8b57). It explicitly uses the existing curation worker profile, `CONTAINER_PROFILE_PRIVILEGED`, to enable nested sandbox namespaces. The setting reaches the coordinator, CPU gate, training workers, and terminal export; Iris's admin authorization remains intact, and grader commands retain their inner bubblewrap sandbox. Cluster policy is unchanged.

[Marin run source `6d6eeaa2bf`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/6d6eeaa2bfc363f7004c1bf0ec192e51a3c02936) pins [trainer runtime `23cdde2a19`](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/commit/23cdde2a19f152727fe42bef9712d1cf7768c5e9). The affected Marin and trainer launch suites pass (37 and 45 tests), and the frozen host environment passes package compatibility checks. The model, full pool, and 10-update recipe are unchanged. CPU grading and optimizer progress remain to be verified live.

🤖 The `.3` CPU gate passed: the published hash and all 100,000 TaskRolloutSpecs validated, and all ten real sandbox grader probes returned grades. All five GPU workers then joined, the trainer loaded 100,000 rows, and the eight inference workers initialized.

GPU attempt 0 failed before its first optimizer update during Hugging Face → Megatron model conversion: `ModelBridge._megatron_global_param_names_all_pp_ranks` called `torch.distributed.all_gather_object(..., group=pp_group)`, which raised `_pickle.UnpicklingError: invalid load key, \x00`. Subsequent NCCL peer-exit errors followed teardown; their presence does not establish a network root cause.

Iris has started the already-configured single retry, currently initializing. No manual resubmission or cluster change occurred. [Live training job](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fdlwh%2Fusers-dlwh-checkpoints-snowball-inventory-smoke-2026.10.20.3-coordinator-c0ef8b57%2Fusers-dlwh-checkpoints-snowball-inventory-smoke-2026.10.20.3-e568c04463bd); [retry W&B run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin-snowball-curriculum-smoke/runs/y2omz966). Diagnosis is tracing the failing collective; zero optimizer steps are verified.

🤖 The ten-update smoke is terminal and unsuccessful: the training job and coordinator both report `FAILED`, the configured retry is exhausted, and no optimizer step or final model export was produced. The CPU gate succeeded, all five GPU workers joined, and all 100,000 rows loaded.

Both GPU attempts raised `_pickle.UnpicklingError: invalid load key, \x00` in Megatron Bridge’s PP-group parameter-name `all_gather_object`, before weight loading and training. Retry logs place the failed operation at sequence 2: a 52,890-byte metadata payload following a completed prior collective. InfiniBand retry-exceeded errors appear during initialization; an earlier peer failure remains possible, so a specific network root cause is unproven.

No manual retry or cluster change was made. The next proposed diagnostic uses two GPUs on separate nodes with the same frozen runtime, a 60-second collective timeout and three-minute probe deadline: validate the length exchange, exact-size byte payload, then pickle objects. It loads no model and runs no training. A separate socket-only comparison would be conditional on reproducing the IB failure. This diagnostic awaits review before submission.

[Failed training job](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fdlwh%2Fusers-dlwh-checkpoints-snowball-inventory-smoke-2026.10.20.3-coordinator-c0ef8b57%2Fusers-dlwh-checkpoints-snowball-inventory-smoke-2026.10.20.3-e568c04463bd) · [retry W&B](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin-snowball-curriculum-smoke/runs/y2omz966)

🤖 A minimal two-rank collective test passed. The larger reproduction stopped during its diagnostic network setup, before reaching the operation that failed in training. That setup is now corrected and under test.

The training smoke remains at 0/10 completed optimizer updates. The full 100,000-task pool, model pin, and ten-update target remain unchanged.

🤖 A cancellation-routing issue was mitigated; see the [incident record](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/797). The training smoke remains at 0/10 completed optimizer updates while the compiled timeout contract is being corrected.
🤖 The smoke is now training on the full 100,000-task pool. Optimizer step 3 of 10 completed with actual rollout grading. Checkpoint and export verification remain pending.

🤖 The requested smoke completed ten optimizer updates using the full 100,000-task inventory, sampling 32 shuffled prompts per update with four answers per prompt. Training and export in Hugging Face format succeeded.

Final checks confirmed the step-10 checkpoint commit marker, completed export request, successful terminal manifests, and exported model inventory against its manifest. This run exercised inference, grading, optimization, checkpoint writing and model export; resumed training and evaluation gains remain untested. Published library releases and the dependent trainer lock update remain open.

topics.title: [sft] Add the GLM 5.3 Harbor trace generation driver
topics.body:
Generate k=8 GLM 5.3 trajectories for TMax and SWE-smith pool tasks with
Harbor, plus v0/GLM relay episodes in which the v0 student acts until a trigger
(a completion claim, a format error or the context budget) hands the turn to
GLM. Each family runs under its eval-campaign Harbor policy, whose YAMLs and
Harbor/Evalchemy pins come from #9569; the runs used that branch, and this
driver needs it merged first. Inside the run, a local OpenAI-compatible proxy
routes each request to the student or the GLM bulk relay and logs every request
and reply per trial. rebuild_traces turns those logs into one row per
conversation with turn authors, triggers and per-author token counts.

The v0 student runs as its own root job (serve_student.py) on non-preemptible
H100 workers, in any cluster. A lane reaches it through a capability URL for
the job's fixed endpoint name, passed only as STUDENT_BASE_URL. The lane waits
until /v1/models answers and takes v0's model id from that reply. On cw-rno2a,
preemptible students were evicted for hours, and each eviction failed every
trial in flight. While Iris moves v0, the proxy retries gateway errors
(404/502/503/504) and refused connections for up to 20 minutes. A run fails
when more than 20% of its trials raised without any proxy reply, since that
means a backend was down, not that the agent failed. httpx logs at WARNING, so
request URLs, the capability URL among them, stay out of logs.

Capability URLs are bearer credentials, so every output is scrubbed of Iris
capability tokens before it is written, including JWTs split across escaped
line breaks. scrub_run re-checks finished runs, and publish_hf refuses to
upload a row that still holds one. During the agent phase the sandbox reaches
only the proxy, and mini-swe-agent installs from pinned constraints. The
null, network and tool-env probe agents record what a sandbox can reach.

Only agents that run inside the sandbox (mini-swe-agent) call the proxy through
its capability URL. Terminus-2 runs in Harbor's own process, so it calls the
proxy at its local address. Under load, each capability-URL round trip into
cw-us-east-02a took 6-10 s (#10318). That raised the gap between a model reply
and the agent's next request from about 1 s to about 25 s. On the local address
it is back to about 1 s. driver_config records which route the agent used.

The traces from these runs are published as
open-athena/GLM-5.3-tmax-swesmith-k8-traces-2026.10.

Part of #10213

topics.title: Marin Eval Policy (2026-10-16)
topics.body:
## Overview

This document is an attempt to formalize Marin’s policy towards what constitutes reportable, public-facing, canonical eval results for Marin models as well as the baselines we compare against.

Why do we need this document? With the first “snowball” release of a 67B A2B MoE, Marin is entering a regime where we regularly compare Marin models to existing open and closed-source models. Because Marin’s unique claim is that we are open development, we will need to hold ourselves to a high standard of transparency on how we report eval scores of Marin models and what claims we make about Marin model capabilities based on those scores.

What is in scope? This document is intended to act as a living snapshot, trustworthy for any given period in time, as to the what and the how of Marin’s canonical set of evals, a set of standards to which we will aspire to hold ourselves. By "the what", we mean “which evals did we run, with what consistent set of hyperparameters and experimental constraints”. By "the how", we mean “where is the self-contained codebase that is both necessary and sufficient to reproduce our eval results independently”.

## Previous version notes

* Released Sept 24, 2026: 18 non-agentic benchmarks, 8 Harbor agentic benchmarks, and 4 reserved out-of-distribution benchmarks.

## Complete eval list, with hyperparameters

### Details on our Evals

- **MATH-500.** OpenAI's [May 2023 process-supervision release](https://openai.com/index/improving-mathematical-reasoning-with-process-supervision/) used a 500-problem subset of the original MATH competition-math benchmark. The campaign scores one zero-shot generated solution per problem by final-answer accuracy.
- **HumanEval+.** The [May 2023 EvalPlus paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.01210) introduced expanded tests for HumanEval programs to catch incorrect code that passes sparse original tests. The campaign executes one zero-shot completion per problem against the stronger tests.
- **MBPP+.** The [November 24, 2023 EvalPlus release](https://github.com/evalplus/evalplus/releases/tag/v0.2.0) extends MBPP with additional functional tests. The campaign's pinned config is zero-shot and scores one generated program per problem.
- **OlympiadBench.** The [February 2024 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.14008) introduced bilingual, multimodal Olympiad-level math and science problems. This campaign uses Evalchemy's 30-question text subset, ten sampled solutions per question, and the configured answer judge.
- **GSM8K.** The [October 2021 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.14168) introduced grade-school math word problems requiring multi-step arithmetic. The campaign uses the zero-shot `gsm8k-0shot` completion route and scores the extracted final answer.
- **PIQA.** The [November 2019 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.11641) introduced two-choice questions about physical commonsense. The campaign selects the answer by length-normalized log-likelihood with no examples in the prompt.
- **WinoGrande.** The [July 2019 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.10641) introduced adversarial pronoun/coreference choices designed to reduce superficial cues. The campaign uses five-shot multiple-choice scoring.
- **BoolQ.** The [May 2019 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.10044) introduced naturally occurring yes/no questions paired with evidence passages. The campaign scores zero-shot choice accuracy.
- **TruthfulQA MC2.** The [September 2021 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.07958) introduced questions that elicit common misconceptions from language models. The campaign's MC2 metric sums probability mass on all true answers within each question's candidate set, rather than counting a single selected answer.
- **TriviaQA.** The [May 2017 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.03551) introduced trivia questions with independently collected evidence documents. The campaign runs five-shot answer generation and reports answer accuracy.
- **AIME24.** The [Mathematical Association of America's 2024 AIME](https://maa.org/maa-invitational-competitions/) supplies the contest problems. Evalchemy samples ten solutions per question in one run through the shared seeded-repeat implementation and scores the integer final answers.
- **MMLU-Pro.** The [June 2024 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.01574) introduced harder, more reasoning-focused multiple-choice questions across fourteen subjects. The campaign runs zero-shot generation with a 65,536-token cap and reports micro-averaged accuracy.
- **GPQA Diamond.** The [November 2023 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.12022) introduced expert-written graduate-level science questions, including the Diamond subset. The campaign averages accuracy over three generated answers per question.
- **CRUXEval (output).** The [January 2024 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.03065) introduced input- and output-prediction tasks for short Python programs. The tracker reports the output-prediction direction, scored on one generated answer per item.
- **FinanceBench.** The [November 2023 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.11944) introduced questions grounded in public financial filings. The campaign scores one generated answer per question with its pinned LLM judge.
- **IFBench.** The [July 2025 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.02833) introduced verifiable constraints that test generalization in precise instruction following. The campaign reports strict prompt-level accuracy, requiring every constraint to hold in the raw response.
- **MRCR.** [Gemini's September 2024 report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.12640) introduced multi-round coreference resolution; [OpenAI's public MRCR release (April 2025)](https://huggingface.co/datasets/openai/mrcr) supplies the corrected multi-needle data used here. The campaign scores nonce-gated sequence similarity and selects only context-length bins that fit the served model.
- **NUPA stratified (Loose).** The [November 2024 Number Cookbook paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.03766) introduced tests of numerical understanding and processing across representations and tasks. The campaign uses Evalchemy's pinned `NUPA5K-Loose` benchmark: a deterministic 5,000-record stratified sample covering 44 tasks and 2,391 strata, scored with permissive answer extraction rather than the paper's direct-answer protocol.
- **SWE-bench Verified.** OpenAI's [August 13, 2024 release](https://openai.com/index/introducing-swe-bench-verified/) introduced the 500-task, human-validated repository-issue repair set. The campaign runs Harbor's canonical `swebench-verified@1.0` implementation with mini-swe-agent 2.1.0, one trial per issue, and executable verification.
- **OpenThoughts-TBLite 2.0.** The [February 18, 2026 release](https://www.openthoughts.ai/blog/openthoughts-tblite) introduced a 100-task, faster-running terminal-agent panel calibrated against Terminal-Bench 2. The campaign runs its pinned `openthoughts-tblite@2.0` tasks with Terminus-2, three trials per task, and reports mean verifier success across trials.
- **Terminal-Bench 2.1.** The [November 7, 2025 release](https://www.tbench.ai/news/announcement-2-0) introduced a harder, more thoroughly verified terminal-agent task set alongside Harbor. The campaign uses `terminal-bench/terminal-bench-2-1` at ref 6 through Harbor, with three Terminus-2 trials per task, a 65,536-token context window, and a 16,384-token per-turn output cap.
- **DS-1000 mini-200.** The [November 2022 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.11501) introduced data-science code-generation problems spanning seven Python libraries. The campaign evaluates a fixed seed-42 200-task Harbor subset with Terminus-2, building task images from the pinned Dockerfiles.
- **BFCL-Parity @ Pi.** Berkeley's [February 2024 BFCL release](https://gorilla.cs.berkeley.edu/blogs/8_berkeley_function_calling_leaderboard.html) introduced executable function-calling evaluation. This campaign uses the Harbor `bfcl_parity@1.0` adaptation with the Pi agent, so its score is the pinned adaptation's verified solve rate rather than an unqualified BFCL leaderboard score.
- **BixBench CLI corrections @ Pi.** BixBench is a computational biology benchmark. The [February 2025 BixBench paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.00096) introduced multi-step computational-biology analysis tasks. This campaign uses Pi on 205 `bixbench-cli-marin-corrections@3` tasks and reports binary answer-equivalence reward, which is distinct from canonical BixBench CLI v1.5.
- **τ³-bench @ Pi.** Tau bench tests whether a model can reliably help someone complete a task from beginning to end. Sierra's [March 18, 2026 τ³-Bench launch](https://sierra.ai/blog/bench-advancing-agent-benchmarking-to-knowledge-and-voice) introduced knowledge and voice tracks alongside corrections to the existing airline and retail tasks. The campaign runs pinned `tau3-bench@1.0.1` in Harbor through the Pi ACP relay and scores task verification.
- **SOTOPIA-hard.** SOTOPIA is a role-playing benchmark where the agent must assume a fictional character and pursue a goal in a simulated scenario, pitted against other agents. The [October 2023 SOTOPIA paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.11667) introduced interactive social-agent evaluation and identified a hard scenario subset. The campaign runs the 100 hard episodes against a fixed `openai/gpt-oss-120b` counterpart and judge. It linearly normalizes each of the seven official dimensions, averages them into an overall score, and applies a cohort-level response-length control. Normalized goal achievement remains available as a non-default diagnostic.

### How do we handle in-distribution and out-of-distribution evals?

#### IN-DISTRIBUTION

**We will** -- dedup against our SFT data, look at model scores while we develop the model, inspect the correlation of our ID evals with our OOD evals, remove or modify ID evals if we think the results are broken, unintuitive or wrong (reporting the eval as modified)

**We may** -- develop synthetic RL tasks modeled on specific tasks in ID evals

**We will not** -- train on teacher rollouts from eval questions, use our ID eval instructions directly as the basis of RL data, deliberately modify ID evals to favor our own models

#### OUT-OF-DISTRIBUTION

**We will** -- de-dup against our SFT raw data, look at meta-data about these evals (e.g., how big they are, general knowledge domain, etc), eval baselines on these evals

**We may** -- evaluate our final models on out-of-distribution benchmarks

**We will not** -- look at the individual questions in the evals, look at any of our own model scores from these evals until our model is frozen, model any synthetic tasks on tasks in the evals (edited), modify OOD evals

### How do we choose which model to release?

We track dozens of candidate checkpoints. Including every candidate in the baseline ranking would
make the critical-difference plot unreadable and would let the number of closely related Snowball
checkpoints bias the cohort. We therefore select one release checkpoint in an internal tournament,
then compare only that checkpoint with the baseline cohort.

The tournament includes every Snowball- or Grug-named candidate with a complete set of observed,
durably linked scores. It does not impute missing cells. FinanceBench and PIQA are excluded because
they did not discriminate reliably within this candidate cohort; TriviaQA is excluded because its
answer extractor proved overly sensitive to response format. The other 23 benchmarks receive equal
weight.

For each model pair and benchmark, let `d = score_a - score_b` and let `s_a` and `s_b` be the
task-level SEMs after multiplying each by `1 / sqrt(0.9)` for the infrastructure-failure tolerance.
The outcome is decisive only when `abs(d) > 1.96 * hypot(s_a, s_b)`. Its sign determines the winner;
otherwise the benchmark is a tie. A win is worth 1, a tie 0.5, and a loss 0. Each pairwise win rate
is the mean of those values across the 23 benchmarks. A candidate's tournament score is the
unweighted mean of its pairwise win rates against every other candidate. If candidates have exactly
the same tournament score, pooled benchmark win rate and then model ID break the tie.

The completed 21-model tournament selected
`open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Merge-Campaign2-DARE-TIES-02-2026.10.10`, with a mean pairwise win rate of
0.627. This checkpoint is labeled **Snowball** in the baseline figures.

### Metric definitions

- **`accuracy`:** the fraction of scored items that pass the benchmark's configured correctness check. Almost all of our benchmarks use this.
- **`mc2`:** Probability mass on all true answers, normalized over the question's answer set and averaged over questions. It is not a binary selection accuracy, and chance performance is above zero.
- **`accuracy (output)`:** CRUXEval output-prediction accuracy. Given a function and input, the model predicts the output; this is distinct from CRUXEval input prediction, which reconstructs an input from the function and desired output.
- **`strict prompt-level accuracy`:** the fraction of IFBench prompts for which the raw response satisfies every required constraint.
- **`mean sequence similarity`:** MRCR's mean `SequenceMatcher` ratio between the response's answer span and the reference answer. A response that fails MRCR's nonce check receives zero credit. 32,768-token models use bins through 16,384 and the 65,536-token model uses bins through 32,768.
- **`length-controlled normalized overall score`:** SOTOPIA-hard's seven official dimensions are each linearly normalized to `[0, 1]`, then averaged per episode. Across the full comparison cohort, a fractional logistic GLM fits model, task, and `tanh`-transformed response-length effects. The reportable score predicts each episode at zero response-length difference from that task's cohort median, then averages those predictions. Length is the evaluated character's total emitted characters over the episode. The counterpart and evaluator are fixed to `openai/gpt-oss-120b` on Together for every model. Normalized goal achievement is retained as an explicit non-default scoring mode.

### Other Metric Notes

- **Scale:** every metric in the suite is reported on a 0-1 scale with 1 the best and 0 the worst; there are no error counts, ranks, or unbounded scores.
- **Allowed context length:** This is allowed prompt + completion context length. If a model's maximum context length is less than the allowed context length, we adopt the model's maximum context length. For single-turn benchmarks, we subdivide the space into max prompt length = longest prompt in the dataset plus a bit of cushion, max response length = the remaining context window. Unless a benchmark specifies another cap, multi-turn generation is limited to 8192 tokens per turn. Context-ablation labels are `context window / per-turn output limit`: both values are passed explicitly, with the first applied to vLLM `max_model_len` and Pi `model_info.max_input_tokens`, and the second applied to Pi `model_info.max_output_tokens`. For example, `65k-16k` means a 65,536-token serving and Pi context window with a 16,384-token per-turn output limit. Ling Lite's native 32,768-token window uses `mrcr-32k.yaml`; the historical 65,536-token Snowball candidate uses `mrcr-65k.yaml`; every release-figure model uses `mrcr.yaml` otherwise.
- **τ³ context selection:** [The Qwen3.6 τ³ ablation](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9743) selected 131,072 total context and 32,768 per-turn output (153/373 scoreable trials; estimated accuracy 0.410) as the optimal for this eval.
- **Pi runtime:** Agentic Pi configs must pin `@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent` explicitly. The corrected context control pins Pi `0.87.0`.

### LLM judges

Five evals involve an LLM judge.

- **FinanceBench:** every scored response is judged. The judge sees the question, the
  reference answers, and the candidate, and returns one label: `correct`, `incorrect`, or
  `not_attempted` (equivalent answers in substance count as correct — algebraic equivalence,
  unit conversions, rounding). Only `correct` scores.
- **BixBench CLI correction set:** every submitted answer is judged for semantic equivalence
  to the task's ideal answer and receives a binary reward. A missing answer receives zero
  without invoking the judge.
- **OlympiadBench:** Minerva/SymPy grades first, and the judge answers equivalence only for
  answers the deterministic check cannot establish. Empty extracted answers score zero before
  any judge request. The reported scores use the fixed-grader replay of sealed responses described
  below, rather than the initial judge labels in the generation jobs.
- **SOTOPIA-hard:** after each completed social interaction, the official episode evaluator
  scores believability, relationship, knowledge, secret keeping, social-rule compliance,
  financial and material benefit, and goal achievement. The verifier normalizes all seven
  dimensions and uses their mean as the default per-episode reward. Cohort analysis applies the
  response-length correction defined above; the judge does not perform that correction.
- **τ³-bench:** the verifier combines deterministic task checks with an LLM evaluator for
  natural-language assertions. The separately configured LLM that simulates the user is part of
  the task environment, not the judge.

Judge deployment is benchmark-specific:

- **FinanceBench** and **OlympiadBench** use locally hosted `MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3-MXFP8` at revision
  `c5454eb03678d8710e54a4e0fc681b9f3b4a3dba` for their final offline regrades. The judge runs
  on eight H100s in RNO2A with tensor parallelism 8, a 262,144-token context window, and the
  `minimax_m3` reasoning parser. The request constrains the response to `correct`, `incorrect`, or
  `not_attempted` with vLLM `structured_outputs.choice`; Evalchemy retains each benchmark's native
  prompt, parsing, deterministic checks, and score aggregation. The replay reads the already sealed
  model responses and changes only the judge deployment.
- **BixBench** uses a co-hosted `MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3-MXFP8` judge at revision
  `c5454eb03678d8710e54a4e0fc681b9f3b4a3dba`. Marin serves it on eight H100s with tensor
  parallelism 8, a 32,768-token context window, the `minimax_m3` reasoning parser, prefix
  caching, and CUDA graphs enabled. The verifier receives the co-hosted endpoint and model
  identity directly from Marin; it does not use the Together judge environment.
- **SOTOPIA-hard** uses `openai/gpt-oss-120b` through Together for both the fixed counterpart
  and the official episode evaluator. Its LiteLLM identifier is
  `openai/openai/gpt-oss-120b`: the first segment selects the OpenAI-compatible provider and
  the remainder is Together's model ID.
- **τ³-bench** uses that same Together-hosted model and LiteLLM identifier for both the user
  simulator and the natural-language assertion evaluator. The two roles are independently
  configured even though this campaign pins them to the same checkpoint.

Judge hyperparameters, per path:

- **Answer-equivalence judge** (FinanceBench, OlympiadBench): a single user message with the
  three-way rubric, `temperature=0`, request timeout 300 s with 5 transport retries, and 16
  concurrent judgments per run. `max_tokens` escalates 128 → 512 → 2048 when a completion is
  empty. Both final replays deploy MiniMax with a 262,144-token judge context window and constrain
  the output to one of the three labels through the pinned vLLM request option. The raw completion
  and parsed label are retained for audit. The judge window deliberately exceeds the 73,664-token
  generation window because responses can expand when re-tokenized by MiniMax.
- **BixBench verifier:** the verifier calls the co-hosted MiniMax Chat Completions endpoint
  with `max_tokens=1024` and a structured response schema containing one boolean score.
  Sampling follows the endpoint's service defaults.
- **SOTOPIA evaluator:** the pinned SOTOPIA v0.1.5 evaluator uses the fixed judge model after
  each episode; the model under evaluation never acts as its own judge. The verifier preserves
  all seven scores, the normalized overall reward, and the evaluated agent's emitted character
  count. `goal` may be selected explicitly for diagnostic runs, but is not the release default.
- **τ³ natural-language assertions:** the pinned τ³ adapter passes only assertions that need
  semantic evaluation to its configured LLM; deterministic assertions remain programmatic.

When a judge call fails after retries, the sample is recorded as grader infrastructure
failure (counted against the run's error tolerance) rather than silently scored zero.

### Thinking mode

The main table records the policy for every benchmark. `on` and `off` set
`enable_thinking` through the model or benchmark config; a benchmark override wins over the model
default. `model default` means the benchmark adds no override, and `not applicable` means the task
does not use a generated chat response. If a model cannot turn reasoning off (e.g. GPT-OSS), an `off` benchmark
uses the model's lowest available reasoning setting instead.

### Errors and Exceptions

#### Infrastructure vs Model Error

We categorize errors during the evaluation process as either infrastructure errors or model errors.
Model errors are scoreable and do not count toward the infrastructure-error threshold. Unless this
policy explicitly identifies an error as a model error, it is an infrastructure error.

#### Infrastructure Error Tolerance

An evaluation may be sealed as soon as at least 90% of its declared trials have valid scores under
the campaign configuration. Up to 10% of declared trials may be absent because of infrastructure
failures; the result does not need to wait for those trials to be recovered. Reported uncertainty
must include this infrastructure-failure tolerance. Task-level outcomes, including agent timeouts
recorded as scores of zero, are scored trials rather than infrastructure failures.

#### Zero-score trace audit

A score of exactly zero shall be reported only after agent review of at least ten representative
traces, or every trace when the evaluation has fewer than ten. The review will check model output,
harness parsing, verifier output, and serving or sandbox errors and accept the zero when the traces support model or task failure and no untracked infrastructure failure explains the result. Otherwise, the result should be rejected and re-run under the policy.

#### Harbor

For Harbor evals, the following error types are currently treated as score-able model errors.

- `AgentTimeoutError`: the agent reached its configured execution timeout; Harbor preserves
  the work produced so far and runs the verifier.
- `ContextLengthExceededError`: the model or agent exhausted the available context; Harbor
  treats that as a classified end to the attempt and runs the verifier.

For these Harbor score-able model errors, we terminate the trial and then run the verifier on the output of the agent, if any output is present. Unlike the Evalchemy timeout rule above, we do *not* automatically score Harbor model errors as 0's. This is because sometimes, agents will solve the task correctly and then get stuck in a loop of self-doubt or fail to submit properly in their harness, and we regard that outcome as closer to a success than a failure.

##### Ambiguous Harbor Errors

- `NonZeroAgentExitCodeError`: the agent process exited non-zero after potentially producing scoreable work. We treat these errors as score-able but if a trial returns more than 30% NonZeroAgentExitCodeError the agent or human executing the policy should review the traces to look for infrastructure errors and invalidate the run if any are discovered.

#### Evalchemy

Under the current Evalchemy pin, `malformed_model_response` is the only named error category that
remains scoreable. It means the model endpoint returned a response that Evalchemy could not parse,
or returned no usable final-answer content. Evalchemy substitutes an empty generation, preserves
the diagnostic category, and lets the benchmark grade that generation normally.

`AgentTimeoutError`, `model_transport`, and `grader_infrastructure` are currently serialized with
the `EVALCHEMY_INFRASTRUCTURE_ERROR` marker and excluded from scored coverage. They therefore count
against the 10% infrastructure-failure allowance rather than as zero-valued model outcomes. Other
task-level failures, including `generation_policy`, `generation`, `grading`, `serialization`,
`incomplete_evaluation`, and `invalid_result`, do not produce a scoreable trial.

This exposes a mismatch with the intended Evalchemy timeout rule below: the release policy says an
`AgentTimeoutError` should score `0.0`, but the current pinned implementation treats it as
infrastructure. Results and coverage from this pin must follow the recorded implementation behavior;
making Evalchemy timeouts scoreable requires a new code pin and provenance.

#### Timeout Policy

The following limits apply to every policy benchmark; there are no benchmark-specific exceptions.

| Evaluator phase | Limit | Outcome when the limit expires |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Evalchemy trial | 30 minutes | Record `0.0` as an `AgentTimeoutError`. This is a scoreable model outcome. |
| Harbor agent setup | 6 minutes | Record `AgentSetupTimeoutError`. This is a retryable infrastructure error. |
| Harbor agent execution | 30 minutes | Record `AgentTimeoutError`, preserve the agent's work, and run the verifier. This is a scoreable model outcome. |
| Harbor verifier | 5 minutes | Record `VerifierTimeoutError`. This is a retryable infrastructure error. |

The Evalchemy limit covers the full trial, including request retries and backoff, after the trial
acquires an evaluator slot.

Harbor launch configs override task-manifest values with
`agents[].override_setup_timeout_sec: 360`, `agents[].override_timeout_sec: 1800`, and
`verifier.override_timeout_sec: 300`. The repository-owned campaign validator checks these values
before submission, so the same limits apply even when a task manifest omits its own timeout.

## Baseline Models

### How we select baseline models

The process for selecting baseline models in our policy is fundamentally heuristic and community-driven. For each new model release, we will strive to select a representative cohort of open-weights and open-source models that are roughly comparable to Marin models in terms of parameter count and document them in the policy. We will look up reported results for those models in the research literature and, where available, use them as targets for internal reproduction, noting, however, that typically the variance in hyperparameters will make published results not directly comparable to our own. We will sometimes substitute quantized variants of the listed models for the canonical models, especially for larger models where our hardware makes it challenging to run inference on the non-quantized variants.
