## Codebase pins

The single pin authority is the checked-out Marin revision. Its generated
[`external_dependencies.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/75a5690b0ff2e1510d73e576649e3e059f06da9a/lib/marin/src/marin/external_dependencies.py#L65-L81)
contains the immutable Evalchemy and Harbor revisions; the campaign validator also requires the
Harbor lockfile to resolve to that same Harbor commit. Do not copy these pins into this document or
an artifact-side environment file. The release pins Marin commit
[`75a5690b0ff2e1510d73e576649e3e059f06da9a`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/75a5690b0ff2e1510d73e576649e3e059f06da9a).
Every launch snapshot records that exact Marin commit, which identifies all three codebase revisions.

### Configuration immutability

For convenience, Marin packages a launcher for policy evals. The launcher must not alter model-serving settings or benchmark semantics (except model-specific chat templates and model-specific Harbor context and compaction values). It may resolve credentials, cluster placement, output locations, concurrency, and other operational values.

Each durable run record preserves the effective model configuration, evaluator configuration, code revision, and Harbor policy digest. Any other semantic change requires a new checked-in config and code revision.

## Eval launch commands (Marin)

These commands require access to the `marin` Iris controller and the `cw-rno2a` federated cluster.
Set `MARIN_DIR` to a clean checkout of the pinned campaign revision and `MODEL` to a filename stem under
the repository's campaign `model-configs/` directory. The launcher validates every pin and canonical config, resolves the
required credentials, snapshots the effective command and configs, and submits one shared-serving
root. It deliberately supplies no eval-policy label.

```bash
REPRO_DIR=$(mktemp -d)
git clone https://github.com/marin-community/marin.git "$REPRO_DIR/marin"
git -C "$REPRO_DIR/marin" checkout 75a5690b0ff2e1510d73e576649e3e059f06da9a
export MARIN_DIR="$REPRO_DIR/marin"
CAMPAIGN="$MARIN_DIR/experiments/evaluation/campaigns/eval-campaign-09-25-unlabeled"
MODEL=REPLACE_WITH_MODEL_CONFIG_FILENAME_STEM
cd "$CAMPAIGN"
./validate-campaign.sh
./launch-campaign.sh --submit --model "$MODEL"
```

Use `--suite nonagentic`, `--suite agentic`, or `--suite terminal-bench` for a complete suite
subset. Use repeatable `--evalchemy NAME` or `--harbor NAME` selectors for a named recovery. AIME24,
OlympiadBench, and GPQA Diamond perform their repeated sampling inside one launch using the shared
seeded-repeat implementation; AIME24 is not launched ten times. Omitting `--submit` is a dry run.

### Three-benchmark reproduction check

For a release-level smoke reproduction, use model-config stem `Qwen-Qwen3.6-35B-A3B` and these
fixed benchmarks: GSM8K 0-shot (`0.908`), MATH500 (`0.984`), and DS-1000 (`0.270`). Launch each
benchmark separately with the Marin command above:

```bash
MODEL=Qwen-Qwen3.6-35B-A3B
./launch-campaign.sh --submit --wait --limit 50 --suite nonagentic --model "$MODEL" --evalchemy gsm8k-0shot
./launch-campaign.sh --submit --wait --limit 50 --suite nonagentic --model "$MODEL" --evalchemy math500
./launch-campaign.sh --submit --wait --limit 50 --suite agentic --model "$MODEL" --harbor ds-1000-local
```

Each launch prints a run ID such as
`20260929-150059-Qwen-Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-piqa-ef1c`. After the waiting command exits, inspect that
run's durable record with the following command. It prints the scoreable-trial count followed by
the primary score; repeat it with the run ID from each launch.

```bash
RUN_ID=REPLACE_WITH_PRINTED_RUN_ID
RECORDS_PREFIX=s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals
bash -lc '
  source ./common.sh
  resolve_coreweave_credentials
  uv run --project "$MARIN_DIR" fsutil cat --raw \
    "'$RECORDS_PREFIX'/'$RUN_ID'/record.json"
' | python3 -c '
import json, sys
record = json.load(sys.stdin)
status = record["status"]
if status != "completed":
    error = record.get("error")
    raise SystemExit(f"run did not complete: {status}: {error}")
coverage = next(iter(record["coverage"].values()))
metrics = next(iter(record["canonical_metrics"].values()))
score = next(value for name, value in metrics.items() if not name.endswith("_stderr"))
print(coverage["n_scored"], score)
'
```

After at least 50 scoreable trials, compare their mean with the corresponding reported score. For this
provisional smoke check, parity means an absolute difference no greater than `0.146`. This is the
worst-case 95% normal half-width for 50 independent `[0, 1]` trial rewards,
`1.96 × 0.5 / sqrt(50)`, expanded by `1 / sqrt(0.9)` for the policy's infrastructure tolerance.
This gate is intentionally a smoke reproduction, not a replacement for the full-run confidence
intervals or release result.

## Run resumption

Resume an interrupted Harbor run only when its model, checked-out repository revision, runtime
limit, and dataset state are unchanged. Read the original run ID and effective configuration from
its durable `record.json`. Use the model and Harbor config from the same Marin commit, then add the
original run ID:

```bash
uv run python -m experiments.evaluation.cli launch \
  --model-config "$CAMPAIGN/model-configs/<model-config>.yaml" \
  --harbor-config "$STAGED_HARBOR_DIR/<harbor-config>.yaml" \
  --resume-run-id <original-run-id>
```

The durable `<records-prefix>/<original-run-id>/results/harbor_jobs/` tree must remain accessible.
Harbor preserves completed scored trials and reruns missing attempts and exceptions in its pinned
resume taxonomy. Use a clean replacement when model, policy, pins, limits, records prefix, or
dataset state changed, or when the unscored error is outside that taxonomy. Never delete a trial
directory to force recovery.

## Baseline-specific launch settings

The YAML files under
`experiments/evaluation/campaigns/eval-campaign-09-25-unlabeled/model-configs/` are authoritative for checkpoint and tokenizer
revisions, serving context, GPU count, tensor and data parallelism, reasoning parser, tool parser,
sampling overrides, and Pi `thinking_format`. Use the matching file unchanged. Pi uses
`qwen-chat-template` for Qwen3.6 and Qwen3-Next and `chat-template` for the other models.

## Updating codebase pins

Use the newest campaign pin for each codebase across the full release, assuming forward
compatibility with earlier score-producing runs. If a pin change causes an observed result
regression, stop launches, fix or revert the change, and issue a new policy version when the
evaluation behavior intentionally changes. Preserve the original run's exact pins in its immutable
config snapshot even after the release-wide pins advance.

## Standards for presenting Marin evals

* Display score cells in the standard tracker and any tournament-only tracker to three significant digits. Apply the same convention to a tracker formed from their union. The linked durable run records retain unrounded scores. Tournament and figure analyses recover full-precision task aggregates from that durable evidence; tracker values are presentation-only.
* Select the release Snowball checkpoint by the uncertainty-aware paired tournament defined in “How do we choose which model to release?” Release figures include only the selected checkpoint, not the other Snowball candidates. The Snowball candidate family includes Grug 67B A2B checkpoints as well as checkpoints named Snowball. For each benchmark, plot the selected Snowball checkpoint and every non-Snowball baseline with an available score and total-training-FLOP estimate. Performance is on the y-axis and total training FLOPs are on a logarithmic x-axis. A baseline with an incomplete suite may appear in the scatterplots for its completed benchmarks, but it is excluded from cross-benchmark critical-difference analysis unless it has the full common benchmark panel.
* Produce uncertainty-aware normalized critical-difference diagrams with and without a FLOP control. Normalize scores within each benchmark across the complete-panel cohort. Estimate each score's task-level sample SEM from the scored trial rewards, then multiply the SEM by `1 / sqrt(0.9)` to account conservatively for the policy's 10% infrastructure-failure tolerance. With a fixed random seed, draw 100,000 score panels from independent normal sampling distributions centered on the reported scores and clipped to the metric's `[0, 1]` range. Rank models within every benchmark for each draw, using average ranks for ties, and report mean ranks with simultaneous 95% bands based on the draw-wise maximum absolute rank deviation. Report the Nemenyi critical difference at `alpha = 0.05`; it depends on the number of models and benchmarks, while score uncertainty affects the simulated rank distribution and its simultaneous bands.
* For the FLOP-controlled diagram, regress the draw's benchmark-normalized scores on `log10(total training FLOPs)` with one common linear slope, rank the within-benchmark residuals, and otherwise use the same uncertainty procedure. Treat FLOP estimates as fixed point estimates and disclose that their estimation uncertainty is not propagated. The uncontrolled diagram ranks the sampled normalized scores directly.
* We use a 6ND proxy for pretraining FLOPS, and 6 * max_tokens_per_rollout / max_context_length * n_rollouts * active_params proxy for RL FLOPS; that said, we are the only lab, as of this writing, which releases RL FLOPS, so meaningful comparisons are impossible. From the few labs who release midtraining / SFT information, we derive an unweighted mean percentage of FLOPS devoted to midtraining. We then estimate midtraining FLOPS for other labs using that mean. We estimate total FLOPS as the sum of pretraining FLOPS + (all midtraining / non-RL) FLOPS + (all RL and OPD) FLOPS. For any model which doesn't give sufficient evidence for any of the three stages, use the mean FLOPS over all models in the cohort as the estimated  FLOPS for that stage.
* In a separate standalone table, include all raw scores in XX.y format, with 95% confidence intervals derived from the trial count and the infrastructure error tolerance -- do not leave gaps, use table captions for results that require further context, use the exact same model family in the table as was present in the x-y scatterplot(s)
* Eval results are reportable IFF the eval in question completed with no more than 10% of trials encountering infrastructure errors
* Eval results are reportable IFF they include provenance, in the form of model traces, and where available, verifier traces
* Any eval result that is publicly presented should clearly distinguish whether the benchmarks are in-distribution (part of the dev set), held out, or a mix of the two
* Any eval result that is publicly presented in a major release should report on *all* ID and OOD benchmarks, avoiding cherry picking, substitution, or new evals outside of a formal policy update
* For active development and internal communication, it is fine to define working subsets of the ID benchmarks and report on those in isolation

### Reproduce SOTOPIA-hard length control

SOTOPIA-Hard length control was introduced post-hoc, after the agent traces were generated. For this generation of eval policy, it needs to be run separately. The details on how to do so live here.

The Harbor verifier writes the unadjusted normalized overall reward and
`sotopia_response_characters` for every completed episode. The release score is a cohort
statistic, so it must be regenerated across all compared models rather than copied from one
Harbor run's aggregate. From the pinned Marin checkout, with CoreWeave S3 read credentials and
the campaign tracker available locally, run:

```bash
TRACKER=/absolute/path/to/TRACKER.md
OUTPUT_DIR=/absolute/path/to/artifacts/sotopia-length-controlled-overall
uv run python experiments/evaluation/campaigns/eval-campaign-09-25-unlabeled/analysis/sotopia_length_control/rank.py \
  --tracker "$TRACKER" --output-dir "$OUTPUT_DIR"
```

The tool reads the seven dimension scores and transcripts from each sealed SOTOPIA-hard archive,
measures only the evaluated agent's emitted characters, and groups cross-validation folds by task.
It writes both raw and length-controlled rankings, plus the tracker SHA-256, every source archive,
the selected regularization strength, and all cross-validation losses. Its counterfactual sets the
response-length difference to zero relative to each task's cohort median. Adding or removing a
model changes that median and requires recomputing the complete cohort. A policy-valid
infrastructure failure retains its configured zero; unscored infrastructure failures are excluded
under the campaign's sealing rule.

The tracker-linked October 15 cohort output is preserved at
`s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/ablations/sotopia-overall-length-controlled-20261015-c5ef5789/`.

### Reproduce the Snowball tournament and critical-difference figures

Use the campaign tracker as a point-in-time input: every numeric cell must contain its durable
S3 result link, either a native `/results` archive or a corrected per-trial replay JSON. The
tournament requires complete observed scores for every Snowball or Grug candidate on its
23-benchmark selection panel; it excludes FinanceBench, PIQA, and TriviaQA. It derives each cell's
full-precision task aggregate and task-level SEM from the durable trial evidence, then expands the
SEM by `1 / sqrt(0.9)`. The three-decimal tracker score is presentation-only. A benchmark is a
win only when `abs(score_a - score_b) > 1.96 * hypot(adjusted_sem_a, adjusted_sem_b)`; otherwise it
is a tie. A win is one vote, a tie half a vote, and each candidate's selection statistic is the
unweighted mean of its paired win rates against the other candidates. Preserve the generated
tracker and recovered-metrics SHA-256 values, and do not combine a tournament selection with
figures generated from a different tracker snapshot.

The analysis tools are in the Marin campaign worktree under
`experiments/evaluation/campaigns/eval-campaign-09-25-unlabeled/analysis/`, in the
`snowball_tournament/` and `critical_difference/` subdirectories. From the pinned Marin checkout,
with the campaign tracker and output directory available locally, run:

```bash
TRACKER=/absolute/path/to/TRACKER.md
OUTPUT_DIR=/absolute/path/to/artifacts
uv run python experiments/evaluation/campaigns/eval-campaign-09-25-unlabeled/analysis/snowball_tournament/pairwise.py \
  --tracker "$TRACKER" --recovered-metrics "$OUTPUT_DIR/recovered-record-metrics.json" \
  --output-dir "$OUTPUT_DIR/snowball-tournament"
uv run python experiments/evaluation/campaigns/eval-campaign-09-25-unlabeled/analysis/critical_difference/plot.py \
  --tracker "$TRACKER" --selection "$OUTPUT_DIR/snowball-tournament/snowball_selection.json" \
  --recovered-metrics "$OUTPUT_DIR/recovered-record-metrics.json" \
  --output-dir "$OUTPUT_DIR/critical-difference"
```

Both commands need read access to the scored results in CoreWeave S3; configure the normal
Marin `fsutil` credentials first. It reads canonical `record.json` files for trial counts and
normalized sample rewards for non-binary metrics. If a NUPA record has not been written, the
tool requires its sealed native Evalchemy archive and verifies its coverage and canonical score.
For cells sealed from an interrupted executor,
`recovered-record-metrics.json` supplies the independently aggregated scored-trial count and
reward standard error; retain that audit file with the tracker. The complete-panel cohort is the selected
Snowball plus the non-Snowball models listed in `critical_difference/baseline_flops.csv`; a
benchmark enters the diagrams only if every cohort model has a numeric, linked score. The output
includes every benchmark-level pair outcome, the full paired-win matrix and selection summary,
per-cell sample statistics, FLOP estimates, rank tables, and uncontrolled and FLOP-controlled PNG,
PDF, and SVG figures. Regenerate
both commands after any tracker change. The uncertainty, normalization, FLOP-control, and
critical-difference calculations are defined above; the random seed and draw count are fixed in
the plotting code.

## Future considerations

* We would like to post-train multiple Snowball checkpoints, experimenting with different degrees of compute applied to post-training, to establish trade-off lines / domains
* We would like to think about a "marin model card" that would set minimum standards for true open development
* amd/Instella-MoE-16B-A3B-Think is not runnable currently from our pinned vLLM fork, but we would like to look at this model in the future
* We still weren't able to land a trusted K2 Horizon baseline set of scores yet
* evaluate our baselines on OOD as well as ID
* JudgeArena multilingual, maybe one of those cultural idiom / include benchmarks, restore simpleQA-mini, a long context supplement for MRCR
* Produce a summary of why we think the previously flagged TB2 / TB4 task description overlap are likely not problematic, if they are not
* Find a better instruction following benchmark than IFBench
* Consider a smaller subset of MMLU-Pro and NUPA so they run faster
* Fix the inconsistency in Evalchemy timeout error handling
* In the future, we may deliberately use subsets of very large benchmarks like BFCL and NUPA as training material; in this case, we must mark the full benchmarks as explicitly contaminated, adding a new section to our eval policy
* Properly unify on the co-hosted MiniMax judge
* Consider using a judge panel and requiring all judges to agree on equivalence
* Consider using cruxeval input as well as output
* Drop PIQA as non-discriminating, TriviaQA needs its grader reconsidered
* biomedical knowledge: MedXpertQA or PubMedQA, Clinical reasoning: HealthBench Professional/ Bedside Bench /ASCENT, Biological discovery: Longevity — genetics regression; LAB-Bench cloning / DNA methylation age comparison, Medical coding: MedConceptsQA — ATC Hard/ MedConceptsQA ICD-10 procedures, hard

topics.title: [eval] Check in the September evaluation campaign
topics.body:
Check in the model, evaluator, and launcher configurations for the September 2026 evaluation campaign, together with the runtime fixes needed for serving, retry, resume, and coverage. The launcher validates external pins, writes immutable effective-config snapshots, and accepts an optional submitter-controlled version label. That label does not attest policy conformance.

Harbor results are bound to the full model and hosted judge configurations, dataset, policy, runtime, and task limit. Resume checks this identity before submission and reuse. A changed checkpoint under the same served name is rejected, as are existing roots without model-bound provenance. Recovery retries known infrastructure failures and unscored trials while retaining scored outcomes and unknown errors.

The frozen Harbor runtime pins 94b118022fe3e677784a638daf33d57a836fa5fe and includes the Tau3 adapter. The Evalchemy lock and generated pin match Marin's external dependency configuration.

SWE-bench uses the native Mini-SWE adapter from merged [Harbor #232](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/pull/232) and [#233](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/pull/233). Its 32,768-token context includes the prompt and reply together. Mini-SWE counts the rendered prompt through the serving tokenizer, including tools and the generation prefix, and caps the reply within the remaining budget and server window. Harbor loads Mini-SWE's base configuration before applying overrides and selects its batch agent, which saves the trajectory on context exhaustion without prompting. Harbor can then verify the existing patch.

Sotopia uses the packaged agent from merged [Harbor #231](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/pull/231). Judge failures become verifier infrastructure errors. The Marin agent wrappers and their harness dependencies are removed. Sotopia's native generation still does not enforce its declared context budget, so those results cannot establish conformance to the 32K context policy.

Part of #9566.

🤖 Holistic review of c67cb190eb37c9c840eea08a33c3f70ee6375488.

This PR checks in the September campaign: about 200 model, evaluator, and ablation configs, plus analysis scripts. It also changes eval-runner behavior: Harbor resume and recovery, brokered `instances`, upstream vLLM with plugins, `stage_local`, hosted-judge startup retry, and orchestrator precache. The campaign configs look reasonable. The library half overlaps three open PRs that solve the same problems in different ways, and the PR also changes `levanter` and `rigging` without saying so in its body.

**Blockers**
1. `experiments/evaluation/launch.py:285` duplicates #9129, which is open and updated 2026-10-14 by the same author. Both add `--retry-unscored-harbor-trials`. #9129 resumes with `--resume-run-id`, reusing the saved record's run ID and results directory. This PR uses `--resume-results-path` plus a separate `harbor_resume_identity.json`. If both merge, Marin has two Harbor resume paths and two validators for the same flag. Pick one design, close the other PR, and land this campaign on top of it.
2. `lib/levanter/src/levanter/model_cache.py:101` fixes the partial-mirror bug from #10039 differently. #10039 is also open and by the same author: it filters `.cache_metadata.json` out of the HF snapshot. This PR moves the marker beside the cache (`<cache_path>.marin-complete.json`). That move turns every existing `quick-serve-models` mirror into a cache miss, so every cached checkpoint in every region is copied again on first use. The 67B models alone are about 90 GB each. Neither PR mentions this. Drop `419343080a` from this PR and land one fix in a levanter PR whose body states the re-mirror cost, or the cleanup of partial mirrors if it keeps the old marker.

**Should fix**
3. `lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/runner.py:369` (from `b983e92751`) removes `EndpointRoute`. Every Evalchemy request now goes through the controller's capability proxy instead of directly to the serving task. That includes MRCR at 65k/128k context and `evalchemy_num_concurrent: 128`. #10033 fixes the same preemption problem without that cost: a loopback relay re-resolves the registry entry and connects directly. The metric window at `:357` still resolves the address once, so after a preemption it scrapes the dead host. Merge #10033 first, then restore the direct route here.
4. `lib/marin/src/marin/inference/iris.py:211`: setting `serve.instances > 1` silently applies the default `BrokerConfig()`. That allows `max_in_flight=16` requests per worker and has a 180 s httpx timeout. Take `model-configs/triviaqa/open-athena-Grug-67B-A2B-BFCL-Recovery.yaml`, which runs DP8 × `max_num_seqs: 32` × 2 instances with `evalchemy_num_concurrent: 128` "to keep the replica pool full". It gets at most 32 requests in flight, and any generation over 180 s fails even though `evalchemy/client.py` sets `_REQUEST_TIMEOUT = 1800`. In `inference_config_for_model`, derive the broker settings from `ServeConfig`: `max_in_flight = data_parallel_size × max_num_seqs`, and set the worker, lease, and proxy timeouts at or above the Evalchemy request timeout.
5. `lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/driver_config.py:27-30`: `Path(__file__).parents[5] / "marin" / "src"` resolves to the same `lib/marin/src` as the old `parents[3]`. The change does nothing, but the new comment says it stops workspace Rigging and FineStore from shadowing pinned packages. Revert to `parents[3]` and drop the comment.
6. Unrelated library changes ride along with the campaign check-in, and the body describes none of them:
   - `rigging/filesystem/conditional_object.py`: forced virtual-host addressing, credentials read from env, and a retry on `PathStyleRequestNotAllowed`.
   - The levanter cache marker from item 2.
   - `inference/worker.py`: path routing.
   - `inference/vllm_server.py`: new streamer fault markers.
   - `runner.py`: `_ORCHESTRATOR_DISK` raised from 16g to 80g, and model precache on the orchestrator.
   
   Split the `rigging`/`levanter`/`inference` changes into focused PRs. Several already exist (#10039, #10033, #9129). Keep this PR to the campaign plus the eval-runner pieces the campaign needs.
7. Checked-in files that nothing reads:
   - `retired-model-configs-2026-09-28/` and `retired-chat-templates-2026-09-28/` (a 1,003-line Jinja template).
   - `config/external/evalchemy-olympiadbench-judge-ablation/`, with its 2,502-line `uv.lock`. Nothing references it by name, and `ablations/olympiadbench_judge/regrade.py` imports `eval.*` without documenting how to run it.
   
   Delete the retired files; git history keeps them. Either document `uv run --project config/external/evalchemy-olympiadbench-judge-ablation …` in an ablation README or drop the project.
8. `lib/rigging/src/rigging/filesystem/conditional_object.py:258,287`: `version()` and `read()` each build the same `ExponentialBackoff(initial=0.1, maximum=5.0, factor=2.0, jitter=0.25)`. Hoist it into one module constant, `_S3_READ_BACKOFF`, next to `_MAX_S3_READ_ATTEMPTS`.

**Tests to drop**
- `test_s3_conditional_object_uses_virtual_host_addressing_without_endpoint` (`lib/rigging/tests/test_conditional_object.py:121`): copies the implementation into the expectation. It asserts the kwargs passed to a mocked `create_client`.
- `test_s3_conditional_object_passes_ambient_credentials_to_botocore` (`:133`): the same pattern. It restates the env-to-kwargs mapping and would not fail if botocore resolved the credentials wrongly.
- `test_pipeline_parallelism_rejects_multiple_serving_instances` (`tests/evaluation/test_model_config.py:260`): mirrors a guard. It only restates the `ServeConfig.__post_init__` check.

- #10039: a competing fix for the cache marker (item 2). Land one; drop the other's version from this PR.
- #10033: a competing fix for Evalchemy endpoint preemption (item 3). Merge #10033 first, then restore the direct route here.

topics.title: [taskcompendium] Tell a failed grading preparation from a failed grader
topics.body:
A grading that fails while the verifier machine is being prepared, unpacking the staged archive, removing it, making the workspace, or making the reward files' directories, was recorded with the same kinds as a grader command that failed or timed out, `EXECUTION` or `TIMEOUT`, with only the message to tell them apart. A verifier deadline that expired before the grader's command ever ran was recorded as the grader timing out. A caller deciding whether a failure is the task's or the host's had nothing typed to go on. In a Taskforge generation run under a saturated cluster controller, 235 of 279 program revisions were spent on host-caused grading failures of this shape (269 deadline expiries during staging commands among them).

Two additions make the distinction typed:

- `GradingFailure.STAGING` for the runtime's own preparation commands. Commands the task's author chose, the grader's own command, its environment's setup commands and its collect commands, keep `EXECUTION` and `TIMEOUT`. The reward files' preparation moves out of the script grader's run into the staging block it belongs to, ahead of the setup commands.
- `GradingProgress`, which the sandbox grading path moves to `STAGING` before it captures the agent's output files and to `GRADER` before the first command the author chose, a setup command or the grader's own. The rollout engine, whose verifier deadline covers the preparation as well as the grader, now reports an expiry before the grader's command as `STAGING` with the error "Verifier deadline expired while preparing the verifier machine", and as `TIMEOUT` with the unchanged message otherwise. A session that grades without the sandbox path leaves the phase at `GRADER`, so nothing changes for it.

Downstream, Taskforge's validation classifier and its build-time grading will map `STAGING` to a host cause instead of a task one; that lands on its own once this is in.

A caller deciding whether a failure is the task's or the host's had nothing typed to go on. - `GradingFailure.STAGING` for the runtime's own preparation commands. A session that grades without the sandbox path leaves the phase at `GRADER`, so nothing changes for it.

```markdown
Tests: the runtime test that fails the archive removal now expects `STAGING`; one test records the phase at each command on the verifier machine (the five preparation commands under `STAGING`, the grader's command and its reward read under `GRADER`); one rollout test stalls the verifier machine on the unpack and on the grader's command in turn and checks the deadline's kind and message for each.

Downstream, Taskforge's validation classifier and its build-time grading will map `STAGING` to a host cause instead of a task one; that lands on its own once this is in.

```

</details>
🤖 Removed the test-inventory paragraph from the body.

🤖 Holistic review of e690c61e14a8fa1ddc95b694a69640538637309b.

This change adds a typed `GradingFailure.STAGING` for failures in the runtime's own grading preparation, and a mutable `GradingProgress` that lets `RolloutEngine` report a verifier deadline that expired before the author's commands as `STAGING`. The split is sound and the tests cover tar, output capture, and the grader. One gap remains: the task author's `collect` commands still run under `STAGING`, which goes against the rule the body states. It should be fixed before Taskforge starts treating `STAGING` as a host cause.

**Before.** Every failed grading command became `EXECUTION` or `TIMEOUT`, whether it was `tar -xf` of the staged archive or the grader's own script. When `verifier_timeout` in `RolloutEngine._run_session` ran out, the result was always `TIMEOUT`, even if the grader never started. **After.** `_run_staging` labels the unpack, archive removal, workspace, and reward-file preparation as `STAGING`. Reward-file preparation moves out of `_script_reward` into `_grade_on`. `grade_in_sandbox` sets the phase to `STAGING` on entry, and `_grade_on` switches it to `GRADER` just before the environment's setup commands. The engine sets `STAGING` around output capture, and `_expired_verifier_grade` maps the phase to the deadline's failure kind.

**Evidence.** I ran the changed tests locally and they pass: `test_a_verifier_deadline_names_the_phase_it_expired_in` (3 cases) and `test_deadline_during_grading_keeps_captured_outputs` in rolloutengine, plus `test_grading_progress_is_staging_until_the_authors_commands` (2 cases) in taskcompendium. The 235/279 revision figure from Taskforge is the PR's own claim. No artifact in the PR backs it, and it is not a merge criterion. No test covers a grader with `collect` or `artifacts`.

**Findings**

- **1. Blocker:** `lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/runtime/grading.py:542`. The `grading.collect` loop runs inside `_grade_staged`, after `grade_in_sandbox` has set `STAGING` at line 469 and before `_grade_on` switches to `GRADER` at line 628. These are the author's commands, and the body says collect commands keep `EXECUTION`/`TIMEOUT`. Each one runs with `timeout=grading.limit`, which is `min(verifier_timeout, grader.timeout)`. The engine's verifier deadline started earlier, before output capture, so the outer deadline always fires before the command's own timeout. As a result, any task whose collect command hangs gets `STAGING` with "Verifier deadline expired while preparing the verifier machine". This is the same misclassification Codex found for setup commands, which 2be6f617a8 fixed only there. Taskforge's planned mapping would then retry a broken task as a host failure. Fix: set `progress.phase = GradingPhase.GRADER` around the collect loop and restore `STAGING` before the artifact downloads and machine creation that follow. Add a `test_a_verifier_deadline_names_the_phase_it_expired_in` case with a `ScriptGrader(collect=...)` whose collect command stalls and expects `TIMEOUT`.
- **2. Should fix:** `lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/runtime/grading.py:133`. `_download_artifact` runs only runtime-generated commands: the `artifact-kind` probe, the protected-directory `mkdir`, and the archive `tar` (via `_run_checked` at lines 184/200/224). It still reports their failures as `TIMEOUT`/`EXECUTION`, which the new `GradingFailure` docstring reserves for the author's commands. Meanwhile, a verifier deadline that expires during the same download is reported as `STAGING`. So one host-side stall gets two different kinds depending on which timer fires first. Fix: use `_run_staging` for those commands and `GradingFailure.STAGING` in the probe's two explicit `_infra_error` calls. Keep `SubmissionFailure` for missing, linked, and wrong-kind artifacts, which are the agent's fault.
- **3. Should fix:** `lib/taskcompendium/README.md:314` still documents `grade_in_sandbox(task, attempt, factory, machine_spec, *, task_machine=None, timeout=None)` without `progress`. The `verifier_timeout` row at `docs/references/task-rollouts.md:345` does not say that an expiry before the author's commands is reported as `staging`. Add the parameter and the `STAGING`/`TIMEOUT` split to both, so downstream classifiers can find the contract without reading `engine.py`.
- **4. Related PR:** #10203 (`[rolloutengine] Replace task sessions with registered harnesses`) rewrites the same verifier-deadline block (`engine.py:420-436`) and the `_grade_rollout` call path. It still builds the literal `GradeResult(..., "Verifier deadline expired", failure=GradingFailure.TIMEOUT)`. Land this PR first. #10203 then needs to pass `GradingProgress` through its new `_grade_rollout` call and use `_expired_verifier_grade`. Otherwise the rebase silently restores the old `TIMEOUT` mapping, and the 3-case deadline test is the only thing that would catch it.

topics.title: [inference] remote_inference keeps a stale address after the served task is rescheduled
topics.body:
`remote_inference` resolves the served endpoint's address once (`lib/marin/src/marin/inference/iris.py:682`) and keeps using it for the life of the client. When the inference task is preempted and Iris reschedules it on another host, every later request goes to the dead address and fails with `httpx.ConnectError: All connection attempts failed` until the client process restarts.

Observed on 2026-10-17 in the SFT-shootout relay collection (#10213): the v0 student server for TMax relay shard-02 round 1 (`inference-7998e252`) shows `preemptions=1` and its log stops at 14:35:18 UTC; from then on the relay proxy logged thousands of `ConnectError`s, 198 of 200 trials in that round raised `InternalServerError` between 14:33 and 15:13 UTC, and the driver still wrote `_SUCCESS` because Harbor exited 0. SWE-smith relay shard-00 round 3 failed the same way earlier that morning (85 of 97 trials raised; both student children of that job show `preemptions=1`).

Reproduce: serve a model through `remote_inference`, start a long-lived client, preempt (or cancel and let Iris reschedule) the inference task, send a request after the task is running again on a different host.

Expected: the client re-resolves the endpoint through Iris when a connection error occurs (bounded retry), so a rescheduled server is picked up without restarting the client; callers that cannot recover should fail loudly rather than report success.

Done when: `remote_inference` (or its client wrapper) re-resolves on connection failure with a bounded retry, a test covers a rescheduled endpoint, and callers that batch many requests (relay collection, eval launchers) surface a failed run instead of a success marker when the server is unreachable. The relay collector's own copy of this fix (re-resolve on `ConnectError`, retry up to 20 minutes, then fail the run when over 20% of trials raise) is on branch `task/212` at `174906474a` and can serve as a reference.

comments.body:
🤖 At Marin commit `753bbb163c78f0e7ea50059522f42156708162c8`, Evalchemy retries can keep targeting a stale address after the serving task moves: `experiments/evaluation/launch.py:219` selects `EndpointRoute.DIRECT`; `lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/runner.py:327` calls `_local_endpoint_session`, which resolves the address once at line 558. `lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evalchemy/client.py` passes this fixed base URL to lm-eval with `max_retries=8`; those request retries do not re-resolve the Iris endpoint. Harbor uses `EndpointRoute.CAPABILITY` at launch.py:236 instead.

The policy branch differs: `benfeuer/eval-campaign-09-25-v2` at `75a5690b0ff2e1510d73e576649e3e059f06da9a` passes the capability-backed session to the evaluation executor unchanged when capability_origin is configured. That revision’s evaluation runner calls `_local_endpoint_session` for inference metrics capture, not the model-request path. This is a source audit, not a live failover test. The learning-rate sweep screens tracked in #10213 will record the exact launch revision and endpoint route; failed/preempted evaluations will be kept separate from valid model scores.

🤖
# Research

At main `2f3897eb`, direct `remote_inference` freezes the serving task's address. Evalchemy selects a direct route and resolves it once more before handing a fixed URL to lm-eval; its eight request retries cannot follow a rescheduled task. Harbor already uses the Iris capability route and a 90% completion gate, while an evaluation step can return successfully after writing a failed record. The relay collector's [address retry](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/174906474a8039d1ff8989e8f6d53103242cfec1) and [unserved-trial gate](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/f547fdf339) are on `task/212`.

**Relevant code**
- [`iris.py#L656-L665`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/2f3897ebfdbdbc2246bbe0a3bf6bca91a89b6f9d/lib/marin/src/marin/inference/iris.py#L656-L665) — initial direct URL
- [`launch.py#L205-L236`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/2f3897ebfdbdbc2246bbe0a3bf6bca91a89b6f9d/experiments/evaluation/launch.py#L205-L236) — Evalchemy direct, Harbor capability
- [`runner.py#L556-L564`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/2f3897ebfdbdbc2246bbe0a3bf6bca91a89b6f9d/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/runner.py#L556-L564) — one-time direct resolution
- [`client.py#L143-L156`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/2f3897ebfdbdbc2246bbe0a3bf6bca91a89b6f9d/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evalchemy/client.py#L143-L156) — fixed URL and eight retries
- [`runner.py#L460-L472`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/2f3897ebfdbdbc2246bbe0a3bf6bca91a89b6f9d/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/runner.py#L460-L472) — failed record returns as step success

# Proposed Fix

`remote_inference` → `_local_endpoint_session` → lm-eval retains the old URL after Iris moves the serving task. This needs changes at the session, evaluator route, and run-status boundaries:

1. Route Evalchemy model requests through the existing Iris capability URL, which resolves the current endpoint per request; retain the direct URL for metrics. Verify long-request timeouts and measure a representative evaluation's throughput before landing.
2. Add a session-owned direct endpoint resolver and use it in direct HTTP callers on `ConnectError`, with a monotonic deadline, bounded poll interval, and terminal-job check. Make `wait_until_ready()` probe the newly resolved address after rescheduling; propagate failure when the deadline expires.
3. After persisting a non-success evaluation record, raise from `run_evaluation_step` so the enclosing step cannot write a success marker. Reuse the existing Evalchemy/Harbor coverage checks and integrate the relay branch's unserved-trial gate without duplicating it.
4. Test a request across two local serving addresses, a permanently unavailable endpoint, Evalchemy's selected route, and failure propagation through the evaluation step. Run the touched package tests and repository lint before opening a PR.

topics.title: Add a fixed-batch Belay+CPLM TPU baseline
topics.body:
Add a native d512 Belay+CPLM baseline on TPU v4-32 with fixed logical batch 16×8192, EP1 dropless routing and the frozen 10980-update optimizer schedule. The entry point retains Belay's copy head, runs a finite-gradient preflight, initializes online W&B before updates, and preserves separate logs and checkpoint paths for every fresh distributed execution. A 400-update calibration mode measures a drained 300-update window without changing the learning-rate schedule.

The TPU path supports ungated ReLU² experts in local scatter, enables exact QB histogram counting at the 8192×512 local shape, and includes the qualified KDA, Inkling attention, projection, embedding and Muon execution paths. The portable CPLM loss is also proposed separately in #10230. This PR targets `ladderclimb_v1_batch14`, the original Belay development branch; that architecture is not yet in `main`.

The native entry point completed 400 TPU updates at commit `1c4e1b334`: **417400 sustained tokens/s, 5.7162% useful MFU and zero drops**. All 400 losses exactly match the optimized harness, ending at NLL 4.25661278. The drained 300-update window took 94.2059 seconds. The preceding harness measured 416823 and 418299 tokens/s in independent runs, versus 230953 for unoptimized EP1, with the same losses. Every run uses seed 0 and unchanged B16×8192. See the [native W&B curve](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/auto-understanding-arch/runs/upstream-native-v2-fcda5d913e534635a7e99856da23cea1) and [frozen evidence](https://github.com/WhenWen/astra-d8-research/blob/4792fab7/research/belay-mfu-native-ep-result.md). Full-run quality, evaluation/checkpoint endpoints and checkpoint restore remain unvalidated for this port.

Remote non-training numerical checks passed for copy loss, ungated/gated scatter, histograms and blocked attention (32 tests). Required lint/type checks and the advisory lint review passed. Reproduction commands, tokenizer hashes, frozen data identities and evidence links are in `experiments/grug/moe_cplm/README.md`; the complete run record is [research issue #236](https://github.com/WhenWen/astra-d8-research/issues/236).

Part of #10229. Related to #9451.

topics.title: [taskforge] Add the agentic author that builds through the program build
topics.body:
Add `stage40_build_with_agent`, the agentic author. `author_round` runs one agent session per program round in a workspace that starts with the standard template, the proposal, the SDK reference and an empty notes file. Its tools read, write and edit workspace files, run the loader in a child process, build the program with the caller's own build stage on the same step store, grade a candidate against the last draft, and search and fetch the web when the proposal lists research; `submit` hands the program in. A host failure or an expired clock never reaches the model: the tool retries a `BuildInfrastructureFailure` with backoff and then ends the round without a record, and re-raises a `BuildExpired` at once, so neither spends a revision.

The agent build is a second package at stage 40. It drives the program build through its `run_build` tool, so `test_imports` gains `BUILDS_ON`: `stage40_build_with_agent` may import `stage40_build_with_program` and never the reverse.

Builds on #10298; #10300 builds on it. The taskforge suite passes 591 tests here (24 more than #10298).

🤖 Branch: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/june_10T_run

Contains the launch script (`experiments/grug/moe/moe_may_d2560_10T.py`) and job summary (`experiments/grug/moe/job_summary_d2560_10T.md`) for the d=2560 / 10T-token run on v4-1024 us-central2.

# Job Summary: d=2560 MoE on 10T tokens

Big-batch d=2560 MoE training run on ~10T tokens (~1.2e23 FLOPs), with the May Recipe baked in. Below are sections on model, optimizer, training, scaling principles, and outputs.

## 1. Model

### Hyperparameters

- **hidden_dim**: 2560
- **num_layers**: 26 (heuristic-derived: `round(2560 / (64 + 4·log2(2560) − 9))`)
- **num_heads**: 20 (`hidden_dim / 128`)
- **num_kv_heads**: 5 (GQA 4:1; largest divisor of 20 ≤ 5)
- **head_dim**: 128
- **intermediate_dim**: 1280 (`ceil(d/2/128)·128`)
- **shared_expert_intermediate_dim**: 2560 (= d)
- **num_experts**: 256
- **num_experts_per_token**: 4
- **vocab_size**: 128,256
- **max_seq_len**: 4096
- **sliding_window**: 4096
- **active_params**: 2.34B (2.01B core + 0.33B lm_head; excludes embed per guidelines)
- **total_params**: 67.1B (66.4B core + 0.33B embed + 0.33B lm_head)

### Features

- **GQA**: 4:1 ratio (20 Q heads, 5 KV heads).
- **QB Routing**: stop-gradient bias updated each step from previous step's QB-β statistics (applied inside JIT).
- **Sigmoid Combine Weights**: sigmoid on unbiased router logits for selected experts.
- **GatedNorm**: rank-128 low-rank gating after RMSNorm, pre-attention and pre-MLP.
- **XSA**: subtracts V-parallel component from attention output per head.
- **Attention Gate**: learned per-head sigmoid gate on attention output, initialized to zero.
- **Shared Expert**: dense FFN (d=2560) in parallel with routed experts per layer.
- **Sliding Window**: every 4th layer (plus last) uses full window (4096); others use half (2048).
- **Half-RoPE on every layer**: RoPE applied only to the first half of Q/K per head (`q[..., :head_dim/2]`, `k[..., :head_dim/2]`). The second half is rope-free on every layer.
- **PKO (Partial Key Offset)**: on every-4th + last layer (7 of 26 layers here), the rope-free second half of K is additionally shifted by 1 position with doc-start zeroing.
- **QK Gain**: `qk_mult = 1.3`.
- **Split w_gate / w_up**: separate weight matrices for SwiGLU gate and up projections (`split_w_gate_up=True`).
- **Routing renorm sum**: 2.5 (combined-feature baseline).
- **Router z-loss**: disabled (`router_z_loss_coef = 0`).
- **Expert dispatch**: ring (May Recipe default; `moe_implementation` not exposed in current model config).

## 2. Optimizer

### Hyperparameters

(Using the refit `MoeAdamHHeuristic` from #5951.)

- **adam_lr**: 0.000432  (= `0.06602 · 1e13^-0.395 · 2560^-0.150 · √(2048·4096)`)
- **muonh_lr (= adamh_lr)**: 0.001870  (= adam_lr · 13/3)
- **beta1**: 0.9062
- **beta2**: 0.95 (clamped; `0.999^(2048/32) = 0.938` → clipped up to 0.95)
- **epsilon**: 1.06e−14  (= `1e-15 · √((32·1e13)/(2048·1.4e9))`)
- **weight_decay**: 0
- **max_grad_norm**: None (1pct-noclip schedule)
- **warmup**: 1% (= 11,921 steps)
- **decay**: None (linear schedule decays to 0 over full run)
- **min_lr_ratio**: 0.0
- **lr_schedule**: linear
- **z_loss_weight**: 0.0

### Features

- **MuonH** (`GrugMoeMuonHConfig`): scale-invariant Newton-Schulz updates on the `muonh` group (matmuls + GatedNorms), Frobenius hyperball step on top. Used in place of AdamH on weight matrices.
- **Multi-group optimizer**: 3 groups —
  - `muonh`: attn matmuls, MoE expert matmuls (gate/up/down), shared expert, GatedNorms.
  - `adamh`: lm_head / output_proj (LR = `muonh_lr`).
  - `adam`: token_embed, router weight + bias, attn_gate, 1-D norm weights (LR = `adam_lr`).

## 3. Training

- **hardware**: v4-1024 us-central2 (= 512 chips).
- **num_train_steps**: 1,192,093  (= `1e13 / (2048 · 4096)`)
- **batch_size**: 2,048 sequences
- **seq_len**: 4,096
- **tokens_per_batch**: 8.39M (= `2048 · 4096`)
- **total_tokens**: 1.00e13 (= 10T)
- **compute_budget**: ~1.21e23 FLOPs (= `6 · 2.01e9 · 1e13`)
- **mixed_precision**: `params=float32, compute=bfloat16, output=bfloat16`
- **expert_parallelism**: 4
- **data**: Nemotron mix (block-shuffled) with default validation sets
- **checkpoints**: every 10 minutes (rolling temporary), permanent every 5,000 steps

## 4. Scaling Principles

All optimizer hyperparameters derived from the refit MuonH May Recipe heuristic (issue #5951, R² = 0.996 on 17 cells).

### Learning rates (current heuristic)

- **adam_lr** = `0.06602 · tokens^-0.395 · dim^-0.150 · √(B·seq_len)`, capped at 0.05.
- **muonh_lr** = `(13/3) · adam_lr`.

### Momentum and precision

- **beta1** = 0.9062 (fixed)
- **beta2** = `clip(0.999^(B/32), 0.95, 0.9999)` → 0.95 at B=2048
- **epsilon** = `1e-15 · √((32·T) / (B·1.4e9))`

### Architecture scaling

- **num_layers** = `round(hidden_dim / (64 + 4·log2(hidden_dim) − 9))` → 26 for d=2560
- **num_heads** = `hidden_dim / 128`
- **num_kv_heads** = 4:1 GQA, largest divisor of num_heads ≤ num_heads/4
- **intermediate_dim** = `ceil(hidden_dim / 2 / 128) · 128`
- **shared_expert_intermediate_dim** = hidden_dim
- **initializer_std** = `0.5 / sqrt(hidden_dim)` ≈ 0.00988
- **num_experts** = 256, **num_experts_per_token** = 4 (fixed for May Recipe; differs from the 64-expert v16 baseline used in the 1e23 summary)

### Schedule

- **warmup** = 1% of training (1pct-noclip baseline)
- **decay** = linear all the way to 0 (no separate decay phase)
- **max_grad_norm** = None (no clipping)

## 5. Outputs

- **GCS checkpoint path**: `gs://marin-us-central2/grug/moe_may_d2560_10T/marin-big-run-moe_may_d2560_10T-XXXXXX/checkpoints` (pending — actual hash assigned at submission)
- **WandB run link**: `https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/marin-big-run-moe_may_d2560_10T` (pending)
- **Final eval metrics**: pending (run not submitted yet)
  - eval/paloma/c4_en/bpb
  - eval/paloma/macro_loss
  - eval/uncheatable_eval/macro_loss
- **Throughput** (mean over last 100 logged steps): pending

🤖 Active branch for these runs: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/june_tpu_67b_a2b

David's idea to use Replica sharding brings it down from 55 days to 45 days. All v4-2048 runs require 2x batch size to get good MFU, up from 33 million to 67 million. However on further testing, 67 million batch size is not training stably, compared to 33 million batch size. https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/Batch-Size-Testing-67B-A2B-MoE-on-10T-tokens--VmlldzoxNzM1MTA2OQ As is standard, we scale learning rate with batch_size^0.5. This assumes that you get a less noisy gradient estimate as you scale up batch size, which typically occurs up until the critical batch size, at which point there are diminishing gains. In a prior [Issue](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/4432) I estimated the critical batch size for compute optimal runs on our prior (similar) architecture. At compute optimal, the critical batch size is much smaller for our model size, estimated to be roughly 6-10M tokens, after which we get reduced performance. However since we are heavily overtraining, a larger batch size can be justified, since when we get to lower loss regime a larger batch size will be helpful. Many works calculate critical batch size as a function of the token budget. 22.91 · T^0.47 for 10 trillion tokens gives 29.5 million tokens, fit on AdamW. https://arxiv.org/pdf/2505.13738. Indications here that critical batch size is higher for Muon compared to Adam: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/1565. Llama 3 report: 3.4.1 Initial Pre-Training We pre-train Llama 3 405B using AdamW with a peak learning rate of 8 × 10−5, a linear warm up of 8,000 steps, and a cosine learning rate schedule decaying to 8 × 10−7 over 1,200,000 steps. We use a lower batch size early in training to improve training stability, and increase it subsequently to improve efficiency. Specifically, we use an initial batch size of 4M tokens and sequences of length 4,096, and double these values to a batch size of 8M sequences of 8,192 tokens after pre-training 252M tokens. We double the batch size again to 16M after pre-training on 2.87T tokens. We found this training recipe to be very stable: we observed few loss spikes and did not require interventions to correct for model training divergence. The key line here is "We use a lower batch size early in training to improve training stability". Training run references: -Arcee trained Trinity nano and mini on 10T tokens pretrain, with batch size 16 million. Then doubled to 32 million midway. -Nemotron 3 Super used 25 million batch size on 25T tokens. Given our atypical hardware setup (1024 tpu chips on a v4-2048) and smaller model size (2B active), batch size is a very high priority axis for achieving MFU, so we want to push batch size as high as possible. (of course there is some theoretical limit where we shift from diminishing gains to near zero gains). It is plausible that we could achieve a stable run start by increasing the warmup percentage from 1pct to 10pct. However, given the literature above, and the fact that we already have evidence that 33 million batch size can perform a stable warmup, it seems more sensible to start the run at 33 million at reduced MFU. If we were to keep the run at 33 million tokens per batch for the full run, we will get 63 days to complete. If we did the full run at 67 million tokens per batch, we will get 45 days to complete. Depending on if/when we shift the batch size, will determine where between 63 days and 45 days the run falls.

🤖 d=2560 throughput at the canonical 10T config (seq=8192, sw2k, MuonH, no PKO, no long-RoPE):

| run | hardware | TPB | EP | replica | state | MFU | step time | tok/s |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `..._d2560_ep1_bs4096..._10T` | v4-1024 | 33.55 M | 1 | 1 | crashed step 4367 | **21.54 %** | 22.58 s | 1.49 M |
| `..._d2560_ep1_rep8_bs4096...` | v4-2048 | 33.55 M | 1 | 8 | finished | 13.36 % | 18.20 s | 1.84 M |
| `..._d2560_ep1_bs8192...` (rep=8) | v4-2048 | 67.11 M | 1 | 8 | finished | 18.62 % | 26.13 s | **2.57 M** |
| `..._d2560_ep2_bs4096...` | v4-2048 | 33.55 M | 2 | 1 | crashed step 9 | 10.13 % | 24.02 s | 1.40 M |

v4-1024 still has the highest per-chip MFU (single-slice FSDP at the natural sharding ratio is hard to beat), but v4-2048 + `replica=8` + BS=8192 wins on absolute throughput at ~2.57 M tok/s. Projected 10T wall-clock at that config: ~45 days vs v4-1024's ~78 days.

Plan:
Start the run on the full v4-2048 at batch size 33 million so we can achieve a stable warmup. Then, discuss with team on timing tradeoffs. 

Option A:
Move to batch size 67 million after 20% of the run. Which will give completion time of 63/5 + 4/5*45 = 49 days, plus some buffer for usual hardware issues.

Option B:
Move to v4-1024 after 20% of the run. Then use the remaining v4-1024 to run early cooldowns + long context extension to 262k. This would enable sending models to posttraining sooner, with more efficient usage of our TPUs. However this is contigent on these early trained models (only 2 trillion tokens, or larger amounts), still being post-trainable. There is some threshold intelligence where we can't get sufficient signal to posttrain.

(This dynamic is how understood but leaving this comment for historical accuracy) Not yet understood dynamic where numerical stability seems to suffer at full node count. Here we do a test on a very small d512 model for 200 steps (with an extremely agressive batch size). On v5p-8 it trains as expected. On v4-2048 it diverges with EP=2, or replica in (2, 16, 1024). If I move to full fp32 on output and compute, as opposed to bfloat16, it not longer diverges, but still performs substantially worse than vp5-8. This confirms that we see numerical gaps, even at fp32. Here we can see that the 33 million tokens per batch on v4-2048 is training stably, but its loss curve is a bit worse than we were getting on v4-1024. The only hardware dependent calc outside numerical precision I am aware of is the local sorting for QB. The difference in trajectory is visible in the first 10 steps, where QB has no impact. This was validated by running a full global sort version of QB and seeing it still follow the v4-2048 trajectory.

The root cause of the issue is that the sharded NS calc in Muon was silently dropping when num_matrices didn't evenly divide into num_chips. This was originally written on v4-1024 where 256*26 is divisible by 512 chips. However it isn't divisible by 1024 chips. The fix was to explicitly replicate the NS calc over the same size as the replica axis, and also patch the silent failure. After doing this, we get stable replication of the v5p-8 d512 200 step run: Increasing precision to fp32 was helping the non orthogonalized approach not diverge, but not addressing the root cause. Lack of orthogonalization explains why the loss curve started better and then got worse over time, similar to how adam can beat muon in first couple steps. Given this knowledge, it is likely that the instability at 67 million token batch size is only due to failing to orthogonalize the gradient. So, we likely could do the full run at 67 million token batch size. However, starting at 33 million batch size for the first 5% of the run will likely be more token efficient, and only add 1 day of runtime. (46 day total). This also lets us validate the full warmup curve against the v4-1024 warmup curve which ran at 33 million batch size. Reflecting on the bug: 1. Transitioning from small scale tests to prod scale implementation will always require iterating on the code. (lax.scan to fit in memory, iterating on the sharding implementation). 2. This introduces risk of incorrect implementation. In particular due to perception of time pressure of having the hardware sit idle. 3. This incorrectness can be subtely incorrect in ML world. (though in this particular case this issue should have errored loudly, but I did not review this agent written resharding close enough) For future runs, recommend we have: 1. Small scale code should have prior code review and be checked into main. 2. After we get large scale code implemented, we should raise PR and get human review on the (ideally minor) changes to get small scale code working at prod scale. 3. Always replicate a small scale run on the prod hardware. (this has now been done for this run) 4. Have a script that runs series of validation checks against the first 200 steps of wandb logs. (checking all param inits, param norms over initial training with hyperball, routing entropy, activity across all layers, train stability, etc). These always get eye-balled but the level of rigor is not the same.

This projection is viewed as our best estimate, but there are a large number of assumptions underpinning it: 1. Assuming an irreducible loss of 1.4. Prior large scale runs at seqlen 4k have indicated an irreducible loss of 1.5. Extending the seqlen to 8k should slightly reduce this, by reducing the number of evals that start a sequence mid-context. 2. The smaller scale runs had no logit z loss. After observing large grad norm on the d1024 run, I did a follow up experiment re-adding z loss to the final logit, which helped control the gradient and gave better evals and train loss. https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/Z-Loss-Under-OverTrain-650B-tokens---VmlldzoxNzMyODk1NQ. 3. We are heavily increasing the batch size for the 10T run, which will increase the final loss. I am assuming that point 2 will roughly cancel out with this. 4. We are extrapolating from 3 points- our prior 1e23 run extrapolated at compute optimal from over 20 points. In particular, runs at d512 seem to extrapolate worse due to heavier parameter skew in lm_head due to high vocab size of 128k. We chose to not extrapolate from more points to enable the 10T run to start sooner. 5. We will be at 24% peak LR at the end of stage 1. Predicting model performance before full LR cooldown may have different dynamics as we scale. Given these assumptions, I anticipate we will be able to use the actual achieved loss to update our knowledge of training dynamics and which assumptions to revisit.

🤖 Job summary for the d=2560 67B / 2B-active MoE 10T pretrain

# Job Summary: 67B / 2B-active MoE 10T pretrain (d=2560, MuonH, v4-2048)

~10.07T-token MuonH MoE pretrain at d=2560 / 67B total params / 2.01B active per token (run_id `moe_67b_a2b_d2560_ep1_rep16_bs4096_seq8192_sw2k_v4_2048_muon_10T`; batch ramp from 4,096 → 8,192 at step 15,000, with total steps reduced so total tokens stay near 10T). Below are sections on model, optimizer, training, and scaling principles.

## 1. Model

### Hyperparameters

- **hidden_dim**: 2560
- **num_layers**: 26
- **num_heads**: 20
- **num_kv_heads**: 5 (GQA 4:1)
- **head_dim**: 128
- **intermediate_dim**: 1280 (MoE expert FFN; `ceil(hidden_dim / 2 / 128) * 128`)
- **shared_expert_intermediate_dim**: 2560 (= hidden_dim)
- **num_experts**: 256
- **num_experts_per_token**: 4
- **vocab_size**: 128,256
- **max_seq_len**: 8,192
- **sliding_window**: 2,048
- **total_params**: 67.1B
- **active_params**: 2.01B per token (2.34B w/ lm_head)

### Features

- **GQA**: 4:1 ratio (20 Q heads, 5 KV heads, head_dim 128)
- **QB Routing**: stop-gradient bias updated each step from previous step's QB-β statistics (applied inside JIT)
- **Sigmoid Combine Weights**: sigmoid on unbiased router logits for the K=4 selected experts (not softmax). Combine weights are then renormalized to sum to **2.5** across the K selected experts (`_ROUTING_RENORM_SUM = 2.5` in `model.py:51`), which effectively rescales the routed-expert contribution per token by 2.5× compared to a standard sum-to-1 (softmax-style) normalization.
- **GatedNorm**: rank-128 low-rank gating after RMSNorm, pre-attention and pre-MLP
- **Shared Expert**: dense FFN (d=2560) in parallel with routed experts per layer
- **Sliding Window**: every 4th layer + final layer uses full window (8,192); the other 19 layers use the short window (2,048). Layout: 7 long / 19 short (`i % 4 == 3 or i == num_layers - 1`).
- **disable_long_rope**: long (full-attention) layers skip rotary embedding entirely. Short (windowed) layers still apply half-RoPE.
- **disable_pko**: no per-key offset on long layers. Plain attention only.
- **RoPE**: partial rotary — only half of `head_dim` is rotated (the leading 64 of 128 dims), the rest is passed through unchanged. Applied on short (windowed) layers only; long (full-attention) layers skip RoPE entirely per `disable_long_rope`.
- **ArrayStacked + scan**: all 26 blocks stacked via `jax.lax.scan` (`use_array_stacked_blocks=True`) for reduced compile time and HBM footprint

## 2. Optimizer

### Hyperparameters

- **muonh_lr**: 0.003733 → **0.005279** at step 15,000 (×√2 with the BS doubling)
- **adam_lr**: 0.000861 → **0.001218** at step 15,000 (= muonh_lr / (13/3); also ×√2)
- **beta1**: 0.9062 (unchanged across the BS ramp)
- **beta2**: 0.95 — clamped both before and after the ramp (raw formula 0.999^(B*S/131072) gives 0.774 pre-ramp and 0.599 post-ramp; both clamp to 0.95)
- **epsilon**: ~8.01 × 10⁻¹⁹ → **~5.66 × 10⁻¹⁹** at step 15,000 (÷√2 with the BS doubling)
- **weight_decay**: 0
- **max_grad_norm**: None (no clipping in MuonH 1pct-noclip schedule)
- **warmup**: 0.01 (1% of training; ~3,000 steps)
- **decay**: None (linear decay over the whole post-warmup period)
- **min_lr_ratio**: 0.05 (decay to 5% of peak by end-of-training)
- **lr_schedule**: linear
- **z_loss_weight**: 1e-4 (logit z-loss; router z-loss = 0)

### Features

- **MuonH (Muon + Frobenius hyperball)**: Newton-Schulz orthogonalization on weight matrices followed by a scale-invariant Frobenius-hyperball projection. Three LR groups:
  - **muonh** — 2D weight matrices and stacked MoE expert weights (NS + hyperball)
  - **adamh** — `lm_head` / `output_proj`. AdamH = Adam moments + Frobenius hyperball (`scale_by_adamh`); no Newton-Schulz. Uses the same LR schedule as muonh.
  - **adam** — biases, RMSNorm scales, router weights, gated-norm scales, and (via `rmsnorm_to_adam=True`) stacked RMSNorm scales
- **Multi-group optimizer**: separate optax chains per group routed by parameter path (see `experiments/grug/moe/optimizer.py:create_mask`).
- **Logit Z-Loss**: penalizes large output-logit norm to stabilize training (no router z-loss in this run).

## 3. Training

- **hardware**: v4-2048 (1,024 chips), us-central2, production priority, --no-preemptible
- **num_train_steps**: 157,500 (reduced from 300,000 to absorb the batch-size doubling and hold total tokens ~constant)
- **batch_size**: 4,096 → 8,192 sequences (step change at step 15,000 ≈ 5% of training)
- **seq_len**: 8,192
- **tokens_per_step**: 33,554,432 (~33.5M) for steps 0–14,999; 67,108,864 (~67.1M) for steps 15,000–157,499
- **total_tokens**: ~1.007 × 10¹³ (~10.07T) — 5.03 × 10¹¹ from the BS=4,096 phase (15,000 steps) + 9.56 × 10¹² from the BS=8,192 phase (142,500 steps)
- **compute_budget**: ~1.69 × 10²³ FLOPs (SWA-aware, with lm_head)
- **mixed_precision**: `params=float32,compute=bfloat16,output=bfloat16`
- **mesh**: `(replica_dcn=16, data=64, expert=1, model=1)`. EP=1, `replica_axis_size=16`. Batch is sharded across (replica_dcn, data, expert) → 1,024 shards.
- **expert_parallelism**: 1 (no expert sharding; routed experts replicated across the expert axis)
- **data**: datakit MoE mixture (`_datakit_data_config`, simulated epoching disabled) with default paloma validation sets
- **eval cadence**: every 3,000 steps; `eval_batch_size=1024`, `max_eval_batches=1` (8.39M tokens per eval)
- **checkpoints**: permanent every 3,000 steps; temp save every 60 minutes; auto-resume on preemption

## 4. Scaling Principles

All optimizer hyperparameters derived from the MuonH May Recipe refit (issue #5951, 17 finished cells across d ∈ {512, 768, 1024, 1280} × R ∈ {4, 10, 20, 60, 120, 240} × lr_mult ∈ {0.4, 0.7, 1.0, 1.3, 1.6}, R² = 0.996). Reference seq_len = 4096; conversions assume `tokens_per_batch = batch_size * seq_len`.

### Learning rates

- **muonh_lr** = `18.31 · T^(-0.395) · d^(-0.150) · sqrt(B)`, capped at 0.05
  - Equivalent to `lr_coeff · T^(-0.395) · d^(-0.150) · sqrt(tokens_per_batch)` with `lr_coeff = 0.06602` (= 18.31 / ((13/3) · 64))
  - At T = 1.007e13, d = 2560, B*S = 33.55M → **muonh_lr ≈ 0.003733**
- **adam_lr** = muonh_lr / (13/3) ≈ **0.000861**
- **adamh_lr** = muonh_lr ≈ **0.003733** (the `adamh` group — `lm_head` / `output_proj` — uses the same LR schedule as muonh, via `scale_by_adamh`: Adam moments + Frobenius hyperball, no Newton-Schulz)

### Momentum and precision

- **beta1** = 0.9062 (fixed)
- **beta2** = `clip(0.999^(tokens_per_batch / 131072), 0.95, 0.9999)`
  - At B*S = 33.55M → raw 0.999^256 ≈ 0.774 → clamped to **0.95**
- **epsilon** = `9.676e-18 · sqrt((B0 · T) / (tokens_per_batch · T0))` with B0=32, T0=1.4e9
  - At T = 1.007e13, tokens_per_batch = 33.55M → **epsilon ≈ 8.01e-19**

### Architecture scaling

- **num_layers** = `round(hidden_dim / (64 + 4·log2(hidden_dim) - 9))` = 26 for d=2560
- **num_heads** = `hidden_dim / 128` = 20
- **num_kv_heads** = largest divisor of num_heads ≤ num_heads // 4 = 5 (GQA 4:1)
- **intermediate_dim** = `ceil(hidden_dim / 2 / 128) · 128` = 1280
- **shared_expert_intermediate_dim** = hidden_dim = 2560
- **initializer_std** ≈ `0.5 / sqrt(2560)` ≈ 0.00988
- **num_experts** = 256, **num_experts_per_token** = 4 (fixed; differs from the 1e23 d=5120 run which used 64 experts)

### Schedule

- **warmup** = 1% of training (~3,000 steps)
- **decay** = none (linear schedule decays over the whole post-warmup period)
- **min_lr_ratio** = 0.05 (decay to 5% of peak)
- **lr_schedule** = linear

Notable updates to architecture:
1. Since we are planning to extend context out to 262k, there will likely be several iterations on datamix and attention scaling to enable this. To minimize possible confounders during this process, PKO has been disabled, along with RoPE on the global layers. This puts our architecture close to published literature on effective long context extension. Once we have successfully extended context using textbook approaches, then we can consider adding back partial rope and PKO. We may be incurring a 10-20% efficiency hit from this, but the risk/reward tradeoff here of taking a controlled approach seems worthwhile to maximize learnings and our later models.
2. Re-adding final logit z loss. At compute optimal scale, z loss had a neglible impact. However on the new data mix and extreme overtrain, we see meaningful gains from including z loss, both on the train loss and evals. https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/Z-Loss-Under-OverTrain-650B-tokens---VmlldzoxNzMyODk1NQ.
3. Batch size schedule. The hardware profile is heavily encouraging us to run at extremely large batch sizes to achieve acceptable MFU. Instead of performing the full run at 67 million tokens per batch, we are running the first 5 pct at half that. Which is the window when smaller batch sizes have the biggest impact.
4. LR decay to 0.05 instead of 0. This is because we will extend out from 64k->262k, and do subsequent posttrain. decay to zero is only optimal if we have no subsequent weight updates.

### Config

| Knob | Value | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Resume step | 141,000 | main run's ~9 T-token mark (89.5% of the 157,500-step horizon) |
| Cooldown steps | 15,000 | 1.007 T tokens = ~last 1 T of the 10 T campaign |
| `seq_len` / `batch_size` | 65,536 / 1,024 | 67.1 M tokens/step (unchanged from source's 8,192 × 8,192) |
| `qk_mult` | 1.57 | matches the winning all-layers YaRN `mscale(coef=0.1)` from the step-102k cooldown |
| LR | 0.000822 → 0.000264, linear | joins source at step-141k, decays to source floor over 15k steps |
| Data mix | phase-1 (mix 2) only | main run's been in mix 2 since step 127,500 |
| `resume_data_offset` | **13,824,000** samples | new field: exact-position continuation — see below |
| `hybrid_attention_flops_accounting` | True | 7 full + 19 sw=2048 layers → MFU reports ~0.44× the naive count (honest) |
| Save + eval | every 1,500 steps | 10 permanent saves + 10 evals over the cooldown |
| Iris retries | `--max-retries 100` | auto-recovery on the recurring coord-service TCP-close failure (#7430) |

### Data-position continuation (new mechanism)

Prior cooldowns (step-39k, step-102k) used a fresh mix-2 shuffle from position 0. This one continues main run's mix-2 stream *exactly*:

- Main run consumed **905.97 B mix-2 tokens** between steps 127,500 → 141,000 (13,500 steps × 8,192 seq × 8,192 BS).
- Cooldown at seq=65,536 wants to start at the same underlying token offset → sample-index **13,824,000**.
- New `resume_data_offset` field on `GrugMoeLaunchConfig2xBS` builds a 3-stage BatchSchedule `[(0, 98), (135000, 99), (141000, 1024)]` that lands `cumulative_size(141000)` at exactly 13,824,000 samples. Zero re-consumption of main run's exposure, zero skip past it.
- Per-bucket read positions in each of the 168 mix-2 buckets exactly continue where main run left off; the mixture-shuffle order differs (unavoidable: mixture-shuffle indexes are in cooldown's seq_len enumeration, which is 8× the main run's).
- 12 small-weight buckets will epoch during the 1 T cooldown budget (aggregate ~1.3% extra re-exposure; largest is `c34q4` at 2.88×).

### MFU accounting

Restored the hybrid-attention FLOPs accounting from the step-39k cooldown (originally commit 5681efbe3f, reverted for hash-continuity at the time). At seq=65,536, `lm_flops_per_token` for our 26-layer model (7 full + 19 sliding-window at sw=2048) is **9.74×10⁹** vs. the naive all-full-attention 2.22×10¹⁰ — so `throughput/mfu` will report about 2.28× lower than a naive counter for the same wall-clock work. Wandb history for the pretraining run is unchanged (naive accounting there); this only applies to the cooldown.

🤖 Follow-up: two 262k context-extension probes from the same step-156000 checkpoint above.

## Runs

| variant | qk_mult | wandb | state |
|---|---|---|---|
| formula-scaled (`1.3 · (0.1·ln(32)+1)`) | 1.75 | [run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/moe_67b_a2b_d2560_ep1_rep1_ctx4_bs256_seq262144_ctxext_step156k) | finished |
| held from step-141k cooldown | 1.57 | [run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/moe_67b_a2b_d2560_ep1_rep1_ctx4_bs256_seq262144_ctxext_step156k_qk157) | running |

## Launchers

- qk=1.75: [`experiments/grug/moe/moe_67b_a2b_d2560_ctxext_step156k_seq262k_bs256_ctx4_muon.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/june_tpu_67b_a2b/experiments/grug/moe/moe_67b_a2b_d2560_ctxext_step156k_seq262k_bs256_ctx4_muon.py)
- qk=1.57: [`experiments/grug/moe/moe_67b_a2b_d2560_ctxext_step156k_seq262k_bs256_ctx4_muon_qk157.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/june_tpu_67b_a2b/experiments/grug/moe/moe_67b_a2b_d2560_ctxext_step156k_seq262k_bs256_ctx4_muon_qk157.py)

Both resume from the step-141k cooldown's `step-156000` checkpoint above.

## Design spec

- **seq_len**: 65,536 → **262,144** (4× extension).
- **BS**: 1024 → **256** sequences → tokens/step stays at 256 · 262,144 = 67.1 M (matches the step-141k cooldown's per-step token budget).
- **Steps**: 1,000 (step 156,000 → 157,000) → **67.1 B tokens** total.
- **LR**: linear decay from 5 % of source peak (0.000264, matches cooldown exit LR) → 1 % of source peak (0.0000528), no ramp. Implementation pins the resume schedule's abstract "peak" to 0.000264 with `min_lr_ratio=0.2` so the floor lands at exactly `0.000264 · 0.2 = 0.0000528`.
- **qk_mult**: 1.75 (`1.3 · (0.1·ln(32) + 1) = 1.7506`, rounded) vs. 1.57 (held from the step-141k cooldown, which used `1.3 · (0.1·ln(8) + 1) = 1.5703`). Both applied Q-only as a single logit multiplier (one-sided YaRN; note this delivers `mscale` on logits, not the paper's `mscale²`).
- **Data continuation**: exact per-token — `resume_data_offset = (13,500·8,192·8,192 + 15,000·1,024·65,536) / 262,144 = 7,296,000` samples. The launcher builds a 3-stage BS schedule `[(0, 46), (36000, 47), (156000, 256)]` that hits exactly 7,296,000 cumulative samples at step 156,000 (zero re-consumption AND zero skip). Post-run cumulative mix-2 consumption = **1.980 T tokens** (98.99% of the 2 T mix-2 design budget).
- **Checkpoints / evals**: every 250 steps (4 total: 156,250 / 156,500 / 156,750 / 157,000).
- **Mesh** on v4-2048 (1024 chips): `(replica_dcn=1, data=256, context=4, expert=1, model=1)`. `batch_shards = replica · data · expert = 256`, `per_device_parallelism = 1`. `context_axis_size = 4` shards the seq axis → `seq_per_device = 65,536` (identical chip-local seq to the step-141k cooldown, our known-good memory point).

## Context-parallel implementation

Landed on this branch as a self-contained addition; `context_axis_size = 1` is a no-op vs. the pre-CP code path.

- **Mesh axis** (`lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/sharding.py`): added `"context"` to `_GRUG_MESH_AXIS_NAMES`; `compact_grug_mesh` now takes `context_axis_size`. `_batch_axes()` returns the full flat-token axes and now includes `"context"` when present so MoE psums / shard_maps reduce over the correct set.
- **Grug MoE model** (`experiments/grug/moe/model.py`): seq axis on Q / residual stream / MLP / embed / output_proj sharded on `"context"` via helpers `_seq_spec_3d` / `_seq_spec_4d` / `_token_spec`. K/V explicitly resharded to seq=`None` before splash (splash's TPU entry refuses `kv_seq_shards > 1`), i.e. the **all-gather-KV** flavor of CP.
- **RoPE cache**: `_apply_half_rope` reshards its precomputed cos/sin to `P(None, "context", None, None)` so the per-shard broadcast against context-sharded Q/K lines up.
- **Segment IDs**: `Transformer.__call__` reshards q_seg to `P(_BATCH_AXES, "context")` and kv_seg to `P(_BATCH_AXES, None)` before passing the mask to splash, so splash's per-shard segment-id shape check matches.
- **Router / QB shard_map**: uses `_token_axes()` (batch + context) for the shard_map in_specs and `pmean` so the QB threshold pmean reduces across both data and context shards.
- **Splash kernel wrapping** (`lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/_core.py`): the splash kernel is now passed as an input to `shard_map` with its own `manual_sharding_spec` (mirroring the classical levanter path). Prior closure-capture would leave `fwd_mask_info.q_sequence` at global shape, and splash's forward broadcast would fail against the local `q_seq_len`. Each mask_info leaf is `jax.reshard`ed to the manual spec before the shard_map, since shard_map now rejects mismatched in_specs.
- **(B,S)↔(B*S) reshapes**: `_flatten_bs` / `_unflatten_bs` helpers wrap `jnp.reshape` with explicit `out_sharding` (`_token_spec()` and `_seq_spec_3d()` respectively). einops's `rearrange` goes through `array.reshape()` with no sharding hint, which JAX can't lower when two sharded axes fuse into one.
- **Trainer mesh** (`experiments/grug/moe/launch_2x_bs.py`): passes `"context": context_axis_size` into the TrainerConfig's `MeshConfig` so `data_axis_size` (used for the BS-divisibility check) reflects only the actual batch shards.
- **Loss parity** verified at `context = {1, 2, 4}` for a small config: identical loss at c=2, bf16-precision noise (~1e-6) at c=4.

## Status

- qk=1.75 finished all 1000 steps. Train loss dropped 1.325 → **1.159** across the extension; paloma macro-loss 2.177 → **2.208** (small uptick from a fresh eval at the new seq/temperature; c4_en, dolma, m2d2, redpajama all continue improving during the 1000 steps).
- qk=1.57 in flight, tracking qk=1.75 closely so far.
- Known artifact: `wikitext_103` and `ptb` paloma tags read `0.0` in both runs. Root cause: `TokenSeqDataset.async_len = total_tokens // seq_len` uses integer division, so any val cache smaller than one 262k window (wikitext_103 ~247k tokens, ptb ~86k tokens) yields **0** eval sequences. Not a training bug; only affects small paloma tags at long seq_len.

Recommendation:
Run multiple experiments, varying the following factors:
- qk_mult. This specifies the attention 'sharpness' (how strongly can it natively pick out a single target). It started at 1.3 during 8k seqlen, then was bumped to 1.57 during 65k seqlen. This is a softer version of yarn mscale. For 262k, could hold at 1.57, or bump to ~1.75 or 2. Increasing may help on longer documents and slightly hurt on shorter documents. Previously tried an experiment bumping it only on global layers, didn't help. (However may be worth it on this 65k->262k extension)
- number of steps. Defaulting to 1k. 67B tokens. Can be varied.
- LR schedule. Defaulting to linear decay from 5 pct peak to 1 pct peak.
- Checkpoint averaging. Am saving checkpoints every 250 steps during this cooldown. EMA over these may give stronger final model.
- Data. First two experiments were on the exact same mix2 from this run, continuing off from where last step was. Alternatively, can upweight long context data (data over 65k seqlen). Or, swap to datamix we are using on the 535B hero run.

Checkpoints exist for the two tests above, both they don't have a long context eval in wandb. This will be good to be comparing against. Need to debug and fix the 0 eval score for the evals with under 262k context length.
Looks like we need to be very careful on comparing evals at 65k and 262k seqlen, due to how eval tokens get chosen and packed.
