> Add an extra loss term to counter the indefinite stretching effect to s, or normalize s and y in the original aux term, in the experiments of Batch 178 (MLP compression).
>
> Choice 1: Instead of lambda * ||s - sg(s + r)||^2 / sg(||y||^2) we should use lambda * ||s - sg(s + r)||^2 / sg(||y||^2) + lambda_1 * ||s||^n
> where n can be 2 or (4 and higher) depending on whether we want the counter force to be smoother or more "hard cap like".
>
> Choice 2: let s' = s / ||s|| and y' = y / ||y||, and the aux term should become lambda * ||s' - sg(y')||^2
> where y = s + r
>
> Rationale: in the aux loss in batch 178, under the random vector assumption, s and r are approximately orthogonal because they are high dimensional, therefore by pythagorean theorem ||s + r||^2 has a very high probability of being larger than ||s||^2, no matter what training phase we are at. In order for the aux loss to minimize ||s - sg(s + r)||^2 / sg(||y||^2) it would both rotate s to be more aligned to (s + r) and stretch s longer to match the norm of (s + r). This optimization pressure of raw norm stretching would never stop at any phase of training. This seems to be the opposite of what we want for a regularized neural network, and might be the real reason why Batch 178 didn't show improvements.
>
> Of course now in choice 1, lambda_1 also needs tuning and my intuition is to start with a value smaller than lambda.

It also logs each layer's output max |x| vs RMS, and dumps every norm gain and output scalar at the end. The control dump shows what the default gains learn per module, which says which gain function fits.

| run | change |
|---|---|
| `ctrl` | none (diagnostics only) |
| `ss_lin` | learned scalar on every attention and MLP output (`sublayer_scales`), linear, init 1 |
| `ss_sig2` | the same scalar as `2·sigmoid(w)`, init `w = 0`, so it modulates in (0, 2) |

| `g_sig2` | `2·sigmoid(w)`, init 0; gain LR ×2 |

**Why the functions could matter:**
- **Scale of an output.** AttnRes scores sources on RMS-normed copies but mixes the raw sources, so an output scalar sets that branch's weight in the mix, and the next RMSNorm removes only the overall scale. Batch 01 found learned output scalars neutral (MoE outputs grew to 1.2–2.1×), but that was a much earlier recipe.
- **Positivity and relative steps.** A linear gain moves additively and can cross 0. `e^w` keeps it positive and makes Adam's steps relative (the same fraction at any size), which suits gains spanning orders of magnitude. `softplus` is linear above about 1 and exponential near 0. `2·sigmoid` bounds it in (0, 2), and that bound is the test of whether large gains are needed.
- **Plain `sigmoid`:** I used `2·sigmoid` rather than a plain sigmoid, which can't start at 1 and can only shrink activations. If the control's gains never exceed 1, plain sigmoid becomes worth a run.

**LR.** Gains train with Adam, so a step moves the raw parameter by about lr, and the gain by `f'(w)` times that. At init `f'` is 1 for `exp`, 0.63 for `softplus` and 0.5 for `2·sigmoid`, so the gain LR multipliers (×1.6, ×2) give every arm the same initial step as linear. A ×0.5 / ×2 sweep follows on whichever helps.

🤖 **Batch 184: two weight sets for the MLA attention (previous step + current)** (candidate 11, d512, 2817 equal steps, seed 0; cw-rno2a; [`2ebb73734a`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/2ebb73734a))

**Idea** (ClassicLarry): keep the previous step's weights for a parameter group, and run half of each batch on them.
- **Implementation** (`dual_attn_prev`): each MLA attention module gets a frozen copy of the previous step's weights, refreshed after every update.
- **Batch split:** in training, odd batch rows run attention at those old weights and even rows at the current ones.
- **Gradient:** the old rows read `sg(θ_old) + (θ − sg(θ))`, so their gradient reaches the current weights. Each update then averages the gradient at both ends of the last step, about its midpoint.
- **Expected effect:** that damps directions that flip sign every step (period-2 bounce) and lags drifting directions by about half a step.
- **Evals** use the current weights only.

|---|---|---|---|

- **A loss at fixed time.** The extra attention pass in the two MLA layers costs 8% step time, about +0.014.

**FP8: microbenchmarks on one GB200** (16k tokens, fwd+bwd of one linear `[16k, d] × [d, n]`)

| d (FFN up, n = 4d) | bf16 GEMMs | per-tensor FP8 GEMMs | MXFP8 GEMMs | JAX MXFP8 linear, end to end |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 512–1024 | launch-bound | no gain | no gain | 0.4–0.6× bf16 |
| 2048 | 2.1 PF | 4.2 PF | 2.7 PF | 0.78× |
| 4096 | 2.3 PF | 4.5 PF | 3.1 PF | 1.02× |
| 6144 | 2.3 PF | 4.6 PF | 3.0 PF | 1.20× |

- **In the training layouts, block-scaled MXFP8 runs as fast as per-tensor FP8.** In the d=6144 profile, cuBLAS's 1×32 block-scaled kernels (`Avec32UE8M0_Bvec32UE8M0`) take 1.44–1.49 ms per GEMM, against 1.43 ms for per-tensor FP8 and 2.7 ms for bf16. Fine-grained scaling itself costs nothing.
- **The overhead is all in quantization.** `jax.nn.scaled_dot_general` re-quantizes both operands for every GEMM. That is six bf16 reads, separate amax / convert / transpose fusions, about 2.1 ms at d=6144 against 4.4 ms of GEMMs. A fused cast kernel would read x, w and g once and write row- and column-wise e4m3 plus e8m0 scales. By bandwidth that is about 0.4 ms, so about 1.9× bf16 at d=6144.
- **Below d≈2048 FP8 can't pay.** The GEMMs are too small to be tensor-core bound. On the d512 H100 rung, FP8 is a numerics question, not a speed lever.
- **Width dependence of the error:** relative error is 3.8% for MXFP8 (e4m3 everywhere) and 5.9% for per-tensor with e5m2 gradients. It is flat from d=512 to 6144 on Gaussian inputs, and four 100× outlier channels don't change it.

**Protocol chosen: MXFP8, just-in-time scales.** Each 32-element block along each GEMM's contraction axis gets a power-of-two (e8m0) scale from its own amax. e4m3 is used everywhere, gradients included. The router, embeddings, lm head, norms, attention core and optimizer stay high precision.
- **Why not modded-nanogpt-style fixed scales:** they are tuned to one width and one activation distribution. The RMSNorm bound `max|x| ≤ sqrt(d)` grows with d, and the gradient scale drifts with depth, LR and training phase.
- **Why not per-tensor current scaling:** a single outlier channel sets the scale for the whole tensor. Massive activations grow with width and training.
- **With 1×32 blocks, an outlier only coarsens its own block,** and no scale state depends on width, step or calibration. It is also the native Blackwell format (same GEMM speed, as above).

**Kalman write strength: parked.**
- Every attempt hit a NaN loss between steps 4 and 31, on both seeds and with either optimizer for the projection.
- A debug run shows why: at step 10 the gradient norm of KDA layer 2's `kalman_b` was **5e18**, with every other gradient below 0.4. Its square overflows fp32 in the global-norm clip, and the loss turns NaN a few steps later.
- The scan itself is not the source. On CPU at 4096 tokens its forward and gradients are finite and O(1) for decays 0.5–0.999 and extreme `ω`/`r`.
- So the blow-up arrives through the kernel's `β` cotangent, on tokens where the Kalman β departs from the sigmoid's narrow range. Finding them needs kernel-level instrumentation; I'm not chasing that further now.

**Why the batch 163 version lost.**
- Batch 163 got −0.003 / −0.004 at equal steps but cost +6.6% step time.
- It added its noise maps on top of the signal heads, as a second full attention call.
- It also tiled each shared noise map out to all `g` heads of its group, so each map was computed `g` times.
- Motif 3's GDLA ([arXiv 2608.09119](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09119)) does neither:
  - The noise heads come out of the head budget: 80 query heads = 64 signal + 16 noise.
  - Each group's signal and noise heads share one KV head, and only the query differs.
  - Its attention kernel therefore runs no extra heads.

**Batch 203: GDLA inside the head budget** (`mla_gdla_noise_heads=m`, MLA layers 3 and 5)
- The `N` query heads form `m` groups of `g` signal heads plus 1 noise head, and run in one kernel call.
- Each group shares one value head, so `w_uv` and the value embeds have `m` heads. Keys stay per head, since MLA up-projections are cheap.
- The output is `D = H_signal − λ·H_noise(group)`, with `λ = sigmoid(x W_λ)` per signal head and token (zero-init, so 0.5).
- Only the signal heads reach `w_o`.

**Batch df1: differential attention with a free noise map** (original idea; on cw-us-east-02a with its own control)
- *Source:* DIFF's noise map is meant to cancel common-mode attention, the broad mass a softmax spreads over irrelevant context. The cheapest estimate of that common mode is a fixed average of the values, so no second softmax map is needed.
- *Mechanism:* `D = softmax(qkᵀ)v − λ·mean_{j≤t}(v_j)` per head, within documents, with the same token-dependent sigmoid `λ`. Cost is one segment-reset scan, with no extra kernel call.
- *Variants:*
  - `uniform`: the plain prefix mean.
  - `decay`: an exponentially decayed mean with a learned per-head decay, half-life 16 / 64 / 256 at init. This makes the noise map a local/recent baseline.
- *Logged:* `knob_mean_noise_lambda_mean` and the learned half-lives per layer.

| run | noise map |
|---|---|
| `df1-ctrl` | none (cw-us-east-02a control) |
| `df1-mu` | uniform prefix mean |
| `df1-md16` / `md64` / `md256` | decayed mean, initial half-life 16 / 64 / 256 |

🤖 **Partial key offset study: what the shifted half of the MLA heads learns** (d512 current best / candidate 12, EMA weights of `lc1-b234-attn-distance`, 2.9528)

With `mla_key_offset`, each MLA head's first 64 key channels come from the previous token (j−1); channels 64–127 come from the current token. I looked at what that split learns: the query/key directions of each head, then a probe of where the heads attend.

**Method**
- **Directions in the attention input x:** the query direction is the `W_q` column. The key direction is backed out through the latent: `W_dkv · diag(latent norm gain) · W_uk`, with the latent RMSNorm linearized.
- **The 128 per-channel pairs aren't unique:** any rotation of a head's channels gives the same scores. So each head is also analyzed through the SVD of its query–key product `B = W_q W_kᵀ`, which gives canonical (query direction, key direction, strength) pairs. The raw-channel and canonical numbers agree closely.

**1. The shifted half is an induction lookup, built into the weights**

Mean query/key cosine on the shifted half (channels 0–63), per head:

| head | layer 3 | layer 5 |
|---|---|---|
| H0 | 0.61 | 0.90 |
| H1 | 0.87 | 0.70 |
| H2 | 0.41 | 0.85 |
| H3 | 0.80 | 0.85 |
| H4 | 0.85 | 0.45 |
| H5 | 0.89 | 0.88 |

- **Query and key point the same way in all 12 heads.** By pair strength, 92–100% sits on positively matched pairs, and no head has negatively matched pairs. So a query scores keys whose *previous* token resembles its own token: "find where I appeared before and read what came next."
- **The current-token half matches only weakly** (+0.14 to +0.40), except L3 H2 (+0.87), a copy head.
- **The attention probe agrees.** Queries at fixed in-document positions (x = 20…4,000), with each query's full softmax row kept rather than averaged:
  - at x = 4,000, 30–49% of the top long-range keys of the sharp layer-3 heads (H1, H4, H5) are induction targets;
  - half of those heads' long-range mass sits on 6–36 keys;
  - L3 H2 picks earlier copies of the query token (33% of its top keys).
- **Layer-5 heads are induction-shaped in the weights too (0.85–0.93), but diffuse in behavior.** Half their long-range mass needs 93–172 keys. They likely match on broader features, so many keys qualify.

**2. The 64 shifted dims are not redundant in weight space**

| per head, shifted half | range |
|---|---|
| directions for 50% / 90% of B's strength | 11–19 / 40–48 |
| effective rank (of 64) | 41–55 |
| stable rank | 12–28 |
| average \|cos\| between different key channels | 0.04–0.07 |
| top 8 channels' share of strength (uniform = 0.125) | 0.14–0.15 |

The channels are near-orthogonal and none dominates. A dozen or so stronger directions plus a long real tail. This is weight space only: whether the data uses all 64 needs an activation-side rank or an ablation, which isn't run yet.

**3. Tying the query to the key on the shifted half costs nothing**

`mla_tie_prev_qk` (`b759695d8f`): the query's shifted half *is* the token's own un-shifted key half, so those channels score `k_prev(x_i) · k_prev(x_{j−1})`, a symmetric similarity. It needs no query projection for those 64 channels.

| run | Paloma | step ms |
|---|---|---|
| current best (`lc1-b217-ctrl`) | 2.9521 | 190.2 |
| **tied shifted half (`lc1-b236-tie-prev-qk`)** | **2.9517** | 190.3 |

Neutral: the free query directions were re-learning the key. That makes it a free simplification, and it drops 64 query columns per head in both MLA layers.

**4. For sparse attention**

The shifted half is close to a symmetric positive form, a learned similarity between the query token and each key's previous token. A low-rank index over previous-token states (around 16–32 dims) could pre-select long-range candidates for the retrieval heads. The diffuse layer-5 heads look better suited to pooled chunk summaries than to top-k selection.

**Next:**
- an activation-side effective rank of the shifted half;
- shifting 16 or 32 channels instead of 64;
- the Inkling relative-position bias by distance. That probe run (`lc1-b235-relpos-probe`) just finished.

🤖 **Config change: KDA write and erase gates dropped** (Gated DeltaNet-2 gates, adopted in batch 88)

They were worth −0.0024 at d512 (batch 88, two seeds) for about +1% step time. At the hero shape, d6144 / 48 layers on one GB200 rack, they cost far more: each is a full 6144×6144 projection in all 36 KDA layers.

| GB200 1-rack, late steps | step time | MFU | tok/s |
|---|---|---|---|
| with write + erase gates | 19.42 s | 25.7% | 216k |
| without (`lc1-gb200-nogate30`) | **17.95 s** | **27.6%** | **232k** |

Kimi K3's KDA has neither gate: it keeps a full-rank output gate, a low-rank decay gate and a per-head β ([arXiv 2607.24653](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.24653v1)). The base config is now `base16` (base15 without `kda_write_gate`, `kda_erase_gate`, `kda_onchip_erase_gate`), and new d512 pairs run against it.

📥 **Intake suggestion** from RavnaBergsndot, approved by ClassicLarry ([original](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9514#issuecomment-6079384012)):

> Try warmup of muonh nesterov momentum, and see if it could shift the optimal momentum from 0.95 to higher ones.
>
> Like how modded-nanogpt introduced it since record 9, start with a lower momentum like 0.85, and linearly increase it to the value we want over the warmup period. Spend more steps in the momentum warmup (like 10% or 20% of total) than common lr warmup settings (<5%). Try higher final momentum such as 0.98 and see whether the momentum warmup schedule could make them better than the default 0.95.
>
> Rationale: 0.95 is a safe number that's widely used, and the kimi paper reported that tuning it makes minimal difference. However, the lack of success from a a higher momentum may be caused by the early-late training dynamic discrepancy, and if this problem is alleviated, it might have some extra potential after training reaches the stabilized phase. A momentum warmup can help with the discrepancy by forgetting gradient information quicker in the early phase. The ademamix optimizer paper has some empirical evidence that the momentum warmup period should be sufficiently long. Since the update size is at the same scale after the short lr warmup finishes, long momentum warmup doesn't have the problem of "too little accumulated update" so it wouldn't require retuning lr and its schedule.

Original description ~~~markdown This issue tracks iterative improvements to the Marin pretraining scaling ladder (`experiments/grug/fast_track`) using the **Marin Belay** process. It is a twist on autoresearch: an agent runs experiments in batches, and anyone can steer it with research directions. > **To suggest a research direction, comment on [Marin Belay Intake (#9514)](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9514).** Suggestions a maintainer approves (👍 from a `marin-devs` member) are copied into this thread automatically, and the agent acts only on this thread. Clean KMA, the current baseline (★), is 0.022 lower at d512, 0.049 lower at d768, 0.040 lower at d1024 and 0.033 lower at d1280, which is about 1.14×, 1.43×, 1.40× and 1.35× the baseline's compute efficiency. They count as ordinary wins; no parity check needed. - **Noise.** Differences under ~0.005 are noise. A win must beat the current best by more than 0.005. ### Gates (both relative to the current baseline, same fixed-time rule at each rung) - **Gate 1:** beat the baseline at d512 and d768. - **Gate 2:** also beat it at d1024 and d1280, **and** project to lower Paloma macro loss at 1e24 FLOPs. Fit a power law of final loss against training FLOPs across the four rungs, for both the baseline and the variant, fixing the asymptote to 1.2. ### Fixed - Training data, the 16k BPE tokenizer, and the eval sets. - Sequence length 4096. - One 8×H100 node per rung. - The FLOP accounting used for the gate-2 projection. ### Judgment calls - **Hero-scale speed is out of scope for v1, so use discretion.** - Robust target criteria would also check training speed and inference speed at hero scale. Marin Belay v1 skips those checks. - Judge whether a change's d512 gain would carry over to hero scale, and avoid changes whose gain comes from d512-only effects. Two examples: - Dropping MoE for dense would be a clear win at d512 because dense gets ~5× higher MFU there, but that MFU gain would not carry over at hero scale. - A much larger KV cache would also be a clear win at d512, but it would hurt long-context inference speed. - **Avoid magic numbers.** - Prefer changes with few new tuned constants. A tuned constant is justified when its gain is above the noise threshold and holds as a pattern across scales. For example, a 2× LR on one parameter group qualifies if it clears the noise threshold and the gain shows up consistently at larger rungs. - The higher a change's risk of curve fitting, the more scales it must be validated at before it counts as a win. - **Spend effort in proportion to an idea's likelihood of improvement.** - Promising ideas deserve several attempts. Long shots can be tried once and dropped. - A first run is not a verdict for a large change. Each goes through a ShortConv followed by SiLU. q and k are L2-normalized, and q is scaled by 1/√128. - **Decay:** per-channel log-decay `g = −5·sigmoid(exp(A_log)·(x·W_a_down·W_a_up + dt_bias))`. - The gate projection has rank 128. - `A_log` is one value per head, initialized to 0. - `dt_bias` is one value per channel, initialized so the decay rate spans 0.02–0.5. - **Write strength:** `β = sigmoid(x·W_β)`, one value per head. - **Recurrence:** `S_t = (I − β·k·kᵀ)·Diag(exp(g))·S_{t−1} + β·k·vᵀ`, read out as `o_t = S_tᵀ·q_t`. - It runs as chunked Pallas kernels, with a stable block-doubling inverse inside each chunk. - **Output:** per-head RMSNorm with a learnable 128-wide scale shared across heads → full-rank per-channel gate `sigmoid(x·W_g)` → `W_o`. - No positional encoding, no window, no XSA, and no ShortConv on the branch output. **Global layers: MLA + Inkling relative position** - **q:** full-rank, D → N·128 (no Q latent). - **k and v:** k = `W_uk · RMSNorm(x·W_dkv)` and v = `W_uv · RMSNorm(x·W_dkv)`. - They share one 512-wide KV latent, with a learnable RMSNorm on the latent. - Heads are 128 wide with no RoPE part. - There's no ShortConv on K, so the up-projections can be absorbed at inference. - **Scaling:** no QK-norm; `qk_mult` = 1, i.e. standard 1/√128 logit scaling. - **Position — Inkling relative-position bias**, added to the pre-softmax logits in place of RoPE: - `bias[h,i,j] = R[i,h,:] · P[:, i−j]`, where `R = x·W_r` is 16 values per head. - `P` is a bank of shape [16 × 1024] shared across heads. The relative extent is 1024. - It runs inside the FA4 attention kernel (forward, backward, and the SM90 backward pass). - **XSA** (exclusive self-attention): subtract the component of each head's output that is parallel to its own value vector. - **Output gate:** per head, `2·sigmoid(x·W_gate)`. `W_gate` is zero-initialized, so the gate is 1 at init. - The branch output also gets a ShortConv. **MoE sublayer (LatentMoE with quantile-balanced routing)** - **Experts:** 384 routed experts, top-8. Each is a SwiGLU with hidden size D/2. - **Latent space:** experts operate in a D/2-wide latent. The input goes through `W_latent_down` → RMSNorm, and the combined expert output goes back up through `W_latent_up`. - **Router:** reads the full-width token and computes logits in fp32. - Experts are selected by top-(8+1) on bias-adjusted logits, where the 9th logit is the threshold α. - Combine weights are the sigmoid of the unbiased logits, renormalized to sum to 2.5. - **Quantile balancing:** each step, each expert's threshold β is the global (1 − K/E) quantile of the logit margins (logit − α), read from a 10k-bin histogram. The router bias is set to −β. - The router bias is not trained by gradient. - **Capacity:** capacity factor 1.15, with pooled-wave expert-parallel dispatch. Receiver ranks are sort-based and the expand backward is gather-based. - **Shared experts:** 2 shared SwiGLU experts that bypass the latent: D → D/2 hidden → D. - **Fused projections:** - The router, latent-down, and both shared experts' gate/up projections run as one GEMM. - The shared experts' down-projections run as one GEMM. **Residual stream: Block Attention Residuals** - **Sources:** the embedding source, one running sum per completed block of sublayer outputs, and the running partial sum of the current block. - The model has 8 blocks. Block sums use the raw sublayer outputs. - **Gates:** every sublayer (attention and MoE) has its own gate, and there is one final gate before the output norm. Each gate has one learned pseudo-query `q ∈ ℝᴰ`, zero-initialized so every gate starts as a uniform average. - **Mixing:** per token, `logitᵢ = q · rms_norm(sourceᵢ)`, using a parameter-free (frozen) RMS key norm, then `softmax` over sources and a weighted sum of the raw sources. - **Implementation:** - Each completed block is scored once against every gate that reads it. - Backward: at d512 the layer's forward intermediates are saved. At d768–d1280 each layer is recomputed. At d1280 the attention branch is also rematerialized. - The model keeps one layer stack per mixer kind. **Optimizer** | Group | Update rule | LR | Parameters | |---|---|---|---| | `muonh` | MuonH | MuonH LR | all attention and MoE matrices: MLA `W_q`/`W_dkv`/`W_uk`/`W_uv`/`W_o`; KDA `W_q`/`W_k`/`W_v`/`W_o`/`W_g`; experts; shared experts; latent down/up. 🤖 **New accepted baseline: Belay Ckpt 1**

Ckpt 1 replaces `base16` as the baseline. From now on, new d512 experiments run against it at a fixed 8 minutes.

**Code:** branch [`marin_belay_v1_ckpt1`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/marin_belay_v1_ckpt1/experiments/grug/fast_track), recipe module [`belay_ckpt1.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/marin_belay_v1_ckpt1/experiments/grug/fast_track/belay_ckpt1.py), which holds the exact flags for every ladder rung and the GB200 rack.

```bash
uv run python -m experiments.grug.fast_track.belay_ckpt1 --size d512 --num-steps 2760 --submit \
    --run-id <id> --target-cluster cw-us-east-02a
```

**Recipe:**
- **Attention:** KDA local layers and MLA global layers (every 4th layer plus the last), with Inkling relative position and Block AttnRes.
- **MoE:** latent MoE with 384 ungated ReLU² experts, top-10 routed. Routed and shared experts are both 0.75·d wide, with one shared expert. The router combine is `sqrt_softplus_renorm`.
- **Embeddings and head:** gated value embeddings, logit soft-cap 10, learnable QK multiplier.
- **Optimizer:** MuonH (pre-norm in, decay power 0.7), with AdEMAMix Adam for the non-matrix parameters. β1 is 0.9 and β2 comes from the heuristic; cosine schedule.
- **GB200 only:** MXFP8 on the routed experts, dense projections and expert dispatch.

**d512, 8 minutes on 8×H100** (2,760 steps, 0.175 s/step, one seed):

| Recipe | Paloma macro loss | Paloma macro BPB |
|---|---:|---:|
| **Belay Ckpt 1** | **3.0270** | **1.2562** |
| Marin Aug Hero Arch | 3.1306 | 1.2980 |
| Basic MoE (128 experts, top-4) | 3.1612 | 1.3108 |
| Vanilla dense | 3.4452 | 1.4275 |

**Scaling ladder.** Ckpt 1 runs at 171 tokens per active parameter and Aug Hero at 235, each at its own hero-budget ratio. The speedup is the extra model FLOPs Aug Hero's fit needs to match Ckpt 1's BPB at that rung.

| Rung | Ckpt 1 BPB | Aug Hero BPB | Speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| d512 | 1.1934 | 1.2309 | 2.20× |
| d768 | 1.0899 | 1.1230 | 2.15× |
| d1024 | 1.0097 | 1.0329 | 1.94× |
| d1280 | training | training | – |

- **Fits:** fixing the floor at 0.498, the fits are BPB = 0.498 + 21.16·C^−0.0822 for Ckpt 1 and 0.498 + 25.49·C^−0.0850 for Aug Hero, where C is analytic model FLOPs.
- **Projection:** at 300k GB200-hours, Ckpt 1 projects **0.729 BPB** against Aug Hero's 0.735. In hardware FLOPs that is a **1.33×** speedup. Two things cut it from the per-rung numbers: Ckpt 1's flatter slope, and its lower 11-rack MFU (26.9% against 28.8%).
- **Caveat:** the advantage shrinks from d768 to d1024. Treat 1.33× as provisional until the d1280 runs finish.

**GB200, one rack (d6144, 48 layers):** 14.59 s/step at 28.9% MFU, counted on analytic FLOPs.

🤖 **Batch plan: X0217, MuonH momentum warmup** (the intake suggestion above, from RavnaBergsndot)

**Idea:** warm MuonH's Nesterov momentum up linearly from 0.85, the way modded-nanogpt does. Then test whether the warmup lets a higher final momentum (0.98) beat the default 0.95.

**Code:** `momentum_warmup_start` / `momentum_warmup` on GrugMoeMuonHConfig, default off. When set, the momentum runs in the existing stage ahead of Newton-Schulz with `m(t) = 0.85 + (m − 0.85)·min(t / W, 1)`, and with a constant `m` it is identical to the current path. Commit [`e8cd1b97ec`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/e8cd1b97ec) on `marin_belay_v1_w2026-10-12`, cut from Ckpt 1.

**Protocol:** d512, 8 minutes (2,760 steps, Belay Ckpt 1), seeds 0 and 1, each arm compared to the same-seed control, ranked by Paloma macro loss. 10 runs.

| Arm | Final momentum | Warmup from 0.85 | Paloma macro loss (s0 / s1) | Δ vs control (s0 / s1) | Δ mean |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---:|
| `ctrl` (Ckpt 1) | 0.95 | none | 3.0269 / 3.0315 | – | – |
| `w95` | 0.95 | 10% of training | 3.0274 / 3.0256 | +0.0005 / −0.0059 | −0.0027 |
| `w98` | 0.98 | 10% | 3.0485 / 3.0477 | +0.0217 / +0.0162 | +0.0190 |
| `w98l` | 0.98 | 20% | 3.0499 / 3.0496 | +0.0231 / +0.0181 | +0.0206 |
| `c98` | 0.98 | none | 3.0509 / 3.0547 | +0.0240 / +0.0202 | +0.0221 |

**Result: no win; X0217 is closed.**
- Warmup at 0.95 averages −0.0027, inside the 0.005 noise threshold, and the two seeds disagree in sign.
- A final momentum of 0.98 is about 0.02 worse. Warmup recovers 0.0015–0.0031 of that, depending on its length, and the longer 20% warmup recovers less.
- So warmup doesn't make the higher momentum competitive here, and 0.95 stays.

`c98` separates the two effects: if `w98` beats `c98`, it's the warmup that makes 0.98 work. Run ids are `belay-X0217-<arm>-s<seed>`; the registry entry is X0217.
Lets test: https://arxiv.org/html/2610.13630v1

🤖 **Batch plan: X0218, Multi-Stream Attention Residuals** ([arXiv 2610.13630](https://arxiv.org/html/2610.13630v1), requested above)

**Idea:** today each Block AttnRes gate reads the depth sources (embedding, completed block summaries, the running partial) with one zero-init pseudo-query. MSAR gives each gate m queries ("streams"):
- **Stream 0** reads the sources as they are, exactly like today.
- **Streams r ≥ 1** first pass every source through its own causal depthwise convolution along the sequence (kernels 4/8/12, zero-init, never crossing document boundaries), then attend over those.
- **Mixer:** a small sigmoid mixer, `sigmoid(α·RMSNorm(concat z)·W + b)`, weights the m reads into the sublayer's input.
- **Final gate:** the one before the LM head stays single-stream.

**Code:** `attn_res_streams` / `attn_res_stream_kernels` / `attn_res_stream_mixer`, default off; with m=1 the model is bit-identical to today. Commit [`0e9cdc7460`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/0e9cdc7460) on `marin_belay_v1_w2026-10-12`. CPU checks passed: future ×1e6 leakage, document boundaries, finite-difference gradients. Not supported with `scan_layers`, so no GB200 runs yet.

**Protocol:** d512, Belay Ckpt 1, **equal data**: 2,760 steps, the same as the Ckpt 1 8-minute run, ignoring MSAR's extra step time for now. Seeds 0 and 1, each compared to the same-seed control from X0217 (`belay-X0217-ctrl-s0/s1`, same base code). Ranked by Paloma macro loss. A fixed-time run follows if it wins.

| Arm | Streams | Convolution kernels | Mixer | Paloma macro loss (s0 / s1) | Δ vs control (mean) |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---:|
| control (Ckpt 1) | 1 | – | – | 3.0269 / 3.0315 | – |
| `m4` | 4 | 4, 8, 12 | yes | 3.0164 / 3.0168 | **−0.0125** (−0.0104 / −0.0147) |
| `m2` | 2 | 4 | yes | 3.0191 / 3.0174 | **−0.0109** (−0.0078 / −0.0141) |
| `m4nomix` | 4 | 4, 8, 12 | no (plain sum) | 3.0163 / 3.0198 | **−0.0111** (−0.0106 / −0.0116) |

The paper's ablation found the convolutions matter most, m=2 captures most of the gain, and the mixer is worth about 0.004.

**Update:**
- **No mixer (`m4nomix`): a clear equal-data win.** It is **−0.0111** on both seeds (−0.0106 / −0.0116), BPB 1.2517 / 1.2537 against 1.2562 / 1.2586.
- **It costs about +18% step time** (0.205 vs 0.174 s/step in 40-step probes), so a fixed-time run has to decide it.
- **The mixer arms diverged from a backward bug.** The gradients of the mixer's α and b are orders of magnitude too large (6e8 at step 0), until Adam overflows. The mixer's W and everything else stay normal. A fix is in progress, then m4/m2 rerun.

**Update 2: mixer arms rerun at [`912bd13876`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/912bd13876).**
- **The NaN was an XLA GPU miscompile.** On 8 GPUs, the bf16 gradients of the tiny mixer α `[2]` and b `[2, m]` leaves come out of the combined float32 gradient all-reduce through a *bitcast* instead of a convert, so the leaves receive raw float32 bit-halves. Keeping those two leaves float32 at compute fixes it; the corrupted runs were rerun under new ids (`m4b`, `m2b`).
- **All three arms win at equal data by about −0.011 to −0.013**, which is 2–2.5× the noise threshold:
  - The mixer adds only about 0.0014 over the plain sum (m4 −0.0125 vs m4nomix −0.0111), inside the noise.
  - m=2 with a single kernel-4 stream (−0.0109) matches m=4.
- **So the gain comes from the convolved streams, not the mixer or the stream count.** Next: a fixed-time run (MSAR costs about +18% step time), and controls for whether the gain is just longer temporal reach (`sconv_kernel` 8/12 on the existing write-side convs) or depends on the per-channel basis (scalar-tap streams).

**Batch 2: finding the minimal version** ([`23bd387bcc`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/23bd387bcc)). Equal data, 2,760 steps, seeds 0 and 1, against the same controls.

| Arm | What it keeps | Question | Δ (s0 / s1) | Mean |
|---|---|---|---|---:|
| `m2nomix` | 1 extra stream over all sources, kernel 4, plain sum | Does the minimal MSAR keep the gain? | −0.0069 / −0.0112 | **−0.0090** |
| `m2embed` | extra stream reads only the conv'd token embedding | Is it an n-gram-like embedding feature? | −0.0072 / −0.0079 | **−0.0076** |
| `m2noembed` | extra stream reads every source except the embedding | Is it the conv'd layer outputs? | +0.0003 / −0.0035 | −0.0016 |
| `m2scalar` | as `m2nomix`, one tap set shared by all channels | Does the per-channel basis matter? | −0.0040 / −0.0079 | −0.0060 |
| `embconv` | no MSAR; embedding source = `emb + conv(emb)` (kernel 4, zero-init) | Is a write-side conv on the embedding enough? | −0.0026 / −0.0044 | −0.0035 |
| `sconv8` | no MSAR; existing write-side SConvs at kernel 8 (also KDA q/k/v) | Is it just longer reach? | −0.0007 / −0.0030 | −0.0018 |

Every arm is bit-identical to its baseline at init. CPU checks for each path: future-token leakage, document boundaries, finite gradients.

**Batch 2 result: the gain is a read-side conv of the token embedding.**
- **Embedding only keeps most of it.** `m2embed` (the conv'd embedding added to every gate's input) gets −0.0076, about 85% of `m2nomix`'s −0.0090.
- **Without the embedding it's gone.** `m2noembed` is −0.0016, which is noise.
- **Write-side is weaker.** The same conv on the embedding source (`embconv`, −0.0035) gets about half: there it only arrives through each gate's softmax weight on the embedding, which is small for later layers.
- **Longer write-side convs** (`sconv8`) do nothing.
- **Per-channel taps matter.** Scalar taps lose about a third.

The seed-1 control is about 0.004 high, so the seed-0 column is the conservative read.

**Batch 3: embedding variants and MLP-side conv placement** ([`00b0b9d102`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/00b0b9d102), [`33aa1753a8`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/33aa1753a8)). Equal data, 2,760 steps, same controls.

| Arm | Change from Ckpt 1 | Δ (s0 / s1) | Mean |
|---|---|---|---:|
| `m2embscale` | `m2embed` with a learned per-gate scale on conv(e) | −0.0066 / −0.0066 | −0.0066 |
| `embout` | embedding out of the layer gates' softmax, added at weight 1 | +0.0123 / +0.0197 | **+0.0160** |
| `emboutscale` | as `embout`, with a learned per-gate scale | +0.0054 / +0.0104 | **+0.0079** |
| `nomlpconv` | MLP-output SConv dropped | +0.0044 / +0.0009 | +0.0027 |
| `mlpin` | MLP-output SConv moved to the MLP input (router, latent and shared all read it) | +0.0022 / +0.0014 | +0.0018 |
| `mlplatent` | MLP-output SConv + a conv on the routed latent output | −0.0004 / +0.0005 | 0.0000 |
| `latent` | routed latent-output conv instead of the MLP-output conv | −0.0018 / −0.0007 | −0.0012 |
| `latentshared` | separate convs on the routed latent output and the shared output | −0.0032 / −0.0010 | −0.0021 |
| `latentin` | routed latent-input conv instead | +0.0014 / +0.0031 | +0.0023 |
| `sharedin` | shared-input conv instead | +0.0016 / no final eval | – |

**Result:**
- **A per-gate scale doesn't improve `m2embed`** (−0.0066 vs −0.0076).
- **Taking the raw embedding out of the softmax clearly hurts,** even with a learned scale. So `m2embed`'s gain doesn't come from bypassing the softmax: it adds the conv'd embedding while the plain embedding stays in the softmax.
- **Where the MLP-side SConv goes barely matters at d512.** Every placement, including dropping it, lands within ±0.003 of Ckpt 1.

The minimal winning change is still `m2embed`: a zero-init causal kernel-4 per-channel conv of the token embedding, added to every gate's input.

**Batch 4: conv'd embedding only at selected gates** ([`fb1caabf39`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/fb1caabf39)). Prompted by `m2embscale`'s learned scales, which stayed large only at layer 0 (both gates) and layer 3's MLP gate, while the other gates fell toward 0.

| Arm | conv(e) added at | Δ (s0 / s1) | Mean |
|---|---|---|---:|
| `m2embed` (reference) | all 12 gates | −0.0072 / −0.0079 | −0.0076 |
| `embL0` | layer 0, attention and MLP gates | −0.0027 / −0.0052 | −0.0039 |
| `embL0L3m` | layer 0 + layer 3's MLP gate | +0.0017 / −0.0017 | 0.0000 |

Restricting it to a few gates loses most of the gain, so the small learned scales elsewhere were still doing work. Only `s_g · conv(e)` is identified, so the conv taps can grow while `s_g` shrinks. `m2embed` (all gates, no scale) remains the minimal winning version.
0.85->0.95 momentum warmup looks like perhaps a minor boost, but not integrating as impact will fall-off as we scale to hero size. (since we'd only apply the warmup for very high loss regime)

topics.title: [levanter] Fuse the EP hero's RMSNorm and GatedNorm
topics.body:
Add `gated_rms_norm` in `levanter.kernels.triton.gated_norm`, which computes `GatedNorm(RMSNorm(x))` as one custom op. The EP hero selects it with `gated_norm_implementation="fused"` (or `--gated-norm-implementation fused` in the diagnostic launcher). The default, `"reference"`, keeps the two separate modules. Parameter names and layout are unchanged, so checkpoints load as before.

Memory bandwidth limits this pair of modules. At the hero's per-GPU shape (65,536 tokens, hidden 6,144, gate rank 128, bf16), they read or write the full `[T, D]` activation 10 times in the forward and 27 times in forward plus backward. The custom op cuts that to about 7 and 23.5:

- It folds the RMSNorm weight into the down projection, `a = rstd * (x @ (w * W_down))`, so the normalized activation is never written to memory.
- The backward saves only `a` (`[T, 128]`) and `rstd` (`[T]`) and recomputes the gate.
- On GPU, the backward's two elementwise passes run as Triton kernels. Elsewhere, and on GPU for shards that are not a multiple of 64 tokens by 128 features, they run on XLA, with a warning on GPU.

All rank-128 matmuls stay on XLA. Moving them into Triton was slower than the reference, because Triton 3.6 reaches only about 150-220 TFLOP/s for that matmul shape on B200. Under a mesh, the op runs per shard inside a `shard_map` over `x`'s own sharding and sums the weight gradients in fp32.

Measured on one B200 at the hero shape, counting 98 calls per step plus the forward that `offload_carry` remat reruns:

| Path | Per step | Saved |
|---|---|---|
| Reference | 444 ms | |
| XLA restructure only | 405 ms | 39 ms |
| XLA restructure with Triton passes | 361 ms | 83 ms |

That is about 0.6% of a 14 s hero step. Error against float32 is about half the reference's on every output (relative RMS 1.82e-3 against 3.71e-3 for `y`, 1.98e-3 against 4.24e-3 for `dx`), because the bottleneck reads the normalized activation in fp32. The op has not run on GB200 or inside the full hero step.

topics.title: [datakit] Replace shuffle-store bucket_token_hint with a self-contained counting pre-pass
topics.body:
## Description
`build_clustered_store_shuffle` (`experiments/datakit/store/datakit_store_shuffle.py`) sizes each `(cluster, quality)` bucket's subshard count from a prior store's per-bucket token mass, loaded via `bucket_token_hint_from_artifact`. This couples the builder to a prior artifact and has a chicken-and-egg on the first build: with no prior store it falls back to `default_subshards`, and no constant wins both goals — `1` sends the hot ~651B-token bucket through one multi-hour / OOM-prone reducer, while a flat `K` re-splits small buckets into many tiny caches (the object proliferation #6687 is fixing).

Replace the prior-artifact hint with a self-contained counting pre-pass: a first map pass that runs the join and counts docs (or tokens) per `(cluster, quality)` — small columns, no payload shuffle — then sizes subshards from the measured distribution. Removes the prior-artifact dependency, is correct on the first run, and adapts to distribution drift, at the cost of one extra cheap pass.

Follow-up to #6687 / PR #6725. Parent: #6037.

### Definition of Done
- `bucket_token_hint` param and `bucket_token_hint_from_artifact` removed from `datakit_store_shuffle.py`
- subshard sizing derived from an in-run per-bucket count pass (reads decon/cluster/quality small columns; no tokenize payload, no scatter)
- hot buckets fan out while small buckets stay at one cache, with no prior artifact required
- `test_datakit_store_shuffle.py` covers pre-pass sizing (a skewed synthetic bucket splits without a hint)

topics.title: [taskforge] Add TaskSpec assembly, lowering, controls and verdicts
topics.body:
Add the `spec` package and `child_process`. `spec.draft` builds a semantic `TaskSpec` from builder outputs (`assemble`, `requirements`, `file`, the answer, Python and script graders), and `spec.draft.lower` alone builds the `LoweredTaskSpec` RolloutEngine runs, choosing each machine's backend for the host. `spec.controls` defines the fixed controls a task's control set must hold (a reference, an acceptance and a shortcut control) and turns a candidate's files and reply into the turns a replay serves. `spec.verdict` reads and writes the per-check verdict a grader program reports. `child_process` stops a child process group, for the loader and build children that come later.

Builds on #10293; the shared modules are complete here, and #10295 starts the stages. Tests that need `spec.draft` land here: the RolloutEngine tests of `llm.rollout_model`, the ShellSim fixture images, and the sandbox factories' two manual machine tests. The taskforge suite passes 322 tests here (110 more than #10293), with one skip for the local backend, which imports on Linux only.

topics.title: Agent MoE Experiment: Inkling relative position vs July Baseline
topics.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This issue tests Inkling-style learned relative attention in the Grug MoE against the fixed July baseline from #6882 at the d512 and d768 Gate 1 cells. The first implementation was stopped immediately because an unfused scan-based attention path was orders of magnitude slower than the fused TPU Splash baseline, so the work shifted to a direct-distance TPU kernel aligned with the released Inkling implementation and covered by value/gradient parity tests. In the corrected rerun, d512 with the current Grug QK scale finished, while the Inkling net-`1/head_dim` QK-scale arm finished with essentially unchanged throughput but materially worse Paloma quality (+13.5% BPB, +0.45972 aggregate eval loss). Both d768 arms were initially stopped for sustained throughput violations around 189k-191k tok/s versus the 249,954 tok/s baseline, then were explicitly continued for diagnostic completion; their first matched step-1,000 comparison also showed a large QKS regression. Current recommendation: reject the net-`1/head_dim` QK-scale variant; treat the relative-position path as not promotable until the remaining d768 continuation data and any separate kernel/quality follow-up change that conclusion.

### Helpful links
- Baseline comparator: #6882
- Kernel bottleneck stop: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7208#issuecomment-4984492475
- Direct-distance parity and rerun reset: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7208#issuecomment-4987514360
- Final d512 Gate 1 result: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7208#issuecomment-4992545932
- d768 continuation status: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7208#issuecomment-4994301965
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Description

The variant in `experiments/grug/moe_relative_position/` replaces the baseline RoPE/NoPE positional scheme with a learned query-dependent relative attention bias. Gate 1 uses the July Baseline's exact 8192-token May-Recipe cells and compares final Paloma macro loss plus last-100-step throughput against #6882.

Initiating prompts:

> Find the new position embedding introduced in https://thinkingmachines.ai/news/introducing-inkling/ and then find the most up to date MoE baseline in the official marin library and replace rope with it

> Follow moe/agents.md and launch gate 1 experiment

> Use this baseline instead https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6882

## Hypothesis or Goal

The learned input-dependent relative bias provides effective wall-clock speedup greater than 1 at both July Baseline Gate 1 cells: d512 at 3.82e17 FLOPs and d768 at 2.81e18 FLOPs.

## Status

Gate 1 is partially concluded and still collecting d768 continuation data by explicit user override. The corrected direct-distance, zero-`W_r`, Adam-routed rerun completed both d512 arms: current-scale d512 reached Paloma BPB 1.28971, macro loss 3.97874, aggregate eval loss 3.74715, and 295,603 tok/s; QKS net-`1/128` d512 reached Paloma BPB 1.46320, macro loss 4.42181, aggregate eval loss 4.20687, and 296,313 tok/s. The QKS d512 result is worse at matched compute with no throughput win. Both d768 arms showed sustained low throughput around 189k-191k tok/s, below the matched 249,954 tok/s baseline, and are being continued to final checkpoints for diagnostics rather than stopped by the original gate.

## Links

* Logbook: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/inkling-relative-position/.agents/logbooks/inkling-relative-position-gate1.md
* W&B project: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/dial_moe
* Baseline: #6882
* Launch snapshot: `a496bc044`
* Submission log: `a11b0d424`

## Decision Log

* 2026-07-15: Use #6882 rather than the newer README baseline, per user direction.
* 2026-07-15: Stop the initial scan-based attention run because the unfused path was far too slow to evaluate the embedding fairly.
* 2026-07-16: Switch the kernel API to direct distance order after checking the official Inkling implementation, then restart with fresh identities.
* 2026-07-16: Reject the net-`1/head_dim` QK-scale variant at d512; continue d768 despite low throughput only because the user requested diagnostic completion.

## Conclusion

The current evidence does not support promoting the Inkling net-`1/head_dim` QK-scale variant. The corrected d512 run is materially worse in quality at matched compute with no throughput gain, and the d768 continuations have already shown low throughput plus an early matched Paloma regression for QKS. Final d768 completion may refine diagnostics, but it would need to reverse both quality and throughput signals to change the recommendation.

topics.title: [rolloutengine] Grade judge tasks on the host
topics.body:
RolloutEngine accepts a `JudgeConnection` and grades judge tasks on the host through TaskCompendium. The engine does not start a verifier machine for this path. The connection stays outside serialized task and rollout records.

[MarinSkyRL #966](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/pull/966) already passes this parameter, but the published `marin-rolloutengine==0.2.201.dev39243773500` rejects it before training. This change extracts the judge path from the open Smartie campaign branch (#10190) so it can reach Marin `main` and the next development release independently.

The verifier timeout bounds the engine's wait for the synchronous judge request. The request thread can continue after that timeout; #10246 tracks deadline handling in Verifyit.
topics.head: bcb0d16fe42394f34f5287642d393f838c66173c

comments.body: @ravwojdyla somehow Skyrl ended up depending on someone's branch I guess?

🤖 SkyRL's root manifest pinned RolloutEngine, Shellbox, and TaskCompendium to Marin commit `b3206ac` on the open Smartie branch (#10190). The published RolloutEngine wheel did not have that branch's `judge_connection` constructor argument, which is why MarinSkyRL #966 failed after switching to PyPI.

Since this PR opened, #10203 merged into `main`. It replaced the task-session engine and already grades judge tasks on the host through `TaskRolloutSpec.judge_connection`. Rebasing this old-constructor patch would restore an API that `main` removed. I am closing this PR as superseded. MarinSkyRL #966 needs a port to the new harness API before a new published Marin release can be used there.

topics.title: [grafana] Unify sync and async RL runs on one RL Post-training board
topics.body:
Merge the sync and async RL boards into one RL Post-training board (`marin-rl-runs`). A training-type picker filters the run picker, and the Job and Execution pickers select attempts for both types.

The board opens with a status strip: step, steps per hour, reward, token rate, record age, services reporting and staleness. Open rows follow for liveness, learning, step wall clock, generation and vLLM engines. Staleness, Megatron, GPU detail, logprob mismatch, resources, Ray and diagnostics sit in collapsed rows.

- Merging this PR deploys Grafana to production.
- The async board (`marin-async-rl`) and `/v1/async-rl/overview` are removed, and the old endpoint returns 404. The board reads `/v1/rl/overview`, `/v1/rl/execution` and `/v1/rl/gpu`.
- Node-GPU detail covers ranges of 7h or less. Longer ranges show a zoom message and send no Finelog query.
- Tested on Snowball sync, Snowball async and Hero async runs. No Hero sync run was found, so that combination is untested.
- A cold 3h page with Cluster = All loads in about 22 s. The GPU and vLLM engine sources each take about 6 s in Finelog.

comments.body:
🤖
# Research

[#9626](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9626) calls `analyze_rollouts()` between evaluation and task generation, but its dummy analyzer groups every reward below 1 by a hard-coded capability ID; the reduced rollout record drops the grade and execution failure evidence needed to tell an incorrect answer from a failed run. #9626 is open and [#9638](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9638) owns the full RSI loop, so this issue can own the analysis stage without duplicating that work. The linked Google Doc redirects to sign-in from this environment, leaving its required grouping and prompt-generation rules unverified.

**Relevant code**
- [`pipeline.py#L82-L97`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/9774e2cd1b4acac2b8b1524e710b217a700fcc22/experiments/post_training/baby_rsi/pipeline.py#L82-L97) — evaluation-to-analysis-to-generation call chain.
- [`dummy.py#L228-L242`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/9774e2cd1b4acac2b8b1524e710b217a700fcc22/experiments/post_training/baby_rsi/dummy.py#L228-L242) — reward-only failure grouping.
- [`interfaces.py#L13-L57`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/9774e2cd1b4acac2b8b1524e710b217a700fcc22/experiments/post_training/baby_rsi/interfaces.py#L13-L57) — prompt and reduced rollout contracts.
- [`contracts.py#L75-L86`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/d8ac9acfd4f1425e8e6caad28fae70b904e5c5bb/lib/rolloutengine/src/rolloutengine/contracts.py#L75-L86) — full grade and failure evidence.

# Proposed Fix

## Design

Implement `AnalysisEngine.analyze_failed_runs` at the #9626 artifact boundary after that PR lands. Preserve each evaluation rollout's task ID, public capability metadata, grade, and execution failure in the analysis input; retain raw task text, expected answers, verifier files, and private traces outside the generator-facing `TaskPromptSet`. Apply the evaluation's explicit pass criterion to completed, valid grades. Count grading and infrastructure failures separately so they do not become training targets. Group valid policy failures by the capability and failure categories specified in the linked document, emit stable prompt IDs and deterministic ordering, and save counts plus source rollout IDs in the private analysis artifact for audit and replay. An empty set of valid policy failures produces an empty prompt set.

## Sequence and validation

1. Rebase on #9626 and keep this PR limited to the analysis input, analyzer, and analysis artifact; leave task generation, training, and the loop coordinator to #9638 and their existing PRs.
2. Add fixture-based tests for wrong answers, partial credit at the configured threshold, successful answers, grader/runtime failures, repeated failures in one category, deterministic output, and exclusion of held-out answer text from prompts. Run the one-round Baby RSI fixture to check that the generated task path consumes the new prompts.
3. Run the touched package's default tests, `./infra/pre-commit.py --all-files --fix`, and the required PR review gate. Record the analysis artifact schema and prompt revision so a later round can reproduce the same selection.

## Open decision

Please provide the linked document's analysis section or read access before implementation. It must settle the failure taxonomy, pass criterion, prompt fields, and whether GLM synthesizes prompts; those choices change the API and tests. The deterministic grouping above is the smallest implementation consistent with the current `TaskPromptSet`, pending that specification.

topics.title: [levanter] Revive rank-level straggler reporting during training
topics.body:
## Description

Levanter still has no in-framework rank-level straggler detection: the trainer logs end-to-end step time but never attributes which rank/host is chronically slow. This was specced in #4235 / #4236 and fully implemented twice — #4240 (host-side, `multihost_broadcast_sync`) and #4241 (JAX distributed KV store), both with tests — but both PRs were closed unmerged (2026-04-28) and the issue auto-closed for inactivity (2026-06-28), not on the merits. `StragglerReporter` is absent from `main` today.

The need is live and recurring:

- The team just merged a **reactive** NCCL collective-hang watchdog (#7350) after a GB200 run silently wedged with all ranks frozen together (#7344). A lagging rank is exactly what straggler reporting surfaces *before* it becomes a wedge — this is the proactive complement to that watchdog.
- Slow-process pathologies keep costing debug time with no per-rank attribution: slow-loader stalls (#7039), prefetch-queue starvation (#7474), and per-host RAM-leak OOMs where engineers hand-rolled per-rank telemetry (#6774, #6908).
- Recent MFU work computes slowest/p50 step time manually per config (#7279, #7201, #7012, #7052); Iris tracks degraded nodes at the cluster level (#2827) but nothing does it inside the training loop.

Rebase #4240 as the starting point (preferred over #4241 — host-side, no KV-store dependency).

### Definition of Done

- A trainer callback logs per-rank step duration to the standard tracker (no profiler trace required), reporting min/median/max + top-k slowest ranks with rolling/EWMA history to separate one-off stalls from chronic lag.
- Cheap enough to leave enabled at moderate cadence during pretraining.
- Focused tests for the aggregation/reporting logic.
- As a byproduct, exposes the slowest-process step time needed for a valid aggregate-throughput denominator.

topics.title: [haliax] Let ragged_dot pick a Triton kernel family explicitly
topics.body:
`ragged_dot` accepts `implementation="triton_group_grid"` and `"triton_tile_map"`, which run one Pallas-Triton kernel family whatever the GPU. `RAGGED_DOT_IMPL` takes the same values, which is how the MoE layers select it. `"triton"` and `"auto"` keep the per-GPU default: tile-map on AMD Instinct, Hopper and data-center Blackwell, and group-grid on every other GPU, such as A100, L4, A6000 and consumer Blackwell (sm_120). Neither family has been measured on those GPUs, so their default does not change.

Tile-map on those GPUs, which this opt-in now allows, used the group-grid blocks (128x128x32, 4 warps, 4 stages). On H100 those blocks made tile-map 0.78-0.89x of group-grid at the Mixtral-like shape (G=8, 4096x14336) at M=16384. A sweep of 96 configs on H100 picked one config per layout among configs whose operand stages fit in 99 KiB of shared memory. 99 KiB is the per-block limit on sm_86, sm_89 and sm_120; A100 allows 163 KiB. Per call in bf16, against group-grid with its own blocks:

| Layout | Blocks (m x n x k), warps, stages, group_m | June, G=32, M=16k and 128k | Mixtral-like, G=8, M=16k and 64k |
|---|---|---|---|
| fwd | 128x256x32, 8, 4, 8 | 1.12-1.16x | 1.18-1.83x |
| dlhs | 128x256x32, 8, 4, 1 | 1.21-1.59x | 1.39-2.22x |
| drhs | 128x128x32, 4, 3, 8 | 1.00-1.08x | 1.03-1.18x |

topics.title: [grug] Add hero launch controls for a context-length switch
topics.body:
The scaling-ladder launcher holds 4,194,304 tokens per rack per update, so the sequence batch shrinks as the context grows (2816 sequences at 16K on 11 racks). The step count (390251), learning rates, decay, and gate/router weight decay therefore match the 4K run. The hero's context length, QK multipliers, and capacity factor live in HERO_MODEL. --qk-mult and --qk-mult-long-scale (global layers only) override the QK multipliers for trial arms and ladder rungs; trial arms set the context length on their branch alongside the history. Eval packs at the training context, as on main, so the eval_dropless/* series shift at each switch. For short trial arms, --eval-every overrides the eval cadence.

The hero's context history is checked in, like the data mix's switch point: HERO_CONTEXT_PHASES in launch_scaling_ladder.py lists each context the d6144 hero trained at before its current one with the step it ended at, and HERO_FLOPS_BASELINE_TOTAL holds the parent's cumulative training FLOPs at the last switch. A context-switch deploy PR edits Python only: it sets the HERO_MODEL fields, appends one entry to HERO_CONTEXT_PHASES, and sets HERO_FLOPS_BASELINE_TOTAL, so a second switch (4K to 16K, then 16K to 64K) is described exactly and trigger_hero.sh is unchanged. The launcher turns the history into a FlopsBaseline at the last end step and, through the prior_context_phases argument of harrier_mix_2026_08_18_data_config, into LmDataConfig.prior_context_phases, with each earlier phase's Harrier stage schedule and shuffle blocks at its own batch size, so the Harrier sources continue from their earlier reads. At d6144 the launcher rejects a history that does not start at 4K, repeats a length between adjacent phases (including the current context), or disagrees with whether the baseline is set. LmDataConfig rejects end steps that do not increase, and rejects any switch below the 1e23-FLOP simulated-epoching cutoff because the data offsets assume each source reads its whole cache. The narrow rungs take no history.

The live run is unchanged: trigger_hero.sh is identical to main and launches the 4K HERO_MODEL with no FLOPs baseline. A switch still needs a GPU rehearsal from the handoff checkpoint and agreed trial thresholds; see the inventory and validation plan in #9615.

Part of #9615

topics.title: [levanter] Continue mixture reads across a context-length switch
topics.body:
Harrier's shuffle blocks change from a fixed 256 sequences to a fixed 2^20 tokens (io_block_size = 2**20 // seq_len). At 4K the two are identical, so the live run's data order is unchanged. At a longer context, the token-sized blocks keep the outer block permutation the same, and only the order of sequences inside each 512-block shuffle window changes. With the old 256-sequence blocks, a 16K relaunch would have re-read an estimated 2.85T already-seen tokens of the remaining ~9T.

The new LmDataConfig.prior_context_phases describes the earlier context lengths of a resumed run, one ContextPhaseConfig per length. With prior_context_phases set, each source skips the unread rest of the shuffle window it was reading at the switch step and starts its next window, so nothing is served twice. At a 216000-step handoff this skips about 52B tokens, 0.65% of the rest of the run. MixtureDataset takes per-source start offsets to apply the skip. Every phase must give positive weight to the same sources, because a training config drops zero-weight sources and that changes the shuffle keys of the rest; a change in the active sources is rejected. So is a phase at the same sequence length as the one before it, since there a source could continue in place and the skip would only discard data. The seed, the source order, and restoring at the last switch step cannot be checked from the config, so the field docstring states them. The offsets come from each source's true position in the earlier phase, so they also absorb the main-mixture boundary moving from step 108000 to 108096 at 16K. The grug train loop builds its mixture through the new LmDataConfig.train_mixture.

Part of #9615
topics.head: aa184d6ddbe72291a0b3c896c6d8f9ed3fe4134d

comments.body:
🤖 Review notes from a walkthrough of the change. None of these block the mechanism; the rename is the main request.

**Rename the prior-phase types.** `PriorDataPhase` is easy to misread: "data" does not say which aspect of the data changed, and in the Harrier code and docs "phase" already means a mixture phase (`_SPEC.phase_weights`, the JSON `phases`, "Phase 1/2/3" in `docs/reports/hero-mixture-log.md`). A context switch can fall in the middle of a mixture phase, so the two divisions of the run need different names. Suggested names:

| Current | Suggested |
| --- | --- |
| `PriorDataPhase` | `ContextPhaseConfig` |
| `LmDataConfig.prior_phases` | `prior_context_phases` |
| `MixturePhase` | `ContextPhase` |

This follows the `FooConfig` → `Foo` pattern: `ContextPhaseConfig` declares a past context phase in steps, and `ContextPhase` is the form `skip_to_window_offsets` uses (start step, `BatchSchedule`, stages in sequence indices). The `ContextPhase` list also holds the current phase. The `MixturePhase` docstring ("A phase of the mixture for ...") should change with it, for example to "One context phase of the run, with its batch schedule and stages in sequence indices." Please also add a sentence to the field docstring that batch-size changes within one context belong in `BatchSchedule`, and that `prior_context_phases` describes earlier context lengths only.

Names and strings that follow from the rename:

- `_prior_phase_offsets` → `_prior_context_phase_offsets`, and `_prior_phase_window_tokens` → `_context_phase_window_tokens`.
- The `"prior_phases ..."` error messages and the `train_mixture` docstring.
- `"Every data phase must draw from the same sources"`, `"Data phases must start at increasing steps"`, and `"Prior phase {phase} must shuffle ..."` → "context phase".
- In `test_context_switch_data.py`: the imports, the `_phase` and `_offsets` annotations, and `test_lm_data_config_prior_phase_resumes_without_repeating_tokens`.
- In #9689: `HarrierPriorContext` and `prior_contexts`, so the stack uses one term. The context history that replaces `CONTEXT_SWITCH_STEP` there (see my comment on #9689) can use the same name.

**Reject adjacent phases with the same sequence length.** `skip_to_window_offsets` accepts two adjacent phases with the same `seq_len`, for example a relaunch that changes only the batch size. In that case the within-window order does not change, so a source could continue at its exact position. `_next_window_start` still rounds up to the next shuffle window and discards up to one window per source (about 537M tokens per source at Harrier's settings). A check that adjacent phases differ in `seq_len` would turn that silent waste into an error. It would also make the `ContextPhase` name exact.

**Rename `counts_before` and make it block-aligned.** `counts_before` does not say what it counts; `sequence_counts_before` does. Its partial-block branch also never runs in this PR: `skip_to_window_offsets` calls it only at block boundaries (rounded up for the old phase, down for the new one). That branch returns a count, but in a partly served block the count is not a read position, because slots are shuffled; a source that served 3 sequences may have served occurrences 0, 7, and 31. Taking a block index instead, as `sequence_counts_before_block(block_id)`, removes the branch and prevents a later caller from using a mid-block count as a position.

**Check source order across phases.** The active-source check compares sets, but order matters as much: it sets each source's shuffle key through `key_iterator`, and the mixture's slot layout through `dataset_index` (including which source receives the rounding remainder). A config that lists the same sources in a different order passes the check and gets a different data layout. Recording the source order in the prior phase and comparing lists would catch this; at minimum, the docstring should say the order must not change.

**Document two assumptions that cannot be checked here.** (1) The shuffle and mixture keys come from the trainer seed, so the seed must be the same in every phase. (2) The offsets assume the current phase starts reading at the last `end_step`. A launch that restores a checkpoint from before that step would re-read data. #9689's trigger checks this for the hero; a docstring sentence on `prior_phases` would cover other callers.

**Optional: give a prior phase a `BatchSchedule`.** `PriorDataPhase.batch_size` is an `int`, so a prior phase cannot have a batch ramp, while the current phase takes a full `BatchSchedule`. A `BatchSchedule` field would give prior and current phases one representation.

**Possible follow-up, not for this PR.** Batch-size history (`BatchSchedule`) and context-length history (`prior_phases`) are both step-indexed descriptions of the run's shape, and could become one schedule. That needs three things this PR should not take on: the trainer must reject a `seq_len` change after the current step, because `Pos` is fixed per launch, while it can follow a batch change; `BatchSchedule` is used in 28 Python files; and the Harrier stage schedule would need to record the realized step of past stage boundaries instead of rounding them again for each batch size.

🤖 Addressed in new commits on top of the reviewed head ([compare 5a2525a4ec..748ad7fe6f](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/compare/5a2525a4ec..748ad7fe6f)):

- **Rename** (86fff8f63b): `ContextPhaseConfig`, `prior_context_phases`, `ContextPhase`, `_prior_context_phase_offsets`, `_context_phase_window_tokens`, the error messages, the `ContextPhase` docstring, and the test names. The field docstring now says that batch-size changes within one context length belong in `BatchSchedule`. In #9689, b596fe391c renames `HarrierPriorContext` and `prior_contexts` to `HarrierContextPhase` and `prior_context_phases`.
- **Same-length adjacent phases** (4ca2f1ba0d): `skip_to_window_offsets` now raises an error.
- **`counts_before`** (c7bdbe68f1): now `sequence_counts_before_block(block_id)`, without the partial-block branch.
- **Source order** (1c99ccec06): documented, not checked. A recorded source list would not catch the case that matters: the Harrier launcher rebuilds the prior phase from the same spec at every launch, so a reordered spec changes the recorded list and the current list together.
- **Seed and restore step** (1c99ccec06): both assumptions are in the `prior_context_phases` docstring.
- **Batch schedule for a prior phase** (748ad7fe6f): `ContextPhaseConfig.batch_size` is now `int | IntSchedule`, the same type as `TrainerConfig.train_batch_size`, so the existing `BatchSchedule(...)` conversion handles both.

The unified schedule is left for a follow-up, as suggested. The `CONTEXT_SWITCH_STEP` history from the #9689 comment is not in these commits.

topics.title: [eval] Prepare Hugging Face weights before starting inference
topics.body:
An evaluation with a cold Hugging Face checkpoint now resolves its commit and checks the regional cache before starting inference. On a miss, the colocated orchestrator waits for a CPU mirror job with a four-hour execution deadline. Candidate and hosted-judge weights finish preparation before either serving job reserves accelerators. Preparation failures write infrastructure-failure records with the child job and log tail.

The serving worker keeps its cache lookup and receives the pinned commit. The affected local suite reported three failures in Levanter checkpoint and Grug mesh tests under parallel execution; all three passed individually on this branch and on main with external access.

Fixes #9233
topics.head: 92ed662bd68fe65e6dfd7ba2a51cc73b09d4c4eb

comments.body: Working on this in loom: https://loom.oa.dev/s/sjx1uct2

🤖 Holistic review of 19d9cb597bb8057cc07998e1836a3f69a4c049f9.

This PR moves Hugging Face weight mirroring for evaluations out of the GPU serving job and into CPU child jobs that the eval orchestrator waits on, as #9233 proposed. All three earlier findings are fixed, and no new problems turned up. I have no remaining findings.

**Before.** `run_evaluation_steps` opened `remote_inference` right away. The GPU worker called `resolve_model_path`, which resolves the commit, mirrors the repo under a lock, and writes `.cache_metadata.json` last. The download counted against the 2400 s endpoint-readiness budget. Any failure in it came back as `RemoteInferenceStartupError` and was written as an `infra_failed` record for every pending eval.

**Design.** `levanter.model_cache` gains `hf_model_cache_entry`, which resolves the repo, commit, and region cache path without downloading. The new `marin/inference/model_cache.py` holds `MODEL_CACHE_PREFIX` and `model_cache_entry`, and has no Transformers import; `model_preparation` imports the prefix from it. `_prepare_inference_models` handles the candidate and the optional judge in one pass. For each model it pins the resolved commit into the served config, keeping `api_model` as the requested name, and checks the completion marker. On a miss it submits a CPU job (4 CPU, 16g RAM, 80g disk, non-preemptible, 4 h execution deadline) running `cache_hf_model(entry.path, entry.repo, revision=...)`, so the child writes to the exact path the orchestrator checks. It then waits on all prepare jobs together with `fray.client.wait_all` for up to 8 h. Resolution, marker checks, submission, and waiting all run inside one guarded block. Any failure terminates every submitted prepare job and is recorded as `infra_failed` through `_record_startup_failure` with the `prepare` role. Placement is safe because the orchestrator runs under the accelerator's region or cluster constraint (`experiments/evaluation/launch.py:498`), and `_resolve_hosted_judge` requires the judge to share that location.

**Evidence and limits.** Locally, the preparation tests pass along with the existing shared-session and startup-failure tests (9 tests). The preparation tests cover: cache miss, hit, prepare-job failure, submission failure, HF revision-lookup failure, and concurrent candidate and judge preparation with judge success and failure. `import marin.evaluation.runner` now takes 1.1 s and no longer loads Transformers (3.1 s at the previous head). The PR has no live run against a cold large checkpoint. `run_served_evalchemy` and `run_served_lm_eval` in `marin/experiment/evaluation.py` still download on the GPU; this PR leaves them unchanged.

No findings.

Earlier findings: 1 resolved (entry resolution and submission are now inside the guarded block; the `resolve-failure` and `submit-failure` cases assert `INFRA_FAILED` records); 2 resolved (`marin.inference.model_cache` has no Transformers import, and the child calls `cache_hf_model(entry.path, ...)`); 3 resolved (`_prepare_inference_models` submits both jobs and waits with `wait_all`).

<!-- marin-holistic-review:19d9cb597bb8057cc07998e1836a3f69a4c049f9 -->

🤖 Addressed the three findings in f1b3102b43 and 19d9cb597b:

- Revision lookup, marker checks, and job submission are converted to `RemoteInferenceStartupError`, so failed preparation writes `infra_failed` records. The fake-client tests now cover resolution, submission, and child-job failures.
- The runner imports a small cache-identity module without importing Transformers. The CPU child calls `cache_hf_model` with the exact cache path checked by the orchestrator.
- Candidate and judge CPU jobs are submitted before `wait_all` waits for them. On failure, both jobs are terminated and their IDs are recorded; neither GPU session starts. A two-model fake-client test covers success and failure.

Verification: 73 evaluation tests and 6 serving resolver tests pass; changed-file lint and pyrefly pass. A live cold-checkpoint evaluation remains to be run.

🤖 Removed misleading snapshot wording from the cache entry docstring and CPU launch narration from the preparation docstring. The existing termination helper logs failed cleanup as an inference job, so I left preparation cleanup unchanged. Targeted tests: 21 passed; pre-commit passed. <!-- marin-deslop:517498f28ab52bf3c0bb79efa7fd728d94fc677f -->

topics.title: [Post-training][Model merging] Initial Experiments in Model Merging with Snowball 67B A2B
topics.body:
We implemented eleven model-merging recipes in Marin and evaluated 113 Snowball 67B A2B checkpoint variants with completed NUPA200 and BFCL-Parity scores. Sequential merging via selective expert transfer retained almost all of the NUPA source's performance and matched the BFCL source's score, but the three best merges retained essentially none of the Base model's routed experts. We have not yet run the complete cohort of policy evals needed to judge non-targeted performance.

[Earlier RLVR experiments](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9735) showed that a small amount of broad-domain RLVR can strongly and unpredictably affect non-targeted benchmarks. It can introduce or repair behavioral defects that change scores while leaving the model's underlying “knowledge” essentially untouched. For example, a model might return every numeric answer, such as “31.7,” as “final_answer.31.7” instead of the requested “Final Answer: 31.7,” collapsing a benchmark score. We conservatively treat these as model defects to remedy under normal use conditions rather than grader defects to smooth. Each RLVR run can repair and break multiple output formats, so we investigated efficient ways to combine checkpoints.

Model merging is popular among hobbyists and is rumored to be used extensively at frontier labs, though the scientific literature is thin. Most merging methods use very few FLOPs and often require no GPUs. This makes merging relevant to our goal of reaching the frontier quickly and FLOP-efficiently.

The target Snowball checkpoint had largely improved but acquired two severe behavioral defects that sharply reduced NUPA and BFCL performance. We used two other Snowball models as merge sources. Each was an expert on one target benchmark, but both were generally inferior to the target, or Base, model. The objective was to raise performance on both disparate target benchmarks without degrading non-targeted benchmarks.

Almost all standard merging approaches we tried failed to raise both target scores strongly. They restored capability weakly on both benchmarks, or strongly on one and not at all on the other. Extensive experimentation led us to try sequential merging via selective expert transfer. It retained performance on both targets, but required discarding essentially all Base parameters from the merge.

| Merge | Pure NUPA | Blended | Pure BFCL | Pure Base |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Shared100 — best score | 87.04% | 0.00% | 12.19% | 0.76% |
| Shared075 | 87.04% | 0.76% | 12.19% | 0.00% |
| Shared050–Attention025 | 86.38% | 1.42% | 12.19% | 0.00% |

These three merges retained almost all source NUPA performance and matched the source BFCL score. None appears to meet the objective of avoiding degradation on non-targeted benchmarks; we will reserve judgment until the complete policy eval cohort has run.

Sequential merging via selective expert transfer appears promising for complex MoE merges. Our best strategy combined weights from the NUPA, BFCL, and Base models:

1. Start with NUPA's configuration files, tokenizer, and chat template.
2. Replace selected NUPA routed experts with BFCL experts. In each layer, select 32 expert positions using BFCL activation measurements and copy BFCL weights into them. This discards all Base routed experts.
3. Change NUPA's shared experts using Base weights. A shared expert processes every token; the router does not select it. We made three versions:
   - 50%: mix equal amounts of NUPA and Base shared-expert weights.
   - 75%: mix 25% NUPA and 75% Base shared-expert weights.
   - 100%: replace the shared-expert weights with Base shared-expert weights.

The percentages describe weight mixing, not token allocation. The 100% version had the highest combined NUPA200 and BFCL-Parity score.

We started with NUPA because its NUPA performance was easier to retain than to transfer into another model:

- Starting with BFCL, copying 16 or 32 NUPA-selected experts yielded only 2.00% or 1.00% NUPA200. BFCL performance remained useful, but the transfer did not recover NUPA performance.
- Starting with NUPA, copying 32 BFCL-selected experts yielded 35.00% NUPA200 and 26.02% BFCL-Parity. This retained most numeric-task performance and added some tool-use performance.
- Using Base as the anchor, the tested task-vector methods generally recovered some NUPA performance but lost most BFCL performance. We found no better joint result with those methods.

Our working explanation is that NUPA performance depends on a combination of tokenization mismatch, weights, and response behavior that a small expert transfer does not reproduce. This was likely an unusually difficult merge target because tokenization and tool calling had drifted between experts.

The tokenizers encoded tool-call markers differently:

| Text | Base tokenizer | NUPA tokenizer |
|---|---|---|
| <tool_call> | One token: 128005 | Four tokens: 27, 14506, 13735, 29 |
| </tool_call> | One token: 128011 | Four tokens: 524, 14506, 13735, 29 |

In NUPA's tokenizer, IDs 128005 and 128011 still had reserved-token names. In Base's tokenizer, those IDs represented the tool-call markers. This affects benchmarks even with unchanged weights: the same input text can produce different token IDs, and the same output token ID can decode to different text. The numerical vocabulary did not change. Both tokenizers encode 337.2571 as [17609, 13, 15574, 16].

The chat templates also formatted tool use differently:

- NUPA's template presents tool definitions as one JSON array; Base's presents individual definitions separated by newlines.
- NUPA's template requests a unique tool-call ID and includes IDs in calls and responses when provided; Base's omits those IDs.
- The templates differ in whitespace, handling of message content, and handling of separate reasoning text.

Using the other template changes the model input and therefore the benchmarks. In one ablation, we kept the weights unchanged and changed the files used to load the model and prepare its input:

| Model weights | With Base configuration and tokenizer | With NUPA configuration and tokenizer |
|---|---:|---:|
| NUPA, with no expert transfer | 0.81% BFCL-Parity | 17.07% BFCL-Parity |
| NUPA, with 16 BFCL experts per layer | 0.81% BFCL-Parity | 21.14% BFCL-Parity |

In another ablation, restoring NUPA's own special-token rows increased NUPA200 from 29.00% to 39.00%. These rows represent control tokens, such as message boundaries.

The agent's experimental design was flawed and needs a follow-up study. It drifted almost immediately from adding specialist capabilities to Base toward combining the two specialists. We will enforce that specialist changes target only a small, measured fraction of Base weights in the follow-up study, and may also control for the tokenizer confound.

---
[Original description](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9975#issuecomment-6074693580) <!-- marin-prose-cleanup -->
