## Parent and finalist scores

| Checkpoint | NUPA200 (%) | BFCL-Parity (%) | Sum |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Base: Grug Antidoom Step12 | 0.50 | 5.70 | 6.20 |
| NUPA: Snowball Mixed-RLVR Step92 | 38.00 | 16.30 | 54.30 |
| BFCL: Grug Reference-KL Step20 | 0.50 | 43.90 | 44.40 |
| Shared100 | 36.50 | 48.78 | 85.28 |
| Shared075 | 36.00 | 40.65 | 76.65 |
| Shared050–Attention025 | 28.50 | 39.02 | 67.52 |

Parent entries are historical policy references, not freshly repeated matched controls; their NUPA200 scores were extracted from the larger policy panel. Finalist entries are the campaign's completed evaluations. See the [tracker](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/TRACKER.md) and [parent subset scores](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/artifacts/nupa200/baseline-scores.json). The historical BFCL parent scores are rounded, so these parent sums use the displayed precision. The third finalist recovers less NUPA than the first two. Only Shared100 exceeds the historical BFCL specialist score; Shared075 and Shared050–Attention025 remain below it. These are not matched reruns.

Shared050–Attention025 combines equal NUPA/Base shared-expert weights with 75% NUPA and 25% Base attention-component weights, on top of the selected BFCL expert transfer; it differs from the shared-only 50% variant. [Exact recipe](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/artifacts/worktrees/marin/experiments/weight_merging/recipes/serial-bfcl032-shared050-attention025-step12.json). Provenance percentages count all stored scalar parameter positions by recipe source: “pure” means copied from that parent, and “blended” means multiple source contributions. They do not measure active parameters or token allocation. In Shared100, the remaining attention, router, embedding, and output-head weights come from NUPA. Blended variants can contain Base contributions even when their pure-Base count is zero.

The metadata ablation swapped the loading/input-preparation file bundle, including tokenizer and chat-template files; it does not isolate individual tokenizer, template, or configuration effects. The 29.00% to 39.00% NUPA200 comparison restored NUPA's native special-token embedding/output rows in a NUPA-weight recipient that previously preserved Base's rows. The [introduction](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9975)'s response-behavior explanation is a working hypothesis; these experiments do not establish that internal knowledge was unchanged.

Broad capability retention is already in doubt: Shared100 scored 89.80% MATH500 and 52.19% GPQA-Diamond, versus the historical Base references of 95.00% and 67.30%; see the [recorded sentinel scores](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/TRACKER.md). “Sealed” means this merge-search campaign is complete. It does not imply that the full policy evaluation cohort was completed or that follow-up work is ruled out.

🤖

# Implemented merging methods

This catalog covers eleven method families implemented in Marin for the Grug/Snowball 67B campaign; coefficient, density, layer-count, and donor-choice sweeps are configurations within these families. Metadata/tokenizer and special-token-row controls are part of checkpoint construction, not additional merging algorithms. An anchor is the starting checkpoint, donors supply weights or updates, and the recipient is the checkpoint receiving transferred experts; Step92 denotes Snowball Mixed-RLVR, Step12 denotes Grug Antidoom-RLVR1, and Step20 denotes Grug Reference-KL, with exact source revisions preserved in each recipe.

Costs are approximate **arithmetic FLOPs per output checkpoint**, estimated from the implementation with `P = 6.7e10` stored parameters, usually two donors plus an anchor, and approximately `2.0e9` active parameters per token during calibration. A multiply-add counts as two FLOPs; comparisons/top-k selection, random-number generation, casts, hashing, storage traffic, and quadratic attention work are excluded, so these are operation-count estimates rather than hardware-profiler measurements.

Wall-clock figures are rounded **observed Iris task durations for representative runs**, including task setup, checkpoint reads, and output writes, but excluding queueing, benchmark evaluation, hyperparameter search, and Hugging Face publication. These timings are not controlled hardware-throughput comparisons: ordinary exports used 16–32 CPU cores; learned calibration and moment collection used eight H100s per job, and their CPU export stages are included explicitly below.

1. **Weighted averaging.** We form a convex combination of aligned parent weights in FP32 and cast the result back to the checkpoint dtype, following the weight-averaging approach of [Model soups (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.05482). With two donors and an anchor, our implementation costs approximately **`3.4e11` FLOPs (`5P`) per merge** and took **34 minutes** for `avg-050-025-025`.

2. **Task arithmetic and delta amplification.** We subtract an anchor from each donor and add scaled donor updates back to the anchor, including the amplified-update sweeps described by [Task Arithmetic (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.04089). The two-donor implementation costs approximately **`5.4e11` FLOPs (`8P`) per merge** and took **34 minutes** for `task-075-075`, with coefficient amplification leaving the arithmetic count unchanged.

3. **TIES merging.** We retain the largest-magnitude updates within each tensor, elect their weighted sign, and average sign-consistent updates using retained coefficient mass, adapting [TIES-Merging (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.01708) with tensor-local pruning. This costs approximately **`1.3e12` arithmetic FLOPs (`19P`) per merge**, excluding top-k comparisons, and took **85–87 minutes** for the 20% and 80% density configurations.

4. **DARE-linear.** We randomly drop task-vector coordinates, rescale surviving updates by inverse retention probability, and add them to the anchor, following [DARE (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.03099). The dense masked implementation costs approximately **`8.0e11` FLOPs (`12P`) per merge**, excluding random-number generation, and took **48–49 minutes** at 20% and 80% retention.

5. **DARE-TIES.** We apply DARE dropping/rescaling before TIES sign election and sign-consistent aggregation, combining [DARE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.03099) with [TIES](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.01708). This costs approximately **`1.4e12` FLOPs (`21P`) per merge** and took **49–51 minutes** at 20% and 80% retention, because the implementation still processes dense tensors after masking.

6. **Structured layer and component merging.** We assign tensor-specific coefficients to early/late layers, depth ramps, attention, routed experts, shared experts, routers, normalizations, or output heads, including exact donor replacements through the [campaign checkpoint merger](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/artifacts/worktrees/marin/lib/marin/src/marin/merging/checkpoint.py). Our two-donor code evaluates the dense weighted expression even for zero/one coefficients, costing approximately **`3.4e11` FLOPs per merge**, with **33 minutes** observed for the `direct-router-step20` representative.

7. **Activation-guided individual-expert transfer.** We favor routed experts used frequently on the target benchmark and infrequently on the other benchmark, then copy or blend their rows while preserving the recipient router, with matched-size random transfers as controls in the [campaign selector](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/artifacts/worktrees/marin/experiments/weight_merging/select_experts.py). With an existing selection, transferring 16–64 of 256 experts per layer costs approximately **`3.6e11–4.2e11` FLOPs per merge**, with **41–43 minutes** observed for the 16/32-expert exports; the reusable BFCL tool-use replay alone adds approximately **`3.8e16` FLOPs across four separate eight-H100 jobs lasting 4–7 minutes each (about 22 summed job-minutes)**, excluding original benchmark captures and NUPA numeric-response activation collection, so this is not a complete fresh-selection setup cost.

8. **Serial merging.** We materialize an intermediate merge and apply another merge to it, including the top recipe by NUPA200 plus BFCL-Parity percentage-point sum: Step20 routed-expert transfer followed by Step12 shared-expert replacement, as specified in the [winning recipe](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/artifacts/worktrees/marin/experiments/weight_merging/recipes/serial-bfcl032-shared-step12-100.json). That two-stage construction costs approximately **`7.1e11` FLOPs and 80 minutes per final checkpoint** when both stages are built afresh, or **`3.4e11` FLOPs and 38 minutes** for its second stage when the intermediate already exists, excluding reusable expert selection.

9. **RAM and RAM+.** We classify task-vector coordinates as active when their absolute update exceeds a threshold in one or multiple donors, retain unique updates, average shared updates, and optionally amplify unique contributions using the tensor-local `ramplus_tl` rule from [RAM (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.13572) and [mergekit](https://github.com/arcee-ai/mergekit/blob/main/docs/merge_methods.md). Both variants execute approximately **`1.1e12` FLOPs (`16P`) per merge** in our implementation, with **53 minutes** observed for `ram-eps1e4` and **49 minutes** for `ramplus-r010-cap020`.

10. **Behavior-trained coefficients: Expert Merging++ adaptation.** We first learn layer/component coefficients for routed experts, shared experts, attention, and routers, then split flattened weight tensors into importance-allocated contiguous chunks and refine their coefficients to match domain-specific parent hidden states and logits before static export, adapting [Expert Merging / Expert Merging++ (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.25712) to native GrugMoE. With 48 calibration examples and 24 warmup plus 96 chunk-training steps, the estimate is approximately **`3.0e14` FLOPs and 7 hours 50 minutes per merge** for `expertpp-hidden`, comprising **7 hours 4 minutes on eight H100s plus 46 minutes of CPU export**, with approximately **`4.0e11` FLOPs** attributable to export alone.

11. **Curvature-aware merging: Optimization Trajectory Aware (OTA) with calibrated tensor-local Fast Fisher Grafting (FFG).** We use square roots of calibrated squared response-loss gradients to weight donor updates and retain coordinates by squared-update-times-moment saliency within each tensor, adapting [OTA + FFG (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.11167) because original optimizer moments were unavailable. A fresh two-donor calibration plus the `ota-ffg-d050` export costs approximately **`6.0e13` FLOPs and 3 hours 20 minutes per merge**, comprising **98 minutes of sequential eight-H100 moment collection plus 102 minutes of CPU merging**, while reusing the moments reduces each additional merge to approximately **`1.3e12` FLOPs and 102 minutes**.

The static estimates count the operations actually executed, including coefficient-zero passes; sparsity therefore does not imply proportional FLOP savings. GPU estimates use `2AT` for forward passes and `6AT` for forward/backward passes, where `A` is active parameters per token and `T` is processed tokens, plus full-weight coefficient mixing or moment accumulation: the learned example used 5,233 teacher tokens and 12,936 student tokens, while the two curvature collectors used approximately 4,175 tokens in total.

Evidence: [cost inputs and formulas](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/artifacts/records/method-cost-inputs.json), [recorded Iris durations](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/artifacts/records/method-timings/index.json), [arithmetic implementation](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/artifacts/worktrees/marin/lib/marin/src/marin/merging/arithmetic.py), [calibration implementation](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/artifacts/worktrees/marin/experiments/weight_merging/calibrate.py), and [campaign results](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Snowball-67B-A2B-Model-Merging-Artifacts-2026.10.09/blob/c4fb17eb44005e01cbb3d5b38c672a2ffa473880/TRACKER.md).

```markdown
What we did: Implemented eleven different model merging recipes in Marin and evaluated 113 checkpoint variants on Snowball 67B A2B with completed NUPA200 and BFCL-Parity scores.

Why we did it: We observed in https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9735 that a small amount of broad-domain RLVR can have strong and unpredictable effects on non-targeted benchmarks; the reason for this is that it can introduce or repair behavioral pathologies which can radically alter benchmark scores while leaving the underlying model "knowledge" essentially untouched. 

e.g., after RLVR, a model might start outputting every numeric answer such as "31.7" in a corrupted format like "final_answer.31.7" instead of the task's requested "Final Answer: 31.7", resulting in a complete collapse in a benchmark score.

Since we do not want our model to behave pathologically under normal use conditions, we conservatively treat these as model defects to be remedied rather than a benchmark grader defect to be smoothed.  The question, then, is how to remediate such defects most efficiently when each RLVR run can repair and break multiple output formats at the same time.

Model merging is a popular technique among hobbyists, and there are rumors it is used extensively at frontier labs, but the scientific literature has always been a bit thin. What is unquestionably true is that most model merging methods are extremely FLOP-efficient, in many cases not even requiring GPUs. Since we want to reach the frontier quickly *and* FLOP-efficiently, it would be irresponsible of us not to take a serious look at model merging.

Results: Our target in this case was a Snowball checkpoint which had largely improved but had acquired two severe behavioral defects causing its performance on NUPA and BFCL to degrade dramatically. We used as merge sources two other Snowball models, each of which was an "expert" on one of these benchmarks, but both of which were generally inferior to the student. The merge objective, then, was narrow and challenging; (1) *boost* target model performance on two disparate benchmarks while (2) *avoiding degradation* on non-targeted benchmarks.

Almost all of the standard model merging approaches we tried failed at (1) -- the typical pattern was that merging either restored capability weakly on both target benchmarks, or strongly on one and not at all on the other. After extensive experimentation, we postulated that *sequential merging via selective expert transfer* might retain performance on both benchmarks, and this turned out to be the case, but at a significant cost; we had to discard *essentially all of the parameters from the base model* in the merge.

| Merge | Pure NUPA | Blended | Pure BFCL | Pure Base |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Shared100 — best score | 87.04% | 0.00% | 12.19% | 0.76% |
| Shared075 | 87.04% | 0.76% | 12.19% | 0.00% |
| Shared050–Attention025 | 86.38% | 1.42% | 12.19% | 0.00% |

Our three most successful merges retained almost all source NUPA performance and matched source BFCL score, accomplishing (1); but none of these three merges appear to have accomplished (2), and it would be surprising if they did. We will, however, reserve final judgment on this until we have run the complete cohort of policy evals on these checkpoints.

COMMENT: Sequential merging via selective expert transfer is a promising approach for complex MoE merges.

Our most successful strategy used weights from three models to build one model: NUPA, BFCL, folding into Base.

1. We started with NUPA's configuration files, tokenizer, and chat template (more on this later).
2. We then replaced selected routed experts in NUPA with BFCL experts. In each layer, we selected 32 expert positions from BFCL activation measurements and copied the BFCL weights into those positions. *All of the Base routed experts were discarded*.
3. Finally, we changed the NUPA shared experts using Base weights. A shared expert processes every token; the router does not select it. We built three separate versions:
   - 50%: mix equal amounts of NUPA and Base shared-expert weights.
   - 75%: mix 25% NUPA and 75% Base shared-expert weights.
   - 100%: replace the shared-expert weights with Base shared-expert weights.

These percentages describe weight mixing, not token allocation. The 100% version produced our highest combined NUPA200 and BFCL-Parity score.

We started with NUPA because the experiments showed that its NUPA performance was easier to retain than to transfer into another model --

- Starting with BFCL: copying 16 or 32 NUPA-selected experts into it gave only 2.00% or 1.00% NUPA200. BFCL performance remained useful, but the transfer did not recover NUPA performance.
- Starting with NUPA: copying 32 BFCL-selected experts into it gave 35.00% NUPA200 and 26.02% BFCL-Parity. This retained most of its numeric-task performance and added some tool-use performance.
- Using Base as the anchor: the tested task-vector methods generally recovered some NUPA performance but lost most BFCL performance. We did not find a better joint result through those methods.

Our working explanation is that NUPA performance depends on a combination of tokenization mismatch, weights and response behavior that a small expert transfer does not reproduce.

COMMENT: This was very likely an unusally difficult merge target because our tokenization and tool calling had drifted between experts.

* The tokenizers encoded tool-call markers differently.

| Text | Base tokenizer | NUPA tokenizer |
|---|---|---|
| <tool_call> | One token: 128005 | Four tokens: 27, 14506, 13735, 29 |
| </tool_call> | One token: 128011 | Four tokens: 524, 14506, 13735, 29 |

In NUPA’s tokenizer, IDs 128005 and 128011 still had reserved-token names. In Base’s tokenizer, those IDs represented the tool-call markers.

This matters for benchmarks, even when the weights are unchanged. The same input text can produce different token IDs. The same output token ID can also decode to different text.

The numerical vocabulary did not change. For example, both tokenizers encode 337.2571 as [17609, 13, 15574, 16].

2. The chat templates formatted tool use differently.

- NUPA’s template presents tool definitions as one JSON array. Base’s template presents individual definitions separated by newlines.
- NUPA’s template requests a unique tool-call ID and includes IDs in calls and responses when provided. Base’s template omits those IDs.
- The templates also differ in whitespace, handling of message content, and handling of separate reasoning text.

Thus, “use the other template” changes the actual input to the model (and therefore benchmarks).

In one ablation, we kept the weights unchanged and changed the files used to load the model and prepare its input.
```

# Research

The reported 87.04% NUPA200 / 12.19% BFCL-Parity merge uses NUPA as its anchor and discards all Base routed experts; broad policy retention is still unmeasured. With NUPA weights held fixed, changing the configuration and tokenizer moved BFCL-Parity from 0.81% to 17.07%, so model metadata is a material confound. [PR #9974](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9974) already adds aligned merging and historical artifacts, but its tools do not enforce the later rule that at least 75% of Base weights stay unchanged.

**Relevant code**
- [README](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1c2b6517e1449f37e54d183255d5a453cf4d4ee8/experiments/weight_merging/README.md#L26-L28) — retention and replay limits.
- [select_experts.py](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1c2b6517e1449f37e54d183255d5a453cf4d4ee8/experiments/weight_merging/select_experts.py#L19-L56) — ranked and random expert recipes.
- [merge.py](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1c2b6517e1449f37e54d183255d5a453cf4d4ee8/experiments/weight_merging/merge.py#L19-L42) — checkpoint merge entry point.

# Proposed Fix

Use #9974 for the follow-up study after review; a second merger implementation would overlap it.

1. Pin the Base, NUPA, and BFCL checkpoint revisions. Keep Base's configuration, tokenizer, chat template, and generation settings fixed for every Base-anchored candidate. Verify tensor and expert-row alignment and specify how donor special-token rows are handled before merging.
2. Audit each export against Base at its stored dtype. Count unchanged scalar weights globally and by component, including embeddings, attention, routers, shared experts, and routed experts; reject candidates that change more than 25% of Base weights.
3. Collect fresh activation measurements, since the archive lacks raw transcripts for exact replay. Compare Base-anchored sequential NUPA/BFCL transfers at predeclared 5%, 10%, and 25% change budgets against matched random expert transfers. Include Base, each specialist, and the prior unconstrained best as reference checkpoints.
4. Evaluate NUPA200, BFCL-Parity, and the complete policy cohort with identical prompts and decoding. Set acceptable non-target regressions before scoring, inspect output-format failures, and publish checkpoint revisions, recipes, changed-weight counts, scores, and negative results. Advance a merge only if it improves both targets within the weight budget and the preregistered retention limits.

## Campaign 2: preserve Base while importing specialist capabilities

TL;DR: We completed 48 additional merges across 12 method families (four variants each), requiring at least 75% of original Base scalar weights and every non-weight model file to remain unchanged. DARE-TIES-02 gave the best observed BFCL + NUPA sum, **45.53**, while changing **6.04%** of Base parameters. Its score was BFCL **45.53%**, NUPA200 **0.00%**; the fresh Base control scored **9.76% / 0.00%** respectively. We improved tool-use performance under the constraint, but did not recover strong performance on both targets together.

[Best checkpoint on Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Merge-Campaign2-DARE-TIES-02-2026.10.10/tree/153f5369f69a0c0a7203779099ec94e98c66748f) · [Implementation PR #9974](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9974) · [Reproduction README](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/4f9f9c6fff3cfc4404d1b8c2c2aeed92329e4f1f/experiments/weight_merging/campaign2/README.md) · [Complete tracker](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/4f9f9c6fff3cfc4404d1b8c2c2aeed92329e4f1f/experiments/weight_merging/campaign2/TRACKER.md) · [Unrounded scores, coverage and timings](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/4f9f9c6fff3cfc4404d1b8c2c2aeed92329e4f1f/experiments/weight_merging/campaign2/results-evidence.json)

NUPA200 tests numerical understanding and arithmetic across number representations, using a fixed 200-item subset of the policy’s 5,000-item set and the pinned loose-format extraction plus exact-match rule. BFCL-Parity uses the 123-trial Harbor `bfcl_parity@1.0` adaptation with the Pi agent; its verified solve rate is not the full BFCL leaderboard score.

Base is Grug Antidoom Step12; the NUPA donor is Snowball Mixed-RLVR Step92, and the BFCL donor is Grug Reference-KL Step20. The README pins all three revisions. This extends the first campaign's 11 families with ISO-Merger and applies the changed-weight constraint to every family. All 48 construction audits passed; actual changed scalar counts range from **3.02% to 23.50%**. The 25% rule is measured against original Base, including both serial stages; blends count as changed wherever stored bits differ. These constraints do not establish non-target capability retention, which was not evaluated for this cohort.

What worked: DARE-TIES-02 had the highest observed summed target score, with 6.04% of Base parameters changed. DARE-TIES-03 scored 41.46 with 8.34% changed; ISO-03 scored 44.09 with 23.14% changed. DARE-TIES-02 is better on both objectives than either of those alternatives. DARE-linear-02 scored 36.27 with effectively the same changed count as DARE-TIES-02 (14 fewer scalar parameters among about 4.05 billion). Thus the ranking is not just a reward for modifying a larger fraction of Base.

What did not transfer well: learned coefficients, curvature grafting and activation-selected expert transfers did not beat the best DARE-TIES candidate on the summed target metric. Activation-02 had the highest observed NUPA200 score, **10.00%**, but BFCL fell to **5.69%**. The byte-identical serial-02 control scored **7.00% / 5.69%**, showing repeat-run variation. The summed objective also permits a winner with zero NUPA; it does not require balanced capability recovery.

Why remains uncertain. Zero-score trace reviews found both arithmetic errors and correct final numbers accompanied by commentary that failed the fixed response-format rule. Weight changes can affect both capability and response behavior; this study does not isolate their causal contributions. Expert Merging++ and OTA+FFG are native-MoE adaptations trained on 48 independent synthetic calibration examples, and ISO operates on selected expert matrices. Their negative results do not establish that the original methods fail generally. NUPA's exact common ancestor with Base remains unestablished despite aligned tensor coordinates.

All 96 target evaluations are complete under the pinned evaluation policy. These are single-run search results, not statistically resolved method rankings. The campaign is sealed; no further OOD evaluations are planned. The README includes regeneration commands and states the remaining exact-replay gaps: historical calibration tensors and raw evaluation transcripts remain in private storage.

## Campaign 3 follow-up: constrained SWE-Bench and Terminal-Bench transfer

**TL;DR:** We completed 32 constrained merges across DARE-TIES, DARE-linear, ISO, and serial DARE-TIES → ISO. Every candidate kept at least 75% of Base scalar weights bit for bit and kept every non-weight model file byte for byte. Serial-01 had the highest observed SWE-Bench-100 + TB2.1 sum at **48.17**, compared with **37.20** for Base. DARE-linear-02 reached **46.36** while changing only **2.36%** of Base scalars and is the published checkpoint.

### Results

| Checkpoint | Method | Changed (%) | SWE-Bench-100 (%) | TB2.1 (%) | Sum | Merge time (min) |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Base | Control | 0.00 | 27.27 | 9.92 | 37.20 | — |
| Specialist | Control | — | 9.09 | 15.27 | 24.36 | — |
| serial-01 | Serial DARE-TIES → ISO | 10.09 | 36.00 | 12.17 | **48.17** | 140.60 |
| dare-linear-02 | DARE-linear | 2.36 | 33.00 | 13.36 | **46.36** | 38.21 |
| dare-ties-04 | DARE-TIES | 2.50 | 34.00 | 11.74 | **45.74** | 42.34 |

The serial family had the highest mean sum, 41.72, and the best single result. Its four 12.50%-support variants averaged 45.43, while its four 25%-support variants averaged 38.00, so changing more Base parameters did not improve this family. DARE-linear averaged 39.61, DARE-TIES 38.48, and ISO 38.17. ISO-08 was ISO's best result at 44.83, but changed 23.93% and took 101.89 minutes.

The specialist control was better than Base on TB2.1 and much worse on SWE-Bench-100. The best merges recovered part of that TB2.1 advantage while preserving or improving SWE-Bench performance. None matched the specialist's 15.27 TB2.1 score, and this campaign did not evaluate any non-target benchmark.

### Protocol

Base was [`open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Merge-Campaign2-DARE-TIES-02-2026.10.10`](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Merge-Campaign2-DARE-TIES-02-2026.10.10/tree/153f5369f69a0c0a7203779099ec94e98c66748f) at revision `153f5369f69a0c0a7203779099ec94e98c66748f`. The specialist was [`laion/snowball-67b-a2b-relay-sft-allkimi-step1203`](https://huggingface.co/laion/snowball-67b-a2b-relay-sft-allkimi-step1203/tree/ff664b48f4c79a81c585dbc9e082b34af3a22b4a) at revision `ff664b48f4c79a81c585dbc9e082b34af3a22b4a`.

Each candidate could change only routed-expert weight matrices. The final checkpoint could differ from original Base at no more than 25% of scalar weight positions. Tensor names, shapes, dtypes, shard layout, configuration, tokenizer, chat template, generation settings, weight index, and all other non-weight files had to match Base exactly. Every export received a full stored-weight and file-inventory readback audit against original Base, including both stages of serial merges.

We ran eight variants in each family. Variants 01–04 used a 12.50% support cap and variants 05–08 used 25.00%.

| Family | Four settings at each support cap |
| --- | --- |
| DARE-TIES | `(keep, scale)` = `(0.20, 0.10)`, `(0.20, 0.25)`, `(0.50, 0.25)`, `(0.50, 0.50)`; magnitude trim 0.20 |
| DARE-linear | The same keep/scale pairs without magnitude trimming |
| ISO | Retain 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, or 1.00 of singular-vector modes |
| Serial DARE-TIES → ISO | DARE-TIES `(keep=0.20, scale=0.25, trim=0.20)`, then the four ISO settings |

Expert support was benchmark independent. For each layer, expert IDs were sorted by SHA256 of `0:layer:expert`, selected round-robin across layers, and applied to all three expert projections. The smaller support was a prefix of the larger support.

Evaluation used Marin commit `554a4b0758448039aa26cf2502ab6eed3c637054`, release base `aaf1878ce65a1a05b386aef257b952fa7205283a`, and Harbor commit `2203bacd03d82e9d4f2a9422f0b3f7e9bb7952cc`. SWE-Bench used `DCAgent2/swebench-verified-random-100-folders` at revision `0c553bd6d05d451907afb8db31dba84759ccc993`, mini-swe-agent 2.1.0, one trial per task, 32,768 input tokens, 8,192 output tokens, and a 90% scored-trial gate. TB2.1 used `terminal-bench/terminal-bench-2-1` ref 6, Terminus-2, 89 tasks with three attempts each, 65,536 input tokens, 16,384 output tokens, and a 75% scored-trial gate.

Both evaluations used 16 concurrent trials, a 360-second setup timeout, a 1,800-second agent timeout, a 300-second verifier timeout, and at most ten retries. Each model used one shared eight-H100 inference server for its two evaluations. At most eight model groups ran concurrently.

The final three TB2.1 runs were early-sealed after they passed the authorized 75% scored-trial gate. Serial-08 sealed at 260/267 scored trials and 12.31%, dare-linear-08 at 222/267 and 9.91%, and iso-08 at 261/267 and 11.49%. Scores are mean reward over valid scored trials, with coverage reported separately.

All 32 candidates and both controls have accepted SWE-Bench-100 and TB2.1 results. All campaign jobs are terminal and zero H100s remain reserved.

## Campaign 4: Policy-compliant sparse routed-expert transfer

### TL;DR

This follow-up tested whether a narrow, audited edit to Antidoom Step12 could recover capabilities from Reference-KL Step20. All 20 candidates passed the weight and file policy, and all 100 evaluation cells completed. The best candidate, `serial-06`, raised the four-target sum from Base's 174.90 to 186.63 while changing 2.40% of Base scalars; its MATH500 canary was 94.00 versus Base's 95.00.

The observed gain was concentrated in BFCL-Parity: `serial-06` moved from 5.70 to 15.45, alongside smaller gains on HumanEval+ (72.60 to 75.00) and MBPP+ (66.90 to 68.52), while OlympiadBench fell from 29.70 to 27.67. Expanding the eligible support to 15.25% and 19.90% did not beat the 9.50%-support winner. The strongest extension, `dare-linear-10`, reached 184.13 while changing 2.26%.

These are single-run, in-distribution search results. The campaign establishes a useful policy-compliant sparse edit, but it does not show broad retention or a statistically resolved ordering between nearby variants.

- **Merge implementation:** #9974.

### Experiment design

**Parents and objective.** Base was [Antidoom RLVR1 Step12](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Antidoom-RLVR1-Step12-2026.10.02/tree/50fe2f488aee7730bbccc721024b35229075602e), pinned at `50fe2f488aee7730bbccc721024b35229075602e`. The extraction target was [Reference-KL Step20](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Antidoom-RLVR1-Reference-KL-Step20-2026.10.04/tree/fd07ef0f2b78a83099a0042e59c00de986e7b647), pinned at `fd07ef0f2b78a83099a0042e59c00de986e7b647`. Selection maximized the unweighted sum of HumanEval+, MBPP+, OlympiadBench and BFCL-Parity percentages. MATH500 was a regression canary and did not enter selection.

**Weight policy.** A candidate could change at most 20.00% of Base's indexed scalar parameters. Only rows of routed-expert gate, up and down projections were eligible. All other weights and every non-weight checkpoint file had to remain byte-for-byte identical to Base. Serial stages were always measured against original Base, so an intermediate checkpoint did not reset the budget.

**Support.** The fixed support ordering reused Campaign 2's seed-0, benchmark-independent R25 ordering. R25 is the deterministic routed-expert support whose whole expert blocks fit under Campaign 2's 25% scalar budget; [this frozen Campaign 2 recipe](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/4f9f9c6fff3cfc4404d1b8c2c2aeed92329e4f1f/experiments/weight_merging/campaign2/dare-linear-02.json) contains the inherited ordering. Campaign 4 took the first 16, 24, 40 or 52 of the model's 256 expert rows per projection and layer. Those prefixes covered approximately 6.10%, 9.14%, 15.24% and 19.81% of Base scalars, below declared caps of 6.25%, 9.50%, 15.25% and 19.90%. The audit counted final stored values that actually differed from Base; the largest observed changed fraction was 6.32%.

**Methods.** Ten DARE-linear candidates varied DARE density and delta scale. Ten serial candidates first applied DARE-TIES with density 0.20, TIES density 0.20, scale 0.25, coefficient 1.00 and seed 0, then applied offline [ISO-Merger](https://iso-rlvr.github.io/) on the same support. ISO-Merger composes donor displacement directions in singular-vector coordinates while reconstructing with Base's singular values. Variants 01–08 crossed the two smaller supports with four DARE settings or four retained singular-mode fractions; variants 09–10 extended both families to the larger supports. `serial-06` used the 24-row support and retained 0.50 of available singular modes after the fixed DARE-TIES stage.

**Construction gate.** Each output was read back and checked for aligned parent tensors, routed-expert-only support, declared support compliance, no more than 20.00% changed scalars, byte-identical non-weight files, unchanged tensor names/shapes/dtypes and shard layout, and a complete object inventory. All 20 candidates passed. Tracker merge time includes construction and this readback audit.

**Evaluation.** Each candidate received its own eight-H100 vLLM server, shared by that candidate's five evaluations; up to eight candidate groups ran concurrently. Serving used tensor parallelism 1, data parallelism 8, enabled expert parallelism, a 73,728-token maximum context, Base's tokenizer and chat template, and the Hermes tool parser. Code was pinned to Marin `aaf1878ce65a1a05b386aef257b952fa7205283a`, Evalchemy `958cdb8019b7a4c8432fe85eb9572538ceb75950`, and Harbor `2203bacd03d82e9d4f2a9422f0b3f7e9bb7952cc`. The suites used all 164 HumanEval+ tasks, 378 MBPP+ tasks, 30 OlympiadBench tasks, 123 BFCL-Parity trials, and 500 MATH500 tasks. The public checkpoint includes redacted copies of `serial-06`'s five records with effective configs, source digests, coverage, metrics, and original record hashes.

## Campaign 4 follow-up: constrained routed-expert transfer

### TL;DR

Campaign 4 tested 71 audited merges that transfer routed-expert rows from Reference-KL Step20 into Antidoom Step12. All 355 fixed-policy evaluation records completed. `adaptive-delta-08` led with a **220.40** four-target sum versus Base's **174.90**, while changing **9.47%** of Base's scalar weights. Its scores were 83.54 HumanEval+, 74.07 MBPP+, 34.33 OlympiadBench, and 28.46 BFCL-Parity; MATH500 was 93.60 versus Base's 95.00.

The top three candidates all used layer-adaptive donor deltas with coefficients above 1.0. Exact donor-row transfer did not match them: the best wide-support serial merge reached 204.66 while changing 27.77% of Base. The result supports selective, task-weighted delta extrapolation for this parent pair. It does not establish broad retention: the four transfer benchmarks selected the checkpoints, MATH500 was the only regression canary, and all scores are single runs.

Each repository contains the evaluated weights, OpenMDW 1.1 license, exact recipe, original-Base readback audit, protocol, final tracker, and sanitized copies of the five sealed evaluation records. The repositories are public and ungated; the links above pin immutable revisions.

### Experiment design

Base was [Antidoom RLVR1 Step12](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Antidoom-RLVR1-Step12-2026.10.02/tree/50fe2f488aee7730bbccc721024b35229075602e). The extraction target was [Reference-KL Step20](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Antidoom-RLVR1-Reference-KL-Step20-2026.10.04/tree/fd07ef0f2b78a83099a0042e59c00de986e7b647). The selection objective was the unweighted percentage-point sum of HumanEval+, MBPP+, OlympiadBench, and BFCL-Parity. MATH500 was a regression canary and did not enter selection.

A merge could change at most 30.00% of Base's indexed scalar weights. Only rows of routed-expert gate, up, and down projection tensors were eligible. Every other weight and every non-weight file had to remain byte-for-byte identical to Base. Serial stages were measured against original Base, so an intermediate checkpoint could not reset the budget. The full public protocol is [here](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Merge-Campaign4-Adaptive-Delta-08-2026.10.14/blob/2fb31748eed37435c7472e80f81f34e306b2fa7a/provenance/campaign4/PROTOCOL.md).

The campaign covered eight method families: DARE-linear; serial DARE-TIES followed by ISO; targeted serial transfer; task-paired serial transfer; exact task-union transfer; layer-adaptive delta transfer; behavioral-residual grafting; and wide-support serial transfer. The initial 20 candidates reused Campaign 2's seed-0 R25 routed-expert support. Later candidates used fixed BFCL, HumanEval+, and MBPP+ routed-expert rankings. Construction wrote a temporary incomplete marker, materialized the candidate, read every stored object back, checked the support and actual-change limits, verified unchanged bytes outside support and across non-weight files, wrote and reread the external audit, then removed the marker.

Evaluation used the pinned October 2026 Marin policy: Marin `aaf1878ce65a1a05b386aef257b952fa7205283a`, Evalchemy `958cdb8019b7a4c8432fe85eb9572538ceb75950`, and Harbor `2203bacd03d82e9d4f2a9422f0b3f7e9bb7952cc`. Each candidate used one eight-H100 vLLM server shared by its five evaluations. The suites contained 164 HumanEval+ tasks, 378 MBPP+ tasks, 30 OlympiadBench tasks, 123 BFCL-Parity trials, and 500 MATH500 tasks. A score sealed only when at least 90% of declared trials were scoreable.

The implementation and reproduction guide are in [PR #10135](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10135). Run the merge commands from the immutable [Campaign 4 implementation revision](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/14a407e045f83f38e4e94a2fb21869707a256997). Exact public replay artifacts are available for the three published checkpoints. For the remaining 68 candidates, the tracker publishes scores and recipe summaries; exact recipes and sealed record contents are not public, so exact byte-for-byte replay of the full search is not possible from public artifacts alone.

### Results

`adaptive-delta-08` recovered 64.08% of the extraction target's aggregate improvement over Base. By benchmark, it recovered 78.12% of the HumanEval+ gap, 84.40% of the MBPP+ gap, 44.98% of the OlympiadBench gap, and 59.57% of the BFCL-Parity gap. MATH500 fell 1.40 points.

The search showed three useful patterns:

- Exact transfer did not improve monotonically with breadth. Exact-union family scores ranged from 188.64 to 200.65; wide serial scores ranged from 195.64 to 204.66 while changing 20.19%–27.81% of Base. Interference at wider supports is one plausible explanation, but this sweep does not isolate its cause.
- Task-specific support was useful, but serially composing exact supports did not add their gains reliably. The best task-paired result was 198.60, and the best targeted serial result was 198.73.
- Layer-adaptive scaling produced the only candidates above 207.77. Its top three changed 8.18%–9.47% of Base, less than half the changed fraction of the widest exact transfers.

These comparisons are retrospective maxima from unequal family sizes. They isolate useful construction patterns for this parent pair; they do not estimate statistical uncertainty or performance on unmeasured tasks.

# Campaign 5 closeout — cross-architecture capability transfer

**Question.** Can a capability that a teacher model has and our 67B-A2B student lacks be moved across the
architecture boundary by mapping and transferring weights?

**Answer: no for the capabilities we tested — and for a more specific reason than "the map is hard to
build."** The map between the two activation spaces is *good*: it predicts the student's activations with
0.933 held-out R². It still does not carry a working feature direction, because predictive accuracy puts
no constraint on where individual directions go. And decisively, the student already *contains* the
capability as a sparse feature and merely under-expresses it. There is nothing to install, so the natural
intervention is training, not mapping.

All evidence referenced below is in
[`open-athena/campaign5-cross-arch-evidence`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/campaign5-cross-arch-evidence)
— one JSON per measurement under `reports/`, the frozen input corpora under `corpora/`, and the campaign's
own working documents under `docs/`.

## Vocabulary used throughout

- **Student / base** — `Grug-67B-A2B-Antidoom-RLVR1-Step12-2026.10.02`, a 67B mixture-of-experts model
  (26 layers, hidden 2560, 256 routed + 1 shared expert, top-4 routing).
- **Teachers** — Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B.
- **Sibling checkpoints** — four other Snowball-family checkpoints trained from related data
  (DARE-linear-02, adaptive-delta-05/06, serial-06). They span `bfclparity-pi` 0.171–0.333, so they are
  useful as comparisons, and they share the student's architecture so any capability is representable in
  them by construction.
- **`bfclparity-pi`** — accuracy on the BFCL-Parity agentic benchmark, 0–1, higher is better. The student
  scores **0.057**; the teachers score **0.800** (Gemma) and **0.764** (Qwen).
- **`ifbench`** — an instruction-following benchmark: student 0.220, Gemma 0.420, Qwen 0.357.
- **SAE** — sparse autoencoder, trained on captured activations to reconstruct them through a much wider
  bottleneck so that individual latents approach single concepts. Ours is **TopK**: exactly `k = 32` of
  16,384 latents may be active per position. (This `k` is unrelated to the student router's top-4.)
- **Capture** — run a model over a set of prompts and record its residual-stream activations at chosen
  layers, one vector per prompt position.
- **Null / "clears its null"** — every search in this campaign reports the *best* result over all
  candidates, so the null re-runs that same search many times with the class labels randomly permuted and
  records the best result each time. "Clears" means the observed best exceeds **every** permuted best, so
  a random labelling of the same data would be unlikely to produce it. The gate's measured false-clear
  rate is in
  [stage1-gate-calibration.json](https://gist.github.com/penfever/eff4cef35ce9e4122581ff1b4550a442).
- **Cohen's d** — standardised mean difference between two groups: how far apart their means are in
  pooled standard deviations. |d| ≥ 1 is a large effect; the sign gives the direction.

## The capability gap, defined by behaviour rather than by category

The student's weakness is instruction following and catching detail in long multi-turn queries, so the
contrast is built from outcomes rather than topic. Per-instance results were joined across three models
over 120 shared `bfclparity-pi` queries:

| label | definition | n |
| --- | --- | --- |
| both teachers pass, student fails | the transfer target | 83 |
| all three pass | matched control | 5 |
| teachers disagree | buffer | 30 |
| student passes, a teacher fails | teacher-style control | 2 |

With a four-model sibling Snowball panel added, 72 of the 83 become **recoverable**: a sibling with the
same architecture solves them, so the capability is representable in this architecture and the deficit is
specific to this checkpoint.

[Gap labels](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/campaign5-cross-arch-evidence/blob/main/reports/gap-labels-bfclparity-pi.json).

## Stage 1A — a usable correspondence exists, and it picks the donor

The correspondence diagnostic maps each teacher's activations onto the student's, per axis, and compares
the observed fit against a null that re-runs the selection. Per axis:

| axis | what it measures | teacherA (Gemma 4) | teacherB (Qwen3.6) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| depth | best-matching layer pair, CKA | 0.526 vs null 0.012 — clears | 0.708 vs 0.017 — clears |
| width (residual) | held-out R² of a ridge map, residual stream | 0.828 — clears | 0.902 — clears |
| **interface** | same, on the **routed-expert input** (the normalised residual the experts read) | **0.933 — clears** | 0.932 — **fails** |
| experts | Spearman ρ of per-expert routing profiles, matched by assignment; n/N = experts matched | 0.576 vs 0.128 (128/128) | 0.409 vs 0.091 (256/256) |

Both donors pass the union rule ("at least one axis clears"), but on the **interface** axis — the space
weight transfer would actually use — they disagree. So the donor is **Gemma 4**, reversing the default we
had assumed. Conveniently Gemma also has the larger `bfclparity-pi` gap (0.800 − 0.057 = 0.74 vs 0.71) and
the larger `ifbench` gap (0.200 vs 0.137).

[Correspondence report](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/campaign5-cross-arch-evidence/blob/main/reports/stage1a-correspondence-gate.json),
[gate calibration](https://gist.github.com/penfever/eff4cef35ce9e4122581ff1b4550a442).

## Stage 1B — a selective feature exists in the teacher; the map does not carry it

First, on a **synthetic** contrast (tool-call prompts vs math prompts, with matched minimal pairs as the
selectivity control — the real gap corpus had not been built yet, and a synthetic corpus allows controls
that real queries do not). A teacher unit clears its null and separates **254 of 256 minimal pairs**
(sign test, p ≈ 3e-73) — but the unit's direction mapped through the 0.933 map does not survive into the
student: Cohen's d +0.50 against a null max of 1.40, i.e. inside the null.

[Synthetic probe](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/campaign5-cross-arch-evidence/blob/main/reports/circuit-probe-synthetic.json).

Then on the **real** gap corpus, whose classes are small enough to state per condition: 72
`gap_recoverable` against 5 `all_pass`. Here **no unit clears its null on either side** — the best unit
reaches AUC 0.969 but the null reaches 3.55 in Cohen's d. The length-matched control is live on this
corpus (it was vacuous on the synthetic one, whose classes did not overlap in length), so the absence is
not a length artefact.

[Gap probe](https://gist.github.com/penfever/fee4a4aa0cbadb6744e7afe3b02b60fa).

## Stage 1C — an SAE feature for the gap, and it is causally load-bearing

A TopK SAE was trained on 66,496 student activations at **each of layers 6, 12, 18 and 24** (the layer
was not assumed; four dictionaries were trained so the choice could be tested). At layer 6 the base's
dictionary contains a latent — 1237 — that clears its null, separates `gap_recoverable` from `all_pass`,
*and* is suppressed more on `gap_hard` than on `gap_recoverable`, which is the selectivity that rules out
"this latent tracks prompt difficulty."

That latent was then tested causally on the gap queries (72 `gap_recoverable`, 5 `all_pass`). The
measurement is the **logit difference** `logit("<tool_call>") − logit("The")` at the last prompt
position, so higher is more tool-call-leaning. "Ablation" removes the feature's contribution to the
residual stream; "amplification ×α" adds α times it. These are inference-time interventions on the
residual stream, not weight edits.

| intervention | gap_recoverable (n=72) | all_pass (n=5) | separation = col1 − col2 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| baseline | −7.3993 | −7.2938 | −0.1056 |
| ablation | −7.6315 | −7.2938 | −0.3378 |
| amplification ×1 | −6.8003 | −6.8125 | +0.0122 |
| amplification ×2 | −6.2569 | −6.3937 | +0.1368 |
| amplification ×4 | −5.6050 | −5.7938 | +0.1887 |

Ablating the feature **widens the gap by 0.232**; amplifying it closes the gap at ×1 and reverses its sign
by ×2. The response is monotone from ×1 upward and saturates past ×2, so the feature is under-expressed by
roughly 1–2× relative to the level at which the separation is zero.

[Causal test + dose-response](https://gist.github.com/penfever/04f22ccd41ab2fbecb3498bc53110096).

The sibling dictionaries were then searched the same way, and **all three contain a latent that clears its
null and separates `gap_recoverable` from `gap_hard` more strongly than the base's does** (Cohen's d
−0.50 to −0.59 against the base's −0.38). Combined with the above: the capability is sparsely
representable in every checkpoint tested including the base, and the base represents it most weakly. The
deficit is a weak feature, not an absent one.

## What was ruled out, and by what

| route | result | evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| dense map (Procrustes / ridge) | 0.933 R² but carries no working direction | [synthetic probe](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/campaign5-cross-arch-evidence/blob/main/reports/circuit-probe-synthetic.json) |
| single units on the gap corpus | no unit clears its null | [gap probe](https://gist.github.com/penfever/fee4a4aa0cbadb6744e7afe3b02b60fa) |
| rank-1 read-side weight edit | **reduced** L6 expression on every set (0.593 → 0.510 on gap queries) | [feature-expression-edit-beta2](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/campaign5-cross-arch-evidence/blob/main/reports/feature-expression-edit-beta2.json), measured by [re-capture](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/campaign5-cross-arch-evidence/blob/main/docs/STAGE1.md) |
| expression explains checkpoint quality | no correlation across 4 sibling checkpoints | [§30.1 "The correlation sweep" in STAGE1.md](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/campaign5-cross-arch-evidence/blob/main/docs/STAGE1.md) |

Two controls did real work and are worth calling out, because both rejected statistically significant
results. On the synthetic corpus the strongest unit had a mean matched-pair difference of **0.001** —
significant, and meaningless. On the gap corpus, two latents cleared their nulls and then fired *more* on
`gap_hard` than on `gap_recoverable`, i.e. they were prompt-difficulty detectors rather than capability
features. Neither would have been caught by a null alone.

## Why cross-architecture mapping fails here

Not because the map is hard to build — 0.933 R² is a good map. It is because **predictive accuracy does
not imply correspondence**: ridge and Procrustes are driven by the data spectrum, and a direction with
small variance contributes almost nothing to the loss, so the map may send it anywhere. Working harder on
the same objective does not fix that; the objective has to change.

Separately, the rank-1 read-side fold of an SAE feature through RMSNorm *reduced* expression on every set.
RMSNorm makes direction the invariant of the residual stream and an SAE coefficient is a magnitude along a
direction, so pre-norm scaling does not survive it. The fold is verified rather than assumed, which is
what makes it a rule-out rather than a maybe.

## Caveats

- The gap-corpus **control class is 5 queries** (and the student passes only ~7 of 123 in total), so every
  gap-corpus result — positive and negative — carries that noise. Growing the scored instance set is the
  fix, and it is why the Stage-1C negative at layer 24 is reported as underpowered rather than proven.
- Everything is measured as a **logit difference on 120 prompts**. The benchmark itself has not been run
  under intervention, so proxy-to-benchmark is still an assumption.
- Cross-dictionary feature matching was **confounded**: all SAEs shared an initialisation, so
  decoder-row similarity across dictionaries is uninterpretable. Retraining one dictionary with a
  different seed is the cheap control.

## Open threads

1. **Feature-expression fine-tuning.** The feature is under-expressed 1–2×, not absent. A hinge loss on
   the post-norm coefficient against a **frozen** SAE encoder — target taken from the student's own
   `all_pass` level — is the direct route. Expected to recover *part* of the gap: the correlation sweep
   says the feature is a lever, not the explanation.
2. **Grow the negative class** and re-run the gap probes.
3. **MRCR labels** need the continuous similarity score rather than a pass boolean.
4. **Feature-aligned map learning**, if anyone revisits transfer: our attempt was confounded, not
   refuted.
5. **What the L6 feature tracks semantically** — unverified, and layer 6 is early.

## Working documents

[STAGE1.md](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/campaign5-cross-arch-evidence/blob/main/docs/STAGE1.md)
is the full log — 33 sections, including every failed job, the bug that cost an hour of compute, and the
two controls that rejected significant results.
[CIRCUIT.md](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/campaign5-cross-arch-evidence/blob/main/docs/CIRCUIT.md)
is the probe design,
[CORRESPONDENCE.md](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/campaign5-cross-arch-evidence/blob/main/docs/CORRESPONDENCE.md)
the axes and gate,
[STATE.md](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/campaign5-cross-arch-evidence/blob/main/docs/STATE.md)
the campaign state.

topics.title: [taskforge] Add the build SDK, standard template and build services
topics.body:
Add the build SDK and the host services required by build programs. `stage40_build_with_program` provides the SDK steps call (`sdk`, `outputs`), `RLEnvBuildServices` for machines, images, web tools, ledger, and agent limits, host effects (`build_machine`, `grade_candidate`, `publish_image`), host failures labeled `infrastructure` separately from program failures, the standard six-step template, `GlmAuthor`, and a wall-clock-bounded build child (`build_process`). Every build receives these services.

`run_build` now takes the services and a `ResearchRequirement`, keys steps on `build_model_digest`, records a `STEP` span for each step, and rejects a task if its solver machine differs from the machine pinned by the proposal. A wall, step, or grader timeout raises `BuildExpired`, distinct from a program `BuildFailure` or host `BuildInfrastructureFailure`. The coordinator holds an expired workpiece without spending a revision.

The changed `run_build` signature requires `StageCoordinator` to hold and pass the services and research requirement to each build. `check_workpiece_id` moves from `step_store` to `ledger.records`. The coordinator and `Author` protocol now type proposals as `TaskProposal`; the walkthrough and capability coordinator test construct them with `stage10_proposal.parse`.

Builds on #10297; #10299 builds on this PR. The loader tests from #10297 land here. Two assertions that lower a built task through `stage50_validate` cover the standard template's RolloutEngine run and the validation verifier deadline; they accompany that stage. The taskforge suite passes 567 tests, 151 more than #10297.

---

```markdown
Add the build SDK and everything a build program runs on. `stage40_build_with_program` gains the SDK steps call (`sdk`, `outputs`), the host's machines, images, web tools, ledger and agent limits passed to every build (`RLEnvBuildServices`), step effects on the host (`build_machine`, `grade_candidate`, `publish_image`), host failures told apart from program failures (`infrastructure`), the standard six-step template, `GlmAuthor`, and a build child bounded by a wall clock (`build_process`). `run_build` takes the services and a `ResearchRequirement`, keys steps on `build_model_digest`, records a `STEP` span per step, and refuses a task whose solver machine is not the one the proposal pins. A build that runs past a wall, step or grader clock raises `BuildExpired`, a third outcome beside the program's `BuildFailure` and the host's `BuildInfrastructureFailure`; the coordinator holds such a workpiece without spending a revision.

The coordinator adaptation lands here because `run_build`'s signature changes here. `StageCoordinator` holds the services and research requirement and passes them to every build, `check_workpiece_id` moves from `step_store` to `ledger.records`, and the coordinator and the `Author` protocol type the proposal as a `TaskProposal`. The walkthrough and the capability coordinator test build their proposals with `stage10_proposal.parse`.

Builds on #10297; #10299 builds on it. The loader's tests from #10297 land here. Two assertions that lower a built task with `stage50_validate` (the standard template's RolloutEngine run and the validation verifier deadline) come with that stage. The taskforge suite passes 567 tests here (151 more than #10297).

```

topics.title: [sft] Preserve the fixed-budget agentic LR sweep
topics.body:
Preserve the Snowball v0 learning-rate sweep with prepared-file hash and cache token-count checks, active-token loss accounting, permanent native checkpoints and BF16 exports. Register W&B and epoch accounting as sibling trackers so the Iris status callback can discover W&B. Offline validation restores each checkpoint without context sharding and reports measured token denominators alongside TMax, SWE-smith and pooled losses.

Each of the three nominal epochs is a fixed-update window under the original block-2048 mixture sampler, which does not visit every row exactly once per window. Window token totals are recorded rather than assumed from the manifest. Resume retains optimizer/data state; earlier window statistics remain in the original run's artifacts.

The Snowball token reshapes carry their output sharding explicitly, and the router query bias remains outside differentiation. The experiment launcher requests non-preemptible H100 workers, disables automatic retries and sets NCCL logging to WARN.

Part of #10213

topics.title: [iris] Move marin-finelog-server into the controller extra
topics.body:
marin-iris listed the 38 MiB native marin-finelog-server wheel as a base
dependency, so every root `uv run` (even `fsutil cp`) installed it. Only the
controller and LocalCluster load the embedded log server, and
`finelog.embedded` already raises an install hint when it is missing.

The wheel now lives in the `controller` extra, which the controller image and
infra/pulumi already install. The iris and zephyr test groups depend on
`marin-iris[controller]` so the version floor stays in one place. Local
`iris cluster start --local` now needs `--package marin-iris --extra
controller`; the README shows it.
topics.head: a4e59b909a5246e29c200f1f99c9faf22f206a01

topics.title: [agents] Add durable experiment logbook workflow
topics.body:
Add a durable public logbook workflow for experimental programs with repeated
launches or controlled comparisons. The research skill keeps ordinary
implementation, debugging, incidents, single reproductions, and one-off
validation out of the workflow.

Detailed attempts live in
[`marin-community/marin-logbooks`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin-logbooks),
milestone updates remain issue comments, and the issue body stays the current
summary. Supporting logbook entries are pushed before issue comments and
cross-session handoffs. The Pallas kernel workflow routes repeated tuning work
through this policy.

The detailed policy lives in a separate research reference so the skill
entrypoint loads it only for qualifying experimental work.

evalchemy209.title: Make Evalchemy results and resume state FineStore native
evalchemy209.body:
Write evaluation aggregates, normalized samples, and request checkpoints directly to FineStore. Resume restores committed requests by default. Before generation, the evaluator validates the stored task list and each task's fingerprint, including all supplied generation overrides. It initializes the model before this validation. Results and samples enter the archive in one transaction, so a retry leaves a completed result unchanged. FineStore result writes use the same guarded SymPy serialization as the CLI display.

`--output_path` and `--finestore_output_path` select the same FineStore archive. Existing scripts keep `--output_path` and use distinct archive paths for distinct evaluations. Native JSON/JSONL result serialization, SQLite resume state, temporary output staging, and the unused TACC listener are removed. The TACC distributed batch scripts remain. The serve-and-eval runner and regression gate read the same archive; the gate keeps `--results` as its archive selector. Concurrent writers to one archive have not been exercised locally.

Part of marin-community/marin#9972. The Marin retry work is tracked in marin-community/marin#9813.

evalchemy214.title: Separate grading from score aggregation
evalchemy214.body:
Use each benchmark's aggregation code for both normal evaluation and partial-result recovery, preserving its metrics and breakdowns. Save grading evidence before aggregation so it can be replayed without rerunning graders.

Repeated evaluations with infrastructure-failed trials still fail the task.

msrl944.title: Refresh the frozen trainer stack to TE 2.20 and Torch 2.14.1
msrl944.body:
Refresh the combined trainer and serving group to Torch 2.14.1+cu132, CUDA 13.2.2, Transformer Engine 2.20.2, Core 0.19.2 and Bridge 0.6.2. Preserve Snowball and Hero MuonH/AdamH math, BF16 compute, FP32 state and router biases, HF import/export, expert routes, repeated weight transfer and fresh-stack save/resume. The recipe and qualified baseline evidence are in https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/610.

Use native FlashAttention versioning, event loops, Core attention selection and expert tags, NCCL transport selection and batch-invariance initialization, and W&B mutable tables. Remove obsolete vLLM API branches, global broadcast replacement, unconditional compile/sampler overrides, wheel migration tools, dead FP8/Qwen helpers, the extra Ray peer-access allocation, copied NCCL settings and startup staggering. Native Harbor already includes its config module, so remove the overlapping standalone distribution. The default uv prerelease policy preserves all 510 package records. Retained fixes have source links and removal conditions beside the code; existing packaging checks refuse unverified runtime, patch-source and build inputs.

The serving changes are in [vLLM PR95](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/pull/95). This draft still selects the qualified [3a wheel pair](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/releases/tag/marin-vllm-gpu-20261012-3a054c458ca8) until the source receives the required GitHub review, lands normally and the official main-only build publishes qualified artifacts. Its native FFI 0.1.11, TileLang 0.1.12 and Tokenspeed MLA 0.1.8 group must then be adopted coherently with [Marin PR10022](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10022). The new published Marin package/projection path and other affected application paths still require qualification.

Focused removal pilots passed 17 cases on H100 and 16 on GB200; a cold GB200 FlashInfer build exceeded the startup deadline and completed separately in 2,464 seconds. A two-GB200 native initializer/shared-group probe passed 18 exact broadcasts without copied NCCL settings. Tiny native Core/MSC S3 save/load passes, while five alternating reader comparisons support retaining record buffering: 69 native GETs versus 9 maintained GETs per read, with exact values in both. Removing Hero's CUDA graph guard produced NaN logprobs after changing batch sizes; retain it. These component results do not qualify the final packaged runtime, full-model continuation or RL throughput.

The bounded High source review and targeted follow-ups found no remaining source blocker. The original four full-model reports apply to the baseline; reuse requires explicit source, lock, payload, build-input and exercised-path comparison. The remaining compiler, dependency-metadata, checkpoint and reload fixes remain maintenance costs. Optional HDO, SGLang, GPTOSS, sandbox and legacy fidelity/cache paths are separate from the required MuonH profile and are not qualified by these pilots.

Keep the qualified fallback branch and artifacts. Final consumer merges remain Romain's actions after final artifacts, affected Snowball/Hero and performance gates, coherent pins and terminal CI. The [native Snowball checkpoint oracle failure](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9400#issuecomment-6129427326), parked [TPU pair](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10023), original Hero/GB200 shutdown anomaly and optimizer-payload sampling limits remain disclosed. Policy-only TE timings do not establish full RL throughput or performance equivalence.
